en: [234] The Section on Daily Duties: The Procedure for the Elimination of Urine and Feces.

The formative forces (*saṃskāra*) have been explained. Now, the daily observance (*āhnika*) that has reached its proper occasion is introduced. Regarding this, Manu says: "Having risen during the *brāhma* hour, one should reflect upon dharma and artha, as well as bodily austerities rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas."
The true meaning of the Vedas consists of valid knowledge (*pramā*). Thus it is said in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should reflect upon dharma and artha;
one should contemplate the physical exhaustion arising therefrom and meditate upon the Lord with the mind."
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, one should contemplate what is beneficial for oneself;
one should not neglect virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) at their proper times, according to one's ability."

The meaning is that whatever duty has been prescribed for a particular time among the various duties and so forth, that alone should be performed at that time. Regarding what must be done in this regard, Viṣṇu says: "Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should perform the voiding of urine and feces. The *brāhma-muhūrta* is the final watch of the night;
for the final watch of the night is called the *brāhma-muhūrta*, according to the traditional teaching of Pitāmaha (Bṛhaspati). Aṅgiras also [says]:
Having risen in the last watch of the night and sipped water,
he should cover the ground with grass and veil his head with a cloth.
"Restraining his speech with effort, avoiding spitting and exhaling, he should void urine and feces in a clean place, being fully composed.

By this, it is stated that wherever the occasion for sipping water (ācamana) arises due to a cause such as dreaming and so forth, one should perform the voiding of urine and feces only after having sipped water. "Grasses unfit for sacrifice"—and thus says Yama:

"One should discharge feces or urine with one's head covered, having covered the ground with grass that is neither fit for sacrifice nor moist. The mention of "grass" is intended to illustrate wood and other such materials as well; for this very reason, Manu says:
"One should utter [the name] after setting aside a piece of wood, a leaf, a clod of earth, or blades of grass;

having restrained one's speech, being pure, with the body covered and the head veiled. Here, "setting aside" (*tiraskaraṇa*) means interposing. "With the body covered" (*saṃvītāṅgaḥ*) means with the body clothed. "Veiled" (*avakuṇṭhitaḥ*) means with the head concealed. Regarding this specific detail, Viṣṇu says: "Having wrapped the nose and mouth with a cloth, and having fastened a clay-bound garment around the neck, one should utter [it]. Āpastamba also says: "A clay-bound garment" (*mṛddhānīm*) refers to a cloth for binding the clay.
The wise person should not look upward, downward, or sideways;
rather, placing a cloth upon his head, he should gaze at the space between the sky and the earth.
Aṅgiras also says:
"Having placed the sacred thread behind him so that it hangs from the neck, a householder may void excrement or urine, or else, being composed, he may do so with it over his ear. [236]

Placing [the sacred thread] on the ear pertains to the case of wearing a single garment. Thus says the *Sāṅkhyāyana-gṛhya*: "If one is wearing a single garment, he should place the *yajñopavīta* on his ear and then perform the voiding of urine or feces. Devala also says:
"One should always void urine and feces facing north in the morning and facing south in the evening; however, one should always avoid doing so during the *saṃdhyā*s."
Manu also says:
"One should discharge urine and feces facing north during the day;
at night, facing south; but during the two twilights, as during the day."

In this regard, an option between these [rules] should be understood. As for what Devala stated—"One should always attend to the voiding of feces and urine, but avoid it during the *saṃdhyās*"—that refers to a situation where other [necessities] are obstructed, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "One should not suppress a natural urge, nor should one perform a ritual act while being obstructed. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu:
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing whichever direction is comfortable, as also when there is fear of danger to life.

This [prohibition] also refers to cases where there is confusion regarding the directions caused by darkness such as mist, whether by night or by day. And this [act] should be performed in the southern direction or in the south-western direction. Thus says Āpastamba: "One should void urine and feces at a distance from the dwelling, toward the south or the south-west. The word "having gone" (*gatvā*) is to be supplied. "At a distance" (*ārāt*) means far away. And thus says Manu:
"One should perform the voiding of urine at a distance from the dwelling, the washing of the feet at a distance, and the disposal of food scraps and water at a distance indeed."
On this point, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states:
"Having gone quickly from the shelter to the southwest for a distance of about a bowshot, one should void excrement while covering the head;
moreover, one should never touch the head with the hand."

*Pratiśraya* means a dwelling. This refers to the daytime. As Āpastamba says: "When the sun has set, one should avoid the act of voiding urine or excrement outside the village, or even at a distance from it. Regarding this, Manu states:
"One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen;
nor on ploughed land, nor in water, nor on a sacrificial altar, nor on a mountain."
Neither in a dilapidated temple nor ever on an anthill,
nor in pits containing living creatures, nor while walking, nor while standing.
One should not study having reached a riverbank, nor on a mountain peak,
nor while looking at wind, fire, Brahmins, the sun, water, or likewise cows.
"One should never perform the voiding of feces or urine [on these].

*Citi* refers to a collection of bricks used for the performance of rites such as the casting of oblations. "In those containing living beings" means "in those with animate creatures. Although the prohibition there is already established by the mention of "mountains" (*parvata*), the specific mention of "mountain peaks" (*parvatamastaka*) is stated in its commentary to indicate that there is no fault in doing so on a mountain when one is in extreme distress. Yama also says:
"Chaff, embers, potsherds, and the abodes of deities..."
Royal highways, cremation grounds, fields, and caves.
One who is under restraint should not frequent the shade of trees, visible crossroads, water, or the edge of a body of water; he should avoid the path as well.
One should avoid the roots of trees, as well as sacred shrines, chasms, and holes.

Hārīta also says: "One should not void urine or excrement at a crossroads, near a door, on cow dung, in a cow-pen, at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), in a place full of grain, on a sacrificial ground, or beneath trees fit for sacrifice. A *catvara* is a courtyard; an *upadvāra* is the vicinity of a door. Āpastamba also says: "One should not void urine or excrement while wearing shoes. Viṣṇu also says: "Not on uncovered ground, nor on saline soil, nor on a grassy plot (*śādvala*), nor near a garden or water, nor in the open air. A *śādvala* is a patch of green grass. Gautama also says: "Facing the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, deities, or cows, one should not cast away urine, excrement, or impure things. The prefix *prati-* here denotes facing toward. Yama also says:
One should not urinate facing the sun, nor should one look at one's own excrement;
having seen it, one should gaze upon the sun, a cow, fire, or likewise a Brāhmaṇa.

Viṣṇu also says: "Not facing the wind, fire, the moon, the sun, a woman, a teacher, or a Brāhmaṇa. Vyāsa also says: "Those men who do not void excrement or urine on the royal highway, among cows, or in the midst of grain are auspicious."

Regarding the rules for urine and excrement, Śaṅkha states: "One should not [perform these acts] without water, nor without earth, nor with one's head uncovered. This refers to the requirement of distant water and earth. For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "First, wrapping the head; second, the *nivīta* (wearing the sacred thread around the neck); third, looking toward the quarters; fourth, concealment; fifth, silence; sixth, the excrement; seventh, taking the earth; and eighth, the water. Then, having wiped the anus and genitals with a clod of earth or similar object, and holding the penis, he should rise. And so says Bharadvāja.

"Then, having removed the feces and urine with clods of earth, wood, grass, or the like, he should rise with his garment lifted, firmly holding his penis. (240) Here, "with his garment lifted" means with his lower cloth raised. "Mehana" refers to the penis. Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule:
"One should wipe the anus with a clod of earth or with dry wood. Thus it is said. Also in the *Purāṇa*:
"Wiping with the left hand, or with *vīraṇa* grass and other materials unfit for sacrifice [is forbidden]."
"One should perform [the evacuation] with urine and feces; thus one's lifespan is not diminished.

As for what was stated by Gautama—"One should not effect the removal of urine and feces with leaves, clods of earth, or stones"—that refers to a situation where the aforementioned wood is unavailable, and is therefore faultless. On this point, Jābāli says:
"If, having performed his bath, he voids feces or urine while still wearing wet clothes..."
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one becomes pure again through bathing.
Hārīta also says:
"One should always take food and perform one's movements in private;
when these two are done in secret, one is endowed with Lakṣmī, but in public, one is deprived of fortune."
Thus ends the procedure for the voiding of urine and feces in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for purification (*śauca*).
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
Having risen with his penis still held [in hand],
he should, unwearied, perform purification with earth and drawn-up water until the odor, the smear, and the impurity are removed.
"With the water-pot and other items drawn up"; "unwearied" means "not lazy. Devala also says:
"One should not release the penis until purification is complete, even during urination or defecation;
having washed the anus and both hands repeatedly with earth and water."
And this [act] should be performed elsewhere than in a reservoir of water. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"When urination or defecation has been performed, purification shall not take place within a reservoir of water;
one should always perform it with a concentrated mind after drawing [water] elsewhere."
Dakṣa also says:
"One should not perform purification at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha); rather, one should do so using water drawn out [from it].
For this person, earth and water are the two attendants for purification."
But when it is not possible to remove the water, Vivasvat has stated this distinction:
"If purification is performed from the current without removing the water, one should leave a span’s depth of water behind;
otherwise, one would become impure."
A *tīrtha* here means a place for purification; hence [the name] Ṛśyaśṛṅga. One should purify with water that place where purification has been performed;
however, there can be no purity for one who does not purify it with earth.
Regarding that, Yama states the nature of the clay:
"A wise man should fetch clay from a bank that contains sand.
The mention of a "bank" is intended to indicate a location that is free from contamination. Marīci also says:
[242] "For a Brāhmaṇa, white clay is prescribed for purification; for a Kṣatriya, red is ordained; for a Vaiśya, yellow like turmeric; but for a Śūdra, one should specify black.

Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Kāśyapīya*: "Likewise, black [clay] is for women and Śūdras. Furthermore, when clay possessing the aforementioned characteristics cannot be found, Manu speaks as follows in response to the inquiry of how one should proceed in such a case:
"In whatever place there is water and whatever clay is found right there, that alone shall be recommended for that place; thus is purification ordained.
Regarding this, those [substances] to be avoided have been shown by Yama:
Nor from earth dug up by rats, nor from an anthill, nor from dusty ground, nor from mud;
nor from a path, nor from saline soil, nor from what has been left over after another person has performed purification.
One should always avoid these [places], for such purification is declared to be in vain.
Devala also says:
[One should avoid ground] filled with charcoal, chaff, insects, bones, gravel, and sand.

One should not take earth brought from within an anthill, from the water of a pond, from a blow against a wall, or from a cremation ground, even if it has been taken for the purpose of another’s purification. This is also stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa.
One should not take earth from an anthill, from that dug up by mice, nor from within water, nor what remains after purification, nor from a house, nor that which originates from a well.
"O King, one should avoid all these types of earth used for purification: that inhabited by living beings, that dug up by a plow, and likewise that from within water.
The phrase "not from within water" refers to locations other than ponds and the like; for this very reason, Yama says:
"One should not take earth from the outer parts of ponds, wells, or tanks;
one should take water from within, however, beyond the wrist (*maṇibandhana*).

Here, a *vāpī* is a long pond. The *maṇibandhana* is the region of the joint between the forearm and the hand. Having thus fetched the water and the earth, one should perform purification during the day facing north. And so says the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*:
"Having drawn out water and taken earth, one should remain silent;
facing north during the day, one should perform [the purification], and if at night, facing south.
Regarding the number of applications of earth here, Dakṣa says:
One application of clay on the penis, three on the left hand, and two on both hands—this is prescribed for purification after urination. As Śātātapa says:
"One [application] on the penis, three on the left hand, and two on each of the two hands."
"The purification for urine has been fully described; however, in the case of semen, it shall be threefold.
Regarding the quantity of earth in this context, Vivasvat says:
"For the purification of the penis, lumps of earth the size of a joint are prescribed."
Dakṣa also says:
"For the funeral rite (liṅga), earth is prescribed which fills [the vessel] in three turns;
water should be offered until the earth is exhausted."
Regarding this, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states a specific rule:
"At the beginning and at the end of the purifications, cleansing with water is prescribed;
once it has been thoroughly cleansed, one should apply earth, and at the end of the application of earth, water itself."
As for the statement of Vivasvat:
"Three applications of clay with intervals should be used for the purification of the private parts;
five applications of clay on the left hand, and three on each of the two hands."

Thus, this refers either to the intention of having an abundance of paste, or to the intention of the small quantity mentioned by Dakṣa. The meaning is that they should be separated from one another by water. Dakṣa also states the rule for purification:
"Three applications of clay for the anus, ten for one [the left hand], and seven for both. Manu also says:
"One [application of] clay should be applied to the penis, three to the anus, ten to one hand, and seven to both hands by one who desires purification. Thus it is said.

Now, is this intended to refer solely to the purification of the penis (*liṅga-śauca*), or rather to the purification performed simultaneously with it (*sahakaraṇa-śauca*)? It cannot be the first, because that would entail the purification of the penis having an invisible spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and because it would be impossible to enjoin two purifications that are mutually independent. Nor can it be the second, because that would result in the omission of hand-washing (*hasta-śauca*), which is included within the purification following urination. And one should not say "let there be an omission here," for there is no evidence for such a thing, and it contradicts the scriptural injunctions that establish the purification after urination. Nor is it a case of "extended application" (*tantra*), because the purification of the anus intervenes, making them occur at different times. Nor is it a case of "incidental inclusion" (*prasaṅga*), since a distinct purpose exists. But if it refers to simultaneous performance, then Manu would have failed to mention the purification for urination when speaking of separate performance; therefore, we do not know what the subject matter of this rule is.

It is said: True, this does not concern the purification of the penis (*viṭchauci*); rather, by the logic already stated in the rule "one [application] on the penis," it serves as an illustration for the aforementioned purifications prescribed in the Sūtras. Thus, it is meant that in each specific occasion (*nimitte*), that particular purification must be performed. Where two occasions coincide sequentially, the performance of the occasional rites (*naimittika*) follows that very sequence. Furthermore, where two occasions occur simultaneously, it is likewise stated—by the aforementioned logic—that the occasional rite must be performed; thus, there is no fault.
Regarding the quantity of clay here, Aṅgiras says:
"The first measure is to be known as a handful (prasṛti), the second as half of that,
and the third measure of clay is to be known as filling one-third of the palm."

Regarding the specific rule for washing the hands, Hārīta says: "One should apply [clay] once to the penis, three times to the anus, ten times to the left hand, six times to the back, and seven times to the feet. The term "back" (*pṛṣṭhe*) refers to the rear part of the left hand, as that is the subject under discussion. Dakṣa also states:
"Six other applications of clay should be given by one desiring purity for the cleansing of the nails;
however, one should never perform purification with streams of rainwater."
After the cleansing of the nails, Śaṅkha states:
"Three applications of clay should be made after performing the cleaning of the nails;
three applications of clay should also be made to the feet for the sake of constant purification."
Regarding this, Marīci states a specific rule:
"The two feet and likewise the two ankles should be washed with three [handfuls] from the heel;
the hands, up to the wrists, should be washed until all traces of the coating and its odor are removed."

[246] And these two types of purity are to be understood as pertaining to the householder. Thus Manu says: "This purity is for the householder; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics."
As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "Five [applications of] clay for the anus, ten for each of the [other] three, and seven for both together"; and also that which was stated by Yama:
Two applications of clay should be given to the penis, five to the anus, and ten to the hands;
seven should be applied to both together, and likewise one more to the anus.
Thus, in this case as well:
"The first clay should be the measure of half a handful;
the other four are proclaimed to be each half the size of the preceding one."

Thus, there is no contradiction because Vṛddhavasiṣṭha prescribes a small quantity; the statement "two [applications] to the penis" intends the greater amount of paste, for earth and water should be taken as necessary for the purpose of purification after voiding feces and urine.

This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu. Furthermore, the act of applying [earth] to the anus is connected everywhere with the purification of feces, as there is no contradiction [in this]. As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha:
"Seven applications of earth are prescribed for the urethra, two for the penis;
twenty are to be known for one hand, and fourteen for the other two."
Three applications of clay should be used after cleaning the nails;
three more are to be known as necessary for the feet by one who desires constant purity.
[247] This is the rule of purification for householders and likewise for those living with their teachers;
it shall be twofold for forest-dwellers and threefold for ascetics.

Thus, here too, there is no contradiction because one may rely on the small quantity mentioned by Marīci: "The *avadāna* (cutting) should be equal to a [morsel of] clay. An *avadāna* is merely the size of a thumb-joint. Here, "urination" (*mehana*) refers to the anus. As for that which was stated by Śātātapa:
"In the moon-vow (*induvrata*), mouthfuls (*grāsa*) the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit are prescribed;
likewise for all oblations (*āhuti*s), and for the clods of earth used for purification."

This refers to the washing of the hands, because for the anus and the penis, a different measure is prescribed. The *induvrata* is the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Thus, even when the aforementioned purification has been performed, Manu states that there is no contradiction even if the number [of applications] is exceeded in cases where neither odor nor stain is removed:
"As long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impurity do not depart from the object smeared by it, so long must earth and water be applied in all purifications of substances."
Devala also says:
"Purification is prescribed for as long as one considers oneself pure;
no fixed measure for the number of purificatory acts is taught by the learned."
As for that which was stated by Dakṣa:
"One desiring purity should not perform purification either deficiently or excessively;
one becomes pure through penance when a prescribed rule has been transgressed."

Thus, this should be understood to apply either before the number previously resolved upon has been reached, or upon its completion, or when the odor and other such qualities have vanished. Consequently, it should be noted that in cases where the odor and so forth vanish even before the stated number is reached, the restriction on the number serves a transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose. Likewise, regarding the performance of the aforementioned purification, Vyāghrapāda states that for one who lacks purity of intention, there is no purification:
"Purification is said to be of two kinds: external and internal.
That which is performed with earth and water is declared to be external, while purity of intention is the internal."
"Even with the entirety of the waters of the Gaṅgā and with loads of earth as large as mountains,
one who acts until death [for purification] does not become pure if his internal disposition is corrupted.
Regarding the specific rule for purification when there is a discharge from the anus during a meal, Bṛhaspati says:
If, while eating, the anus of a Brahmin should ever leak,
resulting in impurity and defilement, how can his purification be accomplished?
Having first performed purification, one should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water;
then, having observed a fast, one becomes pure through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
However, for those who have not been initiated (*anupanīta*), that which was stated by Pitāmaha should be observed:
"As long as the twice-born, the Śūdras, and likewise women have not been initiated,
purification is ordained for them consisting only in the removal of odor and stains."
However, a specific rule regarding women and Śūdras is shown in the Ādi Purāṇa:
"The wise have declared that for women and Śūdras, purification is said to be half [of the prescribed amount].
Furthermore, even for one who has sat down to discharge feces or urine but does not do so, the purification is likewise only half. And thus says Vṛddha Parāśara:

"But one who, while seated, is unable to discharge feces or urine, should always perform half of his prescribed purification. This should be understood to apply at night as well; so it is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:
Whatever purification is prescribed for the day, half of that is declared for the night;
half of that is said for one who is ill, and half of that for one on a journey.
This [rule] regarding the lack of capacity for purification refers to those who are ill; otherwise, however, purification is indeed according to one's capacity. And so says the Ādi-purāṇa:
"Half of the daytime purification is prescribed for the night, for travelers, and so forth;
one who is afflicted should perform it according to his strength, while one who is healthy should perform it as prescribed."
Bodhāyana also says:
"Having understood the place, the time, as well as oneself, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the justification, and the state, one should determine the purification."
On this point, Dakṣa says:
"Effort regarding purity must always be made; a twice-born man is remembered as being rooted in purity.
For one devoid of purity and right conduct, all ritual actions are fruitless."
Even for one whose conduct is lax regarding purity, their character remains unprotected.
Devala also says:
"One who knows the Dharma should employ the right hand for cleansing below the navel;
likewise, one should not cleanse above the navel with the left hand."
Āpastamba also states: "When one has the capacity, one should not remain without performing purification even for a moment.
Thus ends the section on the rules of purification in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the purification of bodily impurities.
Regarding this, Manu says: "Those apertures of the body that are above the navel are entirely pure; those that are below are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body."
The cavities of the sense organs are the [excretory] openings. The impurities have also been mentioned by him [the same author]:
"Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus, phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat—these twelve are the impurities of human beings. Thus it is said.

Fat is the bodily grease; blood is *asṛk*; marrow is the fat of the head; earwax is the impurity of the ears; tears are the water of the eyes. Regarding the purification of one defiled by these, Bodhāyana says:
"For purification from the first six [impurities], one should take earth and water;
but for the latter six, one becomes pure with water alone. Thus it is said.
But regarding humans, he states that even in subsequent cases, purification is by means of earth and water:
"For the purpose of purifying the voiding of feces and urine, earth and water should be taken in appropriate quantities;
and likewise for the twelve purifications of bodily impurities."

That by which feces and urine are discharged is so described; the meaning is "for the sake of its purification. And this, being subject to the aforementioned alternatives, is to be determined in consideration of place, time, and other factors. This is stated by Bodhāyana:
"Having understood the place, the time, as well as oneself, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the circumstances, and the condition, one should determine the purification. [251]
This [rule] applies to contact with one's own impurities; however, regarding contact with the impurities of another, that which was stated by Devala should be observed:
"If one should touch the bone of a human, fat, feces, menstrual blood, urine, semen, marrow, or even the blood of another..."
"Having bathed and wiped off the clothes and so forth, and having sipped water (ācamana), he becomes pure;
by touching those very [clothes] himself and wiping them, he would become purified.

Here, "wiping" (*parimārjana*) means washing. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "If one is defiled below the navel or on the arms by bodily impurities, by *surā* and other intoxicants, or by wine, one should wash that limb with earth and water; if the sense organs are defiled, however, one should fast, bathe, and [purify oneself] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); and if the lips are defiled, likewise. On this point, Yama says:
Three applications of clay on the body, three on the feet, and likewise three on the hands;
there should be fifteen applications of clay for impurity, especially for the hands and other limbs.
This purification has been declared for touching one's own urine and so forth;
however, in the case of another's [excrement], it is taught that it applies at times other than the moment of voiding.
"In the case of contact with another's blood, semen, feces, or urine, thirty-two applications of clay are prescribed for all four castes. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the section on personal purification from bodily impurities in the Smṛticandrikā [252].
Now follows the procedure for sipping water (ācamana).
In this regard, the Elder Parāśara says: "Then,

having performed purification and having washed his feet and hands with earth and water, the twice-born man, having tied up his topknot and his waistband, should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana)."
Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya states a specific rule:
"One should perform the act of sipping water (ācamana) with the hand that holds the *pavitra* grass-ring;
however, that *pavitra* does not become defiled by the [water], but one must avoid using it once it has been defiled by food."
This refers to the intention of using the right hand, because a prohibition regarding the left hand is heard [in the scriptures]. Thus says Hārīta:
"The twice-born man who sips water while holding *kuśa* grass in his left hand becomes defiled by that [act] as if by blood or impurity."

This also refers specifically to the case of using only the left hand, since a distinction in the results for both hands is heard in the scriptures. Thus says Gobhila: "The twice-born who sips water with *darbha* grass placed on both [hands], obtains the fruit of drinking Soma and, having eaten, gains the fruit of a sacrifice."
Regarding this, Hārīta states the rule for the direction:

"Facing the northeast (aiṣānya), one should perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) according to the prescribed rule. Northeast means the intermediate direction between north and east. "One should perform the ritual sipping" means one should rinse the mouth (ācāmet). Yājñavalkya also says:
Seated with his knees together in a clean place, facing either north or east,
a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha.

"Between the knees" means having placed the *aratni* (the space between the thumb and forefinger) between the two knees, according to the traditional teaching of Hārīta: "Having placed the *aratni* between the thighs, one should drink water three times from the heart. The mention of the "Brāhma" [tīrtha] is intended to indicate the *Kāya* and *Daiva* [tīrthas] as well. For this very reason, Manu says:
"A Brahmin should always perform the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*) using the Brāhma *tīrtha*;
or else, he may use the *Kāya* or *Traidaśika* [Daiva], but never the *Pitrya*."

The mention of the *vipra* (Brahmin) is intended to indicate the other two [castes] as well, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) stating, "A twice-born man should always perform ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*). The *prājāpatya* [tīrtha] is that of the body; the *traidaśika* is the *daiva* [tīrtha]. Here, the appropriation of the *tīrthas* should be understood as occurring at the first performance of the *ācamana*, not at every subsequent performance; for if it were so, the expression "at all times" (*nityakālam*) would be untenable. The *tīrthas* have also been shown by Yājñavalkya: "The bases of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, and the tip of the hand, are respectively the *tīrthas* of Prajāpati, the Pitṛs, Brahmā, and the Devas."

The *deśinī* is the forefinger. Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state a specific rule: "The *brāhma* *tīrtha* is on the line running eastward from the base of the thumb; between the forefinger and the thumb is the *pitrya*; and between the little finger and the palm is the *prājāpatya*. Regarding the regulation for the water therein, Śaṅkha says:
"One should perform the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*) with water that has been drawn out, which is free from foam and bubbles, not heated by fire, and not salty."

Yājñavalkya also, in the context of the rule "one should sip water" (ācāmet), states: "But with waters that are in their natural state, free from foam and bubbles. "In their natural state" means unaltered. Hārīta also says:
One should avoid water that is discolored, foul-smelling, and frothy.
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"But those [waters] which are corrupted by color or taste, and those which have an inauspicious appearance.
Pracetās also says:

One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) two, three, four, or twice with water that is not hot, free from bubbles, purified by the "cloth-eye" (a cloth strained over the hand), which reaches the heart, and is silent.
The phrase "not hot" refers to those who are not afflicted by illness; for this very reason, Yama states:
"For the wise, purification at night is said to be by means of water that has not been inspected;
for the afflicted, by water [in general]; and likewise for those who drink hot [liquids], by hot water."

The meaning is that this applies to patients who drink hot liquids, but not to those who are merely ill. Āpastamba also states: "One should not sip water from rain-showers, nor from water in a fissure, nor from heated water without a specific reason. Here, *pradara* means a chasm or pit. The phrase "nor from water in a fissure" refers to water insufficient for a cow; for Vasiṣṭha records: "Even from a fissure, [one may take] as much water as would suffice to satiate a cow. However, when water with the aforementioned characteristics cannot be found, Devala provides the rule for what should be done in such a case:
"In whatever regions there are gods, and in whatever regions there are twice-born [Brahmins]..."
In whatever regions there is water, and whatever soil exists in each respective place;
"In whatever places there is a particular purity and whatever kind of religious practice exists, one should not despise them there; for the dharma is of that very same nature in those places.
Thus says Yama: "This water [for rinsing] shall not be used until one has rinsed with the left hand."
"A wise man should not perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) as long as he does not touch [the water] with his left hand;
for in the left [hand] reside the twelve Ādityas and Varuṇa, the lord of waters. On this point, Dakṣa says:

"Having washed his feet and hands, he should drink water that has been looked at three times. Regarding this, "looked at" refers to the daytime; for at night, purification is said by the wise to be achieved by water that has not been looked at.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Yama. Regarding the specific manner of washing, Hārīta states: "Having washed the hands up to the wrists and the feet up to the ankles. The *maṇibandha* is the region of the joint between the hand and the forearm. Devala also says:
"In this manner, having separately washed the two feet with water up to the knees, and the two hands up to the wrists, one should thereafter sit restrained."
"Then one should drink water equally three times from the first *tīrtha* on the right.
This means from the first [tīrtha], which is that of Brahmā (*brāhma*). Following the washing [of the feet], the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states:
"But having completed the purification of the feet, one should indeed sprinkle the feet again."

"One should drink water three times with that [earth], and likewise wipe [the mouth] with water. Regarding the phrase "one should drink three times," this prohibition applies to drinking less than three times, but not to more; for the Smṛti of Gautama states: "Seated in a clean place, having placed the right arm between the knees, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, having washed the hands up to the wrists, remaining silent, and touching the heart, one should sip water three or four times" (GDh 1.36). This option is intended according to one's own satisfaction. "Touching the heart" means reaching the heart. And so says Devala:
"When the water has been drunk and has reached the heart, the Brāhmaṇa becomes pure;
the Rājanya [is pure] when it reaches the throat; the Vaiśya, when it reaches the mouth; and the Śūdra is pure by mere contact.
The word "contact" (sparśanāt) implies "at the palate" as the ellipsis. The mention of the Śūdra is intended to indicate women as well. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:

"But the twice-born shall be purified by [water] reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; a woman and a Śūdra, by being touched once at the end. Here, "once" means a single time; "at the end" means by being touched with that [part], namely the palate.
When the water has reached the heart, a Brāhmaṇa attains purity;
a Kṣatriya [attains it] when it reaches the throat, a Vaiśya when it reaches the palate, and so too women and Śūdras.

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. Regarding the quantity of water that reaches the heart, Uśanas says: "Water reaching the heart is that which is sufficient for the immersion of a māṣa bean. Bhāradvāja also says:
"Having taken water sufficient for the immersion of a māṣa bean, one should drink it three times. He (Bhāradvāja) also states a specific rule regarding the taking of the water:
Having extended the hand forward and shaped it like a cow's ear,
the twice-born man should take water with his hand, the fingers of which are held together.
"Having released the thumb and the little finger, one should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) with the remaining [fingers].
The word "with the right hand" is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. And likewise, the Purāṇa states:
"Having formed the right hand again in the shape of a cow's ear..."

"One should drink water three times with the right hand and wipe the mouth twice. Thus it is said. That wiping should be performed specifically with the base of the thumb. And so Dakṣa says: "Having wiped [the lips], one should then wipe the mouth twice with the base of the thumb."

The remainder [of the instruction] is that one should wipe the hairless part [of the lips]. Āpastamba, however, says one should wipe around three times: "One should wipe around the two lips three times; some say twice. One should touch [the lips] once; some say twice. Having sprinkled the left hand with the right hand, one should touch the feet, the head, and the sense organs. And here, the two lips include the hairy parts, because of the traditional teaching of Kaṇva: "Meditating on the Atharvaveda, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, one should wipe the hairy parts of the lips with the *brāhma* tīrtha. The remainder is that one should touch the mouth once, because of the traditional teaching of Bhārgava: "Having wiped around the two lips, one should then wipe around the mouth while meditating on Agni. And one should touch the sense organs located in the head, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "And one should touch the apertures located in the head. Dakṣa describes that touching as follows:
Having first gathered [the water] with three [fingers], one should thus touch the mouth;
thereafter, immediately after, the nostrils with the thumb and the index finger.
Again and again, one should touch the eyes and ears with the thumb and ring finger;
the navel with the little finger and thumb; and the heart with the palm.
"And with all [the fingers], he should subsequently touch the head and the two arms with the tips.
Thus [it is said]. The remainder [of the sense] is "with the three middle [fingers]";
that is, one should first touch the mouth with the three middle fingers.

Thus, from the *Yogayājñavalkya-smṛti*: "The forefinger and the thumb; the ring finger and the little finger. The remainder [of the verse] is: "Having repeatedly touched water, having touched all the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), one should touch water. Lord Bhṛgu says: "A Brāhmaṇa should always perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*)."

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Vaiyāghrapāda. Here, the word *śiras* refers to the head, according to the teaching of Viṣṇu: "One should touch the head and the heart. The word *agreṇa* means with the tip of the hand. And so says Vaiyāghrapāda:
"Having touched the two shoulders with the tip of the hand, and having touched water while composed in mind, and having called to mind Padmanābha, the Brahmin becomes thoroughly purified."

In this regard, there is a specific rule in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should mentally remember the Lord of Sacrifice (*yajñapuruṣa*) together with the syllable *Oṃ*. Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi states: "One should pour the remaining water into the left hand. The "remaining" refers to the water left over after the ritual sipping (*ācamana*). Vṛddha-Śaṅkha, however, describes a different method of touching (*upasparśana*): "One should touch the two nostrils by joining the index finger and the thumb; then one should touch the two eyes by joining the middle finger and the thumb."
By joining the thumb and the ring finger, one should touch the two ears;
by joining the little finger and the thumb, a person should touch both shoulders.
"Likewise, one should touch the navel and the heart with the palm;
then one should touch the head—this is the rule for *ācamana*. Thus says Śaṅkha as well."
Then, one should first touch the crown of the head with four fingers;
using the union of the index finger and the thumb, one should touch each of the two eyes separately.
One should touch the nostrils in succession with the middle and ring fingers;
one should touch the ear by joining the thumb with the little finger.
By joining the index finger and the thumb, one should touch the palm to the navel and the heart.

Pāithīnasi also states: "Fire is in the thumb; therefore, one should touch all the [other] parts with that very [thumb]. In this matter, the arrangement follows according to one's own *śākhā*. However, for those belonging to *śākhās* where the touching of the limbs (*aṅgopasparśana*) is not mentioned, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, where the touching of only a few limbs is prescribed, it should be understood that—due to the absence of contradiction or by following the specific injunction—the touching of the limbs immediately following [the ones mentioned] also takes place. For this very reason, Saṃvarta says: "Having wiped the mouth with water, one should touch the twelve limbs."
Vaiyāghrapāda stated the fruit for one who acts in this way:
"The Brāhmaṇa who thus performs the ritual sipping of water (upasparśana) daily shall instantly satisfy the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass."
Vṛddhaśaṅkha also says:
"One should sip water three times; by that, the deities are pleased for him—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; so we have heard."
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are pleased by the act of cleansing;
Viṣṇu is pleased by the two feet, and Brahmā is proclaimed to be pleased by the head.
The Nāsatyas and Dasras are pleased when both nostril-pairs are touched;
the Moon and Sun are pleased when the pair of eyes is touched.
When the two ears are touched in that manner, Fire and Wind are pleased;
by the mere touching of the shoulders, all the deities are pleased.
The lords of the gods are constantly pleased with him by the touch of his navel;
and when his heart is touched, all the deities are pleased.

"By touching [the disciple] on the head, the deity becomes pleased and the person becomes a Puruṣa; the earth, water, mountains, and nāgas, as well as all that is moving and stationary, [reside] in the two shoulders. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the fault incurred by failing to perform this is shown in the Purāṇa:

"Whatever actions an atheist performs out of delusion without having sipped water (ācamana), all those actions indeed become fruitless; of this there is no doubt. Thus ends the section on the rules for sipping water (*ācamana-vidhi*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the occasions for sipping water (ācamana),
Manu says:
"Having voided urine or feces, or having touched the bodily apertures, one who has sipped water should touch [the lips]."
And one who is about to study the Veda, as well as while eating food, [should always do so].

The sense organs are the channels. "Having sipped water" means having drunk water three times. Āpastamba also says: "Upon dreaming, sneezing, touching mucus, tears, blood, hair, fire, cows, a Brāhmaṇa, or a woman; upon walking on a high road; upon touching something impure; upon touching an impure person; and upon putting on the *nīvī*—one should touch water. Here, *kṣavathuḥ* means sneezing; *śiṅkhāṇikā* means nasal mucus; *aśru* means eye-water. By the word *nīvī*, the lower garment (*adhovāsa*) is indicated here. The knotting of the lower garment is the *nīvī*. This is also stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
In conversation with Caṇḍālas or Mlecchas, in eating the remnants of the food of women or Śūdras,
or upon seeing a person who is impure from eating, as well as food of that same nature;
One should sip water (perform ācamana) upon the falling of tears, and likewise upon the shedding of blood;
also after touching fire, cows, or one who is impure.

Regarding the touch of women or oneself, and after adjusting the waist-knot (*nīvī*), Hārīta also says: "One who intends to sleep or to eat should sip water. Prajāpati also [states this] at the commencement of a specific rite, even though one is already pure (*prayata*).
The word "should sip water" (ācāmet) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Also in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"One should perform rites such as the worship of the gods, as well as the salutation of the guru, having properly sipped water; likewise, one should perform the act of eating."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Having performed the necessary duties, one who is intent on purity should sip water (ācamana).
The 'necessary duties' are those that are obligatory. Śātātapa also says:
[262] One should always rinse the mouth after chewing food, except when chewing betel;
likewise, after touching the lips with hair or after changing one's garment.
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, having spoken a false word,
or having stepped upon a road or a cremation ground, one should sip water for purification even if one is already pure.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"Upon the emission of downward wind (flatus), upon a cry of distress, upon the arising of anger,
upon touching a cat or a mouse, upon laughing, and upon speaking untruth— "
While performing ritual acts during all these occasions, one should sip water for purification (*upaspṛśet*).
Hārīta also says: "One who desires to approach the deities should sip water. Yama also says:
"Having emerged from the water, one should sip water; likewise, having entered [the water], one should do the same."
In this way, he shall be endowed with prosperity and honored by Varuṇa himself.

"Having descended" means having entered. Hārīta also says: "One should not cross [water] without having performed *upasparśana*"; the word "water" is to be supplied as the object. *Upasparśana* refers to sipping water (*ācamana*). Also in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"In all cases of doubt, and likewise when the topknot is loosened, one should always perform *upasparśana* without the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)."
Manu also says:
"Having sipped water and being purified, one should always mutter [prayers] upon seeing something impure;
'impure' refers to unclean things such as excrement and the like. [This is stated] in the Padma Purāṇa.
Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla or similar outcaste during the recitation of mantras or the fire sacrifice, the best of the twice-born should sip water;
likewise, upon seeing a dog or other such animal, he should touch his right ear.
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Upon sneezing, spitting, sleeping, laughing, or shedding tears—
one should sip water for purification after these five, or touch the right ear."
Regarding this, Parāśara spoke thus:
"Manu declared that sacred sites such as Prabhāsa and rivers such as the Gaṅgā reside within the right ear of a Brāhmaṇa."
"The Sun, Varuṇa, Soma, Vahni, and likewise Vāyu—these deities always abide in the right ear of the Brahmin.
And this touching of the right ear should be understood as applicable when the sipping of water (ācamana) is impossible; thus says the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Having sipped water properly, one who is pure should indeed perform the rites for the gods, the seers, and the ancestors with great care.
Or one may perform the touching of the right ear;
indeed, this should be done according to one's means, provided that the former [rite] is unavailable.
"The attainment of the subsequent [act] is not desired while the previously mentioned [state] exists.

Alternatively, that which was stated by Baudhāyana should be observed: "Having put on the *nīvī*, a Brahmin should touch water, or he should touch moist grass, the ground, or cow-dung. "Upapeśet" means he should sip water (*ācāmet*). Āpastamba also says: "And having put on the *nīvī*, he should touch water, or moist dung, plants, or the ground. "Śakṛt" means cow-dung. On this point, Baudhāyana says: "As long as one has the capacity, one should not remain impure even for a moment."
Thus ends the section on the occasions for sipping water (*ācamana*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follow the occasions for sipping water twice;
regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or descended from a chariot,
and after putting on a different garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water once more.

Viṣṇu also says: "Having stepped upon a chariot, having voided urine or excrement, having touched the bone or the fat of a five-toed animal, or after speaking with a Caṇḍāla or a Mleccha, one who has sipped water (ācānta) should sip water again. Bodhāyana also says: "In eating, in offering oblations, in giving, in presenting gifts, in receiving gifts, and at the time of consuming sacrificial food (havir), double sipping of water (dvir-ācamana) is prescribed."

Śaṅkha also says: "If one has already performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) during bathing, eating, or spitting, one should sip water again. Vyāsa also says: "During the fire-oblation (homa), at the time of eating, and at both twilights—as well as during the recitation of prayers (japa), the oblation, and worship—one who has already sipped water should sip water again."
The meaning is "giving at home. Also in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
[265] Having washed his hands and feet, one who is eating should sip water twice;
likewise after touching the lips, which have hair on them, and after changing one's garment.
Upon the voiding of feces, urine, or excrement; when speaking harsh words;
after spitting; at the commencement of Vedic study; and likewise upon the onset of coughing or labored breathing.
"Having approached a crossroads or a cremation ground, being composed,
one should likewise sip water again even after having already sipped it during both twilights.
This is the statement of Śukta Nipura.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, [are described] the occasions for double sipping (dvirācamana). Now follows the exceptions to the rules for sipping (ācamanāpavāda).
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
Droplets from the mouth are pure, as are the drops from the act of sipping water;
likewise, the beard and hair within the mouth are pure, and once one has removed what is stuck between the teeth, one becomes pure.

The meaning of this is as follows: drops of phlegm issuing from the mouth are pure and do not cause one to become *ucchiṣṭa* (rendered impure by remnants), provided they do not fall upon the body. Thus says Gautama: "Drops from the mouth do not cause one to become *ucchiṣṭa*, unless they fall upon the body. Therefore, the implication is that one need not perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water). However, if they touch the body, *ācamana* must certainly be performed on account of that contact. Āpastamba, moreover, prescribes *ācamana* even when there is no contact with the body: "Regarding those drops which are perceived falling from the mouth, *ācamana* is ordained for them; some say one need not sip water for those which fall upon the ground" [266]. In this matter, the rule is determined by the distinction of place and time. Furthermore, drops of *ācamana* water, even if they touch the body, are pure and do not cause one to become *ucchiṣṭa*. Thus says Manu:
"Drops that touch the feet of one who is giving water for rinsing to others should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them.

Here, the connection is "the feet of one who is giving water for rinsing to others. The meaning of "those on the ground" is "situated in an uncontaminated place. The mention of the "feet" of the giver is intended to indicate other parts of the body as well, because of the statement of the reason: "they should be known as equal to those on the ground."
And those drops from the body of men that fall while one is eating or drinking—there is no fault of impurity from food remnants in these; they are considered equal to the earth.

And because of the traditional teaching of Yama: "Likewise, the beard that has entered the mouth is pure and does not cause one to become *ucchiṣṭa* (rendered ritually impure by food remnants). Regarding this, Devala says:
"Impurity is not prescribed when the beard enters the mouth."

Regarding this matter, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "One does not become impure by food particles remaining in the mouth as long as one does not touch them with the hand. The mention of the "hand" is intended to indicate other parts of the body as well, based on the traditional teaching of Gautama: "Unless they fall upon a limb. Food stuck to the teeth refers to grains and the like adhering to the teeth. However, that which does not come loose (acyuta) does not cause impurity, provided it is like what remains on the teeth and has not been touched by the tongue. Thus says Manu: "In the case of food stuck to the teeth, one is pure as if it were part of the teeth, unless it is touched by the tongue."
When they have fallen away from those states, he swallows them while remaining pure himself.

"Swallowing" means causing [the food] to enter within; the word "only" (*eva*) is for the purpose of excluding the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). And this swallowing is an alternative to the renunciation mentioned by Yājñavalkya. This rule regarding "what is stuck to the teeth being like the teeth" is to be understood as applying when no flavor is perceived. As Śaṅkha says: "What is stuck to the teeth is like the teeth, except for the perception of flavor, provided there has been no contact with the tongue. "Except for the perception of flavor" means when no flavor is perceived. Some say that even upon contact with the tongue, one remains pure as long as the substance has not fallen away. Thus says Gautama: "Regarding what is stuck to the teeth, it is like the teeth; others say until it falls away, except upon contact with the tongue. One should know that once it has fallen away, it is like saliva; by swallowing it, one becomes pure. "Like saliva" means just as one does not become impure by it. The statement "what is stuck to the teeth is like the teeth" refers to the case where the coating cannot be removed. And so says Devala:
After removing food particles stuck between the teeth during a meal, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
One should regard a particle stuck between the teeth that cannot be removed as being like the tooth itself, and not as a mere coating.
"One should not exert great effort in extracting [the impurity] again;
for if a wound is caused by piercing with grass, there would be excessive impurity.
And thus, that which is devoid of juice, untouched by the tongue, and cannot be removed is said to be like [food stuck between] the teeth. On this point, Śātātapa says:

[268] "When fruit or root remains stuck to the teeth, as well as when oil has been consumed, and likewise with betel leaf and a stalk of sugarcane, a twice-born man does not become *ucchiṣṭa* (impure from remnants). Here,
"when oil has been consumed" refers to that which cannot be removed at all.
Having eaten, one should sip water according to the prescribed rule with a concentrated mind;
one should also cleanse the mouth and hands with earth and by scrubbing.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti of Devala. Also in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"A twice-born man does not become impure by means of water, leaves, roots, flowers, [objects] made of grass or wood, or likewise by fragrant substances."
Atri also says:

"In the case of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), in the Soma sacrifice, in water, and in the oblations to the vital breaths (prāṇāhutis), there shall be no fault for one who has remnants; such is the statement of Atri."

The meaning of the passage beginning with "In the waters you are the covering of immortality" is that there is no fault in the recitation of mantras by one who has remnants [of food] in his mouth. Vasiṣṭha also states:
"In the offerings to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti), in Soma rites, likewise in the Madhuparka, and in all offerings made from the mouth, a twice-born man does not become impure due to remnants."
Thus ends the section on exceptions to the rules for sipping water (*ācamana*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the prohibition of sipping water; regarding this, Devala says:
One should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while wearing shoes, standing in water, with hair disheveled,
wearing a turban, or having the head wrapped in a cloth.
[269] He even wrapped his beard; he wore a turban. Viṣṇu also [did so]:
"Neither walking nor lying down, nor touching clothing nor another person, nor laughing, nor conversing, nor even looking at himself."
Without touching the hair, the waist-knot, the lower body, or even the ground,
if he should touch these, he must wash his hand again.

Gobhila also says: "Having made a portion of the lower garment (*antarīya*) serve as an upper garment (*uttarīya*). Here, *antarīya* refers to the lower garment. Pracetās also says: "One should not sip water while wearing only the inner garment, nor without any garment at all; nor while performing other actions, nor with feet not placed together. Āpastamba also says: "One should not perform useless acts or sip water with the remainder of water used for fire-rituals, nor with water stirred by the hand. Viṣṇu also says: "One should not sip water with the remainder from washing the feet; having poured it out upon the ground, one should sip water. Saṃvarta also says:
A twice-born man of the highest rank is never purified by water given by a Śūdra, by an impure person, or with only one hand; nor is he purified while wearing sandals.
Marīci also said:

"One should not [recite] outside [the sacred area], nor with haste, nor while seated on a seat, nor while standing up; nor while wearing sandals, nor without concentration, but rather being pure and with a restrained mind."
Even while remaining seated after eating, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), but never at any other time.
Bhṛgu also says: "If one has sipped water (ācamana) while lacking the sacred thread, or while wearing unwashed clothing,
or having released the topknot, the entire act must be performed again."
One who wears a turban, one who sits in the full lotus posture, one whose feet are raised, one traveling in a vehicle,
or one standing on improper ground, does not attain purity by sipping water (ācamana).

The word "of that which has been performed" refers to the *ācamana* (sipping of water). One with "propped feet" (*prauḍhapāda*) is one whose feet have ascended onto a seat or the like; or, as it is said: "One who has ascended his feet onto a seat, or likewise onto his knees or calves, and who has crossed his legs—that one is called 'one with propped feet'."
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Gobhila. "Prapada" means the tip of the foot. Pulaha also says:

"Having covered the head or the neck, or even with one's lower garment or topknot hanging loose, one becomes impure even after sipping water (ācamana) if one has not performed the purification of the feet."
Also in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Whether covering his neck or his head, or even while standing in a chariot or a marketplace,
one who has not performed the purification of his feet remains impure even if he has sipped water."
A *āpaṇa* is a place for buying and selling. Kauśika also says: "If some impure-handed Brāhmaṇa should sip water, all of that sipping becomes impure for him."

Gautama also says: "One should not drink from cupped hands, nor should one sip water for purification (ācamana) while standing using water drawn [from a source]. The meaning is that one should sip water for purification only with water drawn [from a source], and one should not drink from the mouth like an animal. The phrase "not while standing" refers to dry land; however, in water, one may indeed sip water even while standing. Thus Viṣṇu states:
"Standing in water up to the knees, one who has sipped water attains purity;
but below that depth, even if one sips water a hundred times, one does not become pure."
By the phrase "below the knees," he states that [the rite] is not contradictory even when the water reaches the knees. And so says the Smṛti:
"Standing in knee-deep water or sitting on dry land facing east, having sipped water thoroughly in both cases, one remains situated in both simultaneously."
The meaning is "of those two who are situated in water. And so says Hārīta:
"Whether standing in water or on dry land, or situated between both;
one standing in water [performs] water-rites, and one standing on dry land [performs] land-actions."
"But one who stands on both sides of both [paths] would be entitled to perform ritual actions. [272] Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: if one sips water while standing in water, then one is authorized only for rites performed in water; but when standing on dry land, then one is authorized only for rites performed on dry land. However, if one does so in both places, then one becomes authorized for all rites being performed in both locations. And thus says Paiṭhīnasi: "One who has sipped water while inside [the water] becomes pure only inside; one who has sipped water while outside [the water] becomes pure only outside. Therefore, having performed one [sip] outside and one inside, one becomes pure in every case regarding the act of sipping. On this point, Dakṣa says:

"When a Brahmin has bathed and then sips water (ācamana) while standing with his feet in the water on one hand, or on dry land on the other, he becomes pure in both cases and thus fit for ritual action. Elsewhere, however, that which was stated by Hārīta should be consulted.
One wearing wet clothes should perform libations, sipping of water, and recitation of mantras in the water;
one wearing dry clothes should perform libations, sipping of water, and recitation of mantras on land.
"If a base man, while standing on dry ground, should sip water while wearing wet clothes,
the *pretas* indeed drink the dripping from his garment.
On this point, Vyāsa says:
If a Brāhmaṇa sips water from the tips of his fingernails, that is equal to the drinking of liquor; thus spoke the Seer.
Yama also says:
"The twice-born who sips water that has been touched by the nails of his hands clearly drinks liquor; such is the word of the Sage."
"Manu, the son of Svayambhū, has declared that if a Brāhmaṇa drinks water using his left hand after lifting it up, that is equal to the drinking of liquor."
In this regard, a specific rule is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"One should not drink water by lifting it with the left hand and taking it directly into the mouth.
Regarding this, there is another *Smṛti* text:
Having taken a gourd, a copper vessel, a water-pot, or a water-jar, one may perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) oneself; by doing so, one does not become impure.

One should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) with one's own hand using a vessel made of horn, gourd, or bell-metal, or with a cup made of a copper leaf; however, one should avoid vessels smeared with oily substances.
"Water that is in a bell-metal vessel, and water that is in a copper vessel,
as well as in a golden or silver one, is never impure.
Thus ends the section on prohibitions regarding *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.

Now, something else regarding the subject of sipping water (ācamana) is also stated; therein Gautama says: "One who has a substance in hand, having become impure through contact with something that makes one ritually unclean (ucchiṣṭa), should set it down and sip water. The meaning of this is: if, while engaged in such activities as feeding Brāhmaṇas, one who has a substance in hand somehow becomes impure through touching something that makes one ritually unclean, then he should set that substance on the ground and sip water. Here, "substance" (dravya) refers to food intended for consumption. And so Vasiṣṭha says:
"If, while dealing with foods intended for consumption, he should touch something that makes him ritually unclean..."
Having wiped that object on the ground and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should proceed once more.
"While moving among the foods and drinks" means while serving them; Bṛhaspati also says:
"If, while moving among the foods and drinks, one should touch anything that is leavings, he should set that object down on the ground, rinse his mouth, and then proceed again."

Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state a specific rule: "One who has something in hand and becomes impure (ucchiṣṭa) should set it down, perform *ācamana*, and then sprinkle that object with water. Thus, it should be understood that for one with an object in hand, purification occurs through *ācamana*, while for the object itself, it occurs through setting it down and sprinkling it with water. However, when the object itself is directly touched by what is impure, then it must simply be discarded. As Vasiṣṭha says: "The food of one who is not a guru, when he himself is impure or when it is defiled by what is impure, is not to be eaten. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu:
If one who holds a substance in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled by food remnants,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that substance down.

This refers to objects such as clothing that are not intended for consumption, because in other cases the rule for setting them aside is prescribed. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya states the following alternative:

"If one whose hands hold an object is touched by something defiled, he should set the object down, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), sprinkle the object with water, and then take it up again."
Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"If a twice-born man becomes defiled by food remnants while holding a metallic vessel,
he should set that vessel down on the ground, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and then sprinkle it with water."
If one has taken up some food here and becomes possessed of a remnant,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) even without setting that substance down.
There may be doubt regarding garments and such; for it is exactly the same when they have been touched.

*Tat-sparśau* means touched by one who is impure (*ucchiṣṭa*). The meaning is that it should be either set down or not set down. Regarding inedible items, Bodhāyana also says: "If, having taken a metallic object, one becomes impure, he should discard it, sip water, and before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water; but if he becomes impure while holding food, he should discard it, sip water, and before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water. This very same procedure is reversed for a vessel. *Udasya* means having set down; *viparītam* means not discarding it. Regarding the voiding of urine and so forth after taking cooked food, the verse stated by Āpastamba should be consulted.
"Having placed that object on the ground and performed purification according to the rule,
one becomes pure after sipping water while holding cooked food in one's lap.
This refers to a situation of distress involving an object that cannot be buried.
In a forest, in a waterless place, at night, or on a path infested with thieves and tigers,
one who carries an object in hand does not incur fault when voiding urine or excrement.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Bṛhaspati. But Mārkaṇḍeya states that even purification should be performed without setting [the food] aside:
"He who voids urine or excrement while holding cooked food, having placed that substance upon his body without setting it down..."
Having performed purification according to the rule and having sipped water according to the prescribed rite,
one should sprinkle the food and, having lifted it up, show it to the sun.
"Or, having discarded even the tip of that [tooth-stick], one attains purity through the remainder.
Thus ends the section on sipping water (*ācamana*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the procedure for cleaning the teeth (*dantadhāvana*).
On this point, Śātātapa says:
"If the tooth-stick remains in the mouth overnight, a man is perpetually impure;
therefore, one should consume the tooth-stick with every possible effort."
Kātyāyana also says:
Having risen, washed his eyes, become pure, and composed himself,
he should recite the mantra and then chew the tooth-stick.
The mantra also says:
"O Lord of the Forest, grant us longevity, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence."
Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya states the rule for the time:
"Having risen in the morning, one should, with speech restrained, consume the tooth-cleansing stick;
having first washed it, one should consume it, and having washed it again, one should discard it."
"In a clean place"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. And thus Vyāsa says:
"Having washed it, one should discard the tooth-stick in a clean place;
when it has fallen properly facing oneself, one obtains the desired food. [277] Thus.
Regarding this, Viṣṇu states:

"Having washed [the hands] and eaten, one should discard that [leavings]; one should not eat it on the day of the new moon (indukṣaya). The term "day of the new moon" (indukṣaya) refers to the amāvāsyā; it is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for prohibited lunar days and so forth. For this very reason, Yama says:
On the fourteenth, the eighth, the new moon, the full moon, and during the sun's transit,
one should avoid oil, meat, women, and the tooth-stick.
"One should avoid cleaning the teeth during a *śrāddha*, on one's birthday, at a wedding, when suffering from indigestion, upon the death of a relative, and while fasting. Thus says Viṣṇu as well.
One should avoid using a tooth-stick on the first lunar day, the new moon, the sixth, the fourteenth, the eighth, the ninth, and on Sundays.
Paiṭhīnasi also says: "O Bhārata, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, on the new moon, on the sixth, and likewise on the ninth,
the contact of a wooden stick with the teeth burns the family unto the seventh generation."
Vyāsa also says:
"At a Śrāddha, at a sacrifice, during a religious observance, when the husband has gone abroad,
on a weekday, on a Pāta, on a Saṃkrānti, and on the Nandā, Bhūta, and Aṣṭa parvans."

"One should avoid oil massage, sexual intercourse, meat, and the tooth-stick. Thus [it is said]. On the day of the Sun (Sunday), Mārkaṇḍeya states the rule regarding the direction: "Facing north or facing east, one should [use] a decoction that is bitter or pungent."
[278] The ellipsis is to be supplied as "one should chew the tooth-stick. "Facing north" means facing either north or east, because a fault is heard of in this regard. Thus Kātyāyana says:
"Facing the east, one should find fortitude and indeed bodily health;
likewise, by facing south, cruelty; and by facing west, defeat."
To the north, there is the destruction of cattle, women, and attendants;
however, in the northeastern direction, one shall obtain all desires.
Regarding this, Viṣṇu states the characteristics of the wooden stick:
"It should be made from thorny or milky trees, measuring twelve finger-breadths in length,
as thick as the tip of the little finger, with a brush-like tuft fashioned at its upper half."
The cleaning of the teeth has been described, as well as the tongue-scraper;
for one with very fine teeth it should be very fine, and for one with even teeth it should be of medium size.
For one with uneven teeth, the tooth-cleansing twig is coarse; thus, there are three types of tooth-cleansing twigs.
The wise have declared that for a Brahmin the wood should be twelve finger-breadths long;
for those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, it should be nine, six, and four finger-breadths respectively.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa as well:
"The tooth-stick should have a thickness equal to the middle finger and measure twelve fingers in length;
it should be provided with a brush-like tip, and one should clean the teeth with its end."
Garga also says: "For Brahmins it should be ten finger-breadths; for Kṣatriyas, nine finger-breadths;
for Vaiśyas, eight finger-breadths; and for Śūdras, it is measured at seven."
For women, however, it measures four finger-breadths; of this there is no doubt.
Vyāsa also says:
One should always avoid those tooth-sticks that are forbidden;
one should use those prescribed by the scriptures, and one should also avoid them on the sacred festival days (parvan).
In response to the inquiry as to which [trees] are seen in the scriptures, Aṅgiras says:
"Having risen in the morning, one should, with speech restrained, chew the tooth-stick of the āmra, punnāga, bilva, apāmārga, or śirīṣa."
Nārada also says:
"All thorny trees are meritorious, and those that yield milky sap are illustrious.
Vṛddha-Manu also says:
Of khadira, karañja, and likewise kadamba;
of arka, karavīra, and especially of kuṭaja.
Viṣṇu also says: "One of these: the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *arka*, *khadira*, *karañjaka*, *karavīra*, *jāti*, *apāmārga*, *mālatī*, *kakubha*, or *bilva*. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"One should consume the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *arka*, *khadira*, and *karavīra*;
as well as *jāti*, *bilva*, *khadira*, and the root of the *kakubha*."
"Arimeda, priyaṅgu, and likewise kaṇṭakini.
Regarding these, Garga stated the results:
"In the case of the *sarja* tree there is dignity; in the *vaṭa*, radiance; in the *karṇaja*, victory in battle."
In the Plakṣa tree there is the attainment of wealth, and in the Vadari tree, a sweet voice.
In the *khadira* there is fragrance; in the *bilva*, abundant wealth;
in the *audumbara*, success in speech; and in the *bandhūka*, firm sacred learning.
From the *saighra* tree one quickly gains fame and good fortune; from the *pālāśa*, supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*);
from the *kadamba*, all forms of prosperity (*lakṣmī*); and from the *āmra*, health itself.
Through Apāmārga, steadfastness, intelligence, wisdom, power, physical form, sacred learning,
longevity, good character, fame, fortune, and good luck are produced.
One should treat dental diseases with *arka*, and pain with *bījapūra*;
likewise, by means of *kakubha*, one becomes long-lived and free from graying hair.
"It destroys bad dreams when [one uses] pomegranate, *sindhuvāra*, *karañja*, *kuṭaja*, as well as *jāti* and *karamarda*.
Thus it is said: "One should avoid those things that are to be avoided. Mārkaṇḍeya states them as follows:

One should avoid the *śālmali*, *aśvattha*, *havya*, *dhava*, and *kiṃśuka* trees; likewise, one should avoid the *kovidāra*, *śamī*, *pīlu*, *śleṣmātaka*, and *vibhītaka* for tooth-sticks, as well as *guggulu* and *kramuka*.

Hārīta also says: "One should avoid the *kāleya*, *pālāśa*, *kovidāra*, *śleṣmātaka*, *bilvaka*, thorny trees, *nirguṇḍī*, *śikhaṇḍī*, *śirīṣa*, *pamālatī*, *karavīra*, *badarī*, *karañja*, and bamboo. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:

"One should reject leaves that are unknown, those that have dried at the tip, those that are split, those lacking bark, and those covered in knots; likewise, one should avoid the *pālāśa* and *śiṃśupā* leaves."
Uśanas also says: "The *tinduka*,
*iṅguda*, *bandhūka*, *moca*, *āmra*, *java*, *balvaja*, cotton,
and the tooth-stick— these would take away even the fortune of Viṣṇu."
Garga also says:
"He who eats *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *pālāśa*,
or *śiṃśupā* grass becomes an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*) for as long as he does not see a cow."

Regarding some of these, an option should be understood to exist through both injunction and prohibition. On this point, Uśanas states: "One should not have tooth-sticks split, nor should one cleanse the teeth with the fingers. This refers to cases other than the ring finger and the thumb. As Vṛddhayājñavalkya says: "With bricks, clods of earth, or stones, as well as with the other fingers—excluding the ring finger and the thumb—one should avoid using them for cleaning the teeth."
A specific detail regarding this is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:

"One should not uproot a tooth-stick, nor should one brush the teeth with the tips of the fingers. And thus, there is no contradiction with what was stated by Paiṭhīnasi: "One should brush the teeth with grass, leaves, water, or even with a finger, excluding the index finger" [282]; for here, the mention of the index finger is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all prohibited fingers. Regarding the settled rule (*vyavasthā*) in this matter, Vyāsa says:

On the first lunar day, the new moon, the sixth, and the ninth, one should clean the teeth with leaves; on other days, however, one may use wood, but the scraping of the tongue should always be done with leaves.
"In the absence of tooth-sticks, or on a prohibited lunar day,
one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with twelve mouthfuls of water.
As for that which was stated by the same author:
If one, out of delusion, should chew a tooth-stick at the time of bathing,
the deities, together with the ancestors, depart from there disappointed.
This refers to the midday bath,
because of the traditional teaching of Dakṣa: "One should perform the morning bath preceded by the cleaning of the teeth."
Thus ends the rule for cleaning the teeth in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the majesty of *kuśa* grass;
on this point, Gobhila says:
Brahmā resides at the root of the kuśa grass, Keśava in the middle of the kuśa, and one should know Śaṅkara to be at the tip of the kuśa; all the gods are present everywhere around it.
Hārīta also says:
"Whatever recitation is performed with kusha grass in hand, whatever gift is given along with kusha grass,
and he who eats while having kusha grass in his hand— for him, there is no limit to the merit."
Also in the Purāṇa:
