"Bathing with *kuśa* grass becomes purified; one should sip water using *kuśa*;
water drawn up with *kuśa* is equal to the drinking of Soma."
But he who always wears a garland of *kuśa* grass around his neck is not defiled by sin, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
He who wears the sacred grass (pavitra) on his hand, his neck, his crest-lock, and on both his ears, is not defiled by sin.
Kauśika also said:
"The kuśa-grass seat is always pure, especially for ascetics;
for one seated upon a kuśa-grass seat, the highest yoga is accomplished."
Also in the Purāṇa:
"Just as no stain is found upon the lotus leaves of water,
so no stain is found anywhere on one who holds the *pavitra* in his hand."
Hārīta also says:
"For these asuras in manifest form, who steal one's recitation and burnt offerings,
flee in the ten directions from one whose hands have been purified by the *pavitraka*."
Gobhila also says:
"Just as the thunderbolt belongs to the Lord of the Gods, the trident to Hara,
and the discus-weapon to Viṣṇu, so too does the *kuśa* grass belong in the hand of a Brahmin."
Thus ends the greatness of the *kuśa* grass;
[284] the ritual for uprooting the *kuśa* grass.
In that regard, Kauśika says:
Having become pure and standing in a clean place, facing either the east or the north,
the best of the twice-born should touch the *kuśa* grass with the mantra consisting of the syllable *Oṃ* alone.
The mantra for uprooting is also:
"O Darbha, born together with Viriñci, produced from the emission of Parameṣṭhin, dispel all my sins and grant me well-being."
Regarding this, Hārīta states the rule for the time:
"In the month of Nabhasya, on the new moon day, the gathering of darbha grass is prescribed;
those darbha blades, being of undiminished potency, may be employed again and again."
*Nabhāḥ* is Śrāvaṇa. For this very reason, they are called *yātayāma*, meaning that they have been cut at another time. With this same intention, Śaṅkha also says:
"Darbha grass, the black antelope skin, the mantras, and especially the Brāhmaṇas—all these are *ayātayāma* and may be employed again and again."
The meaning is that they are fit for repeated application. For this very reason, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"One should perform the act of sipping water (ācamana) with the hand holding a purifier (pavitra);
however, that purifier does not become defiled by the [sipping] residue, but one should avoid [using] what has been defiled by the residue of food."
"This [pavitra] consists primarily of darbha grass free from knots;
one should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with a pavitra that has a knot," according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Hārīta. On this point, Śātātapa says:
During recitation, burnt offerings, giving, Vedic study, and the libations to the ancestors,
one should ensure that the hand is never empty, using gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass.
Mārkaṇḍeya also said:
A Brāhmaṇa who is free from hypocrisy should always carry Kuśa grass in his hand;
he constantly destroys his sins just as fire consumes a heap of cotton.
Also in the Purāṇa:
"One should always wear a silken thread as a purifier on the right hand;
especially while eating, it serves as a purifier of forbidden food."
Atri also says:
"The darbha-strainers, provided with the *brahmagranthi* knot, should be held with effort by the Brahmins using both hands."
"In the *brahmayajña* and in silent recitation (*japa*), the *brahmagranthi* (the sacred knot) is prescribed;
at the time of eating, it is said to be circular; thus the dharma is not lost.
Regarding this, the rule for the fingers is shown in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
The *darbha* grass should be held with the ring finger, or with both the thumb and the ring finger;
however, the two *darbha* strainers (*pavitra*) should be held with both ring fingers.
The ring finger (*anāmikā*) and the next-to-the-pinky finger (*upakaniṣṭhikā*). The characteristics of the *pavitra* (sacred thread) are also stated therein:
"Having abandoned the Vaiṣṇava path and issued forth from the Brahma-path, having circumambulated once, it is designated as the *pavitra*."
One should prepare a Brāhmaṇical purifier with seven tufts of Darbha grass;
for a Kṣatriya, it should be made with five, and likewise for a Vaiśya, with four.
[286] For a Śūdra and likewise for those of intermediate castes, it is ordained by two [stalks].
Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"The purifier (pavitraka) of a Brāhmaṇa consists of four bunches of Darbha grass."
It is taught that there is a reduction of one in each successive caste, in due order.
"One performing the *śāntika* rite should make the *pavitraka* with three *darbha* blades, likewise the *pauṣṭika* with five,
and that called *ābhicāra* with four.
Regarding the *sthālīpāka* and other such rites, however, one should consult what was stated by Kātyāyana.
"Free from internal knots, with a tip, made of kuśa grass, consisting of two blades,
and measuring a span (prādeśa) in length— this is to be known as the *pavitra* wherever it may be used. Thus says Kauśika, concerning the *govāla-pavitra*.
By constantly wearing the hair-strainer of cows,
sins do not touch him, and prosperity dwells upon his limbs.
Whoever performs the fire-ritual using the hair-strainer of cows has,
without a doubt, offered oblations into the five fires for as long as he lives.
"He who performs the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti) with a hair-strainer made of cow-hair, that man indeed becomes one who has performed the twilight worship for twelve years.
Thus it is said; likewise, the characteristics of the *darbha* grass have also been stated by that same author:
Auspicious darbha grass with seven blades, grown in marshy fields or near the ocean,
is recommended for the twice-born in rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors.

Darbha grasses are known as *aprasūtāḥ* (unproduced), while kuśa grasses are known as *prasūtāḥ* (produced). Those with roots are called *kutapāḥ*, those with tips are called *sāgāḥ*, and those with cut-off tips are designated as *tṛṇa*.
Hārīta also says:

A twice-born man should collect auspicious *kuśa* grass that has uncut tips, is accompanied by leaves, possesses roots, and is tender, for the sake of rites for the ancestors, the gods, and the recitation of prayers (*japa*).
This refers to cases other than those involving the *prastara* (sacrificial grass-bundle) and so forth. Accordingly, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states:
"The finest *kuśa* grasses for the purpose of the *prastara* should be taken with their roots severed;
however, in the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and in sacrifice (*yāga*), one should avoid [grass] that has its roots intact."
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the distinction: "Green *darbha* grasses with white tips are for the *pākayajña*;
those with roots are for the ancestors; and those that are speckled are for the Viśvedevas."
"Pitrya" means those whose deity is the ancestors (*pitṛ*). And so says Yama:
"In the ancestral *śrāddha* rite, the *darbha* grass should have its roots;
by means of the root, one conquers the worlds of the high-souled Śakra."
This refers to the subject of the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha, for he himself has said:
"In the *ekoddiṣṭa*, the *kuśa* grass should be used with their roots in the śrāddha rite;
[grass] cut externally and cut once is to be used everywhere in rites for the ancestors."
"Cut at the outside" means cut near the base. Thus, as it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Kuśa grass for the purpose of a *śrāddha* is traditionally prescribed as being cut near the base;
likewise, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, and *dūrvā* grass are also declared [to be used]."

Thus, as for Gobhila’s statement: “In rites for the ancestors, [the grass] is cut near the roots” [288], it should be understood that this refers to matters other than the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha. On this point, a Purāṇa states:
“Until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the ancestral rites are performed with single blades of darbha grass;
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, they should be performed according to rule with double-bladed [grass].”
One should perform the libation for the ancestors with effort using *darbha* grass grown in a sesame field that has been doubled in length; however, for the gods, it may be done at will.

"One who desires prosperity should perform ancestral rites with the root [part] of the *kuśa* grass, bathing and giving gifts with the middle, and divine rites with the tip of the *kuśa*. This means that even by chance— that is, without a fixed rule— if the aforementioned *kuśa* grass is unavailable, Śaṅkha says:"

"In the absence of *kuśa* grass, O best of the twice-born, one should diligently perform the rites of libation (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth with *kāśa* grass; *kāśa* is traditionally held to be equal to *kusa*. Thus [says the law]. Viṣṇu also states: "In the absence of *kuśa*, one should employ *kāśa* or *dūrvā* in place of *kuśa*. However, regarding the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), there is a specific rule stated by Yama:
Kuśa grass, kāśa grass, as well as dūrvā, barley, rice, balvaja grass,
and white lotuses— these are said to be the sevenfold sacrificial grass (barhis).

Regarding this, Hārīta states those [types of kuśa] that are to be avoided: "One should avoid these six kinds of kuśa grass: those on a path, those on a funeral pyre, those on sacrificial grounds, and those used for spreading, as seats, or for piṇḍas."
Those darbha grasses used in the Brahma-sacrifice and those darbha grasses used for the libations to the ancestors,
if they have been defiled by urine or feces, their disposal is prescribed.
[289] One should carefully avoid *darbha* grass that is impure, contemptible, or has been cut by fingernails;
likewise, one should avoid *kuśa* grass that has been boiled or scorched by fire.

"One should know that those *darbha* blades which are placed within the *nīvī* and those which are made into the *brahmasūtra* are purifiers; as is *kāśa*, so too is *kuśa*. Thus [it is said]. "Boiled" means damaged.
Thus concludes the procedure for the uprooting of *kuśa* grass in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the praise of bathing; herein, Yogayājñavalkya says:
By performing the ritual bath, one is liberated from the sins of approaching those who should not be approached, from theft, from accepting gifts from the wicked, and from sins committed in secret.
This bath generates clarity of mind, increases beauty and good fortune,
destroys grief and evil dreams, and likewise bestows liberation as well as knowledge.
All rites for human beings prescribed in the Śruti and Smṛti have bathing as their foundation;
therefore, one should practice bathing, which increases prosperity, nourishment, and health.
Indeed, one who bathes daily does not behold the agonizing suffering of Yama;
even those people who are doers of evil are purified by daily bathing.

For the virtuous person devoted to ritual bathing, there are ten qualities: beauty, splendor, strength, purity, long life, health, freedom from greed, the destruction of evil dreams, austerity, and intelligence.
Satyavrata also says:
"By bathing properly, a person attains strength, beauty, fame, righteousness, knowledge, long life, happiness, fortitude, and supreme health."
Thus ends the praise of bathing in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the classifications of bathing; regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
Bathing is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as secondary and primary;
of these two, the Vāruṇa (water-bath) is the primary, and that, moreover, is of six types.
"The daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the optional (kāmya), that which is an auxiliary to ritual acts (kriyāṅga), that which removes impurities (malakarṣaṇa),
and likewise the sixth, the ritual bath (kriyāsnāna)— thus is the great bath (proḍhā-snāna) proclaimed.
He himself states the definition of these:
A man who has not bathed is unfit for the recitation of prayers, the offering into the sacred fire, and other such rites;
therefore, the morning bath is proclaimed as the obligatory daily bath (*nityasnāna*).
Having touched a Caṇḍāla, a corpse, smoke, or the like, or having touched a menstruating woman who has not yet bathed,
when one who is otherwise fit for bathing does bathe, that is indeed an occasional (naimittika) bath.
Whatever rites such as the Puṣya-bath are enjoined by the rules of the astrologers, that is indeed designated as optional (kāmya); one should not perform it without a specific desire.
An astrologer is one who knows the luminaries. He who, desiring prosperity and wishing to purify the deities and ancestors,
performs a ritual bath, that is proclaimed as the bath that is an integral part of the rite.
The bath preceded by anointing with oil is called "the removal of impurity";
its purpose is indeed the removal of impurity, and not otherwise.
In lakes, in natural pools, at sacred fords, and in rivers, the ritual bath is prescribed;
in those cases, the ritual itself is considered the bath.

The meaning is that bathing alone is prescribed there as a constituent part of the ritual action (*kriyāṅga*). Gobhila also says: "That which is performed constantly is *nitya*; that which is beneficial for a desired object is *kāmya*; and that which arises from a specific occasion (*nimitta*) is remembered as *naimittika*."
By this, the obligatory nature of the midday bath (*mādhyandina-snāna*) is also stated, since that too must be performed continuously. And so says Vaiyāghrapāda:
"One should always be a morning bather; one should be a midday bather.
Thus ends the section on the various types of baths in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the daily bath (*nityasnāna*), which has reached its proper occasion, is described; regarding this, Śaunaka says:
"Having performed the morning sipping of water (*ācamana*) and having performed purification (*śauca*) according to the rules, the knower of the truth..."

"Then, having performed the cleansing of the teeth, one should perform the morning bath. Here, the phrase "having performed the *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water)" is connected to the cleansing of the teeth as well. Thus, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
"Having washed the tooth-stick and having used it according to the prescribed rule..."
"Having sipped water (ācamana) and being purified, one should always perform the morning bath. On this point, Dakṣa says:
"Without having bathed, one should not perform any rite whatsoever, such as recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and so forth."
Covered with saliva and sweat, the man rises from his bed.
The body is utterly impure, endowed with nine openings;
it constantly flows [with secretions] by day and by night. Morning bathing is the means of purification.
They praise the morning bath as beneficial, producing both visible and invisible results.
One who bathes in the morning, being pure in soul, is worthy of performing all [rites] such as the recitation of mantras (japa).
Kātyāyana also says:
"Just as during the day, so too in the morning, one should always bathe without sloth;
having rinsed his teeth in a river or similar body of water, or indeed at home, that [rinsing] is performed without mantras."
The phrase "as if [there were] no mantra" does not intend a total prohibition of mantras; rather, it is for the purpose of prohibiting a multiplicity of mantras. For he himself has said:
"Because the time for the oblation is short and the ritual of bathing is extensive, one should perform the morning bath in brief; the omission of the oblation is censured."
Likewise, bathing is described in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"One should perform the bath with mantras addressed to the Waters (*abdaivata*) and those belonging to Varuṇa, together with earth;
or else with the *vyāhṛtis*, or even with any verse (*ṛc*) whatsoever."
"One should bathe [saying] 'From Drupada' or 'To Jumbuka,' and one should remember sacred fords; thus spoke the sage Uśanas."
Regarding the rule for this time, Jābāli says:
"Having always risen early in the morning and having first brushed his teeth,
he should perform his bath at dawn and offer libations to the gods and humans."

Viṣṇu also states: [293] "One who bathes at dawn should bathe after observing the eastern quarter seized by the rays of the sun. As for that which is stated in the Caturviṃśati: "The bath performed at every dawn, whether at the twilight or after the sun has risen, is equal to the Prājāpatya penance and destroys all sins."

Thus, that [statement] is also identical in meaning to the one from Viṣṇu. That which is the bath at *saṃdhyā* is also at dawn (*uṣas*), or else when the sun has risen, facing the rising [sun]; for that too belongs to the time of dawn. And this is appropriate; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such texts as, "The morning *saṃdhyā* while the stars are still visible," since one who has not bathed is not entitled to perform the *saṃdhyā* and other rites. As Viṣṇu says:
"One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors, as well as for the recitation of purifiers (*pavitra*) and for giving as enjoined by rule."
Dakṣa also says:
"All ritual acts and even the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) have bathing as their foundation;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the bath with a concentrated mind."

If this is so, then by the force of this very statement, the twilight [ritual] (*saṃdhyā*) itself should be postponed. Not so; for there is a traditional prohibition stated by Yogayājñavalkya: "One should perform the twilight ritual at the junction [of day and night], but not when the sun has set or when it has risen. Furthermore:
The two nāḍīs of the final watch of the night are said to be the time beginning with the twilight;
its end is recorded by the sages as being from the sight of the sun’s first streak.

[295] Thus, because of the restriction of time by Dakṣa, the meaning is that the time characterized by the appearance of the sun's rays is the end of the twilight (saṃdhyā). Therefore, the previously stated explanation alone is superior. On this point, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states:
"Bathing is said to be of three kinds: obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya);
however, the libation (tarpaṇa) is proclaimed to be an ancillary part (aṅga) of that."

Therefore, the intended meaning is that one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) immediately after bathing. As for the statement in the *Caturviṃśatimata*, "Immediately after bathing, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the deities," Yama states a specific qualification regarding that.
"Having joined the two hands together, one should fill them with a handful of water;
having drawn up water to the height of a cow's horn, one should pour it into the midst of the water.
As for that which was stated by Vyāghra:
Now, he who offers water with both hands goes to the Kālasūtra hell, headlong, as a fool.
Thus, this refers to the context of a *śrāddha* ceremony. And so says Kārṣṇājini:
"At a *śrāddha* and at the time of a wedding, [the gift] is given with one hand;
but in the libation (*tarpaṇa*), it must be done with both hands—this is the eternal rule."
Concerning the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), that same author says:
"Standing in water reaching up to the navel, with his mind directed upwards and reflecting, [he should say]:
'May my ancestors come; may they accept these handfuls of water.'"
"Standing before the ancestors who reside in the sky, facing south, the wise man should offer three handfuls of water, each higher than the last. Thus it is said.
A specific detail regarding this is shown in another Smṛti:
"Having filled his arms with sesame seeds, one should satisfy the ancestors while standing in water;
one who desires the satisfaction of the ancestors must not perform [the rite] while standing on dry land.
And thus it was said by Gobhila:
If one makes sesame seeds into the shape of body hair and offers libations to the ancestors,
the ancestors are thereby gratified with blood and filth.

Thus, it should be understood that this refers specifically to the occasion of libations performed on dry land (*sthalatarpaṇa*). But how can there be libations to the ancestors here, given the traditional teaching of Jābāli, "One should offer libations to gods and humans," and the Vedic revelation, "The afternoon belongs to the ancestors"? Would it not follow, then, that there should be no libation to the gods during the midday bath? It should not be argued that this is acceptable, for it is said:
"And at every bath, one should indeed offer libations to the ancestors and deities;
one should especially perform that with diligence during both optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites."

Thus, because of the recollection [of this rule] by Vyāghra. In this context, it should be understood that the two scriptural citations refer to matters other than the *tarpaṇa* (libation). Furthermore, Vasiṣṭha has shown the fault incurred even by its non-performance: "If one, out of a nihilistic disposition, does not offer libations to the ancestors after bathing, his ancestors, seeking water, drink the discharge from his own body."
The outflow from the body is blood. Bhāradvāja said: "Those who belong to the group of ten who have died require water for their clothes;
therefore, with every effort, one should pour water upon the ground. Thus it is said.
The meaning is that having emerged [from the water], one should remain there for a short time; thereafter, one should wring out the bathing garment. And so says Pulastya:
"Having thus performed the libations (tarpaṇa) and emerged from the body of water, the wise man should wring out his bathing cloth right there on the bank."
The son of Kṛṣṇāñjanī also [should do so].
Then, having wrung out the bathing garment, he should perform the *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) again, [reciting]:
"Whatever members of our lineage who have died childless, though belonging to our clan..."
"May those who accept this water squeezed from my garment that I have offered.
This is the mantra for the water squeezed from the garment. Regarding this, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states:
"Having bathed in this manner, and thereafter having sipped water (ācamana) again according to the rules..."
Having risen and put on two clean, pure white garments, indeed.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "he should sip water twice. And thus Vyāghra says:
"Then, having taken two clean garments, he should touch [them] twice.
Regarding this, Vyāsa states a specific detail:
A wise man should never wear his upper garment below, nor his lower garment above; he should never dwell in a garment without an inner undergarment.
"One should not apply ointment without having bathed, nor should one wring out one's garment after bathing;
rather, a person, having bathed, should wear their clothes while they are still damp.
(297) Thereafter, one should cleanse the shanks with earth and water. Regarding this, Jābāla says:

"Having bathed and discarded [the upper] garment, the two shanks are to be purified with earth and water, for they have been rendered impure by the water flowing from the privities of the loincloth. Because the phrase "rendered impure" is stated as a reason, the mention of the "shanks" is intended to indicate any part of the body that has become impure. For this very reason, Yogayājñavalkya says:
"Having bathed in this manner and put on two clean, unwashed garments,
one should wash the thighs with earth and water, and then wash the hands.
Regarding this, the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states:
One who has bathed should not wipe his limbs with a cloth or his hands;
he should not shake out his hair, nor should he shake out his garment.
Regarding this, Gobhila states the reason:
"The gods drink from the head; the ancestors drink from the mouth;
all the gandharvas [drink] from the middle; and all living beings [drink] from below."
Therefore, having bathed, one should not wipe oneself with the bathing cloth nor with the hand.
Vyāsa also says:
"As many as there are hairs on the body—three and a half crores—all sacred fords flow through them; therefore, one should not wipe [the body]."
On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:
"Three applications of earth should not be given to the bathing cloth for the sake of purification;
having emerged from the water and wrung it out, one should then complete the remainder of the rite."
Dakṣa states the fruit for one who acts in this way:
"The Brahmin who, having risen in the morning, always bathes in the morning,
dispels the sin committed in seven lifetimes within three years."
Śaunaka also says: "The Brahmin who, having risen in the morning, always performs the morning bath, is liberated from all sins and attains the supreme Brahman. Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the section on the procedure for the morning bath in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now, some other statements concerning clothing are also recorded;
regarding this, Bhṛgu says:

"A Brāhmaṇa’s garment is white; that of a king (Kṣatriya) is intensely red; that of a Vaiśya is yellow; and for a Śūdra, blue is prescribed as being soiled. Here, "intensely" (*ulbaṇa*) means thick or dense. "Red" refers to [red] dyed with mineral pigments, because Uśanas records a prohibition against garments dyed with ochre (*kāṣāya*): "One should not perform rites for the gods or ancestors wearing [garments] with visible veins or those dyed with ochre."

"It is established that what is unwashed and dyed with mineral color (dhātu-rakta) is pure," because of this recollection of its sanctification. With this very intention, Gautama also said: "One should not wear clothing that is dyed, gaudy, or previously worn by another. Pulastya states the definition of the unwashed [garment]:
"That which is slightly washed, new, white, with its fringes intact, and which has not been worn."
"One should know that to be unsoiled (*ahata*), which is purifying for all ritual acts.
Thus [it is said]. "Washed" (*dhauta*) means cleansed. Regarding this, Devala states a specific rule:
"A wise person should perform religious rites with cloth washed by himself."

"But never with one washed by a washerman, nor ever with an *ahata* [unbeaten] cloth. Here, "unwashed" refers to the *ahata* cloth, because the word *ahata* is used in that context as well. As stated by Satyatapas:
"The Self-Existent One declared that a cloth released from the loom is *ahata*."
"That is recommended for auspicious occasions, but not at all times. Here, "auspicious occasion" refers to weddings and the like. On this point, there is a Purāṇa:
"O Lord of Men, the garment for sleeping should indeed be quite different [from that worn during other times]."
For one thing indeed is [the conduct] on the streets of the gods, another in worship,
another in the affairs of worldly life, and yet another in the vision of the Lord.
Bodhāyana also says:
"An upper garment must be worn during these five activities:
during Vedic study, the voiding of excrement, giving gifts, as well as after eating and when sipping water."
"Utsarga" refers to the voiding of urine and so forth; "bhukta" refers to eating. This is intended as an illustration for all prescribed actions:
one who has not tucked up his garment, one who lacks an upper cloth, one who is naked, and indeed one who is unclothed—such a naked person should not even contemplate the Śrauta or Smārta rites.
Thus, because there is a prohibition against merely performing actions while wearing only the upper garment (*anuttarīya*). Yājñavalkya also states:
"A twice-born man should not perform bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, Vedic study, libations to the ancestors, nor the rites of eating at a *śrāddha*, while wearing only one garment."

In the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well: "A twice-born man should not engage in rites such as fire-offerings and the worship of deities, nor in recitation, sipping water, or silent prayer while wearing only a single garment."
Gobhila also says:

"A man wearing only a single garment should not eat, nor should he perform the worship of the deities, nor should he honor the twice-born, nor should he make offerings in the fire; such is the rule for a man in this state."
He (the same author) states the definition of one who wears a single garment:

"One whose cloth is held at the waist, having slipped slightly from the left side—know him to be 'single-garmented' (ekavastra); he should be avoided in rites for the gods and the ancestors. Thus it is said.

He is so described because his garment, which was held at the waist, has slipped from the root of his left arm. This should be understood to apply equally to one who is deprived of the second garment (*dvitīyavāsa*), for there is a traditional prohibition against such a person [performing rites], stating: "one who is without a girdle (*vikakṣa*) and without an upper garment (*anuttarīya*). Regarding the putting on of the garment here, Pāraskara has shown the mantra:
"I shall put it on; I shall bestow glory. For long life, may I reach old age.
May I live a hundred abundant autumns, and I shall clothe myself in the attainment of wealth."
And likewise in the case of the upper garment: "May Heaven and Earth grant me glory; may Indra and Bṛhaspati grant me glory; may Bhaga bestow glory upon me; may glory come to me. Thus it is said.

And these two mantras refer to clothing that has not been worn previously, because it was stated by that same [author]: "If the garment, umbrella, and shoes are new, there is a mantra. Regarding this, Bhṛgu states what should be avoided:
"A wise man should avoid clothing that is red, gaudy, or blue;
he should also avoid cloth that is less than ten days old or stained with dirt."
Jātūkarṇa also says: "They know that, according to the Dharma, ochre-colored cloth, black cloth, or soiled cloth defiled by hair, as well as a lower garment with frayed edges, is contemptible."
Bhṛgu also says: One who wears soiled garments is considered naked; one with a wet garment is likewise considered naked;
one whose garment is burnt is naked; and one whose garment is sewn together is also naked.
"With his hair-locks untied, without an upper garment, naked, and indeed without clothes—one who is naked should not even contemplate the ritual acts prescribed by the Śruti or the Smṛti.
By performing them out of delusion, he would go downwards; that act would become one performed by an Asura. Thus it is said.

And this prohibition against wearing soiled garments and the like should be understood to apply when one has the means. As Gautama says: "If one possesses wealth, one should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states the secondary alternative:
"In the absence of washed cloth, [one may use] those made of hemp, linen, or wool;
or a kutapa blanket or a yoga-cloth; even then, one should certainly not be double-clad."
A *kutapa* is a woolen blanket made from the hair of mountain goats. Furthermore, it is stated in another Smṛti:

"Two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) should be worn during rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti; a third is intended for use as an upper garment (*uttarīya*), and that is desired when no other cloth is available. [302]

Jātūkarṇa states the characteristics of the upper garment (*uttarīya*): "In the absence of a cloth for an upper garment, one should make an upper garment out of urine [as a substitute], circular in shape like a cloth, measuring two, three, or four finger-breadths. Thus ends the section on clothing in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the procedure for the vertical sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*).
In this *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, the Blessed One said to Brahmā:
"I shall declare the measurements of the vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), the substances according to the divisions of finger-widths, the colors, the specific mantras, and their respective fruits."
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, especially in my sacred field,
on the shore of the ocean, at an anthill, or at the base of a *tulasī* tree.
These types of clay should be collected, while other kinds of clay must be avoided;
dark clay is said to bring about pacification (śānti), and red clay brings about subjugation (vaśya).
They say that yellow brings prosperity, while white is said to belong to Viṣṇu;
the thumb is declared to bestow nourishment, and the middle finger brings long life.
The ring finger always bestows food, and the index finger bestows liberation;
one should perform [the ritual] with these specific fingers, but one must not touch [the vessel] with the fingernails.
It may also have the form of a wick-lamp, or likewise the shape of a bamboo leaf,
as well as the form of a lotus bud and that of a water lily.
Alternatively, it may have the shape of a fish or a tortoise, or even the form of a conch shell;
if it measures ten finger-breadths, it is called the most excellent of the excellent.
The middle *puṇḍra* should be nine finger-breadths; beyond that, it may be eight finger-breadths.
The middle *puṇḍra* is traditionally remembered as being of three types: seven, six, or five [finger-breadths].
The three types of sectarian marks (puṇḍra) may measure four, three, or two finger-breadths;
one should know Keśava on the forehead and Nārāyaṇa on the abdomen.
Placing Mādhava in the heart and Govinda in the hollow of the throat,
Viṣṇu is said to be in the belly and on the right side.
One should meditate on Madhusūdana at the side of that [arm], in the middle of the arm;
on Trivikrama in the region of the throat; and on Vāmana in the left belly.
One should remember Śrīdhara on the left arm, Hṛṣīkeśa on the neck, Padmanābha on the back, and Dāmodara on the hump.
These twelve names, with "Vāsudeva" at the head,
[should be used] by one who is composed during the time of worship, during the fire-oblation (homa), and in the evening and morning.
Having pronounced the names according to the prescribed rule, one should wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
Even if he is impure or lacks proper conduct, or even if he commits sin in his mind,
a man marked with the vertical mark shall always remain pure.
"Wherever a mortal dies while wearing the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*,
even if he be a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*), he is honored in my world, seated upon a celestial chariot. Thus says Satyavrata as well.
He on whose forehead a pure vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) made with clay is seen—even if he is a *caṇḍāla*, he is a pure soul and certainly worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt.
Vyāsa also says: "He who bears upon his head the clay produced on the banks of the Gaṅgā bears the very form of the Sun, solely for the destruction of darkness."
Now, regarding occasional ablutions,
Manu says: "A divākīrti, a woman in her courses, an outcaste, and likewise a woman who has recently given birth..."
Having touched a corpse or one who has touched it, one becomes pure by bathing.

A *divākīrti* is a *caṇḍāla*. An *udakyā* is a woman in her menses. Regarding "by bathing," the phrase "with one's clothes on" (*sacelena*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]: "Having touched a corpse, or an *udakyā*, a woman who has recently given birth, or likewise an outcast (*patita*), one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on; of this there is no doubt."

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Aṅgiras. In that context, by the word *tat* ("that"), there is an inclusion of everything from the *divākīrtya* rite up to the *sava* sacrifice, and not merely the corpse (*śava*), since even those are equal to a corpse due to their impurity and because they are mentioned in the same syntactical unit. Nor should one suspect that, due to immediate proximity, the rule regarding contact with a corpse applies here only to the corpse itself; therefore, Gautama says: "Upon touching one who has touched an outcast (*patita*), a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), or a corpse, or one who has touched someone who touched them, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on. By this, it is stated that starting from one who has touched an outcast and so forth, even the third person must bathe with their clothes on. Nor should one suspect that even here, because of the connection between the outcasts and others ending with the menstruating woman and the one who touched the corpse, the rule regarding contact with a corpse applies only there; for in other Smṛtis, the rule regarding contact with a corpse is explicitly stated even in the case of Caṇḍālas and others: "Upon touching a corpse, a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or one who has touched them, there is a bath. The author of the Saṃgraha also [states]: [305] "Upon touching a corpse, a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or one who has touched them, there is a bath. The author of the Saṃgraha also [states]:

"A Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, her husband, and a corpse—upon contact with these alone, the rule regarding those who have touched them is prescribed. The word "alone" (eva) is intended to exclude the application of that same rule to one who touches smoke from a funeral pyre and the like. Thus he [the author] says:
"Having touched one who has been touched by the smoke from a funeral pyre, one who has vomited, one who is devoid of passion (or a eunuch), one who performs the work of a barber,
or one who practices sexual intercourse, bathing is not prescribed. As for that which was stated by Saṃvarta:
If one should touch someone who has touched that [impure object], bathing is prescribed for him;
beyond that, sipping water (ācamana) is declared, as well as the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of objects.
Thus, bathing for only two [of the three] has been prescribed; that refers to the case of touching unintentionally. And so says the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
"In the case of touching unintentionally, bathing is ordained for the two;
but in the case of intentional touching, the same principle is to be applied to those three who touched him."

But for the fourth [act], there is only sipping water (ācamana), because of the traditional teaching of Marīci: "But the fourth should touch [water]; however, after that, sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is prescribed. As for that which is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:

If one should touch, through negligence, someone touched by a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, or a menstruating woman, one should then perform ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and recite prayers with a concentrated mind.

Having intentionally touched one who has been touched by someone who touched that [impure person], the best of the twice-born should perform ācamana for the sake of purification; so said the Lord Pitāmaha.
Thus, both of these [rules] refer to objects other than the second [meal]; otherwise, they would contradict the statements of Gautama and others. With this very intention, Yājñavalkya also says:

"One should bathe when touched by those who are *udakyā* (menstruating) or impure; if touched by them, one should sip water (*upaspṛśet*). One should also mutter verses containing the word 'water' and recite the Gāyatrī once mentally."

One who has been touched by those who are menstruating, impure, or by *caṇḍālas*, outcasts (*patita*), and the like, should bathe. When touched by those [objects] such as a staff that have not been touched by them [the aforementioned persons], one should perform *upaspṛśet*—which means one should sip water (*ācāmet*). However, the authors of the commentaries have explained this as referring to the context of touching objects such as a staff. Alternatively, it has the same meaning as the statement of Saṃvarta: "When touched by those [objects] such as a staff that have not been touched by them [the aforementioned persons], such as a menstruating woman, one should perform *upaspṛśet*—that is, one should bathe. Furthermore, as stated by Devala:

"Having touched something touched by an impure thing, and having touched a second person [who was himself touched], a man becomes pure by washing his hands and feet with water and sipping water (*ācamya*)."
Thus, that too has the same meaning as Yājñavalkya’s [statement]. Furthermore, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"If one should touch another who is impure, he alone becomes defiled;
the other person touched by him does not become defiled—this is the rule regarding all objects."

[307] Thus, that too has the same meaning as the former. Furthermore, in the *Ādityapurāṇa*: "Having touched one who is in childbirth, one who has died, or a woman in her menses, a wise man should bathe; however, from touching one who has touched them, he should merely sip water (*ācamana*)."

Thus, that too has the same meaning as the statement of Saṃvarta. On this point, Kātyāyana says: "Having touched a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, an outcaste, one in a state of impurity, or a corpse—one becomes pure by bathing; having followed a deceased person, one should touch fire."
Thus, this refers to the case of contact with those who are negligent:
having intentionally touched one who has fallen from caste, a woman in childbirth, or a corpse,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.

Thus it is from the Smṛti. On this point, Pracetas says: "Contact mediated by a garment is declared to be direct contact; that which is prescribed for direct contact applies even when there is contact through a garment."
Vyāsa also says: "Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla or an outcaste, a man should look at the sun;
but having looked at these two after bathing, he ought to bathe again with his clothes on."
One should avoid, in order, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, and a Caṇḍāla as the fourth, for one, two, three, and four yugas respectively.
Vaiyāghrapāda also says:
"One should avoid a Caṇḍāla and an outcast from afar;
within the distance of a cow-tail whisk, one should enter the water with one's clothes on."
Some have explained this as referring to a situation involving an extremely perilous circumstance. Viṣṇu also says:
"Upon touching a Caṇḍāla or a menstruating woman, one becomes pure by bathing. Parāśara also says:

"A *caityavṛkṣa*, a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a *caṇḍāla*, and a seller of Soma—a Brāhmaṇa, having touched these, shall enter the water with his clothes on. A *caityavṛkṣa* is a tree planted upon the site of a funeral pyre. Aṅgiras also says:
If a Brāhmaṇa steps upon the shadow of a dog-cooker (śvapāka), he should perform a bath there; by consuming clarified butter, he becomes purified.
Āpastamba also says:
"When a Caṇḍāla or similar person has ascended the same branch [of the tree],
a Brāhmaṇa residing there attains purity by means of bathing."

The mention of "branches" is intended as an illustration for substances of this kind. For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says: "If one sits upon a single grass mat together with those who are untouchable, the fool thinks, 'I am not defiled by those untouchables.'"
"On a bed made of grass" means one constructed from straw. Regarding this, Aṅgiras says concerning a woman in her menses:
"One should prescribe bathing for a woman in her menses on the fourth day;
once the menstrual flow has ceased, she should then perform bathing again for the sake of purification."
Manu also says:
"When her menses have ceased, a virtuous woman who has been menstruating becomes pure by bathing.

This means that immediately after the cessation of the flow, she becomes pure again through bathing and is thus fit for rites dedicated to the gods and other such purposes. Furthermore, as for the statement of Aṅgiras:
A woman who has menstruated becomes pure for her husband on the fourth day after she has bathed;
however, for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors, she becomes pure on the fifth day.

Thus, this is for the purpose of indicating the time of the cessation of the menstrual flow; for he himself has said: "A woman who is menstruating does not become pure in her conduct even after she has bathed, as long as the flowing blood has not ceased."

The meaning is that she is one whose conduct is virtuous and thus fit for rites dedicated to the gods and others. However, she indeed becomes fit for physical contact immediately after her bath. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"A woman in her menses attains purity by bathing on the fourth day.
But when the menses flow due to illness, there is no impurity caused by them; regarding this, Aṅgiras says:

"When the menses of women flow excessively due to disease, they are not thereby impure, because that [excess] is indeed a pathological condition. This should be understood to apply likewise even when menstruation occurs at an improper time. And so it is stated in another Smṛti:

"The wise say that the blood which occurs for women at an improper time is not [the same as] that which is called *rajas* (menstrual flow) when it occurs at the proper time; therefore, she is impure only during that [latter]. On this point, Saṃvarta says:
"Having touched a dog, a boar, a donkey, a camel, a wolf, a jackal, a monkey, a crow, a cock, or a vulture, one should perform a bath. Thus [it is said].

Paiṭhīnasi also states: "Upon touching a crow or an owl, one should bathe with one's clothes on. Upon voiding urine or excrement without water, one should bathe with one's clothes on and perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with the Great Vyāhṛtis. The meaning is that this [penance applies] until water is subsequently obtained.
If, after voiding urine or feces, one does not find water at all,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on once water is later obtained.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Aṅgiras; Vyāsa also says: "Having touched the impurity of a vulture, a monkey, a cat, a donkey, a camel, dogs, or pigs, one should indeed bathe with one's clothes on."
Hārīta also says: "A ram, a cock, a crow, dogs, jackals, and wolves;
funeral pyres, sacrificial posts, cemeteries, village pigs, donkeys, and impure things."
Having touched an Avakīrṇin (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) or an outcaste, one should perform a ritual bath.

Also in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "One who knows the Dharma [should avoid] those whose food is unfit to be eaten, a woman in childbirth, a eunuch, a cat, a rat, a dog, a cock, an outcast, one who has been abandoned, a Caṇḍāla, and those who carry the dead."
Neither a woman in her courses nor a village pig is purified by bathing upon contact;
likewise, two men defiled by the impurity of childbirth are not purified in that same way.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Having touched Buddhists, Pāśupatas, Jains, Lokāyatikas, followers of Kapila, or twice-born men who persist in forbidden acts, one should enter the water with one's clothes on."
But upon touching Kāpālikas, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is considered the superior remedy.
Also, in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Having touched Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Lokāyatas, and atheists..."
Upon touching twice-born men who follow improper occupations or Śūdras, one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
Saṃvarta also says:
"A twice-born man who touches the leavings of a Śūdra, or even a Śūdra who is himself impure with leavings,
or who embraces one who is pure [but has been touched by such], shall enter the water with his clothes on."
"Having embraced" means having touched. It is also stated in another Smṛti:
"Having touched a funeral pyre, wood from a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, a Caṇḍāla, or even a Devalaka, one should enter the water with one's clothes on."
A Brahmin who, desiring wealth, is devoted to the worship of gods for three years is indeed called a *devalaka*; he is censured in rites for the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
Yama also says:
"Upon being touched even for a moment by a dog, by an outcaste (śvapāka), or by the removal of a corpse, one should perform an immersion in water with one's clothes on."

Regarding this specific case, Āpastamba states: "One who has been defiled by a dog shall immerse himself with his clothes on; or, having washed that spot and touched it with fire, and having washed his feet and sipped water, he becomes pure. Immersion with one's clothes on refers to contact with the body above the navel. Likewise, Viṣṇu says:
"If the hand or the tip of the finger is defiled by a dog below the navel, one becomes pure by washing it, sprinkling it with water over darbha grass, and sipping water again."
"If one is touched above the navel by a dog, or smeared with impurity, one should wash the limbs with earth and water and perform a bath with one's clothes on.
This should be understood to apply likewise in the case of touching a washerman or others. And so says Śātātapa:
The washerman, the leather-worker, those who live by snares and hunting,
the dyer, the butcher, the actor, and likewise the stage-player;
A man with a cleft lip, a dog, women of all castes,
one who bears a discus or a banner, an executioner, and village cocks and pigs— [these are inauspicious].
If any part of the body of twice-born men, excluding the head, should be touched by these,
they are considered pure once they have washed that area with water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana).

A *rajaka* is one who dyes wool and other materials; a *nirṇejaka* is a washerman; a *sainika* is a violent soldier; a *naṭa* is a specific caste; an *anaṭa* is also a *śailūṣaka*, one who lives by appearing on the stage; a *mukhebhaga* is a specific type of eunuch; and a *dhvajī* is a seller of liquor. Here too, because of its association with "dogs," the mention of the "head" is intended to indicate the part of the body above the navel. Śaṅkha also says: "If a man is touched above the navel by the mud or water of a street, or by spittle and the like, he becomes pure immediately by bathing."
Jātūkarṇa also says:
"Whatever part of the body above the navel a bird touches, except for the hands—one should perform a bath there; by washing the rest, one becomes pure."

[313] *Khaga* means a bird. Furthermore, if one who is indeed impure touches dogs and other such animals, then a specific rule has been shown by Devala: "A dog-cooker (*śvapāka*), an outcast (*patita*), a person with a physical deformity (*vyaṅga*), a madman, a cremator of corpses, a woman who has recently given birth, a woman in her menses, and a woman overwhelmed by menstrual flow."
Having touched domestic parrots, chickens, and pigs,
a person becomes pure by bathing immediately with their clothes on and including the head.

"If one who is himself impure should touch these [impure things], he becomes pure again by means of a fast or likewise by means of a *kṛcchra* penance. Here, "one who causes birth" refers to a woman in labor. This concerns the case of intentional contact; and so it is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
If a twice-born man, being impure from food remnants or having failed to rinse his mouth, should touch a Caṇḍāla through negligence,
he should bathe and recite the Gāyatrī mantra eight thousand times.
"But if a twice-born man should touch outcasts, fallen persons, and the like out of desire while he is impure from eating,
he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for purification.
With this very intention, Viṣṇu also [states]:
If one is touched by someone who is required to bathe because they have become impure (ucchiṣṭa),
then he who has been touched by that same person becomes pure through a Prājāpatya penance.
On this point, Saṃvarta says:
"A twice-born man, having touched indigo, products of indigo, or even a human bone, as well as the shadow of a Caṇḍāla or an outcaste, should perform a bath."
This refers to the case of bones accompanied by marrow. As Manu says:
"Having touched a human bone with marrow, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
but if it is without marrow, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun."

Regarding non-human [beings], however, that which was stated by Viṣṇu should be observed: "Having touched the corpse of a five-toed animal—excluding those [usually] eaten—as well as its bone or anything oily, one should bathe. On this point, Yama says: "When food is undigested, when the sun has risen, after vomiting, after shaving, after sexual intercourse, upon a bad dream, or contact with a wicked person, mere bathing is prescribed."

On the day after indigestion, when there is belching after eating; when the sun has risen while one is still lying down; and even regarding stale food—one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on after touching the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) of Rudra.
Parāśara also says:
One should perform a bath after a bad dream, sexual intercourse, vomiting, purging, or shaving; and upon touching a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, or a cemetery.

Before the collection of the bones, one should weep and perform a bath; for a Brahmin, it is traditionally taught that within ten days of death, only sipping water (ācamana) is required after that period.

In this context, the connection is that *ācamana* (sipping water) occurs after the removal of bones, provided it is within ten days. However, Yama states a specific rule regarding vomiting and similar cases:
"One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
One who has eaten food should merely sip water; bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse. [315]

The meaning is that after eating food, one should sip water (ācamana) immediately after vomiting. Regarding the bath for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse, this applies specifically to the period of the menses (*ṛtukāla*). As Śātātapa says:
"A bath is prescribed for one who has had sexual intercourse during the menses because of the suspicion of pregnancy;
but when one approaches [his wife] outside the menses, the purification is like that for voiding urine or feces."

The meaning here is that both types of purification must be performed, just as one does after voiding urine or excrement. However, in another Smṛti, bathing is prescribed even outside the fertile period at specific times:

"Having engaged in sexual intercourse on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, during the day, or on a festival day (parvan), one should bathe with one's clothes on and purify oneself with the Vāruṇī verses."
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"One should not perform a bath at night, nor especially the offering of curds;
however, they do perform occasional baths and gifts during the nights."
This refers to the intention regarding the middle watch (madhyamayāma). As Devala says: "The Mahāniśā should be understood as the two middle watches;
therefore, one should not perform a bath during that time, except for one performed for a specific desire or on a particular occasion."
Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"For water is always unfit for drinking during the two middle watches of the night;
likewise, one should not perform bathing or the ritual of sipping water (ācamana)."

From this prohibition of bathing specifically during the "great night" (mahāniśā), it is understood that bathing at other times of the night is not forbidden. For this very reason, Parāśara states: "The 'great night' should be known as the two middle watches; one should perform the bath during the first and last watches of the night just as during the day."
This also refers to a situation of distress. As that same author says:
"Bathing during the day, purified by the rays of the sun, is praised;
bathing at night is not praised, except upon the sighting of Rāhu [an eclipse]."

The meaning is that while bathing during the day is possible, it is not recommended at night. The mention of "seeing Rāhu" (an eclipse) is intended to illustrate other occasions as well, such as the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (*saṃkrānti*) and so forth. For this very reason, Devala states:

"At the sight of Rāhu, at the sun’s passage into a new sign, at marriages, at times of calamity, and on occasions of prosperity, one should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other rites—even at night—and likewise during optional vows."

"Transgression" means death; "increase" means birth. Yājñavalkya also states: "Bathing on occasions such as eclipses, weddings, the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), journeys, calamities, and childbirth is to be known as occasional (naimittika); it is prescribed even at night."

Suffering is death. Parāśara also says: "Bathing is recommended at the birth of a son, during a sacrifice, likewise at the transit of the sun, and during an eclipse of Rāhu; otherwise, it is not [recommended] at night."
Regarding the *avabhṛtha* bath at a sacrifice, Yama states a specific rule for the night-bath:
"If a Brahmin is touched at night by a woman in her courses (*udakyā*) or by an outcast (*patita*),
he should bathe in the presence of the sacred fire using water fetched during the day."

"With water together with gold"—this is the ellipsis. And so Parāśara says: "When water brought during the day has been mixed with gold, one should bathe in its presence when the time for bathing at night arrives" (317).
If water brought during the day is not available, then Marīci states this specific rule:
"If the water brought during the day is not present in the house,
one should kindle a fire and then bathe in a river or a lotus pond."
Kātyāyana also says:
"Due to Varuṇa’s entry into the waters, one should not draw up water at night;
except for [water] in a dwelling, bathing is prescribed when one is situated there."
The meaning is that one should not draw water at night except when accompanied by the mantra "dhāmno dhāmnaḥ. Regarding this, Parāśara states a specific rule:
"If there is no water in the house, how can purification take place?
One should draw [water] from the vicinity of the fire while reciting the mantra 'dhāmno dhāmnaḥ'."
Purified at night by the rays of the house and purified by day by the sun, it becomes pure by this very means; as it is at night, so it is by day.
On this point, the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa states:
"Bathing is said to be of three kinds—daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya).
Libation (tarpaṇa), however, is proclaimed as being an ancillary part (aṅga) of that."
Regarding this occasional bath (*naimittika*), Āpastamba states an exception in certain cases:
"Upon touching an untouchable, after vomiting, upon the shedding of tears, after shaving, or [during menstruation] in the case of the female organ—
an occasional bath must be performed, excluding rites for the gods or ancestors."
Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "He who is entitled to a bath on account of a particular occasion, having first immersed himself in water,
should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and, being self-restrained, carry out the bath according to the prescribed rules."
"Having performed the immersion, [one should remain] silent"—this is the remainder [of the sense]. And so says the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
"When a man becomes impure, he should indeed immerse himself silently;
having sipped water (ācamana) and become purified, he should thereafter perform the bath according to the prescribed rule."
Regarding this, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"Upon touching a Caṇḍāla or similar person, one should perform a purificatory bath (vāruṇasnāna);
the other four [types of baths] are indeed prescribed according to the circumstances."
The others are the *brāhma* and so forth. Yogayājñavalkya also states:
"When an occasion for expiation has arisen, bathing alone is prescribed;
likewise, with the previously mentioned mantras, otherwise purification (*mārjana*) is ordained."
Otherwise, regarding the daily bath (*nityasnāna*), Garga states a specific rule for the bath to Varuṇa (*vāruṇa*):

"One should perform the occasional bath (*naimittikasnāna*) with cold water, as well as the optional (*kāmya*) bath; one may perform the daily (*nitya*) and spontaneous (*yādṛcchika*) baths according to one's preference. Thus he says.

"Because it was stated by that very same author: 'Bathing for the purpose of removing impurity, which has the removal of impurity as its fruit, is occasional (yādṛcchika). Regarding the bath for the sick, Parāśara says:"
When a person who is ill has become defiled, ten times over a healthy person, having bathed and bathed, should touch him; then that sick person shall become pure.
If a woman becomes menstruating when an occasional bath (naimittika-snāna) is required,
she should perform the bath using water filtered through another vessel and then observe her religious vow.
She should somehow have her limbs, including the major and minor parts of the body, sprinkled with water;
she should not wring out her garment, nor should she put on another cloth.

"Ātura" means one who is afflicted by disease. Uśanas also says: "If a woman is overcome by fever and simultaneously overwhelmed by her menses, how can there be purification for her? By what ritual act may she become pure?"
When the fourth day has arrived, another woman should touch her;
she, having suddenly entered the water, should bathe again and again, and then touch [the first woman] once more.
She should sip water ten or twelve times again and again;
however, according to others, she becomes pure only after discarding her garments.
"One should give a gift according to one's ability; then, through a *puṇyāha* ceremony, one becomes purified.
Likewise, a specific rule regarding the death of a woman in childbirth is shown in another Smṛti:
"When a woman in childbirth has died, how do the ritualists proceed?"
Having taken water in a jar, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), likewise.
Then, by consecrating water with meritorious mantras through speech, one obtains purification;
having bathed [the deceased] with that very water, one should perform the cremation according to the prescribed rite.
Regarding the death of a woman in her menses,
[it is said]: "Having bathed the deceased woman who was in her menses with the five products of the cow,
and having covered her with another garment, one should cremate her according to the prescribed rule."
On this point, Śātātapa says:
"In a village, in cases where there is physical contact during travel, in quarrels and the like,
and in the case of defiling a village, no fault of contact exists."

In a village, on the royal highway, and so forth; also in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "During divine processions, weddings, sacrifices that have commenced, and at all festivals, there is no impurity from touching."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"At a sacred ford, at a wedding, on a journey, in battle, during a national upheaval,
and when a city or village is burning, touching one who has been touched does not cause impurity."

Regarding these three statements, some hold that they refer to cases where there is no awareness that one has been touched by such a person. Others maintain that they concern the touching of food-leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) or impure substances (*aśuci*). On this point, Āpastamba says: "When one is capable [of purification], one should not remain impure even for a moment.
Thus ends the section on occasional ablutions (*naimittika-snāna*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the optional ablutions (*kāmya-snāna*).
In this regard, Pulastya says:
"A bath in a river during the Puṣya asterism, one's birth asterism, during Vyatīpāta, during Vaidhṛti, and on the new moon day, purifies the family up to the seventh generation."
Those twice-born who perform ablutions on the days of the Sun, Mars,
or Saturn are not afflicted by diseases, just as deer are not harmed by lions.
Whoever bathes in the presence of Śiva on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra—
especially in the Gaṅgā— does not attain the state of a preta.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"The water that stands before the Śiva-liṅga should be known as the Śivagaṅgā; having bathed there, one shall go to heaven."
Yama also says: "One who has bathed at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika is liberated from all sins;
but one who has bathed at Prayāga on the full moon day of Māgha is released from all defilements."
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, conjoined with the asterism Hasta, the Gaṅgā destroys the sins of ten births; therefore, she is remembered as the remover of evil.
Likewise, having bathed in the Yamunā on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha,
and similarly on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha;
Having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, a person is liberated from all sins.
Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"Whatever fruit results from the perfect gift of ten million cows,
that same fruit is obtained by bathing in the Jāhnavī when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu."
In the Padma Purāṇa as well:
"The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika is for the festival of the ancestors;
on that day, bathing, burnt offerings, and gifts yield infinite fruit."
Viṣṇu also says:
"The seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is equal to a solar eclipse;
bathing on that day at the time of dawn yields great fruit."
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, conjoined with the asterism Punarvasu and the planet Jupiter,
one who bathes according to the rules in flowing waters shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Śātātapa also says:
"When the new moon falls on a Tuesday at the [confluence of the] gate,
by merely bathing in the Ganges, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows."
Also in the *Purāṇa*:
"One who bathes daily throughout the entire month of Kārttika, with senses subdued,
reciting [mantras] and eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), is liberated from all sins once he has bathed."
One should always bathe at dawn during the months of Libra, Capricorn, and Aries;
consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya) and observing celibacy destroys even the greatest sins.
Yama also says:
"He who desires vast enjoyments comparable to the sun, the moon,
and the planets should always bathe in the morning during the two months of Māgha and Phālguna."
Also in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"A man should bathe in the morning for the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha;
having given food to Brahmins, he should become a giver of cows on the full moon day of Kārttika."
He indeed attains the station of Viṣṇu; this is remembered as the vow of Viṣṇu.
The Vṛddhavasiṣṭha also says:
"If a person does not bathe during the meritorious transit of the sun [into a new zodiac sign],
he shall be diseased for seven births and is born here as a partaker of suffering."
For seven births, he shall never be free from diseases.
Mārkaṇḍeya also [says]:
"The sage Vyāsa has declared that bathing with sesame seeds at all times is meritorious;
Viṣṇu is especially pleased by *āmalaka* fruits on the eleventh day."
A man desiring prosperity should always perform his bath with *āmalaka* fruits;
however, he should avoid the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*), the ninth day (*navamī*), and the time of the lunar festivals (*parvakāla*).
On this point, the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa* states:
"Bathing is said to be of three kinds—daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and for the sake of a specific desire (*kāmya*).
The libation (*tarpaṇa*) is proclaimed to be an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of that. [323]

Garga also says: "One should perform the occasional bath (naimittika) with cold water, as well as the optional (kāmya) one; likewise, one may perform the daily (nitya) and voluntary (yādṛcchika) baths according to one's preference."
Thus ends the section on optional baths in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the procedure for the Māgha bath; regarding this, the Nāradīya Purāṇa states:
When the month of Māgha has arrived, which is dear to those who practice austerities,
all waters cry out as the sun rises.
We purify all three kinds of sins, there is no doubt;
even those committed by a slayer of a Brahmin or those performed through violent deeds.
In the month of Māgha, the gods indeed infused splendor into the waters;
therefore, this water is indeed pure and the destroyer of the entire multitude of sins.
One should not bathe in reed-beds, nor in water contained in a well or a vessel;
merit is not obtained easily, for merit is obtained through hardship.
O lady of excellent limbs, the water of a river is indeed recommended in the month of Māgha;
one should not attend to the sacred fire while bathing, nor under any circumstances while not bathing.
Viṣṇu also says:
"Between the months of Pauṣa and Phālguna, one should always be a practitioner of the morning bath;
having begun on either the new moon or the full moon day, one should perform the ritual bathing."
[324] For thirty auspicious days while the sun is situated in Capricorn,
one should rise at that time and undertake a religious observance according to the prescribed rule.
"O Lord Mādhava, having formed this resolution in my mind— 'I shall bathe daily in the waters of this sacred ford throughout this entire month of Māgha'— "
Then, O King, having bathed at the sacred ford and having applied earth to his head,
a householder should offer the *arghya* to the Sun according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
Having gratified the ancestors and then descended from the water,
one should remain silent, pay obeisance to the quarter, and worship Puruṣottama.
One should worship the god named Mādhava, who bears the conch and the discus;
having offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rule, one should thereafter eat but a single meal.
One who is capable should perform his bath while sleeping on the ground and observing celibacy;
for one who is incapable or wealthy, it is said that he may act according to his own will in all matters.
"The Māgha bath must certainly be performed; this is the established rule. One should bathe with sesame seeds, rub oneself with sesame, offer oblations of sesame, and offer water with sesame."
One who plants sesame seeds, one who eats sesame seeds, and one who possesses six measures of sesame does not perish;
sesame seeds and *āmalaka* fruits should always be given at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
In this manner, one should kindle the fire for the sake of fuel for the twice-born;
likewise, at the conclusion of the bath, food should be offered without restriction.
One should feed a Brahmin couple and adorn them with garments and ornaments,
as well as blankets, skins, jewels, and various kinds of clothing.
And garments should be given, as well as cloths for covering;
likewise sandals, and those that fasten at the ankle, and those that fasten at the foot.
One should give [the gift] according to this procedure, saying, "May Mādhava be pleased.
In this regard, there is a specific detail mentioned in the Purāṇas:
"O Savitṛ and Prasavitṛ, the supreme abode, [be present] in my water."
May the sin, fallen away through your splendor, go forth in a thousand directions.
O Divākara, Lord of the World, Maker of Light, homage be to you!
By your command, I shall perform the Māgha bath in its entirety.
This is the mantra for the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
Day after day, sesame seeds mixed with sugar should be given;
likewise, at the end of the month of Māgha, O fortunate one, one should feast the Brahmins.
"May the Sun-god, the stainless embodiment of Viṣṇu, be drunk by me.
[I offer] two fine garments for the couple, accompanied by the seven grains."
Thirty modakas, combined with sugar and sesame seeds, should be offered;
there should be three parts of sesame seeds and the fourth part is sugar.
O lady of beautiful hips, the observer of the vow should spend the entire month without anointing his body with oil.
Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule for one who desires a particular fruit:
"One should travel on the road self-controlled, observing silence and avoiding slander,
if one desires auspicious and abundant enjoyments comparable to the moon and the sun."
But that man who, being desirous and not yet having attained prosperity, performs a ritual bath,
obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step.
Also in the Purāṇa: "The water of a river with great current, likewise [the water] contained in a new jar,
when struck by the *vayuna* [wind] at night, constitutes a vow equal to bathing in the Gaṅgā."
Viṣṇu states the fruit for one who acts in this way:
"Children, youths, the elderly, men, women, and eunuchs—
having bathed in a sacred bathing place during the auspicious month of Māgha, they obtain their desired fruit."
Together with his father, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, as well as with his mother, maternal grandfather, and maternal great-grandfather.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures together with twenty-one generations of his family,
he goes to the world of Viṣṇu after bathing at dawn during the month of Māgha.
Also in the Purāṇa:
"In this manner, when the sun passes through the *māgha-plava* [conjunction], having pierced the solar disc.
Thus ends the procedure for the *māgha*-bath in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some statements concerning the bath for the removal of impurities (*malāpakarṣaṇasnāna*) are written here; regarding this, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"At the beginning of the fortnight, on the new moon, on the sixth lunar day, and likewise on an empty (*rikta*) lunar day..."
But one who is anointed with oil is deprived of wealth and long life.
Hārīta also says:
"He who uses oil on the fifth, the tenth, the full moon, the thirteenth, the eleventh, and the third [lunar days],"
Furthermore, by anointing with it, by touching it, and likewise by consuming it,
there shall be an increase for that person in wealth, progeny, strength, and longevity.
Bodhāyana also says:
"On the eighth, the fourteenth, and especially the tenth day,
as well as at the junction of the lunar phases (parvan), one should avoid anointing the head with oil."
Garga also says:
One should avoid contact with oil on the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, the eighth day, during the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), and on the twelfth, seventh, and sixth days.

Thus, the prohibition of specific days is also demonstrated in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): "From anointing oneself with oil on the days of the Sun and the others, there result distress, splendor, short life, wealth, death, ill health, and the fulfillment of all desires [respectively]."
Also in the Vāmana Purāṇa:

"One should not perform an oil massage on Sunday, nor a haircut on Tuesday; one should avoid meat on Friday and Tuesday, and women on Wednesday and the lunar festivals (parvan). On the remaining days, one should always carry out these activities."
Oil, a razor, and medical treatment should be avoided by a physician under the asterisms of Citrā, Hasta, Śravaṇa, and Viśākhā.
Meat should be avoided under Mūla, Mṛgaśiras, the two Bhādrapadas, Maghā, Ārdrā, Kṛttikā, and the three Uttarās.

Anointing with oil is not recommended on Sundays or Tuesdays, nor during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), the Vaidhṛti yoga, the Niṣṭi tithi, or the sixth lunar day; it is also undesirable on the full and new moon days and the eighth day. However, it is declared desirable on all other days except for Saturdays.

Śanaiścara is the son of the Sun. Thus, it is stated that one should perform an oil-bath (*abhyaṅgasnāna*) on the northern lunar days (*tithis*), excluding the second day which is joined with the [asterism] Uttarā. On this point, Pracetas says:
"Oil made from mustard seeds, fragrant oil, oil scented with flowers, and oil mixed with other substances—none of these ever become defiled."
Yama also says:
"Ghee, mustard oil, and any oil perfumed with flowers—
there is no fault in using these cooked oils for daily bathing and anointing."

Furthermore, this prohibition regarding specific lunar days (tithi) applies only to the ritual bath with oil (abhyaṅgasnāna), and not to the daily obligatory bath (nityasnāna) and so forth. Thus says Garga:
"Upon the birth of a son, during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), at a śrāddha ceremony, on one's birthday, and when performing the daily obligatory bath, no defect regarding the lunar day is found."
Āpastamba also says:

"That bath which is performed by the twice-born for the sake of enjoyment according to whim is forbidden on the tenth day and other such occasions; however, this does not apply to the obligatory or occasional baths."
The same should be understood regarding optional (kāmya) rites as well. For this very reason, Jābāli states:
"One should never neglect the daily (nitya), the optional (kāmya), or the occasional (naimittika) bath;
it must be performed even on the tenth day, but never at one's own whim."

"Because of the traditional teaching of Garga: 'Bathing for the purpose of removing impurity is occasional; that which has the removal of impurity as its result is indeed occasional. And thus, as it was stated by Āpastamba:"
"But one should not bathe on the tenth lunar days except for a continuous bath"—

this [prohibition] should be understood as being intended to illustrate the case of optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) baths as well. Thus ends the section on the bath for removing impurities in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, other prohibitions associated with lunar days (tithis) are also shown; therein, Kratu says:
"The sixth, the seventh, the ninth, and the thirteenth."
One should avoid bathing with *āmalaka* fruits on the occasion of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) and on Sundays.
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"One should not bathe with emblic myrobalan fruits on the new moon day, nor on the seventh or ninth lunar days; for in those cases, one's splendor, longevity, wealth, and sons are diminished."
The *dhātrī* is the *āmalakī*. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"On the seventh lunar day, a man should not touch oil, nor wear blue clothing;
he should neither bathe with *āmalaka* fruits nor engage in quarreling."
Vyāsa also says: "On the sixth, eighth, fifteenth, and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
sin is present in oil, meat, the razor, and the female organ."
This refers to occasions other than the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, because those are prescribed specifically for that time. Vyāghra also says:
"On the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth—the three junctions—one should avoid oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and the tooth-stick."
Sexual intercourse means copulation. Atri also says:
"Oil on the sixth day shortens life, as does meat on the eighth;
likewise, shaving on the fourteenth and sexual intercourse on the new moon day [are forbidden]."
Using a tooth-stick on the new moon day, engaging in sexual intercourse on the fourteenth day,
and taking oil on the eighth day destroys seven generations of men's families.
Also in the Purāṇa: "On the new moon, the full moon, the solstices (saṃkrānti), the fourteenth, and the eighth [lunar days],
a man shall be born in the womb of a Caṇḍāla by the use of oil, women, and meat."
Dhaumya also said:
"The fifteenth day is forbidden for eating meat, the fourteenth for anointing with oil, and the eighth for sexual intercourse; on these days, one would cause even a blazing fire to fall."
Village-dharma is sexual intercourse. Also in the Purāṇa:
"The fourteenth, the eighth, the sixth, the new moon, and the full moon—these, O King of kings, are the festival days (parvan), as is the sun's transit (saṃkrānti)."
That man who indulges in oil, women, and meat on these sacred festival days (parvan) certainly goes to the hell named Viṇmūtrabhojana (Eating Excrement and Urine).
Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"The eighth, the sixth, the ninth, and the fourteenth [lunar days],
as well as the junctions of the lunar phases (parvan-sandhi), should be avoided for the rite of shaving."
On all new moon days, one should not wear new clothing.
Pracetas also says:
