One should not approach a woman even when her season has arrived during the waning of the moon;
one should not touch oil, nor should one cut down raw trees and the like.
Also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"He who cuts down creepers while the moon is situated among the constellations of the Vīrudhas,
or who causes even a single leaf to fall, incurs the guilt of killing a Brahmin."
Śaṅkha also says:
"On new moon days, one should not cut *kuśa* grass nor sacrificial fuel (*samidh*);
for as long as Soma remains present everywhere, to cause injury [to these] would make one a slayer of a Brahmin."
Paiṭhīnasi also states: "One should cut sprouts on the new moon day. And thus, as it was said by Jābāli:
"A twice-born man may take Kuśa grass, Kāśa grass, flowers, and grass for the sake of cattle, even though there is a prohibition, on the day of the new moon."
[332] Thus, it should be understood that this refers to the taking up of *kuśa* grass and other items for the purpose of pacification (*śānti*).
Thus ends the prohibitions occasioned by lunar days (*tithi*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the ritual bath (*kriyā-snāna*).
In this regard, Śaṅkha says:
"I shall explain the ritual bath (kriyā-snāna) according to the rules and in due order;
first, purification must be performed with earth and water according to the prescribed injunctions."

Having emerged from the water after being submerged and having performed the ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) according to the rules, one should perform the invocation of the sacred ford (tīrtha-āvāhana); I shall explain that hereafter.
I take refuge in the god Varuṇa, the powerful lord of the waters;
grant me the sacred ford I have requested for the removal of all sins.
I shall invoke the sacred ford that destroys all sins;
by my grace, may you remain present in these waters of mine.
I take refuge in all the Rudras, the givers of boons; may I be one who walks upon the waters, and I take refuge in all those who walk upon the waters—here, Varuṇa is my witness.
I take refuge in the god who moves upon the waters, the fire that destroys his enemies;
likewise, I take refuge in the holy and purifying waters.
May all the Rudras, as well as Agni, Varuṇa, and the waters themselves,
quickly remove my sin and protect me always within the waters.
Having spoken thus, one should then perform the sweeping with *kuśa* grass,
according to rule and in proper sequence, with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Likewise, with the three *ṛc* verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," and similarly with "śaṃ no devīḥ" and likewise with "śaṃ na āpaḥ."
And one should utter the mantra: "O Waters, carry this away. Having thus performed the sprinkling, [one should recite] the meter, the seer, and the deity.
One who is self-restrained should always recollect the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn;
likewise, while submerged in water, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa three times.
"And likewise, one should offer water upon the head with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
Thus ends the section on ritual bathing (*kriyā-snāna*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*; now follow the waters suitable for bathing.
Regarding this, Manu says: "One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and in mountain clefts and springs."
"Devakhāta" means dug by the gods, but not water created artificially by humans. A "garta" (pit) has been defined by Kātyāyana:
"Those whose course does not extend for eight thousand bow-lengths (*dhanus*), and which do not flow with the name of 'river'—those are proclaimed to be *gartas*."
By this, the definition of a river is also stated. A small flow of water from a mountain or similar source is a *prasravaṇa*. Also in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"One should always bathe for the sake of ritual acts in rivers, streams, ponds, waters excavated by the gods (*devakhāta*), and mountain springs."
[334] One should perform one's bath with water drawn from wells, or on the ground;
or one may bathe with drawn water, or, if that is impossible, on the ground itself.
Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"One should perform the bathing of ancient kings, high-souled sages, and deities at wells and ponds."
By the phrase "of the great-souled ones," he states that one should not bathe in wells and other water sources belonging to outcasts and the like. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"One should not bathe in the wells of one who has acquired wealth by unjust means, of an outcast, or of a usurer; having bathed [there], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance."
The same should be understood regarding those [objects] that have not been relinquished. As Vyāsa says:

"One should not bathe in waters that have not been relinquished, nor likewise in those that have not been consecrated. "Unconsecrated" means not established [as sacred]. "Not relinquished" means not given away; that is to say, belonging to another. For this very reason, Jābāli says:
One should never bathe in another's water, nor eat during the middle of the night;
one should never wear a single garment while it is still wet.
Manu also says:
"One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil karma of the reservoir's builder."

Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Vyāsa— “Having extracted five lumps [of earth], one should perform the bath in another [body of water]”— that refers to a situation where a river or similar source is unavailable. And so says Yama:
"In the absence of natural ponds, lakes,
or rivers, one should perform the bath in another person's water after having drawn out four handfuls [of earth].
With this very intention, Śaunaka also says:
If one should ever bathe in a large pond, a well, or a tank,
one should first scoop out five or ten lumps of earth and cast them away.
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"If one should ever bathe in waters belonging to another,
having then extracted seven lumps [of earth] from there, one should perform the bath."

In this matter, the determination is according to one's capacity. Thus, it is stated that the fault belongs only to him who bathes in another's reservoir without first drawing [the water]. And it has been said by Śaunaka:
"But he who bathes in another's reservoir without having drawn [the water], his bathing becomes in vain, and he is smeared with the sin of the owner."

The meaning is that "in vain" (vṛthā) signifies fruitlessness. The point is that when water has been discarded, since it is no longer for one's own use, there is no fault even in not drawing it out again, because that [personal utility] is absent. Śaṅkha likewise states that bathing in hot water is fruitless:
"For one who has bathed with water heated by fire, or similarly with another person's water, purification of the body should be understood [to occur], but he does not obtain the fruit of the bath."
Yājñavalkya also says: "Bathing in cold water for no purpose, Vedic recitation that is not according to the Vedas,
giving gifts to one who is not learned in the Vedas, and eating in the absence of witnesses— all these are in vain."
[336] As for what has been said by some: "Water alone is always pure, and fire is its purifier;
therefore, at all times, warm water is traditionally held to be purifying."
Thus, as it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Water is pure by its very nature; how much more so when joined with fire? Therefore, the virtuous praise bathing with warm water."
Thus, that refers to the subject of bathing for the sick. And so says Yama:
"Water purified by the rays of the sun and further purified by fire—this water with *kuśa* grass is prescribed and recommended for the bath of one who is ill."
But when water from rivers and the like is not available, even for one who is not ill, bathing with warm water is not prohibited; thus he [the same author] says:
"Whether daily, occasional, or as part of a ritual act, bathing for the removal of impurities must be performed with warm water or other [substitutes] in the absence of a sacred bathing place."
As for that which was stated by Vriddha-Manu: "Upon death, birth, a solar transit (saṃkrānti), a śrāddha ceremony, or on one's birthday,
as well as upon touching someone who is untouchable, one should not bathe with warm water."
On a solar transit, on a Sunday, on the seventh lunar day, and during an eclipse,
one who desires health, sons, friends, or wealth should not bathe with hot water.
"He incurs the sin committed by killing a cow; of this there is no doubt.

Thus, even when death and other such events have been mentioned by him, it is stated that in the absence of a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), one should not bathe with hot water, but rather with water drawn from another source; hence there is no contradiction. Regarding bathing with hot water, Vyāsa states the specific rule:
"Having sprinkled oneself with cold water, [one should bathe] with hot water prepared with a collection of mantras."
"Bathing is praised at home; that which is done outside is inferior and fruitless.
Thus, the "materials" (*saṃbhārāḥ*) refer to clay and so forth. For this very reason, Vivasvat is mentioned in the section concerning midday.
It is called "touching water" (*upasparsana*) when it is conjoined with the materials and the mantras.
"In bathing and immersion, splashing [the body] without following the prescribed rules [is improper].

Likewise, Śaṅkha says that one should not bathe even in water that is too shallow: "One should not bathe in shallow water, nor should one immerse oneself in the waters of the ocean. Also, in another Smṛti:
"Neither when one is ill, nor when the sky is not yet pervaded by the rays of the sun..."
"Neither in another's water, nor in a small amount, nor ever without one's head [submerged]. This refers to the case when abundant water is available. As Yogayājñavalkya says:
"But when abundant and very pleasing water is present..."
A twice-born man should not bathe in a small body of water, nor should he abandon a river to bathe in an artificial pool.
The Purāṇa also says:
"When a river is available, one should not bathe in other waters;
when abundant water is available, one should not bathe in a small amount of water."

[338] The meaning is that one should bathe in meritorious water, not in unmeritorious water. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya speaks of the meritorious waters: "Water situated on the ground is more meritorious than [water] drawn up; then, water from a spring is more meritorious than that; water from a lake is more meritorious still, and water from a river is said to be more meritorious than that."
The water of sacred fords is meritorious, but the water of the Gaṅgā is meritorious in every respect.

The water of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) is water accepted by the virtuous. Viṣṇu also says: "Water remaining on the ground is more meritorious than water drawn [from it]; therefore, one should not take [water] from a riverbed; even more so, that which is accepted by the virtuous; and above all, that which comes from the Gaṅgā. Vivasvat also says: "On one side are all the sacred fords, and on the other is the Gaṅgā alone—that which has fallen upon the surface of the earth from the head of the Lord of the World of Brahmā."
Marīci also said:
Whether it be situated on the ground or drawn up, whether cold or even warm,
the water of the Gaṅgā quickly purifies sin committed until the end of one's life.
The water of the Sarasvatī purifies in three days, that of the Yamunā in five days,
that of the Gaṅgā immediately, and that of the Narmadā by its mere sight.
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"Rivers that do not flow to the ocean yield the fruit of three nights;
those that flow to the ocean [yield the fruit] of a fortnight; and the lord of rivers (the ocean) [yields the fruit] of a month."
The ocean is the lord of rivers. On this point, Vyāsa says:
"A wise man should always avoid bathing when the sun has set over a river;
having bathed in a river, one who knows the Dharma should not praise another river. Thus it is said.
Devala also says:
"One should not speak of a river among rivers, nor of a mountain among mountains; one should not praise another sacred ford (tīrtha) among sacred fords, nor [another] sanctuary among sanctuaries."
Regarding immersion in water, Āpastamba states: "One should avoid submerging the head in water. This refers to stagnant water. Likewise, the Purāṇa says:
"A twice-born man should bathe by entering flowing rivers and remaining within them;
however, in the waters of tanks and the like, he should perform the bath facing the sun."
Regarding this, Vyāsa states which waters are to be avoided:
"One should avoid water that has fallen from a river, water that has flowed out from a river,
and water that has returned after having gone away."
One should not urinate in a water cistern, nor should one cross a river while swimming.

"Paribhraṣṭa" means interrupted. One should avoid that which has flowed out and become interrupted. "Āvartāgata" means that which has gone and returned. Garga also says: "Bathing in a river at a whirlpool of water should be avoided by the twice-born.
Bodhāyana also says:
Twice-born men should avoid bathing in the lower reaches of a river's water;
however, they should avoid bathing within ten cubits of a washerman’s landing place on that same river.
Bathing at the washerman’s ford, eating in a courtesan’s house,
and sleeping toward the northwest— these take away one’s fortune even from Indra.

A *gaṇikā* is a courtesan. The *Yogayājñavalkya* also states: "However, the following waters are not to be taken: those from the first bank of a river, those agitated by anyone, and those that have flowed out from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*)."
The foremost [purifiers] are the new [waters]. In another Smṛti:
"Goats, cows, buffaloes, and Brahmin women who have recently given birth, as well as water that has reached the ground from a rain, become pure after ten nights."
Kātyāyana also says: "One should not bathe in those small streams on earth that dry up in the summer until ten days have passed since they filled again in the rainy season."
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, [the section on] waters suitable for bathing; now follows the determination regarding the impurity caused by menstrual flow in rivers.
On this point, Yogayājñavalkya says:
As long as the Blessed One, the ornament of the southern quarter, does not arise, so long shall the rivers carrying seed avoid the Jāhnavī.

The meaning is that as long as Agastya has not risen, rivers carry semen and are in their menses (*rajasvalā*). His rising is shown in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* to occur only in autumn in the northern regions. Thus, it is stated that during the rainy season, [the rivers] are in their menses. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, all rivers are in their menses;
one should not bathe in them, with the exception of the Jāhnavī. [341]
"When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived" means for a period of two months; this is the remainder [of the sense]. For this very reason, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"For two months all rivers are indeed in their menstrual flow;
therefore, bathing in the new waters at the beginning of the rains is not recommended."
This refers to regions other than those where rivers flow into the ocean. Accordingly, Kātyāyana states:
"For two months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, all rivers are menstruating;
one should not perform ritual bathing in them, except for those that flow into the ocean."

The month is called *yavya*, according to the Śatapatha Śruti: "From the *yavya* month, the well-established year [arises]. He (the same author) also speaks of the impurity of menstrual blood (*rajo-doṣa*) even regarding certain rivers that flow to the ocean:
"During the rainy season, the great rivers are immediately rendered impure by menstrual blood;
one should not bathe in them, with the exception of the Jāhnavī (Ganges)."
The meaning is that even among the great rivers, the Jahnavī (Ganges) is to be excluded. The great rivers are shown in the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Sarasvatī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Suprayāgā, Veṇī, and Kāverikā."
The Dugdhodā, Nalinā, Revā, Vārā, Śītā, and Kalasvanā—
these great rivers also have issued forth from the foot of the Sahya mountain.

In the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa* as well: [342] “The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Taṅgabhadrā, and Kāverī—these are the great rivers. The mention of bathing (*snāna*) is intended to indicate libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other such rites as well. As Kātyāyana says:
“Between the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya, all rivers are in their menses;
a person should not perform ritual acts such as bathing in them.”

The meaning is that she remains in her menses for as long as two months beginning with Karkaṭaka (Cancer). As for what was stated by Kātyāyana, beginning with "during the rainy season" (*prāvṛṭkāle*) and concluding with "excepting the Jāhnavī," that is not intended to establish that the Gaṅgā is entirely free from menstrual flow during the entire rainy season; for he himself says:
"When the month of Śrāvaṇa has begun, the Gaṅgā is in her menses for three days;
when the fourth day arrives, the Jāhnavī becomes pure."
This also refers to the solar measure (*sauramāna*). Otherwise [it would be]:
"O Goddess, first, for three days in Cancer, the Gaṅgā is menstruating;
all the great rivers, including the Karatoyā which carries its waters, are entirely red."

Thus, there would be a contradiction with the statement of Yogayājñavalkya, because of the rule that the *karkaṭa* transit occurs only prior to the commencement of the month of Śrāvaṇa. [This refers to] the Karatoyā river. Regarding this, Yama says:
"The Gaṅgā, the Dharmodbhavā, the Puṇyā Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī—all are pure on every day, even when their internal flow of menstrual-like impurity has occurred."

[343] Those who practice yoga against the current, those who frequent the dust of the streets, and those who bathe in the waters of the road— these are not defiled by the Gaṅgā, for she herself is the source of Dharma.
Also in the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"The river Sarasvatī is meritorious, as is the river Vaitaraṇī;
the Āpagā is greatly meritorious, as are the Gaṅgā and the Mandākinī."
The Madhusravā, the river Aṃśumatī, the Kauśikī which destroys sin,
the highly meritorious Dṛśadvatī, and likewise the river Hairaṇyavatī.
Except for the Sarasvatī, which flows during the rainy season,
the water of all these rivers is meritorious when it rains during the monsoon.
The state of being menstruating never exists for these women at any time.
Kātyāyana also says:
"The Gaṅgā, daughter of Tapaṇa, and the Gomatī, the best of rivers,
as well as those others remembered as merit-bestowing, are not defiled by menstrual flow."
"Yamunā is the daughter of Tapa; Mārkaṇḍeya as well [is so]. Gaṅgā is the daughter of Āditya; Sarasvatī was born from the Plakṣa tree.
And those others known as rivers are not overcome by passion (rajas). Thus it is said.

The Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra originates from the Plakṣa tree. Likewise, Kātyāyana states that for three nights during the period beginning with Cancer (karkaṭa), even the Gomatī and other rivers are defiled by menstrual flow: "For three days, the Gomatī, the Candrabhāgā, the Satī, the Sindhu, the Sarayū, and likewise the Narmadā, are defiled by menstrual flow during the period beginning with Cancer. [344]
Regarding this, the same author states an exception to the defect of menstrual impurity (*rajo-doṣa*) in certain cases:
"At the Upākarma and Utsarga ceremonies, as well as during the morning bath,
and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun, the defect of menstrual impurity does not exist."

"All waters on the surface of the earth become equal to the waters of the celestial river (Svardhunī) during an eclipse of the moon or sun, even those situated in wells; there is no doubt about this. This is the sense [of the objection]: "How, then, can there be the defect of impurity from menstrual blood? Svardhunī refers to the Gaṅgā.

Thus concludes the determination regarding the impurity caused by riverine floods in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now, as an incidental topic, the mantras for bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) are presented:
"O Gaṅgā, born from the lotus-feet of Viṣṇu, who flows through the three paths..."
O Jāhnavī, renowned as the bestower of dharma, take away my sin.
O Goddess Jāhnavī, mother of Śrī, endowed with righteousness through faith;
O Goddess Bhāgīrathī, purify me with your nectar-like waters!
Thus ends the mantra for bathing in the Gaṅgā:
"O Karatoyā, of ever-pure waters, renowned as the best of rivers!
You cause [us] to be immersed; O you who arise from the hand, take away the sin of my grandsons."
Thus ends the mantra for bathing in the Karatoyā:
"O Goddess, daughter of King Gādhi, daughter of the sage Viśvāmitra,
wife of Ṛcīka, noble Satyavatī, Kauśikī— take away my sin!"
[345] Thus ends the mantra for bathing in the Kauśikī. O Goddess, born from the foot of the Sahya mountain, flowing through the lap of Śrīśaila,
renowned as the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, you who destroy all sins!
O Goddess, born from the foothills of the Sahya mountains and renowned as the Kṛṣṇaveṇī,
I shall bathe in your waters for the sake of purification from all sins.
Be gracious to me, O Goddess, who were created by the Lord of Gods with eternal essence for the liberation of the worlds;
by bathing in whom a mortal, having shaken off all sin, attains the very abode of Viṣṇu.

O Kṛṣṇā, people regarded that vessel of the bliss of the nectar of Brahman as if it were full of water; I shall carry it away, I shall drink from it, and I shall satisfy the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
Thus ends the mantra for bathing in the Kṛṣṇaveṇī: "O Goddess,
arisen from Bhīmasena and flowing forth from the rims of chariot wheels,
I shall bathe in your waters for the sake of destroying all sins."
Thus ends the mantra for bathing in the Bhīmarathī:
"May the sky be yours, O you of meritorious waters; salutations, O you who flow to the ocean! O Narmadā, deliverer from sin; salutations, O Goddess of beautiful countenance!"
Homage be to you, served by hosts of sages and perfected beings; homage be to you, who have issued from the body of Śaṅkara.
Homage be to you, bestower of boons upon those who uphold the Dharma; homage be to you, the purifier of all that is pure.
Thus ends the mantra for bathing in the Narmadā:
"O Goddess, sovereign of rivers; O Goddess, most excellent of rivers!
Having bathed at the confluence of the two, I truly release myself from all evils."
Thus ends the mantra for bathing at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean:
"O son of Brahmā, O highly fortunate one, increaser of Śantanu’s lineage,
born from the womb of Amoghā, O Lauhitya, take away my sin!"
Thus ends the mantra for bathing at Lauhitya:
"Agni is indeed your womb and Iḍā your body; you are the seed of Viṣṇu and the navel of immortality.
Speaking this truthful word, O son of Pāṇḍu, one should then plunge into the lord of rivers."
Thus ends the mantra for bathing in the ocean:
"Whatever sin one may commit anywhere throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes,
by merely bathing in the salt waters, one is liberated from all those sins."
The sacred fig tree (aśvattha) and the ocean must never be touched;
however, one may touch the aśvattha on Sundays and the ocean on festival days (parvan).
[347] But on another occasion, O best of the Kurus, the Lord of Waters, who is of divine origin, said: "O son of Kuntī, this great ocean must not be touched even by the tip of a blade of kuśa grass."

In this case, the sipping of water (ācamana) must be performed with water from within [the sacred site] itself, and not with ocean water, because of the traditional law (smṛti): "One should sip water that is non-saline and not hot. Nor is there a rule that the sipping must be done with the very same water used for bathing; for it is stated in the Taittirīya Śruti: "Therefore, they do not drink of the ocean. However, acts such as the *tarpaṇa* (libations) may be performed with that [ocean water], as there is no prohibition against it. This should be understood to apply likewise to bathing in a pool of hot water. In this context concerning sacred sites (*tīrtha*), Paiṭhīnasi says:
"He who goes for the sake of another obtains a sixteenth part [of the merit]."
He who goes there even by chance obtains half the fruit of a pilgrimage site.
Śaṅkha also says:
"He who, having reached a sacred ford, performs a bath there incidentally,
obtains the fruit arising from bathing, but not that which pertains to a pilgrimage."
For men who have committed sins, the holy place (tīrtha) shall bring about the pacification of those sins;
for men of pure soul, the holy place shall bestow the fruits as they have been described.
Vyāsa also says:
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame— he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha also says:
"If one causes his father, mother, brother, friend,
or teacher to perform the immersion, he shall receive a twelfth part of the merit."
Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"He who immerses an image made of kuśa grass in the waters of a sacred ford— indeed,
whoever is intended for that act shall receive one-eighth of the merit."
In this regard, the mantra is as follows:
"You are Kuśa grass; you are pure, fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times.
When you are bathed, he for whom this knot-binding is intended is truly bathed."
Thus ends the section on mantras for bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the secondary modes of bathing (*gauṇasnāna*);
regarding these, Garga says:
The divine, the aerial, the fiery, the pertaining to Brahmā, the pertaining to Sarasvatī,
and likewise the mental— thus should the sixfold secondary ablution (gauṇasnāna) be understood.

Yogayājñavalkya also says: "The seven types of ablution are, in order: that performed with mantras, that on the ground, as well as that with fire, that with air, the celestial, that with water, and the mental."
He [the author] himself states their characteristics:
"The ritual bath with mantras is performed with the hymns beginning 'āpo hi ṣṭhā'; the earthly bath is the touching of clay;
the fire-related bath is bathing with ashes; and the wind-related bath is declared to be [bathing with] the dust raised by cows."
That which occurs during a shower of rain is called divine bathing; immersion in water is Vāruṇa bathing; and the contemplation of Viṣṇu is Mānasa bathing.
Some wise men maintain that mental bathing is the most excellent,
since it was recited by Vyāsa in the praise of the sacred ford of the Self (ātmatīrtha).
In this regard, a specific detail is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The smearing of the body with sacred ash (*bhasman*) from the feet to the head is *āgneya*.
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"May the waters be auspicious to us," "The waters that dwell in the trees," "O Waters, you are most beneficent," and "The dispeller of sin"—
by these five mantras, the mantra-bath is declared.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"The dust of cows is said to be of Vāyu; when that [dust] reaches the Lord of Cows (the Sun), the bath attained through the Sarasvatī of the learned is remembered as the Sārasvata bath."

"Gopati" refers to the Sun; "sarasvatī" is the speech of the learned. The meaning is that which is obtained through her is called "Sārasvata. Vyāsa describes its nature: "One who knows [the ritual] should perform the bath for a twice-born person who has approached spontaneously with humility, as well as for a disciple and for a son."
May there be a bath for those who desire it, performed with jars made of gold from the Dakṣa lineage and with the waters of the Gaṅgā, accompanied by mantras and the auspicious rites of *puṇyāha*.
First, at Prabhāsa, where the waters possess many virtues, or at Madhyama Puṣkara, at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, together with Kanakhala, at Bhadrakarṇa, or at Gayā;
When the Moon is eclipsed by Rāhu while conjoined with the Sun,
through the special conjunction of these aforementioned sacred fords established throughout the three worlds, may my ritual bath be rendered complete and flawless.
"Having performed the bath at Sārasvata, one becomes joyful in mind;
for the speech of the learned is indeed purer than the ablution in all other sacred fords.
These secondary baths (gauṇasnāna) should be performed only when one is unable [to perform the primary ones]. This has been stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
When a state of impurity has arisen, one should perform only the ritual bath;
the wise have declared that when one lacks the capacity [for the full rite], there are baths such as the Brāhma and others.
Yogayājñavalkya also says: "When,
due to the defects of time or through incapacity, one is unable [to perform the ritual], then,
having learned it from the sages, the cleansing (mārjana) is indeed seen to be performed with mantras."
Jābāli also says:
"For those engaged in ritual acts who are unable to perform a full bath, the bath may be headless;
they know that wiping with a wet cloth constitutes the rite pertaining to the gods."
This is the *kāpila* bath. Regarding it, Bṛhaspati says:
"The cleansing of the body with a wet cloth is remembered as the *kāpila* [bath].
Thus ends the section on secondary baths in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the praise of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā).
Regarding this, Yogayājñavalkya says:
"Henceforth, I shall proclaim the definitive rule for the twilight worship."
By worshipping her, one is liberated from the sins committed during a day and night.
A Brahmin who is devoted to the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) in every situation does not fall from his Brahminhood, even if he has entered another birth.
Indeed, for the sake of purifying as many twice-born men on this earth as are established in improper occupations, the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) was created by the Self-existent One himself.
There are thirty crores of well-known Rākṣasas called Mandehas;
they rush toward the thousand-rayed sun as it rises day after day.
Day after day, they all desired to devour the sun;
therefore, a most terrible battle took place between the sun and them.
Then all the hosts of gods and the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
while performing their twilight devotions, daily cast water [into the fire].
Conjoined with the *brahmavyāhṛtis* and consecrated by the *gāyatrī*,
those Daityas were consumed by that water which had become like a thunderbolt.
Having understood this, he who, firm in his vows, performs the twilight devotions shall obtain a long life and be liberated from all sins.
He who performs that exclusive twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) partakes of merit;
but he who performs other rites while neglecting it incurs sin.
The twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) was worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara;
what excellent twice-born man desiring spiritual perfection would not worship that goddess?
Kaśyapa also says:
"Viṣṇu is the heart of Brahmā, and Śiva is remembered as the heart of Viṣṇu;
the Sandhyā is the heart of Śiva, and for that reason she should be worshipped by the best of the twice-born."
Thus concludes the praise of *saṃdhyā* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the word *saṃdhyā*. Regarding this, Dakṣa says:
"The junction of day and night, which is devoid of both the sun and the stars, is declared as *saṃdhyā* by the sages who perceive the truth.
The word "that *saṃdhyā*" implies that it is to be worshipped (*upāsyā*). For this very reason, Yogayājñavalkya states:
One should perform the twilight worship at the junction [of day and night], neither when the sun has set nor when it has risen.

The *Chandoga-śruti* also states: "The exponents of Brahman say: Why does a Brāhmaṇa perform the *saṃdhyā* at the junction of day and night? Why does a Brāhmaṇa sit down to perform the *saṃdhyā* in the evening? Why does he stand in the morning? What is the *saṃdhyā*? What is the time of the *saṃdhyā*? And what is the nature of the *saṃdhyā*? The gods and the Asuras contended with one another. Those Asuras rushed toward the Sun. That Sun was afraid; his heart remained in the form of a tortoise. He fled to Prajāpati, and Prajāpati saw this remedy for him: *Ṛta* (Cosmic Order) and *Satya* (Truth), Brahman, the syllable *Oṃ*, and the three-footed *Gāyatrī*—he saw these as the mouth of Brahman. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa performs the *saṃdhyā* at the junction of day and night. Beginning while there is still light (*sajyotiṣi*) until the appearance of [the next] light (*ā jyotiṣo darśanāt*), that is his time of *saṃdhyā*; that is the *saṃdhyā*; that is the nature of the *saṃdhyā*. In that he sits down to perform the *saṃdhyā* in the evening, by that he conquers the station of heroes. In that he stands in the morning, by that he conquers the heavenly world. Furthermore, when he employs water, those droplets become thunderbolts and strike away the Asuras. By this, it is stated that that which is to be meditated upon is the *saṃdhyā*. The meaning is that one should meditate beginning at the time when the sun is still visible (*sajyotiṣi*) until the appearance of the stars (*ā jyotiṣo darśanāt*). Thus says the *Nārasiṃha-purāṇa*:
Having performed the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) together with the sun according to the prescribed rule,
he should practice the Gāyatrī until the stars become visible.
Having commenced the morning twilight devotion while the stars are still visible, one should practice the Gāyatrī according to the rule for as long as the sun remains in view.
[354] Since there would otherwise be no fixed rule regarding the time "with the stars," Dakṣa states this for the purpose of establishing a restriction:
"The two nāḍīs at the end of the night are called the *kala* of the twilight;
its end is traditionally held by the wise to be upon the appearance of the sun's disc."
The meaning is that the time indicated by the sight of the sun's line is the end of the twilight (*saṃdhyā*). And that twilight has been described by Yogayājñavalkya:
"The morning twilight is Gāyatrī; the midday is remembered as Sāvitrī;
that which occurs as the evening twilight is to be known as Sarasvatī."
Vyāsa also says: "She who is named Gāyatrī in the forenoon, Sāvitrī at midday,
and Sarasvatī in the evening— she alone is remembered as the Saṃdhyā throughout the three periods."
Because she protects one from the defects of accepting gifts, from mortal sins, and from minor offenses, the Gāyatrī is so called; for she rescues him who sings her praises.
She is proclaimed as Sāvitrī because she is the radiance of Savitṛ;
she is Sarasvatī because she is the progenitor of the world and because she has speech as her form.
"He worships at the junction of night and day;
therefore, the wise call that very [junction] *saṃdhyā*.

Here, the sense is that through the mantra presided over by him, it is not contradictory for the object of its expression (*tatpratipādya*) also to possess the nature of being *Sāvitrī*. Therefore, it should be understood that Savitṛ alone—the one expressed by the three names beginning with Gāyatrī—is the *saṃdhyā*. And it is said in another Smṛti:
Gāyatrī is to be worshipped at dawn, Sarasvatī at evening, and Sāvitrī at midday, according to their different names.
Gāyatrī here is red, Sāvitrī is white in color, and Sarasvatī is likewise black; they are to be worshipped according to these distinctions of color.
Gāyatrī is indeed the form of Brahmā, Sāvitrī is the form of Rudra, and Sarasvatī is the form of Viṣṇu; she is to be worshipped according to these distinctions of form.
At sunrise, he is indeed of the form of Brahmā; at midday, he is Maheśvara;
and at sunset, he is of the form of Viṣṇu—the Sun-god is thus truly three-formed.
"Because one performs the worship at the junction of night and day,
the wise therefore call that very [time] 'saṃdhyā' (the junction)."

And here, *upāsana* means meditation (*dhyāna*), as seen in such passages as, "One should meditate on speech as Brahman," and "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman. The Taittirīya Śruti also states: "A learned Brāhmaṇa, performing his duties while meditating on the sun as it rises and as it sets, attains all that is auspicious; 'This sun is Brahman'—being thus [realized as] Brahman, he who knows this reaches Brahman. The meaning is that by meditating in due order during the three periods of time upon the sun—which is designated by the word *saṃdhyā*, endowed with the three names beginning with Gāyatrī, possessed of the three syllables, and consisting of the three forms—one reaches and attains Brahman. Therefore, Vyāsa says:
One should not perceive the Gāyatrī as distinct from Brahman; one should meditate upon it with the thought "I am that," by whatever method possible.
Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:

"Then, standing upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, being well-composed, and having performed the triple *prāṇāyāma*, one should meditate on the *saṃdhyā*; such is the sacred tradition (*śruti*)."
That which is the twilight (saṃdhyā) is the source of the universe, transcending illusion (māyā), indeed partless (niṣkalā);
she is the Lord (īśvara), the absolute power (kevalā śakti), endowed with the three principles (tattvatraya).
Having meditated upon Sāvitrī as situated within the orb of the sun, the wise man should indeed recite her mantra.
In this regard, the location for meditation is also shown in another Smṛti:
"He who meditates upon Gāyatrī as seated within the lotus of the heart, being liberated from both merit and demerit, attains the supreme goal. Thus it is said.

And by the injunction "one should thus worship the twilight," it is meant that one should worship—that is, meditate upon—the deity named Āditya, who is of the nature of Brahman, residing within the solar orb and possessing the form previously described, with the thought "I am He" (so 'ham asmi) in the heart. Therefore, it should be understood that in this context, worship alone is the primary element, while all other acts such as ritual cleansing (*mārjana*) and the like are merely subsidiary (*aṅga*). For this very reason, Yudhiṣṭhira and others, when intent on battle and unable to perform the practice along with its subsidiaries, performed the worship of Āditya alone, omitting all the ancillary parts. This was stated by Vyāsa: [The text continues with the verse: *“Even if one performs only the twilight worship, he is freed from all sins; what need is there to speak of him who performs the sacrifice?”* (MBh 12.208.9) Thus, it is established that the worship of Āditya is the principal rite, while the other acts are its auxiliaries. Furthermore, since the term *sandhyā* here denotes a deity, it cannot be taken in its literal sense as the "junction" between day and night. Nor can it be taken as referring to the recitation of mantras, for that would be redundant with the subsequent mention of *japa*. Consequently, the word *sandhyā* must be understood here as a synonym for the deity Āditya. It is for this reason that the commentator Śaṅkarācārya explains the passage as follows: "One should worship the deity named Āditya, who is of the nature of Brahman, residing within the solar orb. And in the *Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya* (3.3.32), he states: "In the case of the twilight worship, the word *sandhyā* refers to the deity, because it is impossible [to take it otherwise] in the context of the injunction to worship. Thus, the worship of the deity Āditya is the principal act, and the other elements are its subsidiaries. This is also supported by the fact that the *Sandhyā-vidhi* is mentioned in the *Gautama-dharma-sūtra* (2.10) alongside other rites such as bathing and *japa*, which indicates its status as a subordinate component of a larger ritual complex. Finally, the fact that the *Sandhyā-vidhi* is included among the daily obligatory duties (*nitya-karma*) confirms its essential character as a subsidiary act, as it is taught that the omission of even a single such duty results in sin. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal rite, and all other acts are its auxiliaries. This is further corroborated by the fact that the *Sandhyā-vidhi* is prescribed for all four castes (*varṇas*), whereas the *Sāvitrī-japa* is restricted to the three twice-born (*dvija*) classes. Since the former is common to all, it must be considered a subsidiary act, while the latter, being specific to the twice-born, is the principal rite. Thus, it is established that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and the other elements are its auxiliaries. This is also supported by the fact that the *Sandhyā-vidhi* is mentioned in the *Manu-smṛti* (4.94) as a duty to be performed at the three junctions of the day, which indicates its status as a regular, recurring obligation rather than a primary, independent rite. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. This is also supported by the fact that the *Sandhyā-vidhi* is mentioned in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* (1.28) as a duty to be performed before the morning meal, which indicates its status as a preparatory or introductory act rather than a primary, independent rite. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. This is also supported by the fact that the *Sandhyā-vidhi* is mentioned in the *Viṣṇu-smṛti* (66.1–5) as a duty to be performed with specific mantras, which indicates its status as a ritualized act rather than a simple, spontaneous meditation. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. This is also supported by the fact that the *Sandhyā-vidhi* is mentioned in the *Parāśara-smṛti* (2.23–24) as a duty to be performed with specific postures and gestures, which indicates its status as a formal, structured rite rather than a casual act of devotion. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. This is also supported by the fact that the *Sandhyā-vidhi* is mentioned in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* (27.1–3) as a duty to be performed with specific offerings and oblations, which indicates its status as a sacrificial act rather than a mere act of remembrance. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. This is also supported by the fact that the *Sandhyā-vidhi* is mentioned in the *Hārīta-smṛti* as a duty to be performed with specific purificatory rites, which indicates its status as a cleansing act rather than a creative act of visualization. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. This is also supported by the fact that the *Sandhyā-vidhi* is mentioned in the *Śātātapa-smṛti* as a duty to be performed with specific prayers and invocations, which indicates its status as a liturgical act rather than a silent contemplation. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. Therefore, it is concluded that the worship of Āditya is the principal act, and all other elements are its subsidiaries. "O Great King, having thus girded themselves at the front of the battle, they waited upon the thousand-rayed Sun as he had reached the twilight—that is, as he was setting. Thus it is said; "girded" (*daṃśita*) means "armed" (*saṃnaddha*). "Reached the twilight" (*saṃdhyāgata*) means "having reached the juncture," that is to say, "set. And so, as it has been stated by Yājñavalkya in the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
The syllable *oṃ*, the seven *vyāhṛtis*, the *gāyatrī* together with its head,
the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," the *drupadā*, and the *aghamarṣaṇa*.
One should perform the twilight rites with these [mantras] in their proper order: "ud u tyaṃ citram," "tac cakṣuḥ," and "tejo 'si," as well as the fourth foot of the Gāyatrī.

Thus, even in that case, there is no contradiction because the word *saṃdhyā* refers to the deity, [the sense being] that one should perform or worship the *saṃdhyā* by means of these mantras through the purification of the self.
Thus concludes the determination of the meaning of the term *saṃdhyā* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the morning *saṃdhyā*;
regarding this, Dakṣa says:

"Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, the twice-born, having performed the rules of purification, should perform the morning *saṃdhyā* preceded by the cleansing of the teeth. Here, the mention of "purification" (*śauca*) is intended to indicate bathing as well; otherwise, one would lack the qualification for the *saṃdhyā* and other rites. Thus, that same author says:
Without having bathed, a man who has risen from bed and is covered with saliva and sweat should not perform any rite whatsoever, such as recitation or fire-offerings.

Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "It is recorded in the Smṛtis that for men, there is no excellence in ritual acts without bathing, especially in the case of fire-offerings (*homa*) and recitation (*japa*); therefore, one should perform the bath."

[358] Herein is the procedure for the twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā*): having bathed and sipped water (*ācānta*) according to the rules, and having restrained the breaths (*prāṇāyāma*), one should form the resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the morning twilight ritual. Then, one should perform the sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the three verses beginning, "The waters indeed are most beneficent" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*). This has been stated by Yājñavalkya:
"Having restrained the breaths and sprinkled [the site] with the three verses whose deity is Water.
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"Sindhudvīpa is the seer, Gāyatrī is the meter, and the Waters (Āpas) are the deity."
And the application for the wiping is proclaimed as being addressed to the Waters (Abdaivatyam).

This knowledge of the ṛṣis and so forth is indeed necessary, for otherwise a fault is heard [in the scriptures]. Thus he himself says: "He who teaches or even recites [the Veda] without knowing the sage, the meter, the deity, and the application (yoga), becomes a sinner."
Yogayājñavalkya also says: "He who does not know the application, the meter, the seer, and the deity— these five regarding a mantra— does not enjoy its fruit."

Regarding the specific rule for the *mārjana* (sprinkling), Brahmā says: "One who is composed should perform the *mārjana* at the end of a *ṛc*, or at the end of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), or at the end of a triplet (*tṛca*); such is the opinion of the learned."
Yogayājñavalkya also says: "Restrained and pure, one should sprinkle water on the head with the three verses beginning with 'āpo hi ṣṭhā,' joined with nine *praṇavas*. [359]
Regarding this, Śaunaka states the specific result:
"By means of the *Āpo hi ṣṭhā* triplet joined with nine *praṇavas*,
the sin committed during one year is destroyed at the conclusion of the purification (*mārjana*)."
Vyāsa also says:
"One should perform the *mārjana* (sprinkling) with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* using water from *kuśa* grass;
joined with the *praṇava*, one should pour the water at every step."
"One who has conquered [the senses] should cast eight droplets upwards and downwards for the destruction of [impurities];
one should burn these nine defects—born of passion, darkness, and delusion; born of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; and born of speech, mind, and action—with these nine [breaths]. Thus it is said.

In this rite, when the sprinkling (*mārjana*) is to be performed for each foot of the verse, nine drops (*vipruṣaḥ*) are produced. Regarding that, the meaning of the mantra “*yasya kṣayāya jinvatha*” is that one should cast the drop downward. On this point, Hārīta states: “One should perform the acts of sprinkling, worship, the offering of oblations (*balikarma*), and eating with the *tīrtha* pertaining to the gods (*daiva*); the *daiva-tīrtha* is the tip of the fingers. Furthermore, that sprinkling must not be done with water falling from a stream. As Brahmā says:
“The twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsti*) performed with water falling from a stream is censured;
neither the ancestors nor the deities praise it.”
On this point, he himself states the reason: "Since water purified by mantra, consecrated with the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* hymn, falls upon an impure place, one should therefore avoid it. [360] Thus.
When it is asked, "How then is the cleansing performed?", he himself says: "At a river crossing, or in a lake, or in a vessel made of clay,
or one of udumbara wood, or gold, silver, wood, or bamboo."
"Or, having placed [water] in the left hand, one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsti*).
The phrase "having placed water" implies "in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood or copper. And thus, it is as stated:
"Those who perform the twilight worship having placed water in the left hand..."
That twilight should be known as a Vṛṣalī; by her, the Asuras were gratified.

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to the presence of vessels made of clay and other materials. Having cleansed himself according to the aforementioned rule, one should drink water with the mantra "Sūryaś ca. Regarding this, Bodhāyana says: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana). Having gone to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), being pure, having bathed, and having washed his hands and feet, he should sip water (ācamana) and, having drunk water in the evening with the mantra 'Agniś ca mā manyuś ca,' and in the morning with 'Sūryaś ca mā manyuś ca,' he becomes pure after sprinkling himself with water using his hand provided with a ring of *kuśa* grass (*sapavitreṇa pāṇinā*), with the *surabhimatī*, *ābliṅga*, *vāruṇī*, *hiraṇyavarṇā*, *pāvamānī*, and *vyāhṛti* verses, and with other purificatory texts. The two mantras "Agniś ca" and "Sūryaś ca" are recited in the Yajurveda. For the mantra "Sūryaś ca," the meter (*chandas*) is *prakṛti*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Agni, the deities (*devatā*) are Sūrya, Manyu, and Manyupati, and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the morning twilight sipping of water. The *surabhimatī* is "Dadhikrāvṇaḥ. Its seer is Vāmadeva, the meter is *anuṣṭubh*, the deity is Dadhikrāvā, and its application is in cleansing (*mārjana*). The *ābliṅga* verses are those beginning with "Āpo hi ṣṭhā. The *hiraṇyavarṇā* verses consist of the four: "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," "Yāsāṃ rājā," "Yāsāṃ devāḥ," and "Śivena mā. Their meter is *triṣṭubh*, the seer is Agni, the deity is Water, and their application is in cleansing. However, for the followers of the Sāmaveda (*chandogānām*), the two mantras for sipping water are stated by Gautama: "May the Day and the Sun purify me"—this in the morning; "May the Night and Varuṇa purify me"—this in the evening. These two Yajus formulas were seen by Prajāpati. The deities are indicated by the words of the mantras themselves (*liṅgokte devate*). Viṣṇu, however, states a specific rule regarding the twilight sipping of water.
Standing in the water above the knees while wearing dry clothes, one who performs the twilight *ācamana* shall be pure; otherwise, he is considered impure.

"After the twilight rinsing of the mouth, Nārāyaṇa, having touched the consecrated water, should perform the sprinkling (*mārjana*) upon his head with *darbha* grass using the *sūkta* beginning with 'āpo hi ṣṭhā' through the mouth of Brahmā. Thus it is said.
The syllable *oṃ* is to be praised. It is also stated by Manu that it is the mouth of Brahman:
"The three great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, and the three-footed *gāyatrī*—this should be known as the mouth of Brahman. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that, having touched water with that [hand], one should perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with *darbha* grass using the hymn (*sūkta*) beginning with "āpo hiṣṭhā. That hymn consists of nine verses. Regarding this, Bhṛgu states:
"In the nine verses of 'āpo hiṣṭhā,' Sindhudvīpa is remembered as the seer (*ṛṣi*).
Seven of the verses have the Waters as their deity (*abdaivatyā*), and they are all in the *gāyatrī* meter; two are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter."
Regarding the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), Kātyāyana also states:
"One should perform the sprinkling of the head with *kuśa* grass and drops of water;
the *praṇava*, the *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, and the *gāyatrī* as the third."
And the third verse addressed to the Waters (abdaivata) as the fourth—this is the ritual purification (mārjana).
After the cleansing, the Brahmā (the practitioner) should place his hand, filled with water, at the tip of his nose;
having recited "Ṛtam ca," he should then cast that water upon the ground.
Yama also says: Having taken water in his hand, he should mutter the verse prescribed in his own Vedic branch;
then, with the vital breath restrained, he should hold it at the tip of his nose.
"Whoever, being self-restrained, should thus mutter the *drupadā* mantra three times daily, no sins shall remain in the body of that twice-born man.
Thereafter, one should present the *arghya* offering to the Sun; and so Vyāsa says:
Taking water in both hands and consecrating it with the Gāyatrī mantra,
one should stand facing the sun and then throw it upwards three times.

Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule: "Water consecrated with the Sāvitrī mantra and mixed with flowers"—the ellipsis being that one should cast it with the hollowed palms (*añjali*). Nārāyaṇa, however, mentions a different mantra for the offering of the *arghya*:
"Having formed the *añjali* with both hands and filled it with water, being composed, one should cast that water upon the ground with the mantra 'ud u tyam'."
[363] Then, having turned clockwise, one should touch water. This is stated in the *Vāmanapurāṇa*:
"In the evening, having performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) with mantras and having sprinkled [water], [one offers] a handful (*añjali*) to the Sun.
There is also a Vedic text: "In that they proceed clockwise, by that they shake off evil."
Having risen and offered water toward the sun with three handfuls of water,
he should immediately thereafter worship it with the two verses beginning with "uccitram."
The wise say that this worship is to be performed at both twilights;
it consists of a triad: the Praṇava, the three Vyāhṛtis, and the Sāvitrī.
Also in another Smṛti:
"Having performed the worship with the hymns *ud u tyam*, *citram*, and *tat cakṣuḥ* three times always at both twilights, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī to the Sun."

The meters for these [verses] are, in order, *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *uṣṇih*; the seers (*ṛṣi*) are, in order, Praskaṇva, Kutsa, and Vasiṣṭha; the deity is Sūrya; and their application (*viniyoga*) is in the worship of Sūrya. Then, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and meditated upon the *saṃdhyā*, one should worship the Sun immediately after the recitation of the *gāyatrī*. This is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Having sipped water according to the mantra, and having again sipped water while restraining speech, one should purify oneself with *kuśa* grass and drops of water while reciting the mantras."
With the *āpohiṣṭhā* verses, the *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*, and the auspicious *vāruṇa* hymns,
as well as the *gāyatrī*— the mother of the Vedas— joined with the *oṃkāra* and the *vyāhṛtis*.
Having recited [the mantra], one should offer handfuls of water toward the Sun with the mind fixed on Him;
then, remaining well-composed, one should stand upon Darbha grass whose tips point toward the east.
"Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should meditate upon the Sandhyā; such is the Vedic revelation.
That which is the Sandhyā is the source of the universe, indeed beyond Māyā and stainless."
The Lord is pure Power, arising from the three principles;
having meditated upon Sāvitrī as situated within the solar orb, the wise man should indeed recite her mantra.
A learned man, standing facing the east and being self-restrained, should constantly recite the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times at most, a hundred times in the middle, or ten times at the least.
Then, with a concentrated mind, he should worship the rising sun with various solar mantras derived from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.

This refers to the intention of the mantras studied in one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*), because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "One should perform the worship (*upasthāna*) of the Sun with the mantras belonging to one's own [branch]. Therefore, for those belonging to the Yajurveda branch, the worship is performed with these three: "Of Mitra," "Mitra, who impels men," and "O gracious Mitra. Of these, the first is a *gāyatrī* and the latter two are *triṣṭubh*s; the Viśvedevas are the seers (*ṛṣi*), Mitra is the deity (*devatā*), and their application (*viniyoga*) is in the worship of the Sun. The same should be understood for others as well. Bodhāyana, however, prescribes the daily worship at the conclusion of the silent recitation (*japa*): "In this very manner, standing facing the east in the morning, one worships the Day with the two verses addressed to Mitra: 'Of Mitra, the supporter of the people,' and 'Mitra, who impels men. Regarding this, there is a Purāṇic passage:
"At twilight, one should salute one's own feet as well as the earth;
thus a man always obtains long life, knowledge, and health.
Yama states the fruit for one who acts in this manner:
Those who constantly perform the twilight devotions with firm vows,
being cleansed of all sins, go to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Atri also says:
"But that twice-born man who performs the twilight devotions with faith according to the rule—
for him there is nothing unattainable in the three worlds."
Also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"The Brāhmaṇas, whose minds were focused on no other, who were peaceful and had mastered the Vedas,
attained the supreme goal after worshipping the Sandhyā according to the prescribed rules."
Furthermore, the fault in not performing [the twilight devotions] has been shown by Dakṣa:
"One who is devoid of the twilight devotions is eternally impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever other rite he performs, he shall not partake of its fruit."
Even Gobhila says:
"He by whom the twilight has not been understood and the twilight has not been worshipped shall remain a Śūdra while living and,
upon death, is reborn as a dog."
Manu also says:
"But he who does not stand during the morning [twilight] and does not worship during the evening [twilight] should be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra."
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa as well:
"O King, those evil-minded ones who do not attend upon the morning or the evening twilight go to the Tāmisra hell."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa as well:
"O best of the twice-born, he who performs other religious duties elsewhere while neglecting the salutation of the Sandhyā goes to ten thousand hells."
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa as well:
"Therefore, one must not neglect the rite of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana);
for he who does not perform the worship at twilight slays the Sun."
All of this applies to one who is not in distress. For this very reason, the *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
"But that Brahmin who abandons [the fire] while not in distress is equal to a Śūdra;
he must undergo penance and becomes censured in the world."
Atri also says:
Those twice-born who, while in good health, do not attend upon the two twilights,
those sinful ones always injure the blessed Sun.
For those twice-born ones who revile the Sun, the unsurpassed gateway to liberation—
how can the attainment of liberation ever come to those twice-born?
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa as well:
"Attendance at the two twilights is required for kings at all times,
except in cases of birth-impurity, ritual impurity, confusion, illness, or fear."

"Vibhrama" means confusion. The meaning is that there is no fault even in not performing the *saṃdhyā* when one lacks the capacity for such tasks and so forth. However, regarding the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) and similar states, Marīci states that even if one has the capacity, the *saṃdhyopāsana* must not be performed: "During the period of impurity, the abandonment of rituals such as the *saṃdhyā* is prescribed.
As for that which was stated by Pulastya:
One should perform the twilight prayers, the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, the *caru* oblation, and the fire-offering throughout one's entire life;
one must not abandon them even during a period of impurity (*sūtaka*), for by abandoning them, one goes to a lower state.
This refers to the intention of the mental *saṃdhyā*; for he himself has said:
"During both birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), a twice-born man should not abandon the *saṃdhyā* rite;
he should mentally recite the mantras, except for the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*)."

And thus, those passages which prohibit the performance of *saṃdhyā* rites during periods of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and the like should be understood as prohibiting the employment of verbal mantras. As for what was stated by Paiṭhīnasi—"During *sūtaka*, having offered a handful of water with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, having circumambulated, and meditating on the Sun, one should pay homage"—that too is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the entire *saṃdhyā* ritual; it has the same meaning as the phrase "the *saṃdhyā* sacrifice" (*saṃdhyām iṣṭim*). Alternatively, the intention should be understood as follows: only that which belongs to the *saṃdhyā* rite and is prescribed in the Śruti—such as the offering of the handful of water (*añjalidāna*) and so forth—is to be performed here, and nothing else. Whatever has been stated in this regard is to be accepted. On this point, Śātātapa says:
[368] But that twilight devotion which is devoid of darbha grass, that gift which is without water,
and that recitation which is uncounted— all that shall be useless.
Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Facing the east and wearing the sacred thread (*pavitra*), one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*).
Thus ends the section on the morning twilight worship in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the greatness of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
Manu says:
"Even three breath controls, performed according to the rules by a Brāhmaṇa..."
Combined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, this should be known as the supreme austerity.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burnt away when they are being smelted,
so too are the defects of the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava,
performed day after day, purify even the slayer of a learned Brahmin within a month.
Yama also says:
"By fourteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) joined with ten *praṇavas*, one is released even from the murder of a Brahmin; how much more so from other sins?"
Vyāsa says: For those who always recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras, no fear exists anywhere.
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"Whoever should recollect these seven vyāhṛtis during the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama),
by him the entire universe of the seven worlds becomes worshipped."
And in all the worlds, one gains the power to act according to one's will.
Vyāsa also says: "The Brahman consisting of sixteen syllables is known as the head of the Gāyatrī;
by reciting it even once, a wise man is liberated from the cycle of existence."
Thus concludes the greatness of *prāṇāyāma* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for *prāṇāyāma*; regarding this, Yogayājñavalkya states:
Having thus performed the cleansing that effects external purity,
one should then practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the sake of internal purification.
Saṃvarta also says: "Purified by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one should then recite the Gāyatrī.
Breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) is the expansion and restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa). When it is asked what its characteristics are, Manu says:
"Having restrained the breath, one should recite three times the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras; that is called Prāṇāyāma.
Here, the Vyāhṛtis are the seven beginning with Bhūḥ and ending with Satya.
The seven vyāhṛtis are declared to be recited constantly during breath control (prāṇāyāma):
bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, mahaḥ, janaḥ, tapaḥ, and likewise satyam.
Thus, from the *Yogayājñavalkya-smṛti*: "And here, the head [is addressed] with the Yajurvedic mantra 'Om āpo jyotiḥ'. For it is recorded by Vyāsa:

"This mantra 'Om āpo jyotiḥ' indeed belongs to the Taittirīyas. By the phrase "together with the *praṇava*," he indicates the conjunction of the *praṇava* in all nine [levels], beginning with *bhūḥ*. And so says the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, mahaḥ, janaḥ, tapaḥ, and likewise satyam;
these, joined with the syllable Om, as well as that "pada" of Savitṛ.
"One should employ the mantra *oṃ āpo jyotiḥ* at the back of the head;
through the practice of repeating it three times, it is designated as *prāṇāyāma*.
Thus, the syllable *oṃ* should also be understood here at the beginning of the mantra. And so says Yama:
O scorcher of foes, one should likewise mutter the seven vyāhṛtis preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, together with the *śiras* and the *gāyatrī*; this is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
"He should mutter [it] mentally"—this is the remainder [of the statement]. And likewise, Saṃvarta says:
"A twice-born man should always recite the seven Vyāhṛtis joined with the Praṇava, together with the Sāvitrī and the Śiras, three times mentally."

Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says: "Having remembered the seat of the consort (badhvāsana), the restraints (niyama), and the vital breaths (prāṇa), as well as the Ṛṣi and so forth, one should practice prāṇāyāma with eyes closed and observing silence."
In this context, the posture (*āsana*) should be understood as one of the types beginning with *svastika*. Furthermore, the *ārṣa* (seer) and other details have been stated here by Vyāsa:
"Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the *praṇava*, and its meter (*chanda*) is indeed the *gāyatrī*;
Agni is the deity (*deva*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the commencement of all rites."
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"The seer for all the vyāhṛtis is Prajāpati;
their meters are gāyatrī, uṣṇih, anuṣṭubh, bṛhatī, and paṅkti."
The Triṣṭubh and the Jagatī—these indeed are the seven meters;
likewise, Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, Bṛhaspati, and the Waters.
Indra and the Viśvedevas are declared to be the deities;
and their application is declared to be in the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
That [gāyatrī] which has Savitṛ as its deity, Agni as its mouth, and three feet,
whose seer is Viśvāmitra and whose meter is gāyatrī— that one is preeminent.
The application (viniyoga), however, is for the purpose of offering oblations (upasthāna) as well as for breath control (prāṇāyāma);
this is the mantra that is proclaimed as "Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ."
For that [yajus], Prajāpati is the seer; it is devoid of both ṛc and chandas.
"Brahmā, Vāyu, and Sūrya are declared to be the presiding deities;
this is indeed stated to be their application in the regulation of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the vyāhṛtis, however, Brahmā has stated a distinction among the seers (ṛṣis).
"Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, then Gautama, the sage Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa, in due order.
[372] And that breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is to be known as having three characteristics: inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka). Thus says the Yogayājñavalkya:
Inhalation, retention, and exhalation constitute the threefold prāṇāyāma.
He himself stated their characteristics:
"The inhalation drawn through the nose is called *pūraka* (filling)."
"Kumbhaka is motionless breath; when it is being emptied, it is recaka.
Regarding kumbhaka, Atri states the specific detail:
"The wise are able to effect restraint [of the breath] from the tips of the hair to the tips of the nails."
"From cessation wind is born, and from wind fire is born;
from fire water is born, and by these three, one is purified within.
Regarding this, Yogayājñavalkya states the specific distinction between *pūraka* (inhalation) and *recaka* (exhalation):
Having diligently drawn in with the nostrils all the air situated outside, one should completely fill all the channels; that is called *pūraka*, the great restraint (*mahānirodha*).
"One should slowly release the breath through the nostrils, but not with force;
one should not cause the body to tremble—that yogi is considered supreme. Thus says Vyāsa on this point.
One should meditate on Kaṃ, who is red in color, situated in the navel-lotus by means of inhalation (pūraṇa);
and one should meditate on Janārdana, who has the luster of a blue lotus, in the heart-lotus by means of retention (kumbhaka).
One should also meditate upon Śiva, white and located on the forehead, by means of exhalation (recaka);
he resembles pure crystal, is stainless, and is the destroyer of sins.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states the result:
"One should meditate on Prajāpati as red, Viṣṇu as having the luster of a blue lotus, and Śaṅkara Tryambaka as white; by so meditating, one is released from bondage."
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"Through *kumbhaka* one attains union with Viṣṇu; through *pūraka*, proximity to Brahmā;
and by the third, *recaka*, one may attain the state of the Lord."
Here, Brahmā says:
One should place the *vyāhṛtis* in sequence upon the feet, the knees, the shanks, the abdomen, the throat, the mouth, and likewise the head.
Having placed *bhūḥ* on the two thumbs,
the wise one should place *bhuvaḥ* on the two index fingers, and assign the word *svaḥ* to the two middle fingers.

Having performed the ritual placement on the hands (kara-nyāsa), one should commence the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa). Having placed the word "Bhūḥ" upon the heart, one should place "Bhuvaḥ" upon the head.
"Having placed the word *svaḥ* on the crest (*śikhā*), one should place that same word on the armor (*kavaca*).
Having placed the word *bharga* on the two eyes, one should place the word *dhiyaḥ* in the cardinal and intermediate directions. Thus it is said.
Then follows the placement on all limbs (*sarvāṅganyāsa*) with: *oṃ āpo jyotiḥ*.

"One should place the head upon all the limbs during the supreme breath-control (prāṇāyāma)," according to the traditional teaching of Vyāsa. Yājñavalkya states the fruit for one who acts in this manner:
"Having performed three breath-controls at the rising of the sun..."
Being stainless, they go to heaven, just as virtuous people who have performed good deeds do.
Saṃvarta also says:
"Whether it be mental or verbal sin, or that which is committed by the body itself—
all that is quickly destroyed when three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) have been performed."
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, the procedure for breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the nature of the object of meditation (dhyeya-svarūpa).

It has been stated immediately after the description of *prāṇāyāma* that one should meditate upon the *saṃdhyā*. Regarding the nature of that which is to be meditated upon (*dhyeya*), Gobhila says: "In the morning, Gāyatrī is situated within the sun; she is red in color, a maiden, holding a rosary in her hand, mounted upon a swan-throne, having Brahmā as her deity, and reciting the *Ṛgveda*. At midday, Sāvitrī is situated in the center of the sun; she is white in color, in the prime of youth, three-eyed, holding a trident in her hand, mounted upon a bull-throne, having Rudra as her deity, and reciting the *Yajurveda*. In the evening, Sarasvatī is situated in the center of the sun; she is dark in color, an old woman, four-armed, holding a discus in her hand, mounted upon a Garuda-throne, having Viṣṇu as her deity, and reciting the *Sāmaveda*. The remainder of the sense is that one should thus invoke these [forms] in sequence during all three periods of time. This is stated in the *Gāyatrīnirṇaya*.
[375] One should likewise visualize Gāyatrī as a young maiden, not aged, possessing three eyes and four faces,
capable, clad in red garments, and holding a rosary.
The goddess Brahmāṇī, who holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), is seated upon a swan vehicle;
she has Brahmā as her presiding deity and dwells in the world of Brahmā.
One should invoke her with the mantra as she arrives from the solar orb;
thus, at the midday twilight, one likewise invokes Sāvitrī in her youthful form.
She has white limbs and wears white garments; she is mounted upon a bull and possesses three eyes.
Holding a trident and a *ḍamaru* drum in her hands, she is Rudrāṇī, whose deity is Rudra.
Thus, at the evening twilight, one should meditate upon Sarasvatī in her aged state as she approaches from the solar orb toward the goddess whose abode is Kailāsa.
She is black in color, beautiful in form, and four-armed;
she holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and has Viṣṇu as her presiding deity.
"Her dwelling at Badarī-āśrama, she comes from the solar orb.
However, the *Yogayājñavalkya* mentions a reversal of the colors:
"Gāyatrī becomes white; Sāvitrī is of a pale-white color."
"Kṛṣṇā Sarasvatī is to be known; she is declared to be the three junctions (saṃdhyās).
Thus, it is meant that one should meditate upon Saṃdhyā as residing within the solar orb or as dwelling in the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka). And it has been stated by Yogayājñavalkya:
"Likewise, [one should meditate on her] as residing within the solar orb and as having gone to the world of Brahmā."
"Having invoked the auspicious Goddess, who holds a rosary and is seated upon a lotus throne, according to the rule with this Yajurvedic mantra, *tejo 'si* (You are splendor)," so it is said.
*Tejo 'si* is a mantra belonging to the Vājasaneyins; however, Vyāsa mentions a different mantra.
And one should invoke Gāyatrī, the destroyer of all sins:
"Come, O Goddess, granter of boons; be present for my recitation."
Because you protect one who sings, you are declared to be Gāyatrī.
Gobila also says:
"Come, O boon-granting goddess, three-syllabled one, expounder of Brahman;
O Mother of the meters, O Source of Brahman, homage be to you!"
Śaunaka also says: "The invocation and likewise the dismissal are prescribed in the Taittirīya [Saṃhitā].

Therein, the mantra for invocation is: "May the boon-granting Goddess come. Its meter is Gāyatrī; the seers are the Viśvedevas; the deity is Śukra; its application is in the invocation of Gāyatrī. Having thus invoked her, one should meditate in the heart upon the Goddess who is named Āditya, designated by the word *saṃdhyā*, consisting of Brahman, and endowed with the aforementioned names and so forth, thinking, "I am she. This has been stated by Vyāsa:
"One should not treat the Gāyatrī as distinct from Brahman;
one should worship it with the thought 'I am she,' by whatever method is prescribed.

All of this has been demonstrated in the determination of the meaning of the word *saṃdhyā*. Then, having approached her with the fourth foot of the Gāyatrī, one should mutter [the mantra]. That too has been stated by that very same [author]:
Her fourth state, however, is established in the state of Śiva-Brahman;
having approached it with the fourth [state], one should recite her mantra with a concentrated mind.

The fourth foot is "paro rajasi sāvadom," consisting of eight syllables. Its seer (ṛṣi) is Vimala; its meter (chandas) is the Turīya; its deity (devatā) is the Supreme Self (paramātman); and its application (viniyoga) is for liberation (mokṣa).
Thus ends the determination of the nature of the object of meditation in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the majesty of Gāyatrī.
In this regard, Yama says: "The Lord weighed the Gāyatrī and the Vedas on a scale;
on one side were the four Vedas, together with their auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) and their word-for-word sequences (padakrama)."
And on one side is the Gāyatrī; she is remembered as being of equal form.
Manu also says: "Prajāpati milked out from the three Vedas the syllable 'a', the syllable 'u', and the syllable 'm', as well as [the words] 'bhūr', 'bhuvaḥ', and 'svar'."
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that [first] quarter of this Sāvitrī verse, beginning with the word "tat."

Śaṅkha also says: "There is nothing superior to the *aghamarṣaṇa* for recitation while submerged in water; nothing superior to the *vyāhṛtis* for the fire-oblation (*homa*); and nothing superior to the *sāvitrī* for silent recitation (*japa*). Brahmā also says: "There is no recitation superior to the *gāyatrī*;
there is no austerity superior to the *gāyatrī*; there is no meditation superior to the *gāyatrī*; and there is no oblation superior to the *gāyatrī*."
Vyāsa also says:
"If it is recited ten times, whatever sin has been committed over three days, that sin is swiftly dispelled; there is no need for deliberation on this point."
When recited a hundred times, that goddess is known as the pacifier of the flood of sins;
when recited a thousand times, that goddess is the destroyer of secondary offenses.
By a hundred thousand recitations, it likewise destroys great sins;
by ten million recitations, O King of Kings, one shall obtain whatever one desires.
Whether it be the state of a yakṣa or a vidyādhara, or even the state of a gandharva;
or else the status of a deity, or a kingdom on the earth with its thorns removed.
Manu also says:
"He who studies this day by day for three years without sloth,
becomes like the wind and, possessing his own form, attains the state of Brahman."

Vyāsa also says: "The Gāyatrī destroys the sin produced in ten lifetimes by [recitation] a hundred times, and that which was committed in the past threefold [in number] by a thousand [times]. Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the majesty of the Gāyatrī in the Smṛticandrikā; now its seer (ārṣa) and other attributes are stated: therein, Brahmā is the seer.
The meter is Gāyatrī; Savitṛ is recorded as the deity of the Gāyatrī;
the color is white, the mouth is Agni, and Viśvāmitra is likewise the seer.
The three Vedas are the head and the crest-lock, Rudra and Viṣṇu are the heart;
its application is for worship, and the lineage is Sāṅkhyāyana.
"The three worlds are to be known as her feet, and the earth indeed as her belly;
having meditated upon Gāyatrī in this manner, one should recite her twelve-syllabled form. Thus it is said.

In the *Gāyatrīkalpa*, however, the seer (*ārṣa*) and other details for each foot of this [mantra] are stated as follows: "For the verse beginning *tat savituḥ*, the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī; the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Viśvāmitra; the deity (*devatā*) is Brahmā. For the verse beginning *bhargo devasya*, the meter is Gāyatrī; the seer is Viśvāmitra; the deity is Viṣṇu. For the verse beginning *dhiyo yo naḥ*, the meter is Gāyatrī; the seer is Viśvāmitra; the deity is Rudra.
