As for all the syllables (*akṣara*), Prajāpati is the seer; the meter is Gāyatrī; the application (*viniyoga*) is in the ritual placement upon the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*); and the deities should be understood as those spoken by Brahmā."
The first of them belongs to Agni, the second to Vāyu;
the third has the Sun as its deity, and likewise the fourth is of lightning.
The fifth is said to have Yama as its deity, the sixth is called Vāruṇa;
the seventh is Bārhaspatya, and they know the eighth to be Pārjanya.
The ninth is declared to be Aindra, and the tenth is remembered as Gāndharva;
the eleventh is declared to be Pauṣṇa, and likewise the twelfth is Śaiva.
The thirteenth is declared to be that of Tvaṣṭṛ, the fourteenth that of Vāsava,
the fifteenth that of the Maruts, and the sixteenth is remembered as that of Soma.
The seventeenth is that of Aṅgiras; after that, the Vaiśvadeva;
the nineteenth is the Āśvina, and the twentieth is the Prājāpatya.
The twenty-first syllable is said to consist of all the gods;
the twenty-second should be known as Raudra, and beyond that is the Brāhma.

"The Vaiṣṇava [mantra] consists of twenty-four [syllables]; these are the deities of the syllables. By meditating upon them at the time of recitation, one attains union (sāyujya) with them. Thus [ends the section on the deities]. Now, the principles of the syllables (akṣara-tattva).
Therefore, I shall explain the principles, specifically those of the syllables:
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
Smell, taste, and form, touch, and sound, as well as speech;
the two hands, the generative organ, the anus, and furthermore the ear, the skin, and the two eyes.

"The tongue, the nose, the mind, the principle of *ahaṃkāra*, as well as the *mahat* and the three *guṇas*—this is the determination of the principles (*tattvas*) in their respective order. [381] Now, the powers (*śaktis*) of the syllables are also as follows: "Sahā, Nityā, Viśvahṛdayā, Vilāsinī, Prabhāvatī, Lolā, Śāntā, Kānti, Durgā, Sarasvatī, Viṣṇurūpā, Viśālā, Īśā, Āpyāyinī, Vimalā, Tamo’pahāriṇī, Hiraṇyarūpā, Sūkṣmā, Viśvayoni, Jayāvahā, Padmālayā, Varā, Śobhā, and Gadārūpā—these are the powers."
Thus ends the determination of the *ārṣa* and other [factors] in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for *nyāsa*.

First, one should perform the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) with the *astra-mantra*. Then, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the *gāyatrī*, one should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) preceded by the placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), because this is common to all mantras. Regarding this, the placement of the limbs has been shown by Vyāsa.
Having placed "tat savituḥ" upon the heart, one should place "vareṇyam" upon the throat;
then one should place the section beginning with "bhargo devasya" upon the crest-lock (śikhā).
One should place "dhīmahi" on the mouth, and "dhiyo yo naḥ" on the two eyes;
the word "pracodayāt" should be employed for the purpose of the weapon-mantra (astra).
The wise one should place that word on the two ring fingers;
*bhargaḥ* on the two little fingers; and the word *dhiyaḥ* in the middle of the palms.
Having placed *oṃ bhūḥ* at the heart, one should place *oṃ bhuvaḥ* on the head;
having placed *oṃ svaḥ* on the crest-lock, one should [place] the first foot of the Gāyatrī.
The wise one should perform the placement for the armor (kavaca); he should place the second [syllable] on the two eyes;
with the third, he should perform the placement of the weapon (astra); and the fourth he should place everywhere.
In this regard, O twice-born one, Brahmā says: the practitioner should place the syllable *ta* on his own two big toes;
the syllable *sa* on the region of the ankles; and the syllable *vi* on the two shanks.
Know that one should place the syllable *tu* on the two knees, the syllable *va* on the region of the thighs,
the syllable *re* on the secret organ, and the syllable *ṇi* on the testicles.
The wise one should place the syllable *yaṃ* at the region of the hips, the syllable *bha* in the circle of the navel, the syllable *go* in the abdomen, and the syllable *de* on the breasts.
Having placed the syllable *va* in the heart, the syllable *sy* in the throat,
the syllable *dhī* in the mouth, and the syllable *ma* in the middle of the palate;
One should place the syllable *hi* at the tip of the nose, the syllable *dhi* upon the two eyes,
the syllable *yo* between the eyebrows, and the second syllable on the forehead.
One should place the syllable *na* on the eastern face, the syllable *pra* on the southern face,
the syllable *u* on the northern face, and the syllable *da* on the western face.
"One should place the syllable *yāṃ* on the head, which is the all-pervading Lord.
In this context, all mantras end with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and with *namaḥ*. Thus says Bhṛgu:
"Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, one should then [utter] the seed-syllable of the mantra."
"The placement [of mantras] consisting of the name followed by 'namas' at the end is proclaimed as *japanyāsa*.
Thereafter, one should perform the meditation on the syllables (*varṇadhyāna*). Regarding this, Brahmā said:
'And having performed such a complete nyāsa, which destroys all sins...'"
"Afterwards, one should practice meditation endowed with color and form.
This too was stated by that same [author]:
"That [form] is the color of a campaka flower, yellow, and consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva."
One should meditate upon him as peaceful, seated in the lotus posture, established in his own place.
One should contemplate the syllable *sakāra*, dark blue like an *atasī* flower,
situated in the center of a lotus, gentle, and the destroyer of minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
The best of the twice-born should constantly meditate upon the tranquil Piṅgala, who is seated upon a lotus throne and is the destroyer of great sins.
The wise one should contemplate the syllable TUḤ, possessing a luster like sapphire;
it shall utterly consume all suffering arising from the influence of the planets.
The wise practitioner should meditate upon the syllable *va*, which has the brilliance of a blazing fire;
the sin committed by killing a fetus perishes at that very moment.
One should meditate on the letter *re* as stainless, resembling pure crystal;
by this, the sin arising from approaching those who should not be approached is quickly destroyed.
The yogi should contemplate the syllable ṆI, radiant with the flashing of lightning;
the sin born of consuming what is unfit for consumption perishes at that very moment.
One should meditate upon the syllable *yaṃ*, which has the color of a star, is adorned with the moon as its crest-jewel,
grants boons to yogins, and destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having meditated upon the syllable *bha*, which is black in color and possesses a luster like a dark cloud,
the twice-born destroys sins such as the killing of a human being.
One should visualize the syllable *rgo*, red in color and seated upon a lotus throne,
destroying the sins committed through the slaughter of cows and other such acts.
The yogi should constantly meditate upon the syllable *dekāra*, dark green like an emerald and seated upon a lotus throne; by this, even the sin of killing a woman is utterly consumed.
By meditating on the syllable *va*, which is white in color and possesses a radiance like the *jātī* flower,
one instantly burns away the sin committed by killing a preceptor.
Likewise, by meditating upon the yellow syllable *syakāra*, which has a radiance like gold,
a person burns away the sins conceived in the mind.
One should meditate upon the syllable *dhī*, white and radiant like a kunda flower;
one is liberated from the sin of killing one's father or mother—of this there is no doubt.
One should contemplate the letter MA, glowing like a ruby and blazing with splendor;
the sins accumulated in previous births perish at that very moment.
The wise one should constantly meditate upon the syllable *hīṃ*, which is the color of a conch shell, possesses a radiance equal to the full moon, and burns away all sins without exception.
One should meditate upon the white Dhikāra seated upon a lotus;
by its mere remembrance, the sin committed through accepting gifts is destroyed.

O bull among sages, having meditated upon the syllable *yo*, which is red in color and resembles a cochineal insect, one shall burn away the sin of killing living beings. And that second *yo* which has been described is like gold in appearance.
It burns away all sins and one is not tainted by other evils;
first, the syllable *na* is like the face [of the deity], resembling the rising sun.
Having meditated even once upon Him who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, whose face is turned toward the south, that best of the twice-born shall go to the divine abode.
Having meditated upon it once, that best of the twice-born shall go to the state of Īśvara;
[he should meditate on] the syllable Oṃ, which is gentle, yellow as gorocana, and facing north.
Having meditated upon it even once, that best of the twice-born shall indeed go to the station of Viṣṇu—
the syllable *da*, which resembles a conch, a kunda flower, and the moon, and which faces the west.
Having meditated upon it even once, that best of the twice-born shall go to the abode of Brahmā;
the head is said to be the *yātkāra*, resembling four faces.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra bestow their fruits directly; such is the established truth.
Having understood this, the wise person who performs recitation and fire-offerings [attains success].
For him there shall be no birth, nor does death exist;
he becomes manifest as Brahmā himself, the Self-Existent Supreme Lord.
But for one who does not thus know the Gāyatrī according to the rule,
O sinless one, both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka) are ordained by me.
When such a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) exists, one shall obtain neither the fruit of giving, nor the fruit of sacrifice,
nor is the fruit of visiting sacred fords said to accrue to him.

Now, the mudrās: they too were shown by that very same [author]. Now, therefore, one should show the mudrās: the *samukha* (face-to-face) and likewise the *saṃpuṭa* (enclosed); then the *vitata* (extended), the *vistīrṇa* (spread out), as well as the *dvimukha* (two-faced) and the *trimukha* (three-faced).
The four-faced, the five-faced, the six-faced, and likewise the downward-facing;
then the one called the pervasive añjali, and immediately after that, the cart (śakaṭa).
Then there should be the knotted noose of Yama, facing forward;
then the vilamba, the muṣṭika, the fish, and then the tortoise and the boar.
Then follow Siṃhākrānta, Mahākrānta, Mudgara, and Pallava.
He himself states the definition of these:
"The two hands joined together facing each other with fingers bent. Those two hands characterized as described above, whose fingers are bent—that is, curved—are the mudrā named *saṃmukha*.
The *saṃpuṭa* [mudrā] consists of the two hands joined together, resembling the interior of a lotus bud.
The *saṃhata* [mudrā] consists of the two hands joined together, resembling a closed lotus bud.
The *vitata* [mudrā] consists of the two hands joined together, turned upward with the fingers extended.
The two hands characterized as previously described, with the fingers extended and brought forward, are called *vitata*;
when the two palms are joined together, it is the *vistīrṇa* [mudrā].
Those two hands from which the pair of fingers are released are joined together; this is the *vistīrṇa* mudrā by name.
When the two hands are joined face-to-face,
by joining the two little fingers and keeping the remaining fingers slightly apart, one forms the two-faced, three-faced, and other [mudrās].

When two hands are joined face-to-face, by joining the two little fingers and leaving a gap between the remaining fingers, there arise the mudrās named *dvimukha*, *trimukha*, *caturmukha*, and *pañcamukha*, starting from the two thumbs up to the ring fingers. Among these, the *dvimukha* is formed with the syllable *va*, the *trimukha* with *re*, the *caturmukha* with *ṇi*, and the *pañcamukha* with *ya*.
By joining the remaining fingers, the previous configuration is destroyed;
the two circles of joined fingers have their tips joined obliquely.
Those skilled in mudrās have declared that the two hands represent the six-faced one.

The *pūrvayoga* is the joining of the two little fingers. By the separation of those [two], the other fingers are joined; thus, the two hands whose tips are joined crosswise and which possess a circle of joined fingers are the mudrā named *ṣaṇmukha*.
When the two hands are joined with their tips bent and turned downward, it is the *adhomukha* mudrā.
When the two hands are joined with their tips slightly curved and drawn back, it is the *adhomukha* mudrā.
The two hands, being likewise turned upward, form the pervasive añjali gesture.
When the two hands, possessing the characteristics previously described, are joined together, it is called the *vyāpakāñjali* mudrā;
when the two hands have their fists clenched with the thumbs released and turned downward,
it is called the *śakaṭa* [mudrā].
The two hands, which possess the previously described characteristics and have their thumbs and tips released, form the mudrā named Śakaṭa; after this follows Yamapāśa:
with the two fists clenched, the left index finger is turned upward.

The mudrā named Yamapāśa consists of two hands positioned one above the other with fists clenched; the left index finger is turned upward with its tip bent, while it is joined by the right index finger, which is turned downward with its tip bent. The palms have their fingers closed together at the joints and turned upward.
When the two long thumbs are joined face-to-face, it is considered the *grathita* (knotted) mudrā.

Those two hands whose fingers and palms are bound together, with the joints pressed flat; those two [hands] whose long, curved thumbs are interlocked with one another—that is the *grathita* mudrā. Alternatively, when the left hand has its fingers gathered and pointing upward, and is joined by the right hand which is turned downward, it is called *sanmukhonmukha*.

He whose fingers are gathered, joined, and pointing upward is described as such. When he joins his right hand with the palm facing downward, it is called the *saṃmukhonmukha* mudrā. For it is said: "When both hands are turned upward and their tips are raised, that is the *vilamba* mudrā. Thus, those two hands which are turned upward and have their tips raised constitute the *vilamba* mudrā.
The two fists joined together with palms facing upward constitute the *muṣṭika* [mudrā].
The *muṣṭika* mudrā consists of the two hands joined together with palms facing upward; however, when they are turned toward each other, it is the *mīna* [mudrā], with the ring fingers joined.
The two hands have their fingers joined upwards with the tips bent, while the palms of the remaining fingers are flat.

When the ring finger and the little finger are joined and connected as described, and those two hands are thus positioned facing one another, with the remaining fingers curved upward and their palms joined— that is the mudrā named *Mīna*.
When the left hand is in that same position but turned face down,
and the right hand likewise [turned face down] presses against the back of it, it is called by the name *Kūrma*.
With the left hand facing downward or turned face-up, joined with the right hand in the same manner at the region of the back, it is called the *nāma-mudrā*.
When the left arm is raised and the hand rests near the armpit,
it is called the *varāha* [mudrā].
When the hand rests near the armpit, the left arm with the aforementioned characteristics constitutes the Vārāha-mudrā; the Siṃhākrānta-mudrā consists of both hands resting upon the ears.
The two hands, resting on both ears with fingers extended, form the mudrā named Siṃhākrānta; if their tips are slightly bent, it is thereafter called Mahākrānta.
Those same two hands, with tips bent, are the mudrā named Mahākrānta.
When the two hands are raised slightly, it is called the Mudgara;
when the left index finger is grasped by the right hand while both hands are raised slightly upward, that which is held by the right hand is the mudrā named Mudgata.
The right hand is the sprout;
positioned with the face downward upon the head—such is the characteristic of the mudrās.
The hand placed upon the head with the characteristics thus described is the mudrā called *pallava*. Regarding this, there is a specific rule stated in the *Mahāsaṃhitā*:
"One should never display the mudrā in the assembly of great people;
the gods become agitated at that, and what has been performed becomes fruitless."
Thus ends the procedure for the Nyāsa in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the Gāyatrī-kavaca:
Om at the heart, Bhūḥ at the mouth, Bhuvaḥ at the head, and Suvaḥ on all limbs; thereafter, one should practice the recitation of the Gāyatrī according to the prescribed rule.

Vyāsa states the fruit for one who acts in this manner: "He who, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), recites the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, attains the world of Brahmā; such is the word of Vyāsa."
Furthermore, he who, having understood her true nature, worships her according to the prescribed rule,
is not defiled by faults even while accepting the earth filled with jewels.
"O King, it is said that even if that supremely purifying Goddess is recited in any manner whatsoever, she bestows all desires; how much more so when recited according to the prescribed rite?
Thus ends the Gāyatrī-kavaca in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the procedure for the recitation of the *gāyatrī*. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Having sipped water and being purified, one should always perform both the twilight devotions with a concentrated mind."
In a clean place, one should perform the recitation of the mantra to be recited, according to the prescribed rule.

The meaning is "in accordance with the scriptures. When the question arises as to how that is so, Śaṅkha says: "Seated upon a grass mat (bruṣī) or one covered with Kuśa grass, with Kuśa blades as a purifier in hand, facing north or toward the sun, and taking up a rosary, one should perform the recitation (japa) while meditating on the deity. *Bruṣī* means a seat; *kuśottarā* means covered with Kuśa grass. And the deity here is she who is expounded by the Gāyatrī, according to the traditional teaching of Bṛhaspati: "Silence is the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra. And this is its meaning: the connection is "we meditate (*dhīmahi*) upon that Brahman, which is the *bharga*—the form of splendor—belonging to the shining Sun, the Āditya, and which is most excellent (*vareṇya*)," because the word *tat* denotes Brahman. This has been stated in the Bhagavadgītā.

"Oṃ tat sat—this is declared to be the threefold designation of Brahman. Thus, may that Supreme Self (paramātman) impel (prerayet)—that is, inspire—our intellects (dhiyaḥ) toward actions whose fruits are both seen and unseen. And so, it is stated that one should mutter [the mantra] while meditating upon the golden Person (puruṣa) residing within the orb of the sun. Furthermore, it has been stated by Markaṇḍeya in the section concerning the recitation of the Gāyatrī:
"Seated upon a mat of kuśa grass, with kuśa grass in hand, having conquered his senses..."
"One should meditate upon the Person of great splendor situated in the center of the sun. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
"While reciting the prayer, one should repeat the pure mantra consisting of vowels, consonants, and words."
"One should not move the head or the neck, nor should one show one's teeth.
This statement was spoken by Manu.
And reciting this syllable and this [Gāyatrī], preceded by the Vyāhṛtis—
"A Brahmin learned in the Vedas who performs the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) is endowed with the merit of the Vedas.
This "syllable" (*akṣara*) is the *praṇava*; this is the *gāyatrī*. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
"Then one should mutter the *gāyatrī* conjoined with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*."
The *praṇava* (the syllable Om) should also be understood here at the beginning of the mantra; likewise, Saṃvarta states:
"At the morning twilight, one should recite [the Gāyatrī] preceded by the *praṇava*, together with the *vyāhṛtis*.
Here, the *vyāhṛtis* are specifically the three beginning with *bhūḥ*. However, Yogayājñavalkya mentions other [mantras] as well for conjunction with the *praṇava*.
"Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, and likewise *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, and having placed the *gāyatrī* and the *praṇava* at the end—this is declared to be the *japa*.

This is the *saṃpuṭa-gāyatrī*. Regarding this, Bodhāyana states a specific rule: "With the *praṇava* on both sides and accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis*. The phrase "one should repeat the *gāyatrī*" is understood to follow here. Vṛddhamanu also says:
"A Brahmin, pure in mind, who muters the Gāyatrī preceded by six *oṃ*s, is liberated from the sins born of many lifetimes; there is no doubt in this matter.
When it is asked what its characteristics are, he [the same author] says:
First, one should utter the three *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the six syllables ending with *oṃ*;
then, having withdrawn them again, one should likewise place the *oṃ* at the beginning and the end of the mantra.
The *śatākṣarā* (the hundred-syllabled mantra) is to be understood as the syllable *soṃ* repeated four times.
By reciting the *śatākṣarā* completely, one obtains the fruit of all the Vedas. Through constant knowledge of this, the entire realm of speech becomes known.
[394] "By him, the entire sevenfold world-system would have been worshipped.

This is its meaning: by the phrase "with the syllable *oṃ*," he states that the number of the *vyāhṛtis* is included. Thus, together with the syllable *oṃ*, the twenty-five syllables become one hundred syllables through four repetitions. Regarding this, the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa* introduces the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*):
"The sacrifice of recitation is threefold; learn its divisions."
It is traditionally taught as being threefold: that which is called vocal, the whispered, and the mental.
"Among the three types of recitation-sacrifices (*japayajña*), each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
Regarding this, Hārīta says: "Recitation performed aloud is declared to have a single-fold merit; that performed in a whisper is remembered as having a ten-fold merit."
The whispered recitation is said to be a hundredfold [more effective], and the mental recitation is remembered as a thousandfold.
The characteristics of loud and low-voiced recitation are shown in the Purāṇa:
"When one utters the mantra with speech using high, low, and circumflex tones, clearly, with distinct words and syllables,
that is the vocal *japa-yajña*."
One should utter the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly;
one should perceive a slight sound oneself—this is known as whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa).
The definition of mental recitation (*mānasa*) has been stated by Vaiyāghrapāda:
"That recitation which, with the tongue motionless, is free from the covering of eating—that is declared as mental recitation by those devoted to the Vedas. Thus it is said.
Because the phonemes (*varṇa*) are not perceived and only the tone (*svara*) is perceived, it is *dhvāna*. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Vyāsa:

"A wise person should not perform recitation loudly, especially in the case of the *Sāvitrī*," that is intended as a praise of mental (*mānasa*) and other forms of recitation, and is not for the purpose of prohibiting loud recitation altogether. If it were so [intended], [the following would apply]:

There would be a contradiction with the scriptural statement: "For one engaged in whispered recitation (*upāṃśu-japa*), it becomes a hundredfold compared to *śaṃsya*. Here, *śaṃsya* refers to loud recitation (*uccair-japa*). Regarding this, Śaunaka states the method for the rules of recitation:
"Having placed the hands palm-upward in the morning, and then downward-facing in the evening..."
Thus, recitation performed with the hands held stiffly in the middle has been described.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"Withdrawal of the mind, purity, silence, reflection on the meaning of the mantra,
freedom from distraction, and lack of despondency are the causes for the successful accomplishment of japa."
Vyāsa also says:
"Neither walking, nor laughing, nor looking toward the sides;
neither leaning against anything, nor talking, nor likewise with the head covered."
One should not recite while stepping with one foot upon the other, nor likewise with the hands;
nor with an unconcentrated mind, nor while causing others to hear.
One should always perform the oblation, the formal grasping, the giving, the eating, the sipping of water,
and the recitation with the hands placed over the knees and with the thumbs included within them.
Sumantu also says:
"Nor [should one recite] while wearing low-set jewels, nor with a distracted mind, nor with feet or hands crossed; nor with unclean hands, nor naked, nor even with a cloth wrapped around the head."
[396] Or, if one mutters while talking, it is said to be fruitless for that long. Śātātapa also says:
"That twilight rite which is devoid of *darbha* grass, and that gift which is without water," [is ineffective].
And whatever recitation is performed without being counted shall all be rendered meaningless.
Bodhāyana also says: "One engaged in ritual action should avoid touching anything below the navel. Yama also states:
"Having touched the body below the navel, one should wash both hands;
or else, one should touch the right ear or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu."
Śaunaka also says:
"One should remain standing while reciting the morning twilight prayer, but seated for the evening one;
nor should one speak in between, nor should one cease under any circumstances."
Regarding this, the same author states an exception in certain cases:
"One may cease [recitation] when a Brahmin arrives; one may converse with him as desired.
But upon seeing a Śūdra who has arrived, one should by no means recite."
The meaning is that upon seeing a Śūdra, one should simply desist [from recitation] and not speak with him. Vyāsa also says:
"One should not speak at the time of japa, nor during vows, fire-offerings, and the like.
However, if a most excellent twice-born man should arrive while one is engaged in these very acts..."

"Then, having saluted the Brahmin, he should announce his *yogakṣema*. [397] Thus it is said. "Attentive" means focused. However, if there is a lapse in verbal restraint caused by negligence, one should look to what is stated by Yājñavalkya regarding Yoga:
"If, in any way, there should be a lapse in verbal restraint during the recitation (*japa*) and other such acts..."
"One should indeed recite a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Likewise, the restriction regarding place has also been shown by that same [author]:
"One should recite [the mantra] in a fire-sanctuary, at the edge of water, or even in a temple."
At a sacred bathing place, in a cow-pen, in a field of the twice-born, or in one's own home;
On this point, Śaṅkha says: "Recitation performed at home is said to have a single-fold merit; by a river and the like, it is remembered as having a double-fold merit;
in a cow-pen, it is ten-fold; and in a fire-sanctuary, it is more than a hundred-fold."

In sacred fields of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra), at holy fords (tīrtha), and in the presence of deities, [the merit] may be hundreds of thousands of millions; but in the presence of Viṣṇu, it is infinite.
In this regard as well, a specific rule is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Since Guhyakas, Rākṣasas, and Siddhas carry [the mantra] away by force,
one should therefore perform the recitation (*japya*) in a solitary and pure place."
Aṅgiras also says: "Secret gifts, knowledge free from egoism, and well-guarded recitations—these yield infinite fruit. [398]
Regarding the number of recitations here, Yama says:
"One should constantly recite the Gāyatrī— the goddess who destroys all sins— with a maximum of one thousand, a middle of one hundred, or a minimum of ten."

The rule "at least ten [people]" refers to times of distress (*āpad*). Bodhāyana also states: "Seated upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* grass, with his hand containing water, facing the east, he should repeat the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times. The phrase "one thousand times" refers to forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and others. Accordingly, Yogayājñavalkya says:
"A student (*brahmacārin*) and one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should mutter it one hundred and eight times;
a forest-dweller and an ascetic (*yati*) should mutter it more than a thousand times."

The meaning is that because those two [the student and the householder] do not maintain a sacred fire (*anagnika*), there is no lapse in the time for the *homa* offering. The phrase "one hundred and eight" refers to the context of offerings made before sunrise. There is no contradiction even for the religious student (*brahmacārin*), because the performance of the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) prior to sunrise is prescribed by the traditional law (*smṛti*) in the rule: "And the fire-rite at the two twilights. However, for one who performs the *homa* after sunrise, the statement of Manu should be observed: "Standing, he should recite the *Sāvitrī* during the morning twilight until the sun is seen; but sitting, he should perform the evening twilight rite until the stars clearly appear."

*Ṛkṣa* refers to the constellation (nakṣatra). The construction here is inverted, meaning "standing in this [constellation], one should mutter," because the act of muttering (*japa*) itself is the primary element. For this very reason, Śaṅkha says:
"One should mutter during the morning twilight while standing, and likewise during the evening twilight while seated. [399]

But is it not the case that, because of the prohibition against ceasing in the midst of the recitation—"one should not stop in the interval"—it is simply impossible for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and performs the *anuita* oblations to cease? Not so; since that [prohibition] is based on a direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*), there is no contradiction even if one stops in the middle. For this very reason, Āpastamba states: "In a conflict between two rules, that which is based on a direct Vedic injunction is stronger. Regarding the conclusion of the recitation, Gobhila says:
"O Goddess, born from the mouth of Maheśvara, originating from the heart of Viṣṇu, and permitted by Brahmā, go as you desire."
Thus ends the mantra for the dismissal (*visarjana*) of Gāyatrī. Śaunaka also states:
"The invocation (*āvāhana*) is prescribed in the Taittirīya [branch], and the dismissal (*visarjana*) likewise.
Here, the mantra for dismissal is: "O Goddess, on the highest peak... Regarding this, Gobhila says:
"A wise person should never recite the Gāyatrī over water;
the Gāyatrī is said to have Agni as its mouth, therefore one should rise [from the water] and recite it.
Thus says the Śruti: "The Gāyatrī has Agni as its mouth; therefore, one should not recite it in the waters."

Thus ends the section on the procedure for the recitation of the Gāyatrī in the Smṛticandrikā. Now, certain other statements concerning the subject of the Gāyatrī-japa are also recorded. Regarding this, Manu says:
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times,
a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
The *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* constitute the triad. Saṃvarta also says:
"A student of sacred knowledge who eats moderately and shows compassion toward all beings is liberated from all sins by reciting the *gāyatrī* one hundred thousand times."
Having performed sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing, or having consumed food that is censured,
one becomes purified by reciting the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
By reciting the Gāyatrī for five nights, one completely eradicates all sin pertaining to this world and the next, leaving nothing remaining.
Also in the Caturviṃśatimata: "By reciting ten million Gāyatrīs, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin. Vasiṣṭha also says:
Having performed the recitation of the Gāyatrī eight thousand times when the sun has risen,
one is liberated from all sins, provided one is not a killer of an embryo.
He who recites it eighty thousand times is liberated from the sin of drinking liquor;
seventy thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī purify even a thief of gold.
By sixty hundred thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī, one who has violated the preceptor’s bed is liberated.
Yogayājñavalkya also states:
"In whatever situation a twice-born man considers himself defiled,
in that very situation there should be an oblation with sesame seeds or the recitation of the Gāyatrī."
Yama also says:
Having offered oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter into the fire while being well-composed,
restrained, and pure, one is liberated from all sins through the Gāyatrī.
One should bathe while reciting the Gāyatrī a hundred times; one should mutter it a hundred times while submerged in water;
and by drinking water a hundred times while reciting it, one is liberated from all sins.
Vyāsa also says:
"The twice-born who recites [this] according to the rules for a year or for six months shall, before long, obtain all his desires; there is no doubt in this."
Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"When a confluence of all sins has occurred,
the Gāyatrī, practiced ten thousand times, is the supreme purification."
Thus ends the section concerning Gāyatrī in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the rosary for recitation (*japamālā*);
regarding this, Yogayājñavalkya states:
A rosary should be made from crystal, indrākṣa, rudrākṣa, or those produced from the putrajīva tree; each subsequent one is indeed superior to the preceding.
Also in the Purāṇa:
"A rosary should be made auspiciously from pearls;
one may have it fashioned from gold, silver, copper, or crystal."
Hārīta also says:
A rosary may be made of conch-shell or silver, of gold, of nimba fruits,
of lotus seeds, of rudrākṣas, of vidruma, or of gems and pearls.
A rosary made of silver, rudrākṣa seeds, or likewise the joints of fingers,
as well as one made of putrajīva seeds, is indeed recommended for the practice of recitation.
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"Recitation performed with gold, jewels, and gems becomes a hundredfold effective;
with *indrākṣa* seeds it becomes a thousandfold, and with *rudrākṣa* seeds it becomes ten-thousandfold."
It may certainly be a million or ten million, there is no doubt regarding the lotus seeds; however, for the recitation with *putrajīvaka* seeds, there is no fixed limit.
Also in another Smṛti:
"From recitation performed with the counting of fingers, the fruit for those chanting mantras is eightfold by means of *ariṣṭa* beads;
with *putrajīva* beads, the fruit shall be tenfold."

The fruit [of recitation] performed with conch shells or lotuses is a hundredfold; with jewels, it is a thousandfold; and with knots of *kuśa* grass or *rudrākṣa* beads, it becomes a hundred-thousandfold.
Hārīta also says:
"Recitation performed with a rosary of *nimba* and *ariṣṭaka* beads is said to be a hundredfold more effective;
with *rudrākṣa* beads it is multiplied a hundred thousandfold, and with coral beads it is ten millionfold."
With pearls and gems, the merit is multiplied by ten million times ten million; however, the exact calculation cannot be known through the finger-joints of rudrākṣa beads.
There is no limit to the counting [of merit] with lotus seeds and putrajīva seeds;
even Brahmā [cannot count it].
With rudrākṣas, the merit is double that of gold, and with lotus seeds, it is ten billionfold.
O best of the twice-born, ten million times ten million [other merits] are surpassed by a single knot of kuśa grass.
Regarding the rudrākṣa in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One obtains the merit of a thousand lakṣas of koṭis and a hundred lakṣas of koṭis through its recitation; there is no need for deliberation on this point."
Whether one is impure from eating remnants, engaged in forbidden acts, or smeared with all manner of sins,
one is liberated from every evil by wearing Rudrākṣa beads.
"If even a dog, having placed a rudrākṣa around its neck, dies here, it too goes to the state of Rudra; how much more so for humans and others? Regarding this, there is a Purāṇa:
A crystal rosary indeed brings about peace and nourishment;
gold, pearl, and silver likewise bring about all accomplishments.

A rosary made of conch-shell bestows enjoyment and liberation; one made of lotus seeds, indrākṣa, or darbha grass grants all desires, brings prosperity, promotes longevity, and grants all spiritual perfections (*siddhis*). A rosary of *putrajīva* beads, moreover, bestows peace and nourishment.
Hārīta also says:
"A rosary made of conch, gold, or silver is indeed for rites of pacification (śāntika);
one made of lotus seeds, rudrākṣas, or clay is for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika)."
"A rosary made from the finger-joint beads of the *putrajīva* tree bestows liberation and the accomplishment of goals;
likewise, a rosary fashioned from crystal grants both liberation and wealth.
Regarding this, Brahmā states the rule for the number [of beads]:
One should perform [the recitation] one hundred and eight times, or likewise fifty-four;
it should be performed twenty-seven times, and beyond that, no more is considered appropriate.
A rosary of one hundred and eight beads is proclaimed to be the best;
that which consists of fifty-four beads is proclaimed to be the middling.
[404] Even the lowest garland, consisting of thirty-two [beads], is said to be eternal when used for supreme sādhana that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should perform the recitation with a rosary of one hundred and eight beads, or with one of fifty-four; never with an inferior one.
A twice-born man should recite [the mantra] thirty-two times for minor rites such as subjugation (vaśya), as well as for killing, expulsion, inciting enmity, madness, and delusion.

"One should indeed join inferior beads with inferior ones using an inferior string; one should place an inferior garland on an inferior [deity], but one should set aside the superior [garland]. Thus [it is said]. Regarding this, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
One should not touch the thread with the index finger, nor should one shake or vibrate it;
rather, one should perform the turning while the thread rests between the thumb and the middle finger.
If the Meru has been overstepped or the rosary has fallen,
one should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and consume clarified butter.
The drawing [of the breath] with the thumb;
the drawing [of it] with the middle finger bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
One should not draw it with other fingers, nor likewise touch it with the nails. Thus [it is said].

Thus ends the section on the morning twilight devotions (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*, composed by Yājñika Devaṇabhaṭṭopādhyāya, son of Śrī Keśavādityabhaṭṭopādhyāya, who was an expert in all branches of knowledge.
[405] Now, regarding the fetching of water for sprinkling, on this point Śāṭyāyani says:

"Then, having worshipped the sun and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) properly himself, he should take up the sprinkling-water and, with self-restraint, go home. The word "twice" is to be supplied after "having sipped water. And regarding this, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
Then, having sipped water twice correctly, one should perform the sprinkling;
for one who knows the ritual rules should never perform any action without the sprinkling.
Śāṭyāyani states a specific rule regarding the fetching [of water]:
"Wearing sandals, holding *darbha* grass, and wearing an upper garment with its fringe facing upward, one should fetch [the water] contained in a vessel.

The word "fetch" (*āharet*) is to be understood as "fetch by sprinkling" (*abhyukṣaṇam*). "One whose upper garment has its fringe facing upward" means one who possesses such an upper garment (*sadaśottaraḥ*). Pracetās also says:

"Having taken well-protected water for the purpose of ritual practice, one should go home; by sprinkling [himself] with that at the *savanas* (sacrificial sessions), such as morning and so forth, the householder is always pure. "Well-protected" means not seen by anyone. "At the *savanas*" refers to the morning and other times. For this very reason, Garga says:
At the three junctions of the day, one should collect water that is protected while remaining silent and purify it;

one should purify it thoroughly and examine it. Regarding the rule for the timing here, Gobhila says: "Before the time for the *prāduṣkaraṇa* (the lighting of the fires), one should fetch protected water in the evening and morning for the purpose of ritual service. *Prāduṣkaraṇa* means the act of kindling or maintaining the sacred fires. Regarding the rule for the vessel here, Yogayājñavalkya says:
"A vessel made of gold, silver, or copper is proclaimed to be the best."
But if that is not obtained, one may use an earthen vessel, provided it does not leak.
Śāṭhyāyani also says:
A vessel made of stone, gold, silver, wood, or clay— firm,
or one of copper or a leaf-cup— is indeed meritorious for the purpose of sprinkling.
A vessel made of leaves (*patrapuṭa*) refers to the case where no other vessel is available. As Āpastamba says:
"But when all [other] vessels are unavailable, a leaf-vessel is prescribed;
that too should be known as a vessel, provided it does not leak when held."
Likewise, he [Āpastamba] himself stated what things are to be avoided:
"The sage Āpastamba declared that one should not accept sprinkling even with stones, gravel, sand, dūrvā grass, ordinary grass, leaves, or iron."

"A twice-born man should not perform sprinkling (abhyukṣaṇa) with a vessel pierced by a tube, nor with a bell-metal vessel, nor even with one made from a part of a living being or from fruit," so it is said. Here, "nālikā" means made of bamboo; "prāṇyaṅga" refers to conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and the like; and "phalaja" means made from coconut, bilva, and other such fruits. Vṛddhaśātātapa also says:

A wise person should not perform the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) with water containing moss, grass, leaves, and the like; nor with unrefined vessels, nor with sand, nor with cloth, nor with clay coatings.

"By vessels for water that are unconditioned" means, in other words, by those devoid of the aforementioned purificatory rites such as sweeping. Yama also says: "One should not perform sprinkling with water drawn from a vessel using the left hand, nor with water squeezed out from a cloth."
"Taken from a vessel" means brought by hand or other means, not from a vessel. For this very reason, Śāṭhyāyani says:
"One should not carry [water] in a single vessel; neither one who has not taken vows nor a maiden [should do so];
nor indeed should water be carried in the hand or in a cloth for the purpose of sprinkling."
"One bowl" means one that lacks a lid. "Without vows" means one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*). For this very reason, Pracetas says:

"One of a single caste (*ekajāti*), nor a student (*baṭu*), nor a maiden, nor one who has not been initiated, nor one wearing only a single garment, should indeed fetch water for the purpose of sprinkling."
The Śūdra is of a single birth. And so Manu says:
"The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are the twice-born.
But the fourth is of a single birth, namely the Śūdra; there is no fifth. Thus it is said.
Immediately after the sprinkling, Pracetas says:
"The water-pot used for sprinkling should not be set down anywhere until the water for rinsing the mouth has been given and the drops that were sprinkled have fallen away."

By this, it is stated that one should perform the sprinkling with water brought [in], and without setting [the vessel] down, having sipped water (ācamya) and sprinkled [the vessel], one should set it down. Śāṭhyāyani also says: "Having returned home while holding the vessel for sprinkling, even if one has not performed the sipping of water (ācamana), one becomes pure by sipping water upon the ground. [408]

The meaning is that by not performing the ritual sipping (ācamana) and not setting down the vessel for sprinkling (prokṣaṇa-pātra) on the ground, one becomes pure after having sipped water. Regarding what follows the sipping, Pulastya says: "Having sprinkled all the materials with that [water], and having sipped water again at home, the best of the twice-born should then perform his rites and virtuous acts."

The syntactical connection here is that, having again performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) in this house, one should sprinkle the ritual materials (*dravya*) with it. Garga has also pointed out the materials:
"Restraining his speech, one should fetch and purify water at the three junctions of the day [for the following]:
the fire-oblation, the offerings, the ground, the house, the materials, oneself, and the attendants."
Yama also says:
One should diligently sprinkle the house in the morning if it has been left overnight;
one should not perform sacrifice in a house that has not been sprinkled at midday or during the twilight.
Regarding this, Garga says:
"A drop of water the size of a cow-hide, when poured, purifies the earth whether it has been ploughed or not,
provided no smear remains."
Regarding one who is unable to perform the aforementioned sprinkling, Śāṭhyāyani says:
"Having properly sipped water in a river or similar place, being self-restrained, and having returned home,
one should take water from a water-jar and then perform the sprinkling."
Or, having sipped water at home after preparing water with gold and kuśa grass,
and having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth, one who has thus rinsed should again perform the sprinkling.
[409] A jeweled vessel or a water-pot—Pracetā also says:
"Whatever sprinkling a twice-born man performs with Vaiśvānara-water, those who discourse on Brahman declare it all to be equal to the water of the Gaṅgā. Thus it is said.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, [the section on] sprinkling and fetching [water]; now follows the greatness of the Agnihotra, wherein Prajāpati says:
The Vedas, along with their six ancillaries, word-for-word recitations, and step-by-step recitations, have the Agnihotra as their fruit;
a dharma equal to the Agnihotra has never existed before, nor will it ever exist.
Hārīta also says: "There is no duty higher than the Agnihotra; there is no austerity higher than the Agnihotra;
there is no supreme good higher than the Agnihotra; there is no glory higher than the Agnihotra."
There is no accomplishment higher than the Agnihotra; there is no goal higher than the Agnihotra.
There is no purifying bath higher than the Agnihotra; there is no vow higher than the Agnihotra.
That which the wise attain by means of being free from dualities or free from mental constructs—
this is subtle, like fire hidden within wood during the Agnihotra sacrifices.
That which the high-souled ones recite in the Śukriyas, the Rahasyas, the Niṣads, and the Upaniṣads, that shines forth in the Agnihotra.
Well-performed Agnihotra sacrifices lead to the supreme goal;
herein lie both heaven and liberation, for whosoever desires to go there.
The three initial *vyāhṛtis*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *namaḥ*, and *vaṣaṭ*—
he in whose house these are always present truly belongs to the world of Brahman.
Aṅgiras also says:
Even if one were to give away Mount Meru of gold and the entire earth together with its oceans,
that may or may not be equal to the morning and evening fire-oblation (sāyaṃprātar-homa).
Satyavrata also says:
"A twice-born man indeed fully obtains, through the New and Full Moon sacrifices, that which is the righteous duty and the fruit of those who subsist by gleaning grain day after day."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Those twice-born who perform the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices shall never return from the world of Brahmā."
Paiṭhīnasi also says:

"All the sages indeed desire that Brahmanic potency which resides in the self of a Brāhmaṇa who has offered the Agnihotra, performed the fire-rites, completed his recitations, and stands upon the path."
Hārīta also says:
"Indeed, there is no world for one who does not sacrifice; one who does not sacrifice finds no auspiciousness.
One who performs no sacrifice, being impure in soul, falls away like a leaf that has been torn."
By sacrifice the worlds shine forth stainless; by sacrifice the gods attained immortality.
Released from many sins through sacrifice, one reaches the worlds of the supreme Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the majesty of the Agnihotra in the Smṛticandrikā; now, regarding the ritual acts,
Manu says:
One should perform one's own duty as declared in the Vedas constantly and without sloth;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
This is also intended to illustrate the case of Smārta rites; for this very reason Viṣṇu states:
"Whatever injunction there may be, whether Śrauta or Smārta, all must be performed with diligence by one living at home; otherwise, he incurs sin."

The *smārta* [rites] are those prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, such as the *aupāsana* and others; these are to be performed in the nuptial fire (*vaivāhika-agni*). Thus says Yājñavalkya: "A householder should perform the *smārta* rites daily in the nuptial fire, or else in the fire obtained at the time of inheritance; however, the *śrauta* rites are to be performed in the sacrificial fires (*vaitānika-agni*)."

The *śrauta* rites are the *agnihotra* and others; the *vaitānika* fires are the *gārhapatya* and others. Gautama also states: "The fire begins with the wife, or it begins with the inheritance; in that [fire], the *gṛhya* rites are performed. "Inheritance" (*dāya*) refers to paternal wealth. In this matter, whether the fire begins with the wife or with the inheritance, the arrangement is according to one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*. And thus, as stated by Gārgya: "One should not remain even for a moment without the fire after taking a wife;
if a twice-born man so remains, he becomes a *vrātya* and likewise a fallen person (*patita*)."
Just as bathing, just as a wife, and just as the private recitation of the Vedas, so too is ritual worship observed; there is no standing [of the self] apart from that.
Thus, as Vasiṣṭha stated: "Those who are not learned in the Vedas, who do not recite the sacred texts, and who maintain no sacred fires, follow the dharma of Śūdras"; and as Vyāsa also said:
"He who considers himself a householder without having taken the nuptial fire—his food must not be eaten, for he is declared to be one who cooks in vain."

Thus, this should be understood as applying when one has attained the qualification [for such rites]. "Aśrotriyas" means those devoid of the Vedas. "Ananuvākyas"—that is, those lacking *anuvacana* (recitation)—means those devoid of knowledge; this is the sense. On this point, Garga says:
"The Brahmin who, out of delusion, performs Smārta or Itihāsika rituals while disregarding Vedic ones, is not joined with merit."
"Vedic ritual action is primary, while the other [worldly action] is subordinate;
however, one who is intent on the subordinate, having abandoned the primary, goes to a downward state.
This refers to the case where Vedic capacity is present. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
If one is unable to perform the Śrauta rites, one should perform the Smārta rites;
if one is also unable to perform those, the wise person should follow the conduct of the virtuous (Sadācāra).

By this, it is stated that when there is capacity (*sāmarthya*), one must be a follower of the Veda. And it was said by Vasiṣṭha: "One is fit for the *agnyādheya* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) provided he has not failed to establish them; and one is fit for the *soma* sacrifice provided he has not failed to perform the *somayāga*. The meaning of "fit" (*alaṃ*) is "capable" (*samartha*). Capacity consists in such things as not being one whose father has not established the fires, and so forth. Thus, it should be understood that the fault of "not having established the fires" (*anāhitāgnitā*) or "theft" (*steya*), and so on, applies only to one who possesses the capacity for the *agnyādheya* and other rites, and not to anyone else. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says: "A Brāhmaṇa must necessarily establish the fires; he should also sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, *cāturmāsya*, animal, and *soma* sacrifices. Hārīta also says the same.
"He who desires eternal dharma should constantly perform the *pākayajñas* and the *haviḥyajñas*, as well as the *saumya* sacrifices, according to the prescribed rules."

And they were enumerated by Gautama: "The *aṣṭakā*, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, the *śrāvaṇī*, the *āgrayaṇī*, the *caitrī*, and the *āśvayujī*—these are the seven forms of the *pākayajña*. The *agnyādheya*, the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *cāturmāsya*, the *āgrayaneṣṭi*, the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*, and the *sautrāmaṇi*—these are the seven forms of the *haviryajña*. The *agniṣṭoma*, the *atyagniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, the *ṣoḍaśī*, the *vājapeya*, the *atirātra*, and the *aptoryāma*—these are the seven forms of the *soma-saṃsthā*. The *pārvaṇa* is that which is performed on the *parvan* (the new and full moon) and is characterized by the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering). The *śrāddha* is the monthly ancestral rite (*māsi-śrāddha*). The *śrāvaṇī* is the *sarpa-bali* (offering to the serpents). The *āgrayaṇī* is the *āgrayaṇa* (first-fruits offering). The *caitrī* is the rite known as the *holākā*. The *āśvayujī* is the rite known as the *indradhvaja-homa*. The others are well-known. Some, however, state that there are seven *pākayajñas*: the *aupāsana-homa*, the *vaiśvadeva*, the *pārvaṇa*, the *aṣṭakā*, the *māsi-śrāddha*, the *sarpa-bali*, and the *īśāna-bali*. Having thus described the sacrifice consisting of twenty-one forms, Devala says: "The *vājapeya*, *aśvamedha*, *rājasūya*, *pauṇḍarīka*, *gosava*, and so forth, are the great sacrificial rites (*mahāyajña-kratu*). Regarding this, Manu states the rule for the timing:
One should always perform the Agnihotra at the beginning and end of day and night,
and indeed with the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month, as well as with the Paurṇamāsa.
"At the end of the grain harvest, with the sacrifice for new grain; likewise at the end of the seasons, the twice-born [should sacrifice] with the *adhvara* rites;

at the end of the solstice, with an animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, with the Soma sacrifices. Here, "at the beginning and end of day and night" means at the morning and evening twilights (*saṃdhyā*). The term "*adhvaraiḥ*" refers to the *cāturmāsya* (four-month) sacrifices.

"However, when there is a crop, the sacrifice is prescribed as the *naveṣṭi* or the *cāturmāsya*," according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Jābāli. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states an alternative procedure (*anukalpa*):
"The *soma* sacrifice should be performed every year, and likewise the animal sacrifice at each solstice."
The Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must indeed be performed.
"In the absence of these, the twice-born should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that if these [offerings], such as the Soma sacrifice and others, should somehow become impossible, one should perform this *iṣṭi* separately at each respective time as a substitute (*pratinidhi*). This is because, by performing the specific function, one acquires its specific characteristics, according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "A substitute should possess the characteristics of that which it replaces. [Objection: But if this were so, would there not then be the application of other injunctions pertaining to the Soma sacrifice and so forth? [Reply: Not so; for the term "Agnihotra" and the like are intended to bring about the entire group of their respective constituent parts (*aṅga*). Furthermore, as stated by Manu: "One should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara *iṣṭi* at the end of every year."

"For the sake of the expiation (*niṣkṛti*) of the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed"—this [text] also intends to prescribe an *iṣṭi* for the very purpose of performing the rites involving animals and so forth, and not for the purpose of prescribing an expiation for their non-performance. "Expiation" (*niṣkṛti*) means the accomplishment of the ritual purpose of the Soma sacrifice and so on. Having raised the objection, "If this is so, the Vaiśvānarī alone would suffice; what is the use of others?", that same author immediately says:
"The twice-born who performs a duty according to the rule for times of distress when he is not in a time of distress..."
It has been determined that he does not obtain the fruit of that [action] in the hereafter.

"By all the gods, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great Ṛṣis, fearing death in times of distress, a substitute for killing was established. This means [it is a substitute] for the primary injunction. Therefore, even though the term "atonement" (*niṣkṛti*) is used, it should be understood that the Vaiśvānareṣṭi is merely a substitute and not a true expiation (*prāyaścitta*). By this, it is stated that these [rites] are obligatory (*nitya*); and it has been said by Prajāpati that they are so because an expiation is prescribed for their non-performance.
But having performed his duties at the proper time, especially without traveling abroad,
he who practices austerity becomes purified by a three-night fast month after month.
Having omitted either the new-moon sacrifice, the full-moon sacrifice, or both,
purification is achieved by one-quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance for a single omission, and by half for two omissions.

If one is unable to perform the *havis* offerings at sacrifices, even if a single rite is omitted from the beginning, he shall be purified by the *prājāpatya* penance; this applies likewise to the *pākasaṃsthā* sacrifices.
But upon the omission of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana),
as well as the neglect of the daily bath and the obligatory fire-oblation (homa), one becomes pure by reciting the Sāvitrī mantra eight thousand times.
At the end of the year, upon the omission of Soma sacrifices,
one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for failing to perform any one of the sacrifices to which one is entitled.
Indeed, one is purified by fasting in the case of those rites consisting of cooked food.
Kātyāyana also says:
"Upon the omission of the ancestral sacrifice (pitr-yajña), as well as the two Vaiśvadeva offerings,
and likewise upon performing the New Moon sacrifice (navayajña) or the first tasting of new grain, [one must perform the Śrāddha]."
"Food fallen into the vessel becomes the sacrificial porridge (caru) for Vaiśvānara.
Thus [it is said]. Manu also states the prohibition against eating new grain by one who has not performed the sacrifice of the first-fruits:
"A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires shall not eat of the new harvest without having performed the sacrifice of the first-fruits or the animal sacrifice."
One who desires to live a long life should eat fresh grain and meat.

Furthermore, this prohibition regarding new grain is intended with reference to rice (*vrīhi*) and other grains that will be mentioned hereafter. Thus says Āpastamba: "If one should eat of the new grain without having performed the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, he would be eating a portion assigned to the gods without it being properly set aside; he would meet with misfortune. Viṣṇu also states: "Śyāmāka millet, rice, and barley are the subjects for the New Grain Sacrifice (*navayajña*). It is traditionally taught that one who has not performed the *Āgrayaṇa* should not eat these; there is no such restriction regarding other grains."

Regarding this, Āpastamba states the rule for the timing: "One should sacrifice with *śyāmāka* millet in the rainy season, with rice in the autumn, and with barley in the spring; it is known that one may use bamboo-seeds (*veṇuyava*) according to the season. There is also a Śruti text: "A householder should sacrifice with rice and barley in the autumn and spring; with *śyāmāka* or wild rice (*nīvāra*) in the rainy season; in times of distress, he may use either of these alternately, or with old grains. On this point, the Kūrma Purāṇa says:
"He who, out of atheism or laziness, does not wish to establish the sacred fires, or does not sacrifice with a sacrifice, goes to many hells."
"Therefore, with every effort— and especially so for a Brāhmaṇa—
one who has established the sacred fires and whose self is purified should worship the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the section on the Agnihotra and other rites in the Smṛticandrikā.

The definition of the qualified person: The rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) have been described. Now, the person entitled to perform them in each case is defined. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states: "One who is capable of the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) should not fail to establish them; and one who is capable of the Soma sacrifice (*soma-yajña*) should not fail to perform it. The word *alaṃ* means "capable. That capability has been demonstrated by Yājñavalkya:
"A twice-born man who possesses more than three years' worth of food may indeed drink the Soma."
He who possesses food sufficient to maintain his dependents for three years, or even more, may drink the Soma; that is to say, he may perform the Soma sacrifice. And so Manu says:
"He whose food is sufficient for three years to maintain his dependents, or who has even more, is worthy to drink the Soma."

This refers to the *kāmya* (optional) Soma sacrifice, because the scriptural injunction regarding the debt (*ṛṇa*) implies that the *nitya* (obligatory) sacrifice must necessarily be performed, and because it prescribes a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for its non-performance. Furthermore, Manu has stated immediately after this:
"Therefore, even if he has not previously drunk the Soma, that twice-born man who drinks the Soma when his wealth is very meager does not obtain the fruit thereof."

Therefore, even one who has not previously performed the *soma* sacrifice does not obtain the fruit of that obligatory rite when the substance [of wealth] is less than what was mentioned; how much less, then, can he obtain the fruit of the optional (*kāmya*) rite? This is the meaning. Consequently, one who lacks sufficient wealth should not perform the optional *soma* sacrifice. With this very intention, Śaṅkha also says:
"But a twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of food should drink *soma* without weariness;
likewise, a twice-born man with little wealth should perform the Vaiśvānara *iṣṭi*."
The mention of *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offerings) is intended to indicate by synecdoche those rites such as the *agnihotra* that precede the *somayāga*. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"One whose food supply lasts for a year should perform the rites prior to the *soma* sacrifice" [419].
The term *prāksomikyaḥ* means those rites originating before the *soma* sacrifice. Manu also says:
One who is faithful and has conquered the senses should perform other meritorious deeds;
however, one should never, under any circumstances, perform sacrifices here with meager sacrificial fees.
A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys the senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice.
In the Matsya Purāṇa as well:
"A sacrifice lacking food consumes the kingdom; likewise, one lacking mantras consumes the officiating priests.
A sacrifice lacking sacrificial fees consumes the sacrificer himself; there is no enemy equal to such a sacrifice."
The quantity of food has also been stated by Śaṅkha:
"One should feed a thousand Brāhmaṇas at a Soma sacrifice, a hundred at a Paśubandha,
and a hundred at each of the Parvan festivals during all the Cāturmāsya rites."

As for that which is stated in the Śruti: "A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must indeed be given at a sacrifice, even if it be very small," that refers to the obligatory (nitya) requirement. For this very reason, Bodhāyana says: "He whose obligatory rites as well as his perpetual duties (ajasrakāṇi) are omitted stands on a wrong path; he shall not go to heaven, for he is fallen."

"Therefore, one should always perform the daily rites with *skanda* fruits, roots, honey, or juice; and one should not omit the daily rites. By this, the qualification for the daily *soma* sacrifice is established even for one of small means. This should be understood to apply likewise to the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires). And so says Prajāpati:
[420] One who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) shall remain the presiding authority over all ritual stations as long as he possesses wealth;
however, even if he is destitute, a twice-born man should not relinquish the sacred fire out of fear of sin.

One who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and is entitled to perform the *saṃsthā* sacrifices does not refrain from doing so out of fear of sin; rather, [he refrains] only when he lacks wealth, because those [sacrifices] are optional (*kāmya*). "Indigent" means one who possesses little wealth. Manu also says: "If a Brāhmaṇa, while possessing the means, fails to give the horse as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *Agnyādheya* rite dedicated to Prajāpati, he remains one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)."

The meaning is that in the absence of [other property], a Brāhmaṇa who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) remains such even without giving a horse. For this very reason, Āpastamba states: "If one who is not wealthy should establish the fires, he may give a single cow at his pleasure. Regarding the rule for the timing, Viṣṇu says: "If faith toward this [rite] arises on a particular day, he should establish the fires on that very day. Kārṣṇājini also says: "Having procreated a son, a wise man should perform this Vedic rite; or he may establish the fires in any manner whatsoever, provided wealth has been obtained from a virtuous person."
The inclusion of the term "sādhu" (virtuous) is for the purpose of excluding Śūdras and others. For this very reason, Manu says:
"Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice—they are the officiating priests of Śūdras and are censured among those who discourse on Brahman."
"By treading with his foot upon the heads of those who are constantly ignorant and who serve the fire of a *vṛṣala*, the giver shall cross over all difficulties.

By this, the performance of the *agnihotra* preceded by the formal establishment of the fires (*adhāna*) is prohibited, not the *agnihotra* alone; for it says, "of those who serve the fire of a *vṛṣala*," which refers to the fire belonging to a *śūdra*. Yama also [states]:
He who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintains the Agnihotra sacrifice,
becomes a Śūdra-performer of the Agnihotra and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
By constantly performing the work of others and attending upon the fire of a Śūdra,
he indeed lowers himself while delivering others.
Chāgaleya also says:
"If one who has acquired wealth from a Śūdra should maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice,
the donor obtains the fruit of that act, while the performer goes to hell."
In the same way, wealth intended for sacrifice should be viewed with suspicion, for faults are heard of even in that case. And so says Yama:
"A Brāhmaṇa who knows the Dharma should not take wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
by performing a Vedic rite for the sake of a Śūdra, he is born as a Caṇḍāla after death."
Manu also says:
"A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
but a sacrificer who begs it becomes a Caṇḍāla after death."
Yājñavalkya also says:
"One is born as a Caṇḍāla by performing a sacrifice with wealth begged from a Śūdra.
Śaṅkha also says:
One should not beg for wealth from a Śūdra, but one must give away everything that has been begged.
By this, it is implied that not giving everything is prohibited. For this very reason, Manu says:
"He who, having begged wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, does not bestow it all [upon the priests]..."
That brahmin goes to the state of a crane and the state of a crow for a hundred years.
Yama also says: "That evil-minded person who does not utilize all the wealth begged for the sake of a sacrifice shall, after consuming it, be born in the womb of a dog-cooker (śvapāka)."

But when a sacrifice that has already commenced is somehow obstructed in its midst due to the unavailability of an animal or other requirements, then Manu states that it may be taken from a Śūdra or others:
"If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by the lack of even one component—
especially in the case of a Brāhmaṇa— while a righteous king is in power..."
If there should be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but performs no sacrifices and does not drink the Soma juice,
one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of accomplishing a sacrifice.
One may take three or two [grains] at will from the house of a Śūdra,
for the Śūdra has no proprietary right in sacrifices.

"For a Śūdra has no entitlement whatsoever to sacrifices. Even if one possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, or possesses a thousand cows but does not perform sacrifices—one may take from the households of these two as well, without hesitation. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the determination of the qualified persons in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*); regarding this, Dakṣa says:
At the conclusion of the twilight rites, however, the self-performance of the fire-oblation is prescribed;
whatever fruit may accrue from performing the oblation oneself cannot be obtained by another.

When it is asked, "What then is the fruit in the case of another's homa?", he himself says: "The fruit which is prescribed for one who performs the homa himself while offering the oblation—that same fruit is obtained as half when it is offered by another. [423]

Regarding this, Śaunaka states the rule for the performer: "From the time of taking the hand [in marriage], the wife herself, or else the son, the daughter, or the resident pupil (antevāsī) should perform the service. Here, *antevāsī* means a disciple. Dakṣa also says:
"The officiating priest, the son, the teacher, the brother, the sister's son, and the husband of the daughter—whatever is offered by these, that is indeed as if offered by oneself."

The husband of a sister-in-law (the brother-in-law) is the son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*). Āpastamba also says: "Every day the sacrificer himself should offer the *agnihotra*, or on the festival days (*parvan*) a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) should offer it, for he is hired by means of the Veda; or a milk-offerer (*kṣīrahotṛ*) should offer it, for he is hired by means of wealth—so says the *Bahvṛca-brāhmaṇa*. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "Having not offered [the sacrifice] himself, one should not officiate as a priest for another. Also in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "The officiating priest, the son, the wife, the pupil, or even a uterine brother..."
Having obtained permission, one should especially perform the oblation according to the prescribed rule.
All of this refers to the domain of one who performs the oblation himself, for that alone is praised. Thus says the Śruti:
"A single oblation offered by a disciple is better than a hundred oblations offered by others;
a single oblation offered by a son is better than a hundred oblations offered by disciples."
"For one who has offered himself as a sacrifice is indeed better than a hundred sons who have offered oblations.
Furthermore, that which was stated by Manu: "Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool [should perform the sacrifice]."
One who is neither afflicted by illness nor lacking in sacramental rites may be the officiant for the Agnihotra.
For these people fall into hell while offering oblations for one who [is unworthy];
therefore, the *hotṛ* priest should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and a master of the Vedas.

This refers to the domain of the *śrauta* fires, because of the mention of the *agnihotra*. By this, there is no contradiction with the statement of Śaunaka. The mention of the "maiden" (*kanyā*) is for the purpose of illustrating the wife as well. For this very reason, Gobhila says: "The wife may, at her pleasure, offer the evening and morning oblations in the *gṛhya* fire. Regarding the oblation performed by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and others, Kātyāyana has stated that it must take place in the presence of the sacrificer:
"But the offering should not be made in the absence of both husband and wife by the priest or others;
however, if the offering is made in the presence of both, it would be useless."

Here, by the word "api" (even/also), it is stated that there is no fault even if one or the other is absent in some way. For this very reason, the favor of traveling abroad has been shown by that same [author]: "A Brahmin who has business may go abroad after having entrusted his sacred fires to his own wife and likewise appointed a priest; he should not stay away for long without purpose. [425]
On this point, Yajñapārśva says:
"Recreation with one's daughter or even with one's daughter-in-law is not prohibited;
likewise, the cleaning of vessels, the smearing [of the floor], and worship."
*Vihāra* means dwelling. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the rule for the time [of kindling the fires]:
"The kindling of the fires (*prāduṣkaraṇa*) occurs when the sun has not yet reached the sunset mountain by thirty-six *aṅgula*s, and in the morning, upon the appearance of light."
"Making manifest" means carrying [the fire] forth. Likewise, the time for the oblation has also been indicated by that very same [authority]:
"As long as the stars in the sky have not fully appeared in every respect, and as long as they do not yet attain a crimson hue, so long is the evening oblation offered."
Marīci also says:
"The time for the *homa* is to be known as that twilight when the rays have vanished, yet the earth still contains the fire within it through the rays of the sun and the stars."

Āpastamba also says: "This [cycle] is indeed the ocean, namely day and night; its two shallow fords are the two junctions (*saṃdhi*). Therefore, one should offer at the junction—so says the *Śailāli-Brāhmaṇa*. Having seen a star, [one offers] at the onset of evening (*pradoṣa*) or at night. The word "should offer" (*hotavyam*) applies everywhere. That which can be approached is "shallow" (*gādha*). Having seen even a single star, [one offers] at the onset of evening; when all [stars] have risen, [one offers] at night—at that state in which living beings go to sleep. For this very reason it is said: "The lapse of time [is permissible] beyond nine *nāḍikās*. These are the four times for the evening oblation (*sāyaṃ-homa*). Likewise, the times for the morning oblation (*prātar-homa*) are also shown by him: "At dawn (*uṣas*), at the rising of the sun (*upodayam*), when half-risen (*samayāviṣita*), and after sunrise (*udite*)—in the morning. "When half-risen" means when half has risen. Similarly, Manu also [says]: [Manu 2.15–16] "Having kindled the fire according to the rule before the morning meal, one should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice with fuel-sticks and water. One should not let the fire go out; if it should go out, there is a fast-day (*upavāsa*) or an offering of milk. [Manu 2.17] "One should perform the morning *agnihotra* before eating the morning meal, and likewise the evening [offering] after finishing the evening meal. [Manu 2.18] "If the morning *agnihotra* is performed after the morning meal, or the evening [offering] before the evening meal, one becomes a consumer of vomit and excrement. [Manu 2.19] "The *agnihotra* sacrifice is prescribed to be performed with fuel-sticks and water; however, the *brahmayajña* is declared to be the recitation of the Veda. [Manu 2.20] "Having offered the *agnihotra*, one should study the Veda; having studied the Veda, one should offer the *agnihotra*. Between these two, one should not eat anything else. [Manu 2.21] "One should always perform the *agnihotra* twice a day, at the proper times, until the end of life, as long as one possesses the capacity. [Manu 2.22] "One should never neglect the *agnihotra*; for by neglecting it, one falls from the heavenly world. But by performing it, one attains immortality. [Manu 2.23] "The *agnihotra* is the foremost of sacrifices, and the *brahmayajña* is the foremost of them. The ancestors are satisfied by the *pitṛyajña*, and the gods by the *devayajña*. [Manu 2.24] "The *manuṣyayajña* is satisfied by hospitality toward guests, and the *brahmayajña* by the recitation of the Veda. One who performs these five great sacrifices is freed from all sins. [Manu 2.25] "Even if he performs other meritorious acts, he does not attain heaven if he neglects these five great sacrifices, O best of the twice-born. [Manu 2.26] "By performing these five great sacrifices daily, a householder purifies the three worlds, like the sun with its rays. [Manu 2.27] "Those who do not perform these five great sacrifices, though they may perform other rites, are called *vrātyas* and are excluded from the community of the twice-born. [Manu 2.28] "One should always perform the *agnihotra* with diligence, for it is the root of all sacrifices. Without it, no other rite bears fruit. [Manu 2.29] "Whether one performs other sacrifices or not, one must never omit the *agnihotra*, for it is the eternal sacrifice. [Manu 2.30] "Even if he performs hundreds of other sacrifices, he does not obtain the fruit of heaven if he abandons the *agnihotra*. [Manu 2.31] "The *agnihotra* is the most excellent of sacrifices, and the *brahmayajña* is the most excellent of them. The ancestors are satisfied by the *pitṛyajña*, and the gods by the *devayajña*. [Manu 2.32] "The *manuṣyayajña* is satisfied by hospitality toward guests, and the *brahmayajña* by the recitation of the Veda. One who performs these five great sacrifices is freed from all sins. [Manu 2.33] "Even if he performs other meritorious acts, he does not attain heaven if he neglects these five great sacrifices, O best of the twice-born. [Manu 2.34] "By performing these five great sacrifices daily, a householder purifies the three worlds, like the sun with its rays. [Manu 2.35] "Those who do not perform these five great sacrifices, though they may perform other rites, are called *vrātyas* and are excluded from the community of the twice-born. [Manu 2.36] "One should always perform the *agnihotra* with diligence, for it is the root of all sacrifices. Without it, no other rite bears fruit. [Manu 2.37] "Whether one performs other sacrifices or not, one must never omit the *agnihotra*, for it is the eternal sacrifice. [Manu 2.38] "Even if he performs hundreds of other sacrifices, he does not obtain the fruit of heaven if he abandons the *agnihotra*.
