[Manu 2.39] "The *agnihotra* is the most excellent of sacrifices, and the *brahmayajña* is the most excellent of them. The ancestors are satisfied by the *pitṛyajña*, and the gods by the *devayajña*. [Manu 2.40] "The *manuṣyayajña* is satisfied by hospitality toward guests, and the *brahmayajña* by the recitation of the Veda. One who performs these five great sacrifices is freed from all sins. [Manu 2.41] "Even if he performs other meritorious acts, he does not attain heaven if he neglects these five great sacrifices, O best of the twice-born. [Manu 2.42] "By performing these five great sacrifices daily, a householder purifies the three worlds, like the sun with its rays. [Manu 2.43] "Those who do not perform these five great sacrifices, though they may perform other rites, are called *vrātyas* and are excluded from the community of the twice-born. [Manu 2.44] "One should always perform the *agnihotra* with diligence, for it is the root of all sacrifices. Without it, no other rite bears fruit. [Manu 2.45] "Whether one performs other sacrifices or not, one must never omit the *agnihotra*, for it is the eternal sacrifice. [Manu 2.46] "Even if he performs hundreds of other sacrifices, he does not obtain the fruit of heaven if he abandons the *agnihotra*. [Manu 2.47] "The *agnihotra* is the most excellent of sacrifices, and the *brahmayajña* is the most excellent of them. The ancestors are satisfied by the *pitṛyajña*, and the gods by the *devayajña*. [Manu 2.48] "The *manuṣyayajña* is satisfied by hospitality toward guests, and the *brahmayajña* by the recitation of the Veda. One who performs these five great sacrifices is freed from all sins. [Manu 2.49] "Even if he performs other meritorious acts, he does not attain heaven if he neglects these five great sacrifices, O best of the twice-born. [Manu 2.50] "By performing these five great sacrifices daily, a householder purifies the three worlds, like the sun with its rays. [Manu 2.51] "Those who do not perform these five great sacrifices, though they may perform other rites, are called *vrātyas* and are excluded from the community of the twice-born. [Manu 2.52]
"When [the sun] has risen, when it has not yet risen, and likewise when it is the time of twilight—sacrifice is performed in every way; such is the Vedic revelation.
Regarding their definitions, Vyāsa says:
When the sixteenth part of the night has passed, adorned by planets and constellations,
at that time before the morning sun has risen, the wise man should perform the fire-oblation.
Likewise, at the time of dawn, when the circle of stars has vanished,
as long as the sun is not yet visible, though it is already endowed with its rays.
"One should recognize that as 'risen' (udita); therein one should perform the oblation.
By this, it is stated that the third time for the oblation begins from the appearance of the [first] line. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"As long as the sun, having left the earth, does not go higher than the height of the hand..."
For those who offer at the prescribed time, this meritorious rite of oblation is indeed superior to any other.

Āśvalāyana also states: "The morning [period] ends at the *saṅgava* [time]. The phrase "the time for the *homa*" is understood to carry over. On this point, Pulastya says: "If a rite is performed at the wrong time, it must be performed again once the proper time arrives; however, that which one performs after the time has passed should be declared as unperformed."

If an act is performed at an improper time or when the time has not yet arrived, it must be performed again at the proper time. However, if it is performed when the time has already passed, because it is no longer acceptable, the meaning is that even though it was done, it is as if it were never done. But when, for some reason, there is an unavoidable lapse of the primary time (*mukhyakāla*), then the statement of Gobhila should be consulted: "Now, if one should not obtain either the sacrificial offering (*havya*) or the officiant (*hotṛ*) for the evening and morning *homa*s or for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) in the domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*), how should he act? The morning *āhuti* does not lapse until the evening *āhuti*; the evening *āhuti* does not lapse until the morning *āhuti*; the Full Moon day does not lapse until the New Moon day; and the New Moon day does not lapse until the Full Moon day. Therefore, Bhava [the commentator] maintains that one should perform the rite even when the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) has passed. And that must be performed immediately after the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), because Āpastamba prescribes the expiation for the lapse of the primary time in the passage: "If the time for the evening *Agnihotra* should be allowed to pass... Āśvalāyana also says: "If the morning [time] should end with the *saṅgava* period, having let that time pass, one should offer four spoonfuls of clarified butter (*ājya*). This performance during the secondary time applies to cases of distress (*āpad*), according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba regarding the times for *homa*: "In all these times, one should sacrifice in times of distress; one should understand that it is indeed considered offered. And Gobhila has said: "If one should not obtain either the sacrificial offering or the officiant, how should he act? Kātyāyana also intends the secondary time by this very principle.
When the full moon has passed, on whichever day the oblation may fall, one should offer it on that very day; likewise also when the new moon has passed.

*Havya* is the oblation; *hotṛ* is the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). In this case as well, having performed the *pāthikṛta* sacrifice, one should perform the *vaiśvānara* sacrifice for the transgression, according to the Vedic injunction: "One who, being a regular performer of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, should pass over either the new-moon day or the full-moon day, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt; having passed over the new-moon day or the full-moon day, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. This [period of suspension] lasts until the time for another festival (*parvan*) arrives. Upon the arrival of that [new festival], however, there is only the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and not the performance of the missed rite, because the previous entitlement ceases due to the obstruction by another entitlement. And it has been stated by the Commentator: "Then, either the new-moon or the full-moon sacrifice [is suspended] until another festival-time occurs. This same principle applies to the morning and evening fire-oblations (*sāyaṃprātar-homa*) as well. Likewise, in the case of the transgression of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the *āgrayaṇa*, and so forth, having performed the *pāthikṛta* and *vaiśvānara* sacrifices, there is the performance of the missed rites, since those too are modifications (*vikāra*) of them. Herein lies the *vaijāvāpa*.

For some perform the oblation after sunrise, while others perform the oblation before sunrise; others perform the oblation at the time of eating, and likewise there are those who perform the oblation once a fortnight.
The rule that "there should be offerings of food" refers to times of distress; the fortnightly offering (pakṣahoma) should likewise be understood in this way. And so Marīci says:
"Where there is physical distress, or where one becomes destitute due to fear, as well as in other such calamities, the fortnightly offering is prescribed."

"In ancient times, there were indeed sages named Yāyāvaras. They lived as ascetics and offered the Agnihotra sacrifice every half-month. Therefore, according to the rule of the Yāyāvaras, one who is ill, or afflicted by distress, or on the road between birth and death, or in times of calamity, should offer the Agnihotra every half-month. On the first day of the lunar fortnight, he draws fourteen portions of four spoonfuls each in the evening; there is one fuel-stick, a single offering, a single wiping of the hand, and a single recitation of the *upasthāna* prayer; the morning rite is performed in the same manner. Regarding the fortnightly offering (*pakṣahoma*), however, Marīci says that if a calamity ceases in the middle of the period, performing the offering again does not constitute a fault.
Having performed the fortnightly oblations, one should then turn back from that [interruption] and perform the oblation again in the middle; thus, he shall not be a partaker of fault.
Likewise, the *samasyahoma* (combined offering) has also been shown by that same author:

"Or, for one who maintains the *agnihotra* while traveling, whether it be three fortnights, five days, or seven, a single combined offering should be made on one day, separately for the evening and the morning. [430]
Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the rule concerning the substances: "Cooked food such as rice-meal and flour, rice and the like which are both prepared and unprepared,
and unprepared grain such as paddy— thus is the sacrificial offering (havya) declared by the wise to be of three kinds."
Also in another Smṛti: "Oil, curd, milk, Soma, gruel, boiled rice, ghee,
rice grains, meat, and water— these are the ten substances [for which penance is prescribed] when consumed unintentionally."
Kātyāyana also says:
"Among sacrificial grains, barley is primary, and rice is traditionally considered secondary;
in the absence of rice and barley, one may use either curd or milk."
In the absence of that, one should offer either with barley gruel or with water.

Śaunaka also says: "But [one may use] rice, barley, and sesame seeds at will. However, if the primary substances are unavailable, one should follow what was stated by Kātyāyana: "When the prescribed items are not available, that which is similar should be accepted;
for example, wheat for barley, and rice-grains for rice."
Furthermore, regarding those cases where specific substances and so forth are not mentioned, he himself has stated:
"In oblations where no specific instruction is given, clarified butter is prescribed as the offering substance;
as for the mantra and the deity, Prajāpati is the established rule."
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states the measurement of the oblations:
"For grains, sixty-four [grains] are proclaimed as the measure of one oblation;
for sesame seeds, it should be half of that; and for clarified butter, it should be half of that."
Bodhāyana also says:
"A hundred oblations of either rice or barley are prescribed.
As for the fire-offering (*homa*), it is to be performed according to the rules stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*; that has been explained in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*.

"One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the rules prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, in accordance with the injunctions. The phrase "according to the injunctions" means "in accordance with the specific scriptural texts. When the question arises as to how that is done, [it is said]:
"In the morning, with palms turned upward, [one should offer] a full [oblation] at a sacred ford or a sanctuary."
Having passed two finger-breadths beyond the fuel-sticks, one should offer the oblation everywhere.
Viṣṇu also says:
"If one should offer oblations into a fire that is not yet kindled or is accompanied by smoke, the sacrificer will become blind in the next world; so indeed have we heard."
The man who offers oblations into a fire that has no flames and lacks glowing coals is born with weak digestion, afflicted by disease, and impoverished.
Therefore, for the successful completion of the rite, the oblation must be poured into a fire that has been well-kindled with much dry fuel, when it is smokeless and its flames are licking upward.

Āpastamba also says: "That which shines flickeringly when the embers have subsided is the mouth of the gods; therefore it is known that one should offer in such a way that one does not cover that mouth. "When they have subsided" means when they are devoid of flame; "that which shines" means that which blazes forth. Regarding the specific procedure for one who possesses both the Śrauta fire and the Smārta fire, Bharadvāja states:
"Having performed the Vaitānika (Śrauta) oblation, the wise man should perform the Smārta one."
Because the Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda, some have known that which is based on Smṛti as ancient.
Śātātapa also says:
"One should personally perform the Śrauta rites with effort; another may perform the Smārta rites.
In case of inability, even another may perform the Śrauta rites, at the very least performing the Ācāra."

And this must be practiced only after understanding it, for otherwise a fault is heard [in scripture]. Thus says Aṅgiras: "Whatever action is performed according to one's own whim and devoid of knowledge, all that is as useless as the play of children."

Also in the Caturviṃśatimata: "An oblation offered devoid of knowledge and ritual action, or rituals performed through ignorance— by offering these, the blind man is burned, and even the lame man is burned."
But when there is a lapse in ritual action due to negligence, then that which was spoken by Prajāpati should be observed:
"Whatever part of the ritual may lapse for those performing the sacrifices through negligence,
that becomes complete through the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu"— so says the Śruti.
"In the *adhvara* sacrifices. Regarding this, the *Kūrma Purāṇa* states:
"Having entrusted all actions to Brahman, free from attachment and devoid of desire, one who performs them with a serene mind attains that state" (433).

The offering is dedicated to Brahman; that too has been stated in that very same place: "That which is to be given is given by Brahman, it is presented to Brahman, and it is Brahman itself that is given—this is the supreme offering to Brahman."
"I am not the agent; Brahman alone performs all this at that time.
This is declared by the seers who perceive the truth to be the 'offering unto Brahman' (brahmārpaṇa)."
May the eternal Lord, the Master of existence, be pleased by this action;
through his intellect, he constantly performs this supreme offering unto Brahman.
Or else, one may perform the renunciation of the fruits of actions unto the Supreme Lord;
this they call the unsurpassed "offering to Brahman" of all deeds.
"Therefore, with a serene mind, one should constantly practice the yoga of action;
one is satisfied by [serving] the Supreme Lord and attains that eternal state.
Thus ends the section on the rules for fire-offerings (*homavidhi*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the observances for the day of fasting (upavasthya),
Pulastya says therein: "On the festival day (parvan), one should consume ghee once, eat sacrificial food (haviṣya), and take a light meal."
There should be no evening meal, nor should there be a fast; one must abstain from oil and meat.

Regarding this, Āpastamba states the specific rule: "There must be satisfaction with food; and whatever may be dear to these two, that they should eat on this day" [434]. Regarding what is to be avoided here, Hārīta says: "On the day of the vow (*vratya*), one should avoid black gram (*māṣa*), lentils (*masūra*), honey, meat, food given by others, and sexual intercourse. The day of the vow is the day of the *anvādhāna* (the preparatory rite). Bharadvāja also says:
"One should avoid women, oil, and meat on the days of the sacred festivals (*parvakāla*)."

Sāṅkhyāyana also says: One who intends to perform a sacrifice should avoid quarreling, buying and selling, laughter, excessive talking, the threefold arts [song, dance, and music], sleeping at improper times, and idle conduct.
Jābāli also says:
One should avoid field-grown peas, as well as *kuluttha* beans and *kodrava* grain,
falsehood, excessive speech, and buying and selling.
On the day before the sacrifice, a twice-born man observing the vow should avoid these things: cleaning the teeth, lentils, salt,
alkaline substances, chickpeas, *koradūṣaka* grain,
black gram, honey, and food belonging to others.
Also in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"One should avoid vegetables, meat, lentils, chickpeas, millet, black gram, honey, and food belonging to others on the day of fasting."
Bodhāyana also says: "One should avoid all this grain stored in a granary for the entire day, except for sesame.
Thus ends the section on the rules for the Upavasatha day in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, regarding the causes for re-establishing the sacred fires (*punarādheya*),
Kātyāyana states therein:
"If one goes beyond the boundary together with his wife, having left the fire behind..."
If the time for the fire-oblation has passed, the re-establishment of the sacred fires is prescribed for him.
Śaunaka also says: "When the fire has gone out, or when two pairs of oblations are passed over,
or when both [fires] are absent, the common (laukika) fire is prescribed."
But when the husband has gone abroad, if the wife should go even as far as another village,
she is not tainted by fault when the time for the fire-oblation has arrived.
Now, if while staying in that very place the time for the fire-oblation passes by,
a common (laukika) fire is to be prescribed, according to the observation of the Kāṭhaka Śruti.
If both the sacrificer and his wife go on a journey, they must not fail to return before the oblations; otherwise, they must perform the re-establishment of the sacred fires.

Āpastamba also says: "If the sun should set or rise while the wife is within the boundary, the expiation for that is the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*). They should not carry the fires across the village boundary in the absence of the sacrificer; if they were to carry them across, the fires would become worldly (*laukika*). When they cross as many river-boundaries as there are in the village, they should hold onto one another; if they do not hold onto one another, the fires would become worldly. Śaunaka also says:
"In the case of the omission of the two daily oblations, and likewise in the case of the omission of the New and Full Moon sacrifices..."
"One should establish the sacred fire once again"—this is the instruction of Bhārgava.

According to the opinion of Āpastamba, if the fire being maintained is extinguished even after four days, there must be a re-establishment (*punarādheya*) of the fires, even if the *homa* offerings have been interrupted. Āśvalāyana also says: "If the sun should rise or set while all the fires have gone out, there shall be either a new establishment (*agnyādheya*) or a re-establishment (*punarādheya*); and when the fires have been transferred [to the kindling woods], the destruction of the kindling woods [constitutes a cause for re-establishment]. Some have explained this as referring specifically to the case of the fires that have been separated (*vihṛta*). Āpastamba also states: "For one whose two fires [the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya] have both gone out, if the sun should set or rise [while they are unlit], the re-establishment is his expiation. Both refer to the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya. Likewise, if one should let three fortnights pass without performing the fortnightly *homa*, the re-establishment is his expiation. Śaunaka also says the same.
The fire pertaining to the gods, that pertaining to the elements, and the fire drawn out for the purpose of sweating—
all these are to be known as worldly when they have departed from the single fire.
This refers to a case where the sacred fire has been removed through negligence. Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"For one who has caused his dharma to falter and is being oppressed by enemies, there is exile for two months; beyond that, he is like one who has never maintained the sacred fires."
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, [section 437], the causes for re-establishing the sacred fires regarding the subject of the *agnyādheya*.
Now, in connection with the *agnihotra*, something else regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) is also stated. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having cremated his virtuous wife with the *agnihotra* fire, the husband shall, without delay, take another wife and the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule."
"One who possesses virtuous conduct" means one who is observant of proper behavior. And she must be of the same caste (*savarṇā*). Thus says Manu:

"A twice-born man who knows the Dharma should cause a wife of the same caste who has possessed such conduct and who dies before him to be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire and the sacrificial vessels."

"Of such conduct" means one who follows the prescribed rules of behavior. By this, it is not absolutely prohibited to cremate a woman of a different caste (*asavarṇā*) with the *agnihotra* fire; rather, [the prohibition applies] only when a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) exists, because in that case she lacks the entitlement [to perform the rite]. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"When another wife of the same caste exists, one should not have her perform religious duties."

The meaning is that when a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) is available, one should have religious duties performed by a wife of a different caste (*asavarṇā*), but one should not perform religious acts together with her. By this, it is stated that even a wife of a different caste has the right [to participate] when no wife of the same caste is present. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha also states a prohibition against performing religious rites together with a Śūdra woman: "Women of dark complexion (*kṛṣṇavarṇā*) are indeed for pleasure alone, not for dharma. Here, "dark-complexioned" refers to a Śūdra woman. However, when there are several wives of the same caste, one should not perform religious acts with the others except for the eldest; rather, one should perform them only together with the eldest. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
[438] "In the performance of the religious rite with women of the same caste, the eldest is not to be bypassed.

This means that in a religious rite, the other—whether the middle or the youngest—is not to be appointed without the eldest; rather, she must be together with the eldest. Nor should one suspect an interpretation such as "the other is the partner in dharma (sahadharmacāriṇī) excluding the eldest," for Kātyāyana says:
"The twice-born should not perform the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) even without a single wife."
One should know that as unperformed, for they all take hold of whatever [is performed].

The meaning is that all wives touch the fires being established. Āpastamba also says: "For when the establishment [of the fires] has taken place, she becomes connected with the ritual acts. Bodhāyana also says: "One should lead forward each one individually. Therefore, it is established that the other wives have the entitlement [to perform the rites] only together with the eldest, and not without the eldest. This too applies only when the eldest wife is not defective. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states:
"If a man possesses the sacred fires while his younger wife is present and his eldest wife is free from defect, he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin at every ritual session, indeed for all time."
The meaning is that if she is corrupted by defects, one should abandon her and practice dharma with another. And so Dakṣa says:
"She is declared to be the lawful wife if she remains free from defect; if a defect exists, there is no fault in taking another who is endowed with virtues. [439]
As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "In sacrifices such as the Agnihotra, one should not perform [the rite] with a second [wife];
otherwise, it is fruitless for him, even with hundreds of well-performed sacrifices."

Thus, this refers to the case of one who has a second wife of a different caste (*asavarṇa*). Alternatively, it may refer to the case where the elder wife is not defective, or to the case of a woman who was married after [the elder] while the sacred fires (*agni*) were still present; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the previously cited statements. Furthermore, as stated by Kātyāyana: "The first wife shall be the partner in dharma (*dharmapatnī*); the second increases pleasure (*rativardhinī*).
In that case, only the visible fruit is produced, not the invisible."

Thus, that [text] also has the same scope as the Vaiṣṇava [text]. But surely, remarriage for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is strictly prohibited. As Āpastamba says: "One should not take another wife while the current wife is endowed with both virtue and offspring; in the absence of either, [another] may be taken before the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). This is not so; its meaning is that just as it may be done before the *agnyādheya*, so too after it, provided there is a specific occasion (*nimitta*), remarriage must be performed. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states: "A man who already has a wife may, for some other reason, somehow take another wife."
If one wishes to become possessed of the sacred fire, where is his fire-oblation prescribed to be performed?
The oblation must indeed be offered in the sacred fire, never in a worldly fire;
for the ritual duty of one who has consecrated the fires is not prescribed to be performed in a worldly fire.

This refers to the case of a wife who was previously ineligible [for the rites], until her remarriage; after the marriage, having abandoned the fires with the *utsargeṣṭi* sacrifice, one should establish them again with another wife—this is the meaning. Now, an objection is raised: if one may perform the *agnihotra* and other rites even with a remarried wife, then why does the rule "one should not perform [the rites] with a second wife" apply specifically to that case? It is said in reply: True, we do not say it applies to that specific case; rather, we say it applies to a case where, because she is childless or for some other reason, there is no fault even in remarrying, and thus there is no destruction of the additional ritual obligations (*adhika-karma*). For this very reason, another Smṛti states:

"One may abandon a wife who is diseased, one who has given birth only to daughters, one who is barren, one who is insane, or one whose menses have ceased—provided she is not otherwise defiled—but this is [abandonment] by way of the *tīrtha* (the source), not according to *dharma*. Here, "by way of the *tīrtha*" means "by way of the womb" (*yonitaḥ*). Therefore, in this case, there is no re-establishment of the fires (*punar-ādhāna*) along with a second wife, because there is no cause for abandoning the sacred fires. Thus, if a husband has cremated his previously deceased wife with the *agnihotra* fires, and being without a suitable wife, marries again, he should perform the *ādhāna* (establishment of the fires) together with that new wife; however, it should be understood that for others, there is only the *ādhāna* itself. As for what was stated by Kātyāyana:
If his wife dies here, even though he has a second wife,
he might somehow abandon the *agnihotra* sacrifice, deluded by the eye of ignorance;
one should know that such abandonment constitutes a rejection of the Veda, as does he who abandons it out of desire.
Viṣṇu also says:
"If one should burn a second wife with the sacrificial fires while the first wife is still living,
that act is equal to the drinking of liquor."

Thus, this refers to the case of a second wife who has not been included in the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration). Otherwise, the scriptural injunction, "They cremate those who have maintained the sacred fires," would become a contradictory authority. [Objection: But surely this scriptural statement can also be understood as referring to anyone other than the second wife. [Reply: Not so; for it is improper to restrict the scope of a Śruti text on the basis of a Smṛti. On the contrary, since the Smṛti may apply to other subjects, it is proper to restrict its scope. However, where no other subject is possible, a restriction indeed occurs by virtue of that [Smṛti]. As it was stated by Kātyāyana:
A virtuous wife who has lived righteously should be cremated with the sacred fires when she dies;
one who has acted contrary to this should not be cremated, and in such a case, the marriage rite must be performed again.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having cremated his virtuous wife with the Agnihotra fire, the husband..."

"Vṛttavatīm" means one who possesses proper conduct (*ācāravatīm*). Regarding this, the following is the established rule concerning the sacred fires (*agni-vyavasthā*): In the case of one who has performed the *sarvādhāna* (the complete establishment of the fires), if his wife dies first, he should abandon the *agnihotra* there, marry again, and perform the *ādhāna* with her. If he is unable to perform the *punar-āharaṇa* (re-establishment of the fires), he should perform the *agnyādheya* for his own sake alone, because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Āpastamba: "If he is incapable of the act of marriage, he should perform the *agnyādheya* for his own sake; the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and the *āgrayaṇa* [remain], but the remaining rites do not take place. The *Bahvṛca-brāhmaṇa* also states: "Therefore, one who is without a wife should establish the fire" [442]. Thus, what has been stated by others—that "this statement refers to when the wife is menstruating"—is also refuted. Alternatively, that which was stated by Viṣṇu in this regard should be consulted.
"Even when his wife has died, he must not abandon the Vedic fire;
even by means of a substitute, he should perform that rite for as long as he lives.
Here, the "substitute" refers to a wife made of *kuśa* grass.
Other householders, having fashioned a wife out of kuśa grass,
perform the agnihotra sacrifice tirelessly for as long as they live.
In another place as well:
"But Rāma, having fashioned a golden Sītā as his illustrious wife,
performed various kinds of sacrifices together with his brothers, O Acyuta."

As for what Satyāṣāḍha stated: “There is no substitute for ownership, a wife, a son, a country, time, the sacred fire (*agni*), a deity, a ritual act, or a word,” that refers to human wives and the like; for the substitution of a wife made of *kuśa* grass and so forth is expressly enjoined by scripture. Therefore, the claim made by some—that because a wife made of *kuśa* grass cannot perform the functions [of a real wife], she cannot serve as a substitute, and thus the statement “others [make] one of *kuśa*” is merely for the purpose of praising the *agnihotra*—is also refuted. According to this injunction, if the sacrificer dies after the rite has commenced, the *pitṛmedha* (funeral sacrifice) must be performed upon his three sacred fires (*tretāgni*). Even in the case of the initial consecration (*ādhāna*), if he is unable to complete it, the *pretādhāna* (consecration for the deceased) alone is performed. This too was stated by Āpastamba: “If one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*) should die while having abandoned the fires, having let them go out, having interrupted them, or while they are extinguished, they do not burn him with the other three fires. Wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), having dug up the fire-places and sprinkled them, having placed the deceased at the sacrificer’s place, and having placed the two churning sticks (*araṇi*) at the site of the *gārhapatya* fire, he churns [the fire] with the mantra: ‘Those fires of his which, desiring flesh, wait for the one offering oblations—let them know the sacrificer’s flesh; let them lead this deceased one to the heavenly world for this tasted oblation. Having silently distributed the fires, having filled the ladle (*sruk*) with twelve portions of clarified butter and having offered it silently, he proceeds with the rites beginning with ‘The kinsmen (*āmātyāḥ’)’ [etc. In this very case, if the sacrificer dies first, the *pitṛmedha* is performed on his three fires, but for the wife, it is only the *pretādhāna*. Or, in the case of one who has performed the full consecration (*sarvādhāna*) and has multiple wives, if the eldest wife dies first, he should abandon the fires there and perform the consecration again together with the second wife. If she too dies, he should again abandon the *agnihotra* there; and in the absence of another wife, he should marry again and perform the consecration and so forth with her. If, however, he is unable to marry again, he should perform the consecration of the fires for himself as before. In this same situation, if the sacrificer dies first, the *pitṛmedha* is on his three fires, but for the wife, it is on the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), according to the traditional rule of Āpastamba: “Of those two, whichever dies first—the sacrificer or the wife—for him this *pitṛmedha* is accomplished with the *agnihotra*; for the one who dies later, it is with the *aupāsana*. In this very case, if the wife dies first, he should abandon the *agnihotra* and the *aupāsana* there, marry again, and perform the consecration with her. For Āpastamba himself prescribes the disposal of the *aupāsana* as well, starting from “Then he fasts” and continuing with “Before the *sabhyāvasathya* and the *aupāsana*. If she dies again, the same principle applies. If he is unable to take another wife, he should perform the consecration of the fires for himself. If it is certain that he will be unable to do even that, the *pitṛmedha* for the wife is performed on the three fires, while for the sacrificer it is on the *aupāsana*, because he lacks any other fire, and because of the traditional rule: “For the one who dies later, it is with the *aupāsana*.”

But surely, even in this case of half-consecration (*ardhādhāna*), since there is a traditional rule stating, "Of those two, that which is the first," why could the *pitṛmedha* of the wife not take place in the three sacred fires (*agnitretā*), while the consecration and other rites for the sacrificer take place in the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) alone?

Not so; for the *Kāṭhaka-śruti* states, "These funeral fires are maintained when the wife has died," thereby declaring that their sole purpose is the *pitṛmedha* (funeral rite). Therefore, the previously mentioned view alone is superior. In the case of one who maintains the fires (*āhitāgni*) but has more than one wife, if the first wife dies, her *pitṛmedha* is performed using the three fires (*agnitretā*). However, for the other wives, it is performed with the respective portions of their own *aupāsana* fire. As it is stated in the *Kalpabhāṣya*: "Or there may be an offering with the respective portions of the *aupāsana* fire. In this very case, if the wife dies first, one should abandon the *āhavanīya* and *aupāsana* fires there and perform the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) again together with the second wife. But when husband and wife die simultaneously, their *pitṛmedha* is performed together. As Āpastamba has stated: "If they have both died together, the *pitṛmedha* is performed together" [445]. He thus reconciles the mantras containing dual-number indicators. For one who is not an *āhitāgni*, the *pitṛmedha* is performed with the *aupāsana* fire. This too has been stated by him: "They burn one who is not an *āhitāgni* with the *aupāsana* fire; the wife with the *nirmanthya* (churning) fire, and the others with the *uttapana* (heating) fire. The "others" refers to students (*brahmacārin*) and so forth. Regarding the death of the sacrificer even when the fires have been consigned within himself or the two churning-sticks (*araṇī*), he has stated the following: "If the sacrificer should die while the fires are consigned within himself or in the two churning-sticks, one should prepare the fire-places as before. Having placed the deceased in the place of the sacrificer and having established an ordinary fire (*laukikāgni*) in the place of the *gārhapatya*, the son, brother, or another close kinsman of the deceased, grasping the deceased's right hand, consigns the fire into the ordinary fire with the mantra: 'Descend, O Jātavedas, lead him knowing the way to the heavenly world. Bestow upon us long life, progeny, and wealth; accept his funeral oblation. Or, having consigned it into the two churning-sticks, he should churn the fire. While the fire is being brought back from the churning-sticks, he should mutter the mantra: 'The deceased has taken hold [of the fire]' (*pretānvārambhe*). The distribution of the fires and subsequent rites are the same."
Thus ends the section on fire-offerings (homakāṇḍa) in the Smṛticandrikā; now follows the section on looking into a mirror and so forth, wherein Dakṣa says:

"Then, having performed the rites for the gods and having looked upon the Guru and auspicious objects"—here, "looking upon auspicious objects" refers to looking at a mirror and so forth. It is also stated in the Purāṇa:
"Saffron, sandalwood, gold, a drum, a mirror, and a gem..."
"A wise man should always look upon his gurus, the fires, and the sun at dawn. Thus [it is said]. Nārada also says:
"In this world, there are eight auspicious things: a Brahmin, a cow, and fire..."
Gold, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise the king as the eighth.
Whoever should constantly behold these, pay homage to them, worship them,
and circumambulate them, their lifespan shall not diminish.
Manu also says:

"A cow with well-developed humps, a Kapila cow, a performer of a sacrificial session, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean—these purify by the mere sight; therefore, one should look upon them constantly."
Kātyāyana also says: "He who, having risen in the morning, beholds a Vedic scholar, a beautiful woman, fire, a cow, and one who has maintained the sacred fires, is liberated from calamities."
He who, having risen in the morning, sees a most wicked person, an unfortunate woman, an outcaste, a naked man, or one with a severed nose— that is a characteristic sign of the Kali age.
Also in the Vāmapurāṇa:
"Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the touching of auspicious objects, it is recommended to go outside;
[carrying] *dūrvā* grass, clarified butter, curd, a water-pot, a cow with its calf, a bull, and gold."
Clay, cow dung, a svastika, unbroken grains of rice, oil, honey, and Brahmin maidens;
white flowers, as well as the śamī tree, fire, sandalwood, and the orb of the sun.
One should touch an *aśvattha* tree and thereafter perform the duties of one's own caste.
Also in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"If one desires long life, one should look at one's own self in clarified butter."
Bharadvāja also says:
"Having scratched his back and performed the salutation of the *aśvattha* tree,
he should approach all his elders and greet the Brahmins."
Thus ends the section on looking into the mirror and so forth in the *Smṛticandrikā*; now follows the study of the Vedas,
regarding which Dakṣa says:
And in the second part likewise, the study of the Vedas is prescribed:
first the acquisition of the Veda, then its investigation, its practice, and its recitation.
Giving to one's disciples and the study of the Vedas—this is indeed fivefold;
that time is proclaimed as the proper occasion for [offering] fuel-sticks, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth.
In the second division of the day divided into eight parts, the Kūrma Purāṇa also states:
"Then the twice-born should diligently practice the study of the Vedas according to his ability;
he should recite them, teach them to disciples, retain them in memory, and indeed investigate them."
"And the best of the twice-born should study the treatises on dharma and other subjects. So too says Manu:
"Those which quickly increase the intellect, and which are righteous and beneficial..."
"One should constantly study the treatises and the Vedic scriptures.
Whatever is to be said regarding this has already been stated in the section on purificatory rites (*saṃskārakāṇḍa*).
Thus ends the section on the study of the Vedas in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Then, he is skillful in the acquisition of wealth;
likewise, in the third part [of his life], he accomplishes the means for supporting those who are to be maintained. Thus it is said.
"In the third part of the day divided into eight parts, or even at the twenty-fourth [muhūrta],
a wise man should desire wealth for the sake of accomplishing the needs of those he must support.
The group of those to be supported has also been shown by Dakṣa:
"Mother, father, teacher, wife, offspring, the poor, those who have sought refuge, the guest, and the sacred fire—this is declared to be the group of dependents.
This too must be carried out according to one's means of livelihood. And so says Manu:

"For the sake of accomplishing mere subsistence, one should accumulate wealth without causing distress to the body by means of one's own irreproachable occupations. Here, "subsistence" (yātrā) refers to the maintenance of life. "By one's own occupations" means by those activities which serve as one's livelihood; these too have been shown by that very same [author].
"Teaching, studying, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts—these are the six duties of the *agrajanman*.
Here, the *agrajanman* is the Brāhmaṇa. Among these, three are for the sake of livelihood and three are for the sake of dharma. As he himself says:
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
performing sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts from distinguished persons.

By this it is stated that only three duties—study and the others—are mandatory, whereas officiating at sacrifices and the rest are not. And it has been said by Gautama: "For the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving; for the Brāhmaṇa, additionally, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts; these last three are not obligatory for those mentioned before. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of excluding the Kṣatriya. For this very reason, Manu says: "Three duties cease with respect to the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, receiving gifts."
"In the same way toward a Vaiśya, they should desist; such is the established rule.
And thus, as it was stated by Manu:
"In times of distress, study from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa is ordained."

Thus, that statement refers to teaching for the sake of one's livelihood; otherwise, it would contradict the previously cited injunctions. When it is asked, "What then are the means of livelihood for these two? Manu says: "Bearing weapons and missiles is for the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are for the Vaiśya. But their duty consists of giving gifts, study, and sacrifice. (MDh 10.78)

The bearing of weapons and missiles is for the purpose of livelihood by means of protecting the subjects. By the word "merchant" (vaṇik), the occupation of trade is indicated; by the word "cattle," their protection is meant. Therefore, Yājñavalkya says:
"The primary duty of the Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects;
money-lending, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing are prescribed for the Vaiśya."
Since it is primary and foremost for the sake of dharma and livelihood, the supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of his subjects.

This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu. *Kusīda* is the lending of money for the sake of interest; *vāṇijya* is buying and selling for the sake of profit; and *pāśupālya* is the tending of cattle. Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state a specific rule: "One should guard the cows; while they are drinking, one should not drink, nor sit while they stand, nor rise oneself [to make them move]; one should gently strike them from behind with a moist branch; one should not lead them down by an improper path, through uneven ground, or where there is little water; one should attend to the young, the old, the sick, and those in need; and one should provide remedies according to one's ability. This is the duty regarding cows; otherwise, there is ruin. Regarding this, Manu speaks of another means of livelihood.
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, professional labor, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous.

*Ādāya* (inheritance) is wealth acquired through lineage. *Lābha* (gain) refers to the discovery of a treasure-trove; for it is recorded in the *Viṣṇu-smṛti*: "Upon finding a treasure-trove, a Brāhmaṇa shall take it all. A Kṣatriya, having given one-fourth of the share to the king, shall give one-fourth to the Brāhmaṇas and take half for himself. A Vaiśya, having given one-fourth to the king and taking one-fourth for himself, shall give half to the Brāhmaṇas. A Śūdra, having divided what he has found into twelve parts, shall give five parts to the Brāhmaṇas, five parts to the king, and take two parts for himself. *Kraya* (purchase) is well known. These three modes of acquisition are lawful for all four social classes (*varṇas*). *Jaya* (conquest) belongs to the Kṣatriya alone. *Prayoga* is the lending of money for the sake of interest. *Karmayoga* consists of agriculture and trade; these belong to the Vaiśya alone. *Satpratigraha* (acceptance of gifts from the virtuous) belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone.
One should live by truth through two truths, or by falsehood or even by a mixture of falsehood; or even by both truth and falsehood, but never by the "dog's life" (śvavṛtti).
Gleaning ears of grain (*uñcha*) and picking up single grains (*śila*) should be known as *ṛta*; that which is obtained unasked is *amṛta*.
Begging for alms is called *mṛta*, while cultivation is remembered as *pramṛta*. Trade is *satyānṛta* (truth-and-falsehood), and one may even live by that.
"Service is called the livelihood of a dog; therefore, one should avoid it.
*Uñcha* is the gathering of individual grains that have fallen or been discarded. *Śila* is the taking of stalks of rice and other crops that have fallen or been abandoned. Yājñavalkya also says:
"One may possess grain in a granary or a jar, or enough for three days, or even for a single day."
"Or he may live by gleaning ears of grain; each subsequent mode among these is superior.

[452] *Kusūla* means a granary. One who has accumulated grain sufficient for that amount is a *kusūladhānya*. Or he may be a *kumbhīdhānya*, one who has accumulated grain sufficient for a *kumbha* (a large jar).
He may be either a *kusūladhānya* or indeed a *kumbhīdhānya*.

This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu. One who collects wealth sufficient for three days is a "tryāhika" (one who lives on a three-day supply). One who does not have a store for the morrow is an "aśvastana" (one who lives from day to day); the meaning is that he washes [his bowl] immediately [after eating]. Or he may be such [an aśvastana]. The modes of livelihood for these, ending with the aśvastana, are to be understood as stated by Manu: "One among these performs six duties; another proceeds with three; one with two; but the fourth lives by the thread of sacred knowledge (*brahmasūtra*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: one may be a *kusūladhānya* (one who possesses enough grain in a granary for three years), performing the six duties such as officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and so forth; another, the second type, subsists by three—officiating at sacrifices, teaching (*adhyāpana*), and receiving gifts (*pratigraha*); the third subsists by two, namely those other than receiving gifts; and the fourth subsists by the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) and teaching alone. These statuses, beginning with being a *kusūladhānya*, belong exclusively to the Brāhmaṇa, because for others, activities such as receiving gifts are not permitted. However, the practice of gleaning (*śiloñcha*) is common to all three social orders (*varṇa*). Thus Āpastamba states: "The specific duty of a Brāhmaṇa consists of study, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving, receiving gifts, inheritance, and gleaning (*śiloñcha*). Other things that have not been specifically appropriated [are also permitted]. For a Kṣatriya, these same duties apply, excluding teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts, but with the addition of wielding the rod of punishment and warfare. For a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, these duties apply with the exception of wielding the rod and warfare, but with the addition of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. [453] Parāśara, however, speaks in favor of agriculture for all four classes without distinction during the Kali age.
Henceforth, [I shall describe] the ritual conduct of the householder in the Kali age,
the common dharma pertaining to the four castes and stages of life according to one's capacity.
I shall declare that first, according to the words of Parāśara:
a Brahmin engaged in the six duties may also perform the work of agriculture.
In a field ploughed by himself, and with grains earned by himself,
he should perform the five great sacrifices and cause the initiation for Vedic rites to be undertaken.
A Kṣatriya, having practiced agriculture, should worship the gods and the Brahmins;
likewise, a Vaiśya and a Śūdra should engage in agriculture, trade, and the arts.
This is the eternal dharma for all four castes as well.
Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule:
"One should not drive [the oxen] on the lunar festival days (parvan) or at the two junctions (saṃdhi).
A plough for the sake of dharma should have eight oxen; for those seeking a livelihood, six oxen."
Four oxen for those who are cruel, and two oxen for those who have killed a Brahmin.
Taming and riding young animals is not recommended, nor is it praised for the elderly or the weak; such is the word of Prajāpati.
Parāśara also says:
One should not yoke an ox that is hungry, thirsty, or exhausted;
a Brahmin should not drive an ox that is deficient in limb, distressed, or impotent.
One should drive them for half the day and thereafter perform the bathing;
here, the bathing refers to the oxen. For this very reason, Hārīta says: "Having bathed the oxen and adorned them, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas."
On this point, the Kūrma Purāṇa states:
"Having obtained the gain, he should worship the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins;
when they are satisfied, they undoubtedly pacify that fault of his."
One who practices agriculture does not incur sin if he gives a twentieth part as a share to the gods and the ancestors, and a thirtieth part to the Brahmins.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"One who performs agriculture incurs no fault if he gives a sixth part to the king, a twentieth part to the deities, and a thirtieth part to the Brahmins."
Hārīta also says:
"This sacrificial post has been set up here in the midst of the fields by the cultivators;
therefore, one should unweariedly give there offerings of grain and wealth."
Having broken the earth, cut through plants, and killed insects and ants, farmers purify themselves by means of the sacrifice of the threshing floor; of this there is no doubt.
For this very reason, Parāśara has shown the fault in failing to perform it:
"He who does not give to the twice-born when the king's treasury has been depleted is a thief, he is most sinful; one should designate him as a stealer of Brahman’s property."
In the Purāṇa, Śaṅkara also says:
"O Goddess, I shall describe the sin of that farmer who, overcome by greed, should enter his grain into storage without having given it away."
For a thousand divine years, that evil-souled cultivator shall become a tree in a desert region, devoid of flowers and fruit.
At the end of that [existence], having become a human being after the lapse of some time,
he is born sometimes poor, diseased, foolish, and of low birth.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, however, the regulation of livelihoods is shown according to the divisions of householders:
"The householder should be known to be of two kinds: the seeker (*sādhaka*) and the non-seeker (*asādhaka*).
For the former, they prescribe teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and the acceptance of gifts."
Furthermore, a householder practitioner may also adopt the practice of alms-gathering;
however, he who is described as a non-practitioner remains established in the stage of a householder.
Two modes of livelihood, śila and uñcha, have been declared for him by the supreme seers:
he may live either on nectar or even on death.
"Amṛta is that which is unasked for; however, food obtained by begging is as good as death. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the occupations of a Śūdra have been shown by Uśanas:
"Service to the twice-born, or indeed all crafts, are the duties of a Śūdra."

"The sale of all commodities is declared to be the work of a Śūdra. "Arts" refers to various crafts. Service to Brāhmaṇas for the sake of dharma is the specific duty proclaimed for a Śūdra; indeed, service to Brāhmaṇas alone is cited as his distinguished task.

Thus, according to the *Manusmṛti*, "distinguished" means excellent, because it is the cause for the practice of dharma. The phrase "all crafts" refers to times of distress (*āpad*). As Yājñavalkya says:
"A Śūdra's duty is service to the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant.
Or he may live by various crafts, provided he performs what is beneficial to the twice-born."

The meaning is: by those crafts through which the twice-born are served. And so says Manu: "Those activities which, when practiced, serve the twice-born—those are the works of artisans and various crafts."

And these were shown by Devala: "The duty of a Śūdra consists of service to the twice-born, avoidance of sin, the maintenance of his wife and others, agriculture, cattle-rearing, carrying loads, trade in goods both permitted and forbidden, and the performance of various crafts, as well as dancing, singing, and playing the flute, lute, drum, mṛdaṅga, and mouth-organs. To him, moreover, the remnants of food and so forth should be given. And thus says Manu: "Remnants of food should be given, as well as worn-out garments, the chaff of grains, and old household utensils."
The straw mats were poorly woven; the belongings consisted of sandals and other such items.

Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, the acquisition of wealth through means such as receiving gifts has been described; it was stated therein that the Brāhmaṇa possesses a general entitlement to receive gifts and so forth. Now, his specific entitlement is being defined. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"One who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from kings, pupils, or those for whom he performs sacrifices.
The meaning is that one who is suffering—that is, being oppressed—by hunger is authorized to accept gifts from kings and so forth. Manu also says:
"A *snātaka* who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king."
It is the established rule that [the initiation] may be performed for either the sacrificer or the pupil, but not by anyone else.

And this [prohibition] is intended to forbid the acceptance of wealth from others when other means are available; it is not for the sake of an absolute prohibition, because that same author [Manu] has stated: "But a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone. For this very reason, Nārada also says that accepting gifts from kings and others is indeed superior.
The acceptance of gifts from kings is superior [to that of others], except for those from other Brahmins;
for both the Brahmin and the king are observers of firm vows.
There is no difference between these two, because both protect the dharma of the subjects;
just as the meeting of pure and impure waters attains equality in the ocean, so too does the influx of wealth for kings.

"Just as gold situated in fire indeed attains purity, so do all acquisitions of wealth attain purity when [given] to a king. Regarding this, the intention is that when one possesses wealth, one should seek to obtain more from kings and others. For this very reason, Manu says:
A learned Snātaka shall never suffer from hunger,
nor shall he wear worn-out or dirty clothes, provided that he possesses the means.
By the phrase "one should not perish from hunger," it is stated that when hunger does not exist, one should not engage in accepting gifts and the like.
However, a twice-born man who, while possessing wealth, takes pleasure in receiving gifts,
falls into the Raurava hell and is there thoroughly cooked.
Yama also says: "That mortal who is a beggar is not a fit vessel for heaven;
he agitates living beings just like a thief."
"But for those who are attached to receiving gifts and never to giving them,
Vaivasvata has declared that there is no upward journey for them at all. Thus says Śātātapa as well.
For as many syllables of the Veda as one employs for the sake of profit, for so many instances of killing an embryo does the seller of the Veda incur.

The employment of Vedic syllables for the sake of wealth is the sale of the Veda; one who does so is a seller of the Veda. The meaning is that he incurs the sin of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*). The sixfold nature of the sale of the Veda has been shown by Chāgaleya:
"Proclaiming it, prattling about it, receiving gifts on its account, officiating at sacrifices for its sake, teaching it, and debating it—this is the sixfold sale of the Veda. Thus it is said.
In this same way, a fault should also be seen in giving preceded by a request. Thus said Śātātapa:
"But he who gives a gift to a Brāhmaṇa preceded by a request goes first to hell, and the Brāhmaṇa immediately after."

[Objection: If the prohibition of accepting gifts applies only to one who possesses wealth, then for one who is destitute, the previously mentioned fault would not exist. [Response: True; however, even in that case, the fault described by Vyāsa remains:
"One should not have a desire for accepting gifts, yet one may practice them for the sake of a livelihood.
A Brāhmaṇa who accepts more than what is required for his livelihood goes to a low state. [459]
One should seek the restriction of one's livelihood and not strive for the accumulation of wealth;
for by being intent on the acquisition of wealth, one falls away from the very state of a Brahmin.
Livelihood means subsistence. Manu also says:
"Seeking happiness, one should remain self-restrained by relying upon supreme contentment;
for happiness has its root in contentment, while the opposite is the root of suffering."
He is self-restrained, having withdrawn his senses. Vyāsa also said: "Who, being contented, is unable to subsist on fruits and roots?
But everyone, through greed for the objects of the senses, plunges into difficulties."
"The poor man desires wealth; from that, a kingdom; likewise from that, the status of Indra; and from that, the imperishable state. There is no end to this; therefore, one should abandon craving.
Thus, the intended meaning is that the accumulation of merit alone is necessary, not the accumulation of wealth. And so says Manu:
For in the next world, neither father nor mother remain for the sake of companionship;
neither sons, nor daughters, nor kinsmen remain—dharma alone stands by one.
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone it experiences the fruit of its good deeds, and alone that of its evil deeds.
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; Dharma alone follows him.
"Therefore, for the sake of a companion, one should always follow Dharma; thus Dharma follows him.

Thus it is established that even when one lacks wealth, one may accept from kings and others only as much wealth as is sufficient for mere subsistence, and not otherwise. As for that which was stated by Yama regarding Brahmins who have not disciplined themselves and are consumed by the sins of the king:
Just as with seeds that have been steamed, rebirth is no longer found.
Thus it is said; and also by Hārīta:
"A king indeed commits ten thousand slaughterhouse-deeds in a single day;
he commits those very same deeds at night, for his acceptance of gifts is terrible."
And as it is said in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Accepting gifts from a king is terrible; though it tastes like honey, it is like poison.
It is better to eat the flesh of one's own son than to accept gifts from a king."
Therefore, this refers to the acceptance of gifts from a king who acts contrary to the scriptures. For this very reason, Manu says:
"He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures goes, in succession, to these twenty-one hells."
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, the hell Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahānaraka.
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana,
Sahāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pratimūrtika.
The Iron Spike, the Residue of Grain, the Path, the Śālmalī River,
the Forest of Sword-Leaves, and indeed the Iron Teeth.
"Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king.
Thus [says] Yājñavalkya as well.
One should not accept gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures;
for among those who receive gifts, the butcher, the oil-presser, the liquor-seller, the prostitute, and the sovereign are the most censurable.
Each of these is ten times more wicked than the preceding one, respectively:
the butcher, the hunter, the oil-presser, the liquor-seller, and the executioner.
[This applies] to a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste and who acts according to his own whims.
The acceptance of gifts by him is terrible; though it tastes like honey, it is like poison.
"In the same way, the queen, the royal ministers, and the domestic priests—all those who perform the duties of kings are joined with sinful wealth.

[The term] *arajanaprasūtaḥ* means born of one who is not a Kṣatriya. Likewise, Hārīta states the fault even in officiating at sacrifices for the fallen (*patita*): "By officiating at sacrifices for the fallen, or by officiating at sacrifices for those who cause mixture of castes (*saṃkari*), one becomes a mixer of castes; by officiating at sacrifices for those of mixed caste, one becomes mixed with mixtures; and by officiating at sacrifices for Śūdras, one falls from one's birth-status."

"By performing a sacrifice for one, forming a matrimonial alliance with one, studying together with one, or eating together with one who has fallen (patita), one falls immediately; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding purification after accepting gifts from a fallen person, Uśanas states the following distinction:
"If a Brāhmaṇa eats food after taking property from one who has fallen [from his caste], that twice-born man, having renounced that food, should perform the Atikṛcchra penance. Thus it is said.

The same should be understood regarding officiating at sacrifices for Śūdras. And thus Sumantu says: "One who officiates for a Śūdra becomes purified by the renunciation of all his property. Regarding this renunciation, Hārīta states a specific rule: "One who officiates for a Śūdra, having cast the censurable object into a lake of the Nāgas, should approach Brāhmaṇas and say: 'May you protect me; [grant me] equality with the [other] castes. A "lake of the Nāgas" (nāgahrada) is an "unshakeable lake" (akṣobhyahrada). On this point, Manu says: "Prajāpati considered that alms brought and offered, even if not previously solicited, may be accepted even from one of evil deeds."

The meaning is that Prajāpati considers alms to be acceptable when they have been brought—that is, brought to the place of offering—and when they are offered as a gift, having been intended for donation, yet previously unasked and not previously mentioned by saying, "I give this to you. Thus says Āpastamba:
"Prajāpati considered alms that are brought forward, offered, and not previously announced to be fit to be eaten even from one who has committed evil deeds."
The mention of "receiving alms" (bhikṣāgrahaṇam) is intended as an illustration for other items such as bedding and so forth. For this very reason, Manu says:
"One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, gems, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or even vegetables."
Yājñavalkya also says: "Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, earth,
meat, beds, seats, parched grain, and water— these should not be refused."

Gautama also states: "Fuel, water, fodder, roots, fruits, honey, protection from fear, beds, seats, dwellings, vehicles, milk, curd, small fish (*śaphari*), *priyaṅgu* grain, garlands, paths, and vegetables are not to be refused by anyone. Small fish (*śapharyaḥ*) are tiny fish. "Not to be refused" means they are not to be rejected. Regarding this, Bharadvāja provides the reason:
"For there is no fault in accepting what is offered unasked;
the gods know that to be nectar (*amṛta*); therefore, one should never turn it away."
Manu also states the fault in rejecting [such a gift]: "The ancestors of him who disregards her do not eat for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his sacrificial oblation. Thus it is said.
In this regard, there is a specific rule stated by Yama: "He who treats with contempt that [woman] who goes to the womb of a *rakṣas* [through a *rākṣasa* marriage]...
This too should be understood as applying to all cases except in times of distress (*anāpad*), excluding those who are outcastes (*patita*) and so forth. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"Even from one of evil deeds, that which is brought unasked may be accepted—except from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, and likewise from an enemy. Thus it is said.
One who wanders from family to family is an *akulaṭā*, a wanton woman. Yama also says:
One should avoid food offered by a physician, a hunter, a courtesan, a gambler, a eunuch, and a woman recently delivered of a child.
A hunter is a fowler; a gambler is one who plays at dice; a butcher is a violent man—Hārīta says the same.
One should avoid the food offered by a physician, an ungrateful person, a surgeon, a usurer, a eunuch, and an unchaste woman, even if it is being served.
The definition of a usurer has been stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"He who, having acquired goods at a low price, sells them at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda."

Furthermore, for one for whom the acceptance of praised gifts and the like is impossible due to their purity, and who does not resort to the livelihood of a Vaiśya or others, even the acceptance of censurable gifts and the like does not constitute a fault; thus Manu says:
"A Brāhmaṇa who does not adopt the livelihood of a Vaiśya, remaining on his own path, if he is distressed by lack of livelihood and perishing, should practice this rule."
"Emaciated by lack of livelihood," meaning oppressed by the absence of means of subsistence; "this," meaning that which is about to be stated.
"There is no fault for Brahmins [in teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or accepting gifts] from censurable sources, for they are like fire and water."
That a purifier should become defiled— this is not logically tenable according to dharma—
for one who, having fallen into a life-threatening crisis, eats food from whatever source it may come.
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into misfortune may accept gifts from anyone;
like space, he is not defiled by that sin.
Yājñavalkya also says: "A Brahmin who,
having fallen into distress, accepts or eats from whatever source,
is not tainted by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun."
Bṛhaspati also says: "An aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son— Manu declared that these must be supported even after they have committed a hundred improper acts."
Regarding this, Manu relates an ancient account:
"Ajīgarta, being famished, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not defiled by sin, as he was acting to counteract his hunger."
Desiring to eat dog-meat when afflicted by hunger, Vāmadeva, though discerning in matters of dharma and adharma,
was not defiled because he did so for the sake of preserving his life.
But Bharadvāja, the great ascetic, being afflicted by hunger along with his son in the lonely forest,
accepted many cows from Pṛthu, the carpenter.
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.

A dog’s haunch or a dog’s tail—since a primary mode of livelihood is impossible in such cases, one must resort to a secondary one; therefore, it should be understood that even a defective livelihood belonging to one's own station is superior. And so it was said by Manu:
"Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well-performed; for by living according to the duty of another, one falls immediately from one's caste."
With this very intention, Vyāsa also said:
"The best of the twice-born should seek wealth from praiseworthy members of the twice-born, or even from those who are merely twice-born by birth, but never from a Śūdra under any circumstances."

But when even accepting gifts from censured twice-born persons is no longer possible, then it is implied that one may accept from a Śūdra as well. This has been stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "If one is perishing [from hunger], one should accept from Brāhmaṇas, then from a king, and then from Vaiśyas and Śūdras; such is the word of Śaṅkha."
Regarding the specific rule for accepting gifts from a Śūdra, Aṅgiras says:
"But that grain which may be heaped together in a threshing floor or in a field—this may be accepted even from a Śūdra; such is the statement of Aṅgiras."
Vyāsa states that when it is impossible to receive gifts even from a Śūdra and the livelihoods of a Kṣatriya or others are unavailable, then theft is prescribed:
"In times of distress, theft is permitted from those who are superior, equal, or inferior;
one should first take from an inferior, or after that, from an equal."
"But in the event of impossibility, one may take even from a distinguished righteous person.
Regarding this, Manu states the rule for the time:
"Likewise, having fasted for six meals, at the seventh meal-time..."
One may take from a person of inferior conduct by means of a "no-tomorrow" provision.
Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found—
if someone asks, that [stolen property] must be declared to him who inquires.

"A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa; however, he may take the property of a Dasyu or one who neglects his religious duties (niṣkriya) when he has no other means of subsistence. This refers to the morning of the fourth day, at the time of the seventh meal. "From one of lowly conduct" means from a non-Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
Having remained hungry for three days, one may take grain from a non-Brāhmaṇa.
On this point, Manu says:
"Roots and fruits from trees, as well as wood for the sake of fire," [may be taken].
"Manu has declared that taking grass for the sake of fodder for cows is not theft. Yama also says:
"A twice-born man may openly take grass, wood, fruit, or roots."
"Indeed, one who takes [wealth] for the sake of cows and Brahmins is not tainted by sin.
Thus says Nārada as well:
"A handful of rice, grain, or sesame seeds is prescribed as the amount that may be taken."
Or even in the case of barley and wheat, or perhaps of mung beans and black gram.
These may be seized by men standing in times of calamity;
when taken in the measure of a potherb, as a potherb, it does not constitute an offense.
Flowers should be taken for the purpose of worshipping the deities;
one who desires more than that should be known as a thief of what is not given.

[468] The meaning is that there is no fault for those situated in times of distress; for the Smṛti states: "There is no fault for travelers in taking handfuls of grain such as sesame, mung beans, black gram, barley, and wheat. Yājñavalkya also says:
"A twice-born man may take flowers from everywhere as he pleases, as if they were his own."

The meaning is "like one's own property," that is, without hesitation. All of this refers to situations of distress (*āpad*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [statements such as] "otherwise it is theft" being devoid of intended meaning. However, in non-distress, Gautama has stated: "For the sake of cows or fire, one may take grass, herbs, and the flowers of shrubs and trees as one's own, and also the fruits of those that are not enclosed. "Like one's own" means it should be taken in such a way that no injury is caused to them;
"gathering leaves and flowers, one should avoid cutting the roots, like a gardener in a grove, and not like a charcoal-maker."

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Vyāsa: "Of those not enclosed," meaning those for whom no livelihood has been provided and who are not protected. For this very reason, Manu states the punishment for taking from what is so appropriated:
"Whether it be grass or wood, or whether it be a flower or a fruit, one who takes them without having asked permission deserves the amputation of the hand."
On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"A gift must never be accepted by one who is deficient in learning and austerity;
for by accepting it, he leads both the giver and himself downward."
Just as milk, curd, ghee, or honey placed in an unbaked clay vessel would perish—both those liquids and that container—due to the weakness of the vessel; [469] so too is it with the mind.

"Thus, one who accepts gold, a cow, a horse, clothing, an umbrella, sesame seeds, and so forth, without having been asked, is reduced to ashes like a piece of wood. And thus it is established that only one who possesses knowledge is entitled to accept wealth, and no other. Furthermore, regarding the fruit for one who does not accept [wealth] even though he is qualified to accept what has been offered, Yājñavalkya says:
Even though he is capable of accepting gifts, he who does not accept them attains those abundant worlds that belong to those whose nature is to give.
Yama also says:
"For one who is capable of receiving gifts but has desisted from receiving them,
the merit that belongs to the giver is indeed the same as that of one who does not receive."
Than the mastery of all the Vedas, than the service of all the gods,
and than the gift of ten million cows, non-acceptance [of gifts] is superior for him.
Thus concludes the determination of acceptance of gifts and other matters in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follow the modes of livelihood in times of distress;
regarding this, Manu says:
But if he cannot subsist by his own prescribed Brahminical occupation,
he may live by the dharma of a Kṣatriya, for that is the next best alternative for him.
If it be asked how one should live if unable to subsist by either of these two,
one should indeed live by the livelihood of a Vaiśya, resorting to agriculture and cattle-rearing.

"Next in order" means closely proximate. The meaning is that if one cannot subsist by either of the two occupations of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, one may adopt the occupation of a Vaiśya to live, but not that of a Śūdra. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"If a Brāhmaṇa cannot subsist by his own duty, he may resort to the [occupation] of a Kṣatriya;
or he may perform the work of a Vaiśya, but he must avoid the [work] of a Śūdra."

A *vṛṣala* is a *śūdra*. Regarding the specific duties of a Vaiśya, Gautama states: "Agriculture and trade, provided they are not performed by himself, as well as usury. Usury (*kusīda*) is the lending of money for the sake of interest. Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"One may engage in usury, agriculture, and trade, provided they are not performed by oneself.
One should practice agriculture in the absence [of other means], trade in the absence of that, and usury in the absence of those."

Furthermore, as stated by Manu: "Even if living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which consists mostly of violence and is dependent on others."
They consider agriculture to be good, yet that livelihood is greatly censured;
for the wooden plough with its iron tip destroys both the earth and the creatures dwelling within it.

Thus, that refers to the intention of self-performed labor; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the previously stated injunctions. "Dependent on others" means dependent on oxen. However, when agriculture and other such activities performed by others are impossible, even self-performed agriculture and so forth certainly take place.
As it has been said by Bṛhaspati:
"One should personally carry out money-lending, agriculture, and trade."
"In times of distress, a twice-born man may perform [these tasks] himself; he is not tainted by sin.
Also, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Or he may himself engage in agriculture, trade, or money-lending."
"A miserable and sinful mode of livelihood is usury; one should avoid it.
Likewise, Nārada also states that living by means of interest is forbidden:
"Even in times of dire distress, a Brāhmaṇa must not engage in usury."

Vasiṣṭha also states: "A Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya should not practice usury. The meaning is that they should not engage in the lending of money for the sake of interest. All of this refers to the prohibition of lending after having received [money] from the hand of another; for immediately thereafter, he says the same: "He who, having taken wealth at its ordinary price, gives it back at a high price, is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda."

The meaning is that he who, having taken wealth from one person's hand at a small rate of interest, gives it to another at a high rate of interest, is a usurer (*vārdhuṣika*) and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda. Immediately following this, the fault [of usury] was also demonstrated by that very same [author]:
"He weighed the killing of an embryo against interest on a scale;
the killer of the embryo remained steady at the end, while the usurer trembled."
Hārīta also says:
"If one were to weigh a slayer of a Brahmin against a usurer on a scale,
the slayer of a Brahmin would remain at the top, while the usurer trembled."

The same should be understood regarding the sale of grain and other such goods. And so says Manu: "He who, having acquired a commodity at a fair price, sells it at a high price, is indeed called a usurer, as is he who deals in interest."
In this regard,
he who, having taken a loan at a moderate price, employs it at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
He weighed the killing of a Brahmin against usury on a scale;
the killer of a Brahmin remained steady at the end of the beam, while the usurer trembled.

This is the specific rule stated by Baudhāyana. Since this prohibits only a specific case, it is understood that the lending of wealth for the sake of one's own personal interest is not prohibited in every instance. For this very reason, Manu says:
"Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor even a Kṣatriya should ever lend at interest;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may indeed give a small amount to a person of evil character."

The meaning is that one may give a small amount for the sake of dharma to one who is more wicked or of inferior conduct. And so Paiṭhīnasi says: "One may indeed give to a more wicked person, but one should not take a higher rate of interest. And that interest has been shown by Manu:
"A moneylender may employ the interest prescribed by Vasiṣṭha to increase his wealth;
he may take an eightieth part of a hundred per month" (MDh 8.140).
As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
