"Many means of increasing wealth have been proclaimed by the sages;
yet among all of these, they know usury to be the most superior."

Thus, that [statement] is intended to demonstrate the superiority [of moneylending] in terms of the increase of wealth, and not to assert its absolute preeminence; for immediately thereafter, that same author says: "Loss may occur in agriculture and other [occupations] due to drought, royal oppression, or calamities such as rats; such loss is not found in moneylending."
Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark, by night or even by day,
in heat, rain, or cold, it increases and does not turn back.

"The increase that accrues to those who have gone abroad, subsisting by various kinds of merchandise, arises exactly for one who remains at home and practices usury. Thus it is established that a Brāhmaṇa, if he should fall into distress, may live according to the dharma of a Kṣatriya; and if that is unavailable, he may live according to the dharma of a Vaiśya, but never according to the dharma of a Śūdra. In the same way, it should be understood that for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya as well, the livelihood of the one immediately following their own rank is permissible in times of distress. And so says Manu:

"A Kṣatriya who has fallen into misfortune may live by all of this [means], but he should never at any time consider a higher mode of livelihood for himself. By "this," is meant the way of life of a Vaiśya; "fallen into misfortune" means having encountered calamity.
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may also live by the occupation of a Śūdra;
however, he should avoid improper conduct and desist from forbidden acts as soon as he is capable.

[474] "Improper acts" refers to eating the remnants of food and so forth. "Capable" means one who has crossed over his misfortune. The meaning is that he should subsist by the occupation of a Śūdra. Vasiṣṭha also says: "If unable to live by his own duty, he may adopt the next lower occupation, but never a higher one. "Lower" refers to occupations pertaining to inferior castes; "higher" refers to occupations pertaining to superior castes. For a Śūdra, however, even an occupation pertaining to a superior caste is indeed permitted. As Nārada says:
"Between those two (the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya), there exists neither a superior nor an inferior occupation for him (the Śūdra)."
"Having abandoned the two middle actions, for those two are common to all."

The meaning is that between those two—the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra—there is no degraded Śūdra-work for the Brāhmaṇa, nor is there any exalted Brāhmaṇa-work for the Śūdra. Some, however, maintain that even Śūdra-work may be performed in extreme distress. To this effect says Gautama: "Not by Śūdra-work; some say that even that [is permissible] when life is in danger. This means one should live by work other than that of a Śūdra; the meaning is that even that [Śūdra-work] may be done for the sake of survival when life is at risk. The modes of livelihood for a Śūdra in times of distress have been shown by Yājñavalkya: "Service to the twice-born is the duty of a Śūdra; if unable to subsist by that, he may become a merchant."
"Or he may live by various crafts and perform what is beneficial for the twice-born.
This means: by those occupations through which the twice-born are served. And so says Manu:
"By those occupations which, when practiced, serve the twice-born..."
"Those are the crafts of artisans and various skills.
Regarding that, Yājñavalkya states other means of livelihood:
"Agriculture, craftsmanship, wages, learning, usury, a cart, and the mountain."
A king who lives by service or by begging during times of distress, however, is indeed a livelihood.

Crafts refer to cooking and the like; service refers to being a servant; learning refers to teaching for wages and the like; usury refers to lending money for the sake of interest; the cart refers to making a living by means of transporting grain and other goods; the mountain refers to making a living through the grass and such found thereon; service refers to following the will of another; a marshy region (anūpa) is a place with many trees and water; and the king refers to the monarch. Because of the statement that "these are means of livelihood in times of distress," whichever mode of subsistence is prohibited for a particular person is permitted for him when he is in a state of calamity. Manu also [says]:
"Knowledge, craft, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury—these are the ten means of livelihood.
Here, "contentment" (*dhṛti*) means satisfaction; by which one may live even with what is extremely meager. Regarding this, Aṅgiras says:
"Alms-seeking is prescribed for one who is diseased, for one who is impoverished, for one who has fallen from his family, or for one who has set out upon a journey.
This recourse to the livelihood of another is intended for a situation where even one's own deficient means of subsistence cannot be obtained. And so says Manu:
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the well-performed duty of another;
for by living according to the duty of another, one immediately falls from one's caste.

Gautama says: "Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts—among these, each preceding one is more weighty than the following for all. In the absence of those, the livelihood of a Kṣatriya. The phrase "for all" implies Brāhmaṇas and the other castes; here, the term "alternative course in times of distress" (*āpadkalpa*) is understood to carry over. Thus, by the use of the word "all," those [livelihoods] that are not commendable are included, since the commendable ones have already been prescribed even in the absence of distress. By this, it is stated that among sacrificing, teaching, and receiving gifts, receiving gifts is the most commendable. Yama also says: "Among receiving gifts, teaching, and sacrificing, they declare the receiving of gifts to be the most excellent."
One is purified from accepting gifts through recitations and burnt offerings; however, the Vedas do not purify one from the sins of officiating at sacrifices for the unworthy.

"Yājya" means the sacrificer; this refers specifically to the acceptance of gifts from the twice-born. This is because Manu, regarding the case of Śūdras, has stated that [officiating at sacrifices and teaching] are inferior to accepting gifts: "Between accepting gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and likewise teaching, accepting gifts is the lowest and is censured for a Brāhmaṇa. (MDh 10.109)
The inferior one is the low-born. He himself states the reason for this:
"Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed for those whose souls have been refined;
however, the acceptance of gifts is performed even from a Śūdra of the lowest birth."

"Sin caused by officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*) is removed by recitation (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*); however, that which arises from receiving gifts (*pratigraha*) is removed only by renouncing them and through austerity (*tapas*).

(477) This refers to the twice-born (*dvijāti*) whose souls have been refined. Therefore, it should be understood that for a twice-born person, receiving gifts is actually superior to officiating at sacrifices and teaching. Regarding even this matter of receiving gifts, Manu states a distinction:
"Unplowed land is better than plowed land; likewise, cattle, goats, and sheep;
gold, grain, and food—each preceding one is free from fault. Here, "unplowed" means uncultivated. Yājñavalkya states what is not to be sold for one living by the occupation of a Vaiśya:
Fruit, fruit-stones, linen, soma, humans, cakes, creepers, sesame, cooked rice, meat broth, honey, curd, milk, ghee, and water.
Weapons, liquor, beeswax, honey, lac, and the feathers of a peacock;
earth, leather, flowers, a woolen blanket, hair, buttermilk, poison, and the ground.
Silk, indigo, salt, meat, one-hoofed animals,
lead, vegetables, half-ripe grains, oil-cakes, livestock, and perfumes— likewise [these are not to be sold].

"Even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, one should never sell [these]. Regarding fruits, this excludes the *badara* and *iṅguda*. Under the recurring rule "that which is to be sold," [it is stated]: "The husks of *badara* and *iṅguda* fruits may be sold when they have become rotten on their own."
If that thread made of jute or cotton should remain unaltered.

Thus, from the Smṛti of Nārada: "Stone" refers to rubies (*māṇikya*) and the like; "linen" (*kṣauma*) is that made from flax fibers; "cake" (*apūpa*) refers to *maṇṭka* and similar items; "creepers" (*vīrudh*) are climbing plants; "liquids" (*rasa*) are sugarcane juice and so forth; "distilled liquor" (*āsava*) is intoxicating drink; "beeswax" (*madhūcchiṣṭa*) is *sikthaka*; "honey" (*madhu*) is *kṣaudra*; "lac" (*lākṣā*) is *jatu*; "barhis grass" is *kuśa* and the like; "kutapa" is a specific type of woolen blanket; "hair" refers to that belonging to yaks (*camari*) and other animals; "single-hoofed animals" are horses and the like; "animals" include both wild and domestic ones, according to the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha: "Among animals, single-hoofed ones, hairy ones, all wild animals, those with cloven hooves, and fanged ones [are forbidden]. Here, "hairy ones" refers to humans. Gautama also states: "His forbidden articles for sale are: perfumes, liquids, prepared food, sesame, hemp, linen, skins, dyed and washed garments, milk and its products, roots, fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, water, and salt; animals when associated with slaughter; barren cows, cows that miscarry, and cows that have recently calved; and, according to some, land, rice, barley, goats, sheep, horses, bulls, milch-cows, and oxen. "Prepared food" (*kṛtānna*) means cooked food. "Dyed" refers to woven cloth, according to the Smṛti of Manu: "Dyed items include those made of hemp, linen, and wool. "Washed" means cleansed. "Roots" are turmeric and the like; "fruits" are betel nuts and the like; "unwholesome" (*apathya*) refers to poison. Regarding "associated with slaughter," animals that have been slaughtered are not to be sold. A "barren cow" (*vaśā*) is one that does not conceive; a "miscarrier" (*vehad*) is one that destroys her fetus. Some maintain that land and the others are also always unsaleable. The commentary on that text explains that because of the use of the singular "some" (*eke*), this does not apply to Gautama. Nārada also repeats the rule "it is unsaleable" (*avikreya*).
Safflower, coconut, eggplant, and likewise stinking herbs;
Soma, Śleṣmātaka, the sacrificial post, water, and clarified butter—these are always [permissible].

Manu also says: "Milk, honey, curd, ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and *kuśa* grass. Here, "honey" (*kṣaudra*) refers to that produced by bees. Furthermore, this prohibition against trading applies specifically to the Brāhmaṇa, as Nārada states:
"Even by means of the occupation of a Vaiśya, milk and curd must not be sold by a Brāhmaṇa. Thus [it is said].

Āpastamba also says: "Trade is not prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa. In times of distress, he may engage in commerce, avoiding articles that ought not to be sold. The meaning is that he should trade with goods while excluding those items that are forbidden as merchandise. Regarding this, he (Āpastamba) states a further distinction: "He trades with goods not purchased. This means by means of goods obtained through sources other than purchase. By this, it is implied that even in times of distress, one should not trade using goods acquired through purchase. Thus, regarding the fault incurred in transgressing the aforementioned prohibitions, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "A Brāhmaṇa falls immediately from his status by trading in sesame, curd, honey, salt, lac, liquor, meat, cooked food, women, men, elephants, horses, bulls, perfumes, liquids, black antelope skins, Soma, and water. Yājñavalkya also [says]:
Lac, salt, and meat are causes for falling [from one's caste] if sold;
however, milk, curd, and liquor cause one to become of a lower caste.
[480] One of inferior caste is a Śūdra. Manu also says: "One falls immediately through the sale of meat, lac, or salt; a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra in three days by selling milk."
But by intentionally selling other commodities here,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.
Yama also says:
"The seller of oily substances, flavors, living beings— even those still alive—
and of goods for sale as gifts, is declared by the wise to be a slayer of a Brahmin."
But one who sells cows shall become a worm in a cow-pen for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on those cows.
If one uses sesame seeds for any purpose other than giving them away, as anointing oil,
or for consumption, that evildoer becomes a worm in excrement because of that action.
Manu also says:
"Whatever one does with sesame seeds other than eating, anointing, or giving them away,
he becomes a worm in excrement and sinks there along with his ancestors."
But as for what was stated by that very same [author]:
"A farmer, having personally undertaken cultivation,
may at his pleasure sell pure sesame seeds that have not been kept for long, for the sake of dharma."

Thus—meaning pure, unmixed with other substances—even though Vasiṣṭha says: [481] "Or, at their own will, having produced sesame by cultivation themselves, they may sell them," this refers to sale characterized by barter. As Nārada says: "In case of inability, for the sake of medicine, and likewise for the purpose of a sacrifice, if sesame must necessarily be sold, it should be exchanged for an equal amount of grain."

The meaning is that sesame seeds may be sold only as an equivalent measure of grain, and not for coin or similar currency. Yājñavalkya also states: "Sesame seeds, being equal to those [grains], may be sold for the sake of dharma in exchange for grain. Manu likewise says:
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors;
prepared food may be exchanged for unprepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equal.

*Kṛtānna* means cooked food (*pakvānna*). *Nimātavyāḥ* means they are to be exchanged; this is the meaning. This should be understood in the same way regarding humans and so forth. For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "Food for food, humans for humans, liquids for liquids, fragrances for fragrances, and knowledge for knowledges. Here, the term "exchange" (*vinimaya*) is understood to carry over. Regarding liquids, Vasiṣṭha states a specific rule: "Liquids may be exchanged for liquids that are equal or inferior. "Equal" means of equivalent measure; "inferior" means of smaller quantity. Gautama, however, states a specific rule concerning food: "But cooked food may be exchanged for uncooked food of equal value. The meaning is that an exchange of cooked food takes place with uncooked food of equal value. On this point, Hārīta says:
However, the exchange or sale of rasa and other such substances is not at all blameworthy,
just as the word of Prajāpati permits the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of a sacrifice.
Nārada also says:

"But for a Brāhmaṇa, dry wood and grass may be sold. Having thus crossed over the calamity by resorting to the livelihood of another, and having purified himself through penance, he should return to his own proper mode of life. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"In times of distress, a twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or even that of a Vaiśya;
having emerged from that distress and purified himself, he should then set out upon his proper path.
Thus ends the section on times of distress in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Then follows the midday bath;
regarding this, Bodhāyana says:
"Then, at the time of midday, one should perform the bath once again."
Then follows the worship of the Sun, as well as the recitation of prayers, fire offerings, and so forth.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Then, at the time of midday, one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing.
"At the time of midday" means during the fourth part of the day divided into eight parts. For this very reason, Dakṣa says:

Likewise, on the fourth part of the day, one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing, as well as sesame seeds, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth; and the bath should be performed in natural water.
Vasiṣṭha and Hārīta also state:
"With the sacred grass (pavitra) in hand, one-pointed in mind, not looking toward his sides,
and free from illness, one should perform the bath during the day, especially before midday."
"Aroga" means one who is free from disease. By this it is stated that one who is ill should not bathe for the sake of [auspicious] purposes. And it has been said by Vyāsa:
"One should perform the midday bath when the food is well-digested and when free from illness;
one should not bathe after eating, nor while adorned, nor while ill, nor in water whose depth is unknown, nor while agitated."
And this bath is to be understood as applying to the householder and the forest-dweller. Thus says Dakṣa:
"The morning and midday baths are for the forest-dweller and the householder;
the ascetic's bath is at the three sessions of the day, and that of the student is once [daily]."
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
They declare that bathing with waters purified by mantras yields fruit;
for those who merely immerse themselves in water without such means, there is no fruit, just as there is none for aquatic creatures.
The meaning is "of aquatic creatures," that is, water-dwelling beings. Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"Fish, tortoises, and frogs dwell submerged in the water day and night;
even though they reside there, they do not obtain the fruit of bathing anywhere."
Therefore, the intention is that the rite must be performed exactly as prescribed by the mantra. For this very reason, Vivasvat stated the fault incurred by failing to perform it:
"He who performs the ritual bath without knowing the procedure for bathing goes to a terrible hell; such is the established law of Dharma. [484]
This also pertains to the twice-born. To that effect, Viṣṇu says:
"O descendant of Kuru, the bath accompanied by mantras is prescribed for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas; however, for Śūdras and women, it is indeed to be performed silently."
Regarding the materials for bathing here, Yogayājñavalkya says:
"One who is self-controlled and pure should, at the time of bathing, collect earth, sesame seeds, cow dung, darbha grass, and fragrant flowers for the purpose of bathing."
Śātātapa describes the nature of clay:

"Clay from an anthill, from a molehill, from what has been used for smearing, from water, from a road, from a tree, and that which remains after purification— these seven types of clay are not to be taken."
One should collect earth from a clean place, free from gravel, stones, and the like;
it is traditionally held that there are three kinds of earth: red, pale-yellow, and white.
One should not collect earth or cow dung during the night.
"A wise man should not collect cow urine during the evening watches.

Thus [it is said]. After collecting earth and other materials, Yogayājñavalkya states: "Having gone to the water's edge, he should place it separately upon the ground according to the prescribed rule."
The wise man, having divided that clay and the cow dung into three parts, [should proceed].
One should perform the cleansing of the lower, upper, and middle parts of the body with those [substances] in separate portions;
in the act of cleansing, there must be no mixing of the earth.
"Having washed both feet with water and earth and having sipped water (ācamana), one is indeed pure.
[485] Regarding this, Vyāsa speaks concerning the bath for removing impurities:
"The feet with six [applications of earth], the shanks with four, and the navel and hips with three."
The head should be washed with one application of clay, and likewise the area above the navel with two.
"Then one should perform [the cleansing] with three [applications of earth] below, and likewise with six for the feet;

having washed the entire body, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice according to the rule. In this matter, the arrangement is determined by one's own *śākhā*. The measurement of the clay and so forth is shown in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Clay for the purpose of bathing should be taken in a quantity equal to a fresh *āmalaka* fruit;
that is the measure for the cow-dung, with which one should then smear the body.
And this bathing, which consists of removing impurities, should be performed on the riverbank. Thus it is said in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*.
Having sprinkled water upon a clean spot, one should place kusha grass and earth there;
having diligently purified one's own body externally with earth and water.
Dakṣa also says:
"Bathing is said to be of three kinds: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya). Among these, that which is the daily is further divided into three types."
"The removal of impurity on the side [of the body] is prescribed in water with the recitation of mantras;

the twilight bath (*saṃdhyā-snāna*) is performed by both [methods]. Thus the locations for bathing are proclaimed. Here, "on the side" means on the bank. "Twilight bath" refers to the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*). The meaning is that this should be performed by both [methods]: in water and on land. In this context, the inclusion of the term "obligatory" (*nitya*) even regarding the bath for removing impurity is so that its obligatory nature may apply even to those who do not belong to the specific Vedic schools mentioned. Following the bath for removing impurity, Yama says:

"Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), standing facing the east, he should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and then meditate upon the Sun. Thereafter, he should perform the ritual preparation of the sacred site (tīrtha-parikalpanā) and so forth; and thus says the Matsya Purāṇa:
With darbha grass in hand, having sipped water according to the rule, being self-controlled and pure,
the wise knower of mantras should fashion a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) with the root mantra.
"Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" is declared to be the root mantra.
[The area] should be a square on all sides, measuring four cubits.
Having prepared [the vessel], the wise one should invoke the Gaṅgā with these mantras:
"You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu; you belong to Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu is your deity."
"Save us from that sin which begins at birth and ends with death," said Vāyu to the three and a half crores of holy fords.
May those [names] of yours exist for me, O Jahnavi, in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space;
for your name among the gods is indeed Nandinī, and [on earth] it is Nalinī.
Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Vihagā, Visvarāyā, Śivāmṛtā, Vidyādharī, Suprasannā, and likewise Lokaprasādinī.
Kṣamā, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī—
these auspicious names one should recite at the time of bathing.
The Gaṅgā, flowing through the three paths, would be present there;
likewise, the words of the Gaṅgā also state:
"Nandinī, Nalinī, Sītā, and Mahāpagā Mālatī."
Born from the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, the Gaṅgā flows through the three paths;
she is known as Bhāgīrathī, Bhogavatī, Jāhnavī, and Tridaśeśvarī.
In whatever reservoir of water these twelve names are present, [there one should bathe].
One intent on bathing should always remember that "I am present there, there. Vyāsa also says:
Kurukṣetra, Gayā, Gaṅgā, Prabhāsa, and likewise Naimiṣa.
"May all these sacred fords (tīrthas) be present for me at the time of bathing.
This entire [formula] refers to artificial water;
one should mentally recall the Gaṅgā and all other sacred fords within such artificial waters.
Thus it is from the *Yogayājñavalkya-smṛti*. Devala also says: "In rivers one should not speak of a river, nor of a mountain in mountains;
staying there at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and shrines, one should not praise anything else."

Having thus invoked [the earth], one should bathe according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā). For this very reason, the *Matsya Purāṇa* states immediately after the rules for purification:
"One should perform a bath with clay, likewise having addressed it according to the rule:
'O Vasundharā, traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, traversed by Viṣṇu!'"
On this point, Jamadagni says:
"Now I shall proclaim the ritual bathing that destroys all sins.
A twice-born man should not bathe in a small body of water, nor should he abandon a river to bathe in an artificial one."
One should spread out a washed cloth with its ends pointing either eastward or northward;
then, being pure, one should fetch clean earth with the mantra "Aśvakrānte."
Having offered [the water] to the Sun with the mantra "namo mitrasya," one should wash one's hands;
having recited "gandhadvārām," one should smear [the remains] upon one's own limbs.
With the mantra "To Varuṇa with the golden horns," he approaches the waters;
having cast [the water] into the waters with the mantra "May they be friendly to us," he should cast that which is unfriendly outside.

Having stirred the water three times with his hand while reciting "Whatever is cruel in the waters," he should immerse himself facing the sun while reciting the two-verse hymn beginning with "May the waters [purify] us."
At midday, he should sip water with the mantra "May the waters purify me";
in the evening and in the morning, he should do so with "May Agni and I... and "May Sūrya and I...".
One should sprinkle [the materials] with water from the *surabhimatī* and *ābliṅga* verses while holding *kuśa* grass in the hand,
as well as with the *hiraṇyavarṇīya* and *pāvamānī* verses.

"One should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, beginning with 'ṛtaṃ ca,' three times within the waters; as there is an *avabhṛtha* bath at the end of a horse sacrifice, so is the *Aghamarṣaṇa* at this bath. All other rites, such as the libations (*tarpaṇa*) of water and so forth, are to be understood as prescribed for the morning bath. The instruction "one should immerse oneself facing the sun" refers specifically to standing water. Thus says the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"A twice-born man should bathe in rivers and flowing streams standing against the current;
in the waters of tanks and the like, he should perform his bath facing the sun.
Regarding this, the *Kūrma Purāṇa* speaks concerning the *Drupadā* [mantra]:
"Having taken water in the hand and performed the sprinkling with those waters,
by placing that water upon the head, one is released from all sins.
Regarding this, Yogayājñavalkya states a specific detail:
Taking water in one's hand, one should recite the Drupadā verse three times;
by placing that water upon one's head, one is liberated from all sins.
He himself has also stated that this [mantra] is inherently effective for muttering while submerged in water:
"Even after destroying these three worlds, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa three times;
Manu has declared that it is indeed equivalent to the final purificatory bath of a horse sacrifice."
That goddess named Drupadā is established in the Yajurveda;
by reciting it three times while submerged in water, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Vyāsa also says: "The Gāyatrī named Drupadā, which belongs to the Brāhmaṇa Vājasaneyaka,
removes even the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa for one who recites it once while submerged in water."
Then, having become purified and recited the Sāvitrī mantra three times while submerged in water,
one is released from all sins, provided that one is not a slayer of a Brahmin.
Hārīta also says:
"The Gāyatrī named Jumbukā, found in the Vājasaneyaka Veda,
removes even the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa when recited once while submerged in water."

Sumantu also says: "Having killed one's mother, sister, maternal aunt, paternal aunt, daughter-in-law, female friend, or having committed any other forbidden sexual act, one becomes purified from this by reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times while submerged in water. Hārīta also says: "By muttering the verse, *āyaṃ gauḥ pṛśnir akramīt*, three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sin; or else, by muttering the *vyāhṛtis* three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sin. Gautama also says: "Or else, by muttering the *Gāyatrī* verse—foot by foot, half-verse by half-verse, and the whole—three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sin; or else, by muttering the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sin. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states the rule for bathing.
Now I shall proclaim in due order the entire procedure for bathing,
by performing which with faith, the best of the twice-born go to heaven.
Being self-restrained, having taken earth, durva grass, and fresh cow dung,
and having set them down and likewise performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then perform the bath.
The head should be washed with one portion of clay; likewise, the area above the navel with two portions, the body below it with three portions, and the feet with six portions.
Having washed all his limbs and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice according to the rule,
the knower of mantras should then first perform the cleansing with earth.
O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, trodden by Viṣṇu!
You were lifted up by the boar, by Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms.
O clay, I take you along with offspring and wealth;
O clay, you are bestowed by Brahmā and consecrated by Kāśyapa.
O Earth, destroy my sin, whatever evil deed I have committed;
O Earth, grant me prosperity, for everything is established upon you.
And again, speaking with cow dung, "tip by tip," he [gathered] the tips of the tips of the herbs as they grew in forest after forest.
O cow dung, the purifier that cleanses the body of those wives of the bull,
drive away my diseases, my sorrows, and my sin.
With the two verses beginning "From joint to joint," one should touch each limb.
The word "with *dūrvā*" is to be supplied [to the verse]. These two mantras belong to the Yajurveda.

Having thus performed the purification (*mārjana*) with the mantras beginning with "aśvakrāntā," one should then [invoke] the immortal Goddess right here, as in the *Pārāvata* and other [texts]: "O Pārāvata, [I invoke] the immortal Goddess right here..."
Having meditated that "these are the hundred [tīrthas]," the wise man should invoke the sacred fords:
Kurukṣetra, Gayā, the Gaṅgā, Prabhāsa, and the Puṣkara lakes.
Then one should consecrate [the water] with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the Gāyatrī,
and also with the verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," "idam āpaḥ," and "drupadād iva."
Likewise, with the *hiraṇyavarṇā* verses and the *pāvamānī* hymns,
the wise man, having looked at the sun while uttering the syllable *oṃ*, should immerse himself within the water.
One should perform breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the Gāyatrī, and the Aghamarṣaṇa;
then, having been agitated by those [faults], one should immerse oneself three times like a staff as prescribed.
Having bathed according to the aforementioned methods— consisting of the inflation, retention, and expulsion of breath— one should take another garment and cleanse the thighs with earth;
however, if they have been made impure by the discharge from the private parts, one should cleanse them with water.
A wise man should never wear his upper garment below, nor his lower garment above; he should never dwell in a garment without an inner undergarment.
Having sat down in a clean place facing either the east or the north, he should sip water twice;
whichever body of water a twice-born man bathes in according to this rule, [he gains its merit].
He obtains the fruit of a sacred ford, and at a sacred ford the fruit is indeed twofold;
yet whatever sin he commits through thought, word, or deed, [it is all purified].
All that goes to destruction, like an unbaked clay vessel in water. Thus [it is said].

Having removed dirt with earth and water, one should immerse oneself and touch water while reciting the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and the verse *idam āpaḥ pravahata*. Then, one should consecrate the bathing place (*tīrtha*) with these mantras. Thereafter, submerged in the water, one should mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times—either *tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam*, or the *drupadā* verse, or the *sāvitrī*, or the section beginning with *yuñjate manaḥ*, or the *puruṣasūkta*. Having bathed, while still wearing wet clothes, one should perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods, sages, and ancestors while remaining in the water. Āpastamba also states: "One should descend into the water slowly, striking the water [with one's hands], and touch the water facing the sun; this is the rule for touching water in all cases. [493] Regarding this, the commentary on that [text] explains that the mention of "touching water" here refers specifically to forest-dwellers (*vanastha*), because it is recited within that specific context. In this regard, Yogayājñavalkya states the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*):
If one is unable to perform this extensive and supreme procedure for bathing that has been described, then this following rule is prescribed.
Bathing within the water, as well as sprinkling, sipping,
the consecration of the water, and the visualization of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
"By means of the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta recited three times daily,

this is declared by the great sages to be the performance of the ritual bath. Thus, some have explained that this prescription for the preparation of the sacred site (tīrtha) refers to the rule of reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta three times during the consecration of the water, the sipping of water (ācamana), the sprinkling (mārjana), and the bath within the water.
Thus ends the midday bath in the Smṛticandrikā;
now follows the midday twilight (saṃdhyā) rite.
Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
One should perform the morning and midday twilight devotions during the ritual bathing,
and one should worship the western twilight together with the sun according to the prescribed rule.

"In the rite of bathing" means immediately after the midday bath. Here is the procedure: Having bathed and sipped water (*ācamana*) according to the rules, one should restrain the breath (*prāṇāyāma*) and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the midday twilight worship (*mādhyāhnasaṃdhyā*). Then, as before, having offered oblations with the three verses beginning with *apo hi ṣṭhā*, one should drink water with the verse *āpaḥ punantu*. Its meter is *anuṣṭubh*; Viṣṇu is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the waters are the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sipping of water during the midday twilight worship. Thereafter, all rites from the sprinkling (*mārjana*) onwards, up until the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*, are to be performed as at the morning twilight worship. A specific detail regarding this is shown in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Then, at the midday twilight, one should recite while seated facing the east;
a twice-born man should always recite while standing, facing the sun.
This means that if he stands, he should recite while facing the sun. For this very reason, Yogayājñavalkya says:
If standing, he should gaze at the sun; if seated, he should recite the prayer facing the east.
In this case as well, he should worship the Sun with the mantras prescribed in his own Vedic branch;
indeed, he should perform the worship of the Sun with the rituals belonging to himself.
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha. All of this was stated by Nārāyaṇa:

"Wearing the sacred thread, with his topknot tied, having sipped water according to the tradition, and with the *pavitra* grass in hand, he should mentally remember the Lord of Sacrifice (*yajñeśa*) preceded by the syllable *oṃ*."
Having remembered the meter, the seer, and the deity according to the rules for the morning twilight ritual,
and having sipped water (ācamana), one should restrain the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) while holding darbha grass in the hand.
One should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with the mantra "May the waters purify" and "O Waters, stand," and likewise,
having properly offered a handful of water, one should recite "ud u tyam" and "citram."
With the mantra "That eye, beneficial to the gods" and also "The swan dwelling in purity," he should recite this with arms raised, gazing at the sun with a concentrated mind.
"Having worshipped the Sun with the Gāyatrī according to one's ability, a wise person should not perform the recitation (*japa*) loudly, especially that of the Sāvitrī. Thus it is said.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), sipping of water (*ācamana*), and so forth, are prescribed precisely within the midst of that bath.
Then, at the time of midday, one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing,
as well as flowers, unbroken rice grains, *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and pure cow dung.
The head should be washed with one portion of clay; likewise, the area from the navel upwards and downwards should be washed with two portions each;
the body with three portions, and the feet likewise with six.
And clay is prescribed, along with three fresh *āmalaka* fruits;
that is the measure for the cow dung, with which one should then smear the body.
Having washed his hands and sipped water according to the rule, he should then bathe with a concentrated mind,
having consecrated the water with auspicious Vāruṇa mantras containing the word "water."
Purified by meditation, he should hold that unmanifest, imperishable Viṣṇu;
for the waters are called "nārāḥ," and they are indeed his place of rest (ayana).
Therefore, at the time of bathing, a wise person should meditate upon the god Nārāyaṇa;
having looked at the sun while uttering the syllable *oṃ*, he should immerse himself three times in the body of water.
Having sipped water once, the knower of mantras should sip again with this mantra:
"You move within all beings, dwelling in the secret cave, facing in every direction."
You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, the waters, light, essence, and immortality.
Thereafter, one should perform the purification with the verses beginning *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*.
"O Waters, carry this away," with these words and likewise with the *vyāhṛtis*;
then, having consecrated that water with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Having entered the water and submerged himself, he should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
then he should worship the sun with water and flowers held above him.
Having cast [the flower], he should gaze upon the deity with the mantras "ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ pari," "ud u tyaṃ citram," and "tat cakṣuḥ."
With the mantra "haṃaḥ śuciṣad," especially with the Sāvitrī,
and with other Vedic mantras dedicated to the Sun that destroy sin.
"One should indeed recite the Sāvitrī afterwards; that is traditionally known as the *japayajña* (recitation-sacrifice).
Thus [says] Bodhāyana as well:

Then, having washed his hands and taken hold of his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a lump of clay, he goes to the bathing place (*tīrtha*) and washes his feet three times and himself three times. Then he approaches the water with the verse: "Varuṇa with golden horns... He takes up water in his joined palms with the formula: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us. He sprinkles that water toward the direction in which someone whom he hates resides, saying: "May they be unfriendly to him! Then, having touched water, he turns the water clockwise three times with the verse: "Whatever is cruel in the waters... Having submerged himself in the water and emerged, he sips water and sips again with the verse: "May the waters purify... Having made two strainers (*pavitra*) and purified himself with water, he purifies himself with the three verses beginning with "The waters are best," with the four verses beginning with "Golden-colored," and with the entire section beginning with "Pavamāna, the source of light. Having gone into the water, held three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, and having emerged, wrung out his garment, and put on clothes that have been washed, aired, and unworn, he sips water, sits upon *darbha* grass holding *darbha* blades, and facing eastward, repeats the *Sāvitrī* a thousand times. Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the determination of the Mādhyandina twilight ritual in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the praise of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*).
Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says:
"The four types of *pākayajña* sacrifices, even when accompanied by the ritual sacrifices (*vidhiyajña*),
are all not worth a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*)."
The *pākayajñas* are the sacrifices to the gods (*devayajña*) and so forth; the *vidhiyajña* is the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other such rites. Manu also says:
"The sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is superior to the ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*) by tenfold merit.
A Brāhmaṇa may attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter."
Yama also says:
Among livelihoods, agriculture is the best; among duties, the practice of hospitality is supreme;
and among all sacrifices, the sacrifice of silent recitation (japa-yajña) is remembered as the highest.
Also in the Purāṇa:
"Yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and all terrifying grahas do not approach one who recites [the mantra]; they flee from afar."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Just as fire, fanned by the wind and fed with oblations, blazes up,
so too does the twice-born man who is constantly devoted to silent recitation and always joined with the mantra."
Thus ends the praise of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the recitations (*japyāni*),
Yājñavalkya in the *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
Indeed, the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) should be performed with the various purificatory mantras prescribed in all the Vedas,
as well as those from the Gṛhyasūtras and the Upaniṣads.
[498] Various internal sciences (*adhyātmavidyā*) are to be recited; indeed, through the recitation of these, one succeeds in *japa*.

This is also accomplished by other means, such as the praise of deities and so forth. Viṣṇu also says: "Having bathed and with pure hands, one should recite according to one's ability, especially the *Sāvitrī* or the *Puruṣasūkta*; there is nothing superior to these two. And those purifiers (*pavitra*) have been shown by Vasiṣṭha:
"Henceforth, I shall declare all the purifiers of the Vedas."
By whose recitations and burnt offerings one is purified—of this there is no doubt.
The Aghamarṣaṇa, the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, the Taratsamās, the Kūṣmāṇḍyas, the Pāvamānīs, as well as the Durgā and the Sāvitrī.
The Abhiṣaṅgas, the Padastobhas, the Sāmans, as well as the Vyāhṛtis,
the Vāruṇa Sāmans, the Gāyatra, and likewise the Raivata.
The *abliṅga*, the *bārhaspatya*, the *vāksūkta*, the *madhvṛca*s,
as well as the *śatarudra*, the *atharvaśiras*, the *trisuparṇa*, and the *mahāvrata*.
The *gosūkta*, the *aśvasūkta*, the two *sāmans* known as *indraśuddha*,
the three *ājyadohas*, the *rathantara*, the *agnivratam*, the *vāsudevyam*, and the *bṛhat*—
these, when recited, purify living beings; one who so desires shall attain the memory of former births.

The three beginning with *aghamarṣaṇam* and *ṛtam ca*; those beginning with *devakṛtam* and *devakṛtasyainaḥ*; the three *śuddhavatyaḥ* beginning with *eto nv indram stavāma*; the three *taratsamāḥ* beginning with *taratsamandī dhāvati*; the three *kūśmāṇḍyaḥ* consisting of the three sections beginning with *yad devā devaheḷanam*; the *pāvamānyaḥ* beginning with *svādiṣṭhayā madiṣṭhayā*; the single verse of Durgā, *jātavedase sunavāma somam*; the *sāvitrī*, *tat savituḥ*; the specific Sāman chants beginning with the *abhiṣaṅga*s and ending with the *raivata*; the *abliṅgāḥ* beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*; the *bārhaspatyam* consisting of eleven verses beginning with *yas tastambha sahasā*; the *vāksūktam* consisting of eight verses beginning with *ahaṃ rudrebhiḥ*; the three *madhvṛcaḥ* beginning with *madhu vātā ṛtāyate*; the *śatarudrīyam* consisting of eleven sections beginning with *namas te rudra manyave*; the *trisuparṇam* consisting of three sections beginning with *brahma metu mām*; the *mahāvrata* consisting of the *rājana* Sāman; the *gosūktam* consisting of eight verses beginning with *ā gāvo agman*; the *aśvasūktam* consisting of twenty-two verses beginning with *mā no mitro varuṇaḥ*; and the specific Sāman chants beginning with the *indraśuddha*s and ending with the *bṛhat*. These are the purifiers (*pavitrāṇi*), meaning they are the *aghamarṣaṇa*s. This also applies to the *caturviṃśati* hymns.
By reciting the Devavrata, Ājyadoha, and Agnīdhra hymns, as well as the Rathantara and the Gharma-sāmans dedicated to Rudra, one is liberated from all sins.
Having recited the Yajñāyajñiya, the Āditya, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, the Rājana,
and the Gāruḍa Sāmans, one shall be liberated from sin.
Manu also says:
"One should constantly study the Veda itself at the proper times without weariness;
for they do not call anything superior to this his duty; any other practice is called a secondary duty."
Through constant study of the Vedas, through purity, through austerity,
and through non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth.
Remembering his former birth, the twice-born one shines as Brahman;
and by shining as Brahman, he enjoys infinite bliss incessantly.
Yama also says:
"Or one should recite for him the Vāmīya hymn, or the Pāvamānī verses,
or the Kuntāpa, the Vālakhilyas, the Nivid, the Praiṣas, and the Vṛṣākapi."
Having recited the Hotṛ, Rudra, and Pitṛ mantras, one is liberated from all sins.

The *Asyavāmīya* consists of fifty-two verses beginning with "Of this lovely, grey-haired Hotṛ. The *Hotṛs* are those beginning with "Thought is the ladle. The *Rudras* are the five Rudra-hymns beginning with "O Rudra, who... The *Pitṛs* are those beginning with "He who has gone forth. Also in the *Caturviṃśa*: one should mutter this unsurpassed *anuvāka* of Agni;
the twice-born should mutter this *anuvāka* beginning with "May my fury be like that of a lion."
By reciting these, one shall be liberated from sins, according to the word of Bodhāyana:
namely, the Trimadhu, the Trisuparṇa, and likewise the three Nāciketas.
One should mutter the Nārāyaṇa hymn; one is liberated from every [sin], even the killing of a Brahmin.
Whatever sin one may commit, whatever it may be, one should mutter this *ṛc*.
One should also mutter the verse beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat," or the "tryambaka" mantra,
as well as the Brāhmaṇas, the Kalpas, and likewise the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga).
Likewise, by reciting other Ākhyānas, as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and hymns of praise to the deities, one is liberated from sins.
By reciting [these], one is liberated from sins, as well as by other narrations of the Dharma. Yājñavalkya also says:
"The recitation of the Śukriya and the Āraṇyaka, and especially that of the Gāyatrī."
For these, as well as the Rudraikādaśinī, are indeed removers of all sins.

"Śukriyam," "Viśvāni deva savitar," and "Āraṇyakam priyam śukriyam viśvāni deva savitar"—one enters into the beloved speech (*vācam*). Both of these [mantras] are recited in the *Vājasaneyaka*. When the Rudras are repeated eleven times in a ritual of silent recitation (*japa*), it is called the "Elevenfold Rudra" (*rudraikādaśinī*). Atri also says: "Even one who has been touched by great sins is liberated by repeating the Rudras eleven times, provided he knows the Dharma; of this there is no doubt."
Also in the Purāṇa:
"For he who might give away the entire earth, together with its oceans, filled with mountains and forests, covered in gold, and endowed with medicinal herbs made of gold..."
A twice-born man who recites the Rudra-mantra even once certainly attains a superior fruit;
as one who is self-restrained, he performs intense austerity for thousands of years.
He who recites the Rudra-mantra even once does not obtain that fruit which one receives by bestowing ten million cows upon a guru according to the prescribed rites.
He who recites the Rudra-mantra even once does not merely obtain that fruit;
[he obtains] sacrifice, austerity, gifts, and various sacred pilgrimage sites.
These do not equal even a sixteenth part of the recitation of the Rudra.
Regarding this, Saṃvarta says:
"Even if it is devoid of vowels and measures, or lacking syllables in its quarters, or having been made deficient or excessive, one should nevertheless utter it with these words: 'ābhir gīrbhiḥ'."
Thus ends the section on recitations (*japyāni*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, in connection with the topic of recitation, another recitation is also described; regarding this, Pulastya says:
One should recite the names Kāma, Kāmaprada, Kānta, Kāmapāla, Hari, Ānanda, and Mādhava for the sake of the complete fulfillment of one's desires.
Rāma, Paraśurāma, Nṛsiṃha, Viṣṇu,
Trivikrama, and others— these names should be recited by those desiring to conquer their enemies.
By those constantly practicing sacred knowledge, Puruṣottama should be recited;
a man who has fallen into captivity should always recite Dāmodara.
One should constantly recite the name Keśava Puṇḍarīkākṣa for all afflictions of the eyes, and Hṛṣīkeśa in times of fear.
One should remember Acyuta and Amṛta during the administration of medicinal herbs;
one going forth to face battle should remember Aparājita.
One who travels abroad seeking security should constantly remember the Lord as bearing the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and likewise the sword, in the directions beginning with the east.
A person should always remember Ajita, Ādhipa, Sarva, and likewise Sarveśvara with devotion during all worldly activities.
One should always invoke Nārāyaṇa at all times—in cases of hunger, stumbling, and the like;
during afflictions caused by planets and constellations; and always when faced with obstacles from the gods.
In the face of bandits, enemies, or obstructions; in peril from lions, tigers, and the like; and in blinding, pitch-black darkness—one should recollect Narasiṃha.
One afflicted by suffering crosses over all difficulties by recollecting the One who reclines upon the waters;
through the remembrance of the one whose banner is Garuḍa, the potency of poison is pacified.
During bathing, worship of the deity, burnt offerings, prostration, and circumambulation, one should,
being intent upon Him, chant the name of the Blessed One, "Vāsudeva."
When storing wealth, grain, and so forth, or when consuming unwholesome food produced from impure sources,
one should remain focused on that task while chanting the names of Ananta and Acyuta.
In dreams of ill omen, one should always remember Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the bearer of Śrī, the Supreme Person, Vāmana, and the one who holds the sword.
A person should remember Balabhadra reclining on his couch at the beginning of the single ocean for the sake of prosperity;
one should remember him in heroic deeds.
One who desires offspring should praise the Source of the World with devotion and shall not come to grief;
for all rites intended for prosperity, one should quickly invoke the Lord of Śrī.
One should always recite the Viśoka [mantra] even when faced with all manner of portents of death,
such as being carried off by the wind, falling from a height, fire, water, or imprisonment.
In both the independent and dependent systems, the wise man should mutter the name of Vāsudeva,
the wielder of the discus, the God of gods who is endowed with his own inherent power.
Or whatever name one prefers, one should recite it for all purposes;
for by means of the single meaning inherent in all names, one attains the accomplishment of all aims.
O sinless one, all these names belong to the supreme Brahman.
Thus concludes the determination of other recitations (*japya*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the *brahmayajña*;
regarding this, Manu says:

"Restrained and established in the daily rule, one should go to the forest with a concentrated mind and recite even the Sāvitrī near water"—this means that one should go to the forest in such a way that the roofs [of houses] are no longer visible. And so says the Śruti: "One intending to perform the Brahma-sacrifice (Brahmayajña) shall go from the village toward the east, or where the roofs are not visible, or toward the north, or toward the northeast, when the sun has risen. The meaning is "after the rising of the sun," and not "at the very moment of its rising. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:

"And that [offering] should be performed either before the libation (tarpaṇa), or after the morning oblation (prātar-āhuti), or at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva; it is not to be done on any other occasion except when prompted by a specific cause."

By the term *vaiśvadeva* here, the entire ritual up to the *manuṣyayajña* (sacrifice to humans) is indicated, not the *vaiśvadeva* alone, because that [entire sequence] is prescribed in that very context. Thus says the Śruti: "These five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) are continuously extended and continuously completed: the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*), the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*), and the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*)" [505]. "Continuously" (*satati*) means incessantly, day after day. Also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"If the *brahmayajña* has not been performed prior to the libation (*tarpaṇa*)," and so forth.
"Having indeed performed the sacrifice to men, one should then begin the private recitation of the Veda."

By the phrase "except when there is a specific cause," it is stated that when such a cause exists, [the recitation] is not prohibited even at other times. For this very reason, the Śruti says: "In the village, one should study the Veda mentally, whether by day or by night; so said Śauceya Ātreya. Or in the forest, with strength, or with speech; standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—one should indeed study the Veda. Thus he becomes a performer of austerity and becomes meritorious. Here, the connection is: "So said Śauceya Ātreya. Regarding the specific rules for study, however, Yogayājñavalkya says:
Having circumambulated clockwise, paid homage,
and sat down upon *darbha* grass with palms joined in reverence and *darbha* blades held in both hands, he remained thus.
One should perform the private recitation of the Veda according to one's ability for the sake of the Brahma-sacrifice.
Śaunaka also says:
Having purified his faults through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), wearing white garments and being pure,
he should, having sipped water according to the rule, prepare a bed of darbha grass.
"Having placed the sacred grass in his hand, he should place his right hand over his left thigh. Thus it is said.

The word *adhīyīta* (he should study) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. That ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) is shown in the *Taittirīyaka-śruti*: "When the sun has risen, having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*upavīya*), having sat down, having washed both hands, he should sip water three times, wipe his mouth twice, and touch [the organs] once: the head, the two eyes, the two nostrils, the two ears, and the heart. By the fact that he sips water three times, he gratifies the *ṛc*s; by the fact that he wipes his mouth twice, he gratifies the *yajus*s; by the fact that he touches [the organs] once, he gratifies the *sāman*s; by the fact that he sprinkles water on his left hand and feet, and touches the head, the two eyes, the two nostrils, the two ears, and the heart, he gratifies the *Atharvāṅgiras*s, the *Brāhmaṇa*s, the *Itihāsa*s, the *Purāṇa*s, the *Kalpa*s, the *Gāthā*s, and the *Nārāśaṃsī*s. Having spread a large quantity of *darbha* grass and made a seat for himself, sitting facing the east, he should study his own Veda. For *darbha* grass is indeed the essence of waters and plants; thus he makes the *brahman* possessed of essence. Having placed his hands with the right over the left and his feet with the right over the left, and holding a blade of grass, he begins with *Oṃ*. Thereafter, having recited the *vyāhṛti*s, he should recite the *Sāvitrī* verse foot by foot, half-verse by half-verse, and then the whole. Regarding this, Śaunaka says: "He recites the *vyāhṛti*s preceded by *Oṃ*, followed by the *Sāvitrī*, foot by foot, half-verse by half-verse, and then the whole. There are only three *vyāhṛti*s. Thus says the *Śruti*: "He employed only three: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svar*. This is indeed the truth of speech; whatever is the truth of speech, that he employed. Then he recites the *Sāvitrī*, the *Gāyatrī*, three times—foot by foot, half-verse by half-verse, without pausing. Savitṛ is the progenitor of glory; thus he obtains glory. Moreover, by means of a well-known opening, he enters upon the *Chandas*s. "Opening" refers to the beginning. By this, it is stated that one should begin from the very start of the Veda and study further and further in due order. And it has been said by Yogayājñavalkya:

"Starting from the beginning of the Veda, having bathed, that which one studies day by day according to one's ability in successive order is known as *svādhyāya*. *Svādhyāya* is the *brahmayajña*, according to the Vājasaneyaka Śruti: "Now follows the *brahmayajña*; *svādhyāya* is the *brahmayajña*. Regarding this, Śaunaka states a specific rule:
In the morning, the voice should indeed be soft; when midday has arrived, it should be loud;
but in the afternoon it should be loud, and at the time of twilight, one should conclude softly.

The *aurasa* [recitation] is low-pitched. Gṛhyaśaunaka also says: "Gazing at the junction of heaven and earth, or with eyes closed, one should recite while composed in whatever manner one feels appropriate. Viṣṇu also says:
"Having mentally recollected the syllable *oṃ*, the three *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*, and the verse beginning with *tat*, one should commence the Vedas."

Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the Purāṇas and other such texts are included. For this very reason, the *Yogayājñavalkya* states: "One should recite the Vedas, the Arthaśāstras, the Purāṇas, the Sāṃkhya and Yoga systems, and spiritual knowledge (*adhyātmikī vidyā*) according to one's ability, for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*)."

[508] The sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). The *Śruti* also states: "When one studies the *Ṛgveda*, one satisfies the gods with oblations of milk; when one studies the *Yajurveda*, with oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta*); when one studies the *Sāmaveda*, with oblations of Soma; when one studies the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ*, with oblations of honey; and when one studies the *Brāhmaṇas*, the *Itihāsas*, the *Purāṇas*, the *Kalpas*, the *Gāthās*, and the *Nārāśaṃsīs*, one satisfies the gods with oblations of fat (*medas*). Being satisfied, they satisfy him with long life, splendor, luster, prosperity, fame, the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*), and the enjoyment of food. In this regard, a specific distinction is shown concerning the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as characterized by its indicative mark (*liṅga*).
"O Brahmin, the study of one's own Vedic branch is traditionally known as the Brahma-sacrifice."

As for the statement in the Śruti: "Whatever one may study from one's own Vedic recitation—even a single Ṛc, Yajus, or Sāman—that constitutes the completion of the Brahmayajña," that refers to occasions when there is no formal suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "Now, if the wind blows, or it thunders, or it lightens, or it flashes [with lightning], one should recite a single Ṛc, or a single Yajus, or a single Sāman, saying: 'Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ! Truth, austerity, I offer into faith. By this, indeed, on that day his private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) becomes as if undertaken. This also is intended to indicate all occasions of suspended study. For this very reason, Manu says:
In the daily obligatory recitation there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice.
It is meritorious, offered with the oblation of Brahman, and consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call even during times when study is otherwise forbidden.

[509] Regarding *naityaka*, the meaning is the daily recitation (*nityasvādhyāya*), which is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). The Śruti also states: "For this very sacrifice, there are two occasions for non-study: when one is impure oneself, and when the place is [impure]. The meaning is that there are only these two occasions for non-study, and no others. Having studied in this manner, one should recite the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*), "Obeisance to Brahman" (*namo brahmaṇe*), three times. And so says the Śruti: "This sacrifice is indeed performed immediately and completed immediately. Its purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) takes place in the evening; having recited the concluding verse 'Obeisance to Brahman' three times and touched water, he should say, 'Enter the house. Then, whatever he gives is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Yājñavalkya states the fruit for one who acts in this way:
Whatever sacrifice one may study, one shall obtain the fruit of each;
one enjoys the fruit of giving away the three worlds, filled with the earth.

The Śruti also states: "Whatever extent of this world one conquers by giving away a full measure of wealth, to that same extent of a world he conquers, and even more—indeed, an inexhaustible world; he conquers non-returning death and attains union with Brahman.
Thus ends the section on the Brahma-yajña in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the Tarpaṇa.
Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"Thereafter, the twice-born Snātaka should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) every day, for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors, in their proper order. [510]
And this should be performed immediately after the recitation (*japa*). Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"One should recite the mantras and Yajus formulas declared in the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda;
having thus completed the recitation, one should then perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods, sages, and ancestors."
As for that which was stated by Yogayājñavalkya:
"With one-pointed mind, on the bank [of a river], with palms joined in *añjali*, he should slowly recite the beginning of the Veda,
or likewise the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), for the sake of accomplishing the *brahmayajña*."
Or, having recited the Praṇava according to one's capacity, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa).

Thus, the libation (tarpaṇa) is stated to follow immediately after the Brahma-sacrifice (brahmayajña); however, that refers to the performance of the Brahma-sacrifice after the morning oblation (prātarāhuti), since it is prescribed there as well. Accordingly, Bṛhaspati says: "It should be performed either before the libation or after the morning oblation, or at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva; it is not [performed] otherwise except on account of a specific occasion."

"At the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva [offering] and at the end of the *manuṣyayajña*. And so it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "If the Brahmayajña has not been performed prior to the libation (*tarpaṇa*), then after performing the *manuṣyayajña*, one should indeed practice the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*)."
Regarding the libation (*tarpaṇa*), Śātātapa states:

"One should cause the satisfaction of the gods, sages, ancestors, humans, and others— prescribed by the rules of one's own Vedic branch— to be proclaimed with a single handful [of water] for each, using [their names] ending in the nominative case."
In the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa as well:

"Pure, wearing clean garments, and having bathed, one should perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors with great concentration, using the very *tīrtha* (parts of the hand) belonging to them."
One should offer water three times for the gratification of the gods;
then, according to the rule, once for the Ṛṣis and once for Prajāpati.
O Lord of the Earth, one should offer water three times for the sake of pleasing the ancestors.
Vyāsa also says:
"The gods [receive] one handful each, while Sanaka and the others receive two each."

"The ancestors eat three [handfuls], but each [descendant] eats one handful. Regarding this, the rule is determined according to one's own *śākhā*. However, for those whose *śākhā* does not prescribe it, there is simply an option (*vikalpa*). As for that which is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"With the left hand holding [the vessel] and with the right hand..."
The wise man should satisfy the celestial sages and the ancestors with handfuls of water.

Thus, that [is performed] for the purpose of an alternative to the previously mentioned joining of the palms (*añjali*). For this very reason, Yogayājñavalkya says: "Facing the Aparājita direction (the northeast) with both hands, one should join the thumbs together, or indeed begin with the left hand."
"Having uttered either 'May they be satisfied' or 'May they be satisfied,' the one who knows the ritual procedure should pour water for the gods and the others without exception.
The direction Aparājita is the north-eastern (aiśānī) direction. As for that which was stated by Vyāghra:
He who offers water with both hands is a fool; he goes head-first to the Kālasūtra hell.
Thus, this refers to the context of *śrāddha* and similar rites. For this very reason, Kārṣṇājini states:
"In a *śrāddha* and at the time of marriage, the gift is given with one hand;
but in the libation (*tarpaṇa*), it must be done with both hands—such is the ancient rule."
And this libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed with water and other substances; thus says Gobhila:
"Water that is not offered upon the ground does not reach [the ancestors], whether it is offered in water, in vessels, by one who is angry, or with only one hand."
Therefore, the intention is that the offering should be made on the ground itself. Śaṅkha also says:
"One should never offer water to the ancestors while standing in water;
rather, having stepped out onto a clean spot, one should perform the libation of water."
Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule:

"Having put on dry clothing upon a wide expanse of sacrificial grass (barhis) on dry ground, one who knows the ritual procedure should perform the libation (tarpaṇa); never [should it be done] in vessels."

"Or, having taken water from the vessel, one should pour it into another auspicious vessel, or into a hole filled with water; but not on dry ground, nor where the sacrificial grass has been removed. Thus [it is said]. And regarding the vessel here, it was stated by Pitāmaha:
A vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal should be used here for the libation to the ancestors; however, one should avoid using an earthen vessel.
Regarding the spreading of the seat, however, a specific rule has been shown by Yogayājñavalkya:
"Having invoked [the deities] with mantras as before and having spread many *kuśa* grasses,
one should properly place the gods upon those with tips pointing eastward, and the ancestors upon those with tips pointing southward."

The word "should satisfy" (*tarpayet*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Furthermore, Viṣṇu states that where there is an impure place, one should offer the water into the water: "If a man, standing on dry land, offers water into the water, that water does not reach the ancestors; it is useless for them."
"Whether one is in an impure place or in water, one should satisfy the deities and the ancestors according to one's desire; for everything is established in the waters.
With this very intention, Kārṣṇājini also [said]:
"One should offer handfuls of water for the deities and the ancestors in the water;
however, for those who have died without the proper funeral rites (asaṃskṛtapramīta), one should again offer water on dry land.
Regarding this, Bodhāyana states the rule concerning the handful of water:
One should offer three handfuls of water for those others who have been consecrated on earth;
for those deceased who were not consecrated, one should cast only a single handful upon the bank.
In this regard, the mantra is as follows:

"May those beings in my family who have been consumed by fire, and those who have not been consumed by fire, be satisfied by what is given upon the earth; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal. Thus it is said.
In this regard, Hārīta has also shown the restriction of place according to the distinction of the qualified person:
"One whose garment is wet should perform libations, sipping of water, and recitation in the water;
one whose garment is dry should perform libations, sipping of water, and recitation on land."
The word "staying in water" is to be understood as the ellipsis. For this very reason, Sumantu says:
"If one who is on dry land offers a handful of water while his clothes are still wet from the water, the *pretas* drink that water after it has dripped from his garments."
"Having set aside" means having excluded one who is entitled to a share. It is also stated by Likhita:
"Whether inside water with dry [clothes], or outside with wet clothes, bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and the libation to the ancestors are fruitless."

The bath is the Brāhma-bath. For this very reason, Hārīta says: "One who performs the Brāhma-bath, as well as giving gifts and the libations to the deities and ancestors, while standing in the midst of water, becomes defiled even if he is wearing dry clothes."
On this point, another Smṛti states:
"The libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) should be performed with a sword, a pearl, or with gems, gold, and darbha grass; it must never be done with anything impure."
Yogayājñavalkya also says: "Gold worn on the ring finger, silver on the index finger,
and a sword worn on the little finger— by these a man becomes purified."
Marīci also says:
"Without silver and gold, without copper and sesame seeds,
and without mantras and *darbha* grass, [the offering] does not reach the ancestors."
This statement is not intended to mean a combination of silver and the other materials; for as Marīci and Yogayājñavalkya state:
"In the absence of even sesame seeds, one should use gold accompanied by silver;
in its absence, one should sprinkle with *darbha* grass or again with the mantra. [515]

By this, the necessity of using sesame seeds in the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) is stated. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Manu says: "Just as a righteous king goes forth preceded by thousands of warriors, even so does water mixed with sesame seeds go to the deceased."

"Whatever in the Rāmāyaṇa consists of washing the feet without anointing them, or offering libations without sesame seeds— O Trijaṭā, all that belongs to you, as does any śrāddha performed without a priestly fee."

Thus, even when sesame seeds are available, that [injunction] intends a libation performed without them; otherwise, it would contradict the statement of Marīci. Regarding the specific rule for taking sesame seeds, Marīci says:
"The gift should be given with an open hand; one should not display a seal (mudrā) therein.
Sesame seeds are to be held in the left hand, while the right hand remains open."

The *mudrā* is the joining of the forefinger and the thumb. This refers to the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with water that has not been drawn up, because a specific rule is stated for when water has been drawn up. And so says Yogayājñavalkya:
"If, however, one pours out water that has been drawn up, one should mix sesame seeds into the water;
otherwise, sesame seeds should be taken with the left hand by the wise."
Otherwise, it would not be extracted. This [rule] also refers to limbs that are hairless, because otherwise a fault is heard [in the scriptures]. And so says Gobhila:
"If one offers libations to the ancestors after making sesame seeds adhere to their body hair, the ancestors are satisfied by that blood and water."
"A twice-born man should satisfy the gods with white sesame seeds, humans with variegated sesame seeds, and the ancestors with black sesame seeds, satisfying them at all times. Thus,
a specific distinction is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* regarding the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors.
"One should satisfy the gods and the Brahmanical seers with unbroken grains and water,

and the ancestors with devotion using black sesame seeds, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra. Regarding this aforementioned libation of sesame seeds, Marīci states an exception in certain cases:
On the seventh lunar day, on Sundays, at home, and always on one's birthday,
one who desires servants, sons, and a wife should never perform the libation with sesame seeds.
Also in the Purāṇa: "O King, on the seventh day of both fortnights, at night, and during the two twilights—
one who desires knowledge, sons, or a wife should avoid sesame seeds on these five occasions."
"One should never consume nimba, apply oil as an eye-salve, offer libations with sesame seeds,
or eat from a copper vessel on the seventh lunar day.
Regarding those who are to be offered libations here, Satyavrata says:
Having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder for the gods,
one should then place it around the neck (nivītī) and satisfy the humans with devotion, as well as the sons of Brahmā and the sages.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder and bent the left knee to the ground,
he should satisfy the deceased ancestors with darbha grass in hand according to the prescribed rite.
Also in the Purāṇa:
"Then, one should constantly gratify the gods and the hosts of gods, as well as the sages and the hosts of sages, and the ancestors and the hosts of ancestors."
Also in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "The gods, yakṣas, as well as nāgas, gandharvas, apsarases, asuras, serpents, cruel beings, suparṇas, trees, jambhakas, and birds."
Those beings who have the wind as their support, those who have water as their support, likewise those who move through space,
those who are without support, and those who are devoted to the Dharma.
For their nourishment, this water is offered by me.
Having performed the *upavīta* rite for the gods,
one should thereafter become *nivītī* and satisfy the humans with devotion, as well as the sons of Brahmā and the sages (*ṛṣis*).
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
as well as Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha.
May all of them without exception attain satisfaction through the water offered by me:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
One should satisfy Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada,
as well as all the celestial and brahminical sages, with water and unbroken grains.
Then, having placed the sacrificial thread over the right shoulder and bent the left knee to the ground,
[he should address] the Agniṣvāttas, the Saumyas, the Haviṣmants, and the Uṣmapās.

One should devoutly satisfy with water mixed with sesame seeds and sandalwood those ancestors who carry the Pināka bow, those who sit upon the sacrificial grass, and others who move according to their will.
"Then, with darbha grass in hand, one should satisfy the deceased according to the prescribed rule.
Thus says Yogayājñavalkya:
"One should first satisfy Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati."
The gods, the meters, the Vedas, and the sages whose wealth is asceticism—[518]—all these he honored.
The Gandharvas who are teachers, as well as the sons of teachers,
the year with its constituent parts, and the divine Apsarases.
Likewise, he [beheld] the gods, the followers of the gods, the nāgas, the oceans, and even the mountains;
as well as the rivers, humans, yakṣas, and indeed the rākṣasas.
The Piśācas, the Suparṇas, the Bhūtas, as well as the animals,
the trees, the medicinal herbs, and the fourfold collection of living beings.
Then, having touched his left knee and facing south,
he should satisfy all the classes of ancestors with mantras containing their respective names.
"A wise man should always satisfy his maternal grandfathers with faith.
In this context, the formula is "May Brahmā be satisfied," while [the rite is performed] with the left hand supporting the right hand.
One should sprinkle water while saying "May they be satisfied," preceded by the syllable Om and followed by their names.
For this was stated by that very same [author] immediately after the libation to the deities; Śaunaka also says:

Agni, Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, Brahmā, the Vedas, the gods, the seers (ṛṣis), the meters, the syllable *oṃ*, the syllable *vaṣaṭ*, the *vyāhṛtis*, the *Sāvitrī*, the sacrifices, Heaven and Earth, the atmosphere, day and night, the Sāṃkhyas, the Siddhas, the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, the fields, herbs, trees, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, birds, cows, the Sādhyas, the Brahmins, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and all beings ending with these; then the seers: the Śatarcins, the Madhyamas, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, the Pragāthas, the Pāvamānyas, the Kṣudrasūktas, and the Mahāsūktas. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*): Sumantu, Jaimini, Vaiśampāyana, Paila, the authors of the Sūtras and Bhāṣyas, the teachers of Dharma of the Mahābhārata, Jānanti, Vāhavi, Gārgya, Gautama, Śākalya, Vābhravya, Māṇḍavya, Māṇḍūkeya, Gārgī Vācaknavī, Vaḍavā Prācitheyī, Sulabhā Maitreyī, Kahola Kauṣītaki, Mahākauṣītaki, Bharadvāja, Paiṅgi, Suyajña, Sāṅkhyāyana, Aitareya, Mahaitareya, Bāṣkala, Gārgya, Sujātavaktra, Audavāhi, Mahaudavāhi, Saujāmi, Śaunaka, Āśvalāyana, and whatever other teachers there may be—may they all be satisfied. Having thus gratified the ancestors for each individual person, he concludes.
In this case as well, the ritual application is as before: "May Agni be satisfied. Alternatively, it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Then one should satisfy the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors;
having first uttered the syllable *Oṃ*, [one says] at the end of the name, 'I satisfy' (*tarpayāmi*)."
Alternatively, as stated in another Smṛti:
"Having uttered either 'May they be satisfied' (tṛpyantu) or 'Let them be satisfied' (tṛpyatām), one who knows the ritual rule should pour water for the gods and the others without exception. [520]
In this matter, regarding those to be gratified, the arrangement follows one's own specific *śākhā*. For this very reason, Satyavrata says:

"Having performed the libation to the gods, sages, and ancestors according to this procedure, one should perform that which is prescribed by one's own *śākhā* as a separate rite, for it is indeed a distinct limb of the ritual bath."
In the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇī* of the followers of the Yajurveda, however, the libation to the seers of the sections (*kāṇḍarṣi*) is prescribed:
"Then, being pure and composed, one should daily offer libations with handfuls of water to these seers of the sections on the festival days and on the eighth lunar day, using the sacred formulas."
Regarding the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa), Paiṭhīnasi states:
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and standing facing the direction of the ancestors,
one should satisfy the divine and non-divine ancestors with the *pitṛ-tīrtha* [the part of the hand between the thumb and forefinger]."
