The divine ones are Vasu and the others; the non-divine ones are one's own ancestors and so forth. And those divine ones have been shown by that very [author]: "Dhruva, Dhara, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus."
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, Raivata, Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Sureśvara.
Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pitṛnāka, and Aparājita—
these are declared to be the eleven Rudras, the foremost among the gods.
Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Mitra, Varuṇa,
Aryaman, Arcis, Vivasvat, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu.
"These twelve Ādityas are considered the foremost among the gods;
these divine Pitṛs are all to be worshipped with great effort.
In this context, the ritual application is simply "Obeisance to Dhruva" (dhruvāya namaḥ). For this very reason, Yogayājñavalkya states:

One should satisfy the Vasus, the Rudras, and likewise the Ādityas with salutations; "one should satisfy" is the understood remainder of the sentence. Thereafter, one should satisfy one's own ancestors and others. Regarding this, Satyavrata states the specific rule:
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and having bent the left knee to the ground..."
Then, with darbha grass in hand, he should satisfy the deceased according to the prescribed rule.
Kātyāyana also says:
"Then one should satisfy the gods with water mixed with sesame seeds, and the ancestors as well,
saying 'Oṃ' at the beginning and 'I satisfy [you] with homage' (namas tarpayāmi) at the end."
Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"Mentioning the name and lineage of each individual man,
one should cast three handfuls of water with sesame seeds aloft for each."
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"One should sprinkle water according to the rule with the Pitṛ-tīrtha on the right;
with a concentrated mind, one should take [the water] with the Pitṛ-tīrtha itself on the right."
"A salutation with joined palms (añjali) should be offered to those of the same caste and even to those of a different caste;
one should satisfy them in due order by uttering their names, gotras, and the word *svadhā*.
Regarding the specific procedure for pronouncing the names and so forth, Bodhāyana says:
It is said that the name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in "śarman," that of a Kṣatriya in "varman," that of a Vaiśya in "gupta," and that of one born as a Śūdra in "dāsa."
For the ancestors of all four castes, the ancestral lineage is determined by the father's gotra;
for unmarried daughters, it is the father's gotra, but for those who are married, it is the husband's gotra.

And the application [of the rite] is as follows: "Oṃ, I satisfy with *svadhā* and obeisance the ancestors of the Śrīvatsa lineage, Viṣṇuśarman. In this manner, one should satisfy the grandfather and the others as well. Thus, there is a sprinkling of three handfuls for each individual. Then, for the mothers: "I satisfy with *svadhā* and obeisance Gaṅgādāyī of the Śrīvatsa lineage. In the same way for the grandmother and the great-grandmother. Then for the maternal grandfather and the others. This has been stated by Satyavrata: "One should offer daily to the fathers, and likewise to the mothers;
then to the maternal grandfather and the others, and to the paternal uncle and the son."
Bodhāyana also [says]:

With the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*): *Oṃ*, I satiate the fathers with *svadhā* and homage; the grandfathers with *svadhā* and homage; the mothers with *svadhā* and homage; the grandmothers with *svadhā* and homage; the great-grandmothers with *svadhā* and homage; the maternal grandfathers with *svadhā* and homage; the maternal grandfathers’ fathers with *svadhā* and homage; the maternal grandfathers’ grandfathers with *svadhā* and homage; the maternal grandmothers with *svadhā* and homage; the maternal grandfathers’ mothers with *svadhā* and homage; the maternal grandfathers’ grandmothers with *svadhā* and homage; *Oṃ*, I satiate the teachers with *svadhā* and homage; the wives of the teachers with *svadhā* and homage; the gurus with *svadhā* and homage; the wives of the gurus with *svadhā* and homage; the friends with *svadhā* and homage; the wives of the friends with *svadhā* and homage; the kinsmen with *svadhā* and homage; the wives of the kinsmen with *svadhā* and homage; the ministers with *svadhā* and homage; the wives of the ministers with *svadhā* and homage; I satiate all of them with *svadhā* and homage.
In all these cases, the names and lineages (*gotra*) and so forth should be connected [to the ritual]. This has been stated here by Yājñavalkya in the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
"One should likewise satisfy all the hosts of ancestors with mantras possessing their respective characteristics.
And those mantras have been shown by him as follows:
"May the Aṅgirases rise up," "May they come," "For strength," "To the ancestors," "And those who are here," and the triplet beginning with "Honeyed are the winds."
Meditating upon the ancestors, one should indeed sprinkle [the water] and recite the mantras in their proper order;
then, with palms joined and body bowed, one should say "Be satisfied" three times.
"Having said 'Namo vaḥ' (Salutation to you), he should then offer libations to his maternal grandfathers as well, out of compassion and established in the highest dharma. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: at the end of the mantra *udīratām*, one should first pour an *añjali* of water with sesame seeds, saying: "O ancestors (*pitaraḥ*), of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*) and such-and-such name (*śarmāṇaḥ*), may you be satisfied; *svadhā*! The same applies at the end of the second and third mantras, *aṅgirasa āyantu naḥ* and so forth. Then, at the end of each of the mantras *ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ*, *pitṛbhyaḥ svadhāvibhyaḥ*, and *ye ceha pitaraḥ*, one should separately offer an *añjali*, saying: "O grandfather (*pitāmaha*), of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, may you be satisfied; *svadhā*! Similarly, for the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), one should do so at the end of each of the mantras beginning with *madhu vātāḥ*. The same procedure applies to the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) and others. However, the mantra *namo vaḥ* is the only one that is to be repeated again and again. Some have explained that for the mother and other female ancestors, one should offer the oblation using only their names and so forth. Regarding the specific rule for one whose father is still living, Yājñavalkya says: [524] *Yogayājñavalkya states the special rule for one whose father is alive:* *(Note: The source text provided does not contain the actual verse by Yogayājñavalkya.)*
Kavyavāha, Anala, Soma, Yama, and Aryaman,
as well as the Agniṣvātta, the Somapa, and the Barhiṣad Pitṛs.
If one whose father is still living should know these ancestors, then he should cause the offerings to be given to them;
or else, he should cause them to be given to those to whom his father would give. And a twice-born man whose father is deceased should offer to these [ancestors] who have passed away.
[525] Here, the formula is "I satiate Kavyavāha," according to the traditional rule: "And one should say 'I satiate' at the end of each name. Regarding this, there is a Purāṇa:
"One should offer water separately to the deceased while mentally recollecting their respective stations; Dvaipāyana declared that one should also offer water for oneself."

Regarding this, Kātyāyana speaks of the final *añjali*: "I satiate those belonging to my father’s lineage, those belonging to my mother’s lineage, and whoever else deserves water from me—this is the final *añjali*. Thereafter, one should offer the optional (*kāmya*) water. As stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "O King, having performed the libations for the gods and others, one may either recite this [verse] over the water or pour it into the water according to one's own desire, for the benefit of all living beings."
The gods, asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas;
the piśācas, guhyakas, siddhas, kūśmāṇḍas, trees, and birds.
May all creatures— those that dwell in water, those that live on land, and those that depend on the air—
quickly attain satisfaction by means of this water given by me.
This water is offered by me for the nourishment of those who abide in all the hells and amidst the various torments.
May those who are not kinsmen become kinsmen, and those who were kinsmen in another birth—
may they all attain complete satisfaction, as well as those who desire water from us.
Also in the Purāṇa:
"For those who are situated anywhere, their selves afflicted by hunger and thirst—
may this water with sesame seeds offered to them be inexhaustible."
For those in my lineage whose ancestral offerings have been interrupted, and who are deprived of sons and wives—
may this water with sesame seeds offered for them be inexhaustible.
"May this water offering with sesame seeds be inexhaustible for those who have died in my mother’s lineage and likewise in my father’s lineage. Thus it is said.
However, in the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa*, a concise libation is prescribed for one who is unable to perform the elaborate rite.
Saying, "May the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied," one should offer three handfuls of water while performing the abbreviated libation.
Śaṅkha states the fruit for one who acts in this manner:
"Having bathed and performed the libation for the ancestors with water and sesame seeds,
he attains the world of the ancestors and likewise gratifies them."
Also in the Purāṇa:
"In this way, the twice-born who daily satisfies all beings shall go to the supreme abode, which is of the nature of light and free from ailment."
Even in performing [the rites] in that manner, the fault has been shown in that very same place:
"He who does not satisfy the deities, the sages, and the ancestors,
having become a debtor to the gods and others, goes downward to hell."
Yogayājñavalkya also says: "If one,
out of an atheistic disposition, does not indeed satisfy those ancestors,
then his ancestors, seeking water, drink the discharge from his own body."
Blood is the discharge from the body. Kātyāyana also says:
"Just as one distressed by the autumn heat desires shade, the thirsty desires water, and the hungry desires food;
so the child [desires] the mother, the mother the child, the woman the man, and the man the woman."
In the same way, all beings, both stationary and moving,
desiring prosperity, seek water from the Brahmin.
Therefore, it must always be performed; by not performing it, a Brahmin incurs great sin, for by performing it, he indeed sustains this entire universe.
Regarding this, Yama speaks of the ancestors' longing:
"May there be someone born in our family who would offer us handfuls of water,
especially in rivers abounding with cool waters."
Viṣṇu also says: "In our lineage, may that being be born who shall offer us handfuls of water in rivers abounding with water, especially those that are cool."
For this very reason, Hārīta says: "One should not cross flowing rivers in vain; for thus it is said:
'Both the gods and the ancestors long for the handful of water;
if it is not offered, they depart from hope to the abode of Yama.'"
Regarding this, the *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
"As long as a twice-born man who has not bathed does not offer libations to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors, he must not wring out his garment."

"He who wrings out his garment or bathing cloth before the libation has been offered, the ancestors depart in despair, having uttered a most terrible curse. (528) Thus, the meaning is that one should wring it out immediately after the libation. A specific rule regarding this is shown in another Smṛti:
"The water squeezed from a garment and the food remaining from a *śrāddha* meal—the Śruti declares these to be one's allotted portion; therefore, one should squeeze [the garment] on dry ground.
After the squeezing, Yogayājñavalkya says:

"Having wrung out the bathing garment, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), being self-controlled and pure, one should perform the worship of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, free from envy. The phrase "having performed the ritual sipping of water" implies that one should offer the *arghya* oblation to the Sun. And so it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Having properly offered the desired water to these [ancestors] endowed with faith,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then offer a handful of water to the Sun.
A specific detail regarding this is shown in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
Then one should offer the *arghya* to the Sun, accompanied by sesame seeds, flowers, and water,
while reciting "The Swan dwelling in purity" (*haṃsaḥ śuciṣat*), rising [the offering] up to the crown of the head.
"Having paid homage to the God in the water, the wise man should then go home;
he should then worship Viṣṇu with the Pauruṣa Sūkta.
The phrase "he should go home" implies that he should do so taking the sprinkling water with him.
Restraining his speech at the three junctions of the day, he should fetch water from a protected source and purify the sacrificial ground,
the house, the ritual materials, himself, and his attendants.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Garga.
Thus concludes the determination regarding libations (*tarpaṇa*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the libation to Yama.
In that regard, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"When the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight coincides with a Tuesday,
one should bathe in auspicious water and offer libations using the names of Yama."
Those names were revealed by Vṛddha Manu:
"Having reached any river whatsoever on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight—
and especially the Yamunā— one who is self-restrained and has controlled his senses [should perform the rite]."
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, to the Ender,
to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the Destroyer of all beings.

"Salutation to Audumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, Parameṣṭhin, Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta. The word "should satisfy" (tarpayet) is to be understood as the ellipsis here; the formula used in this context is "namo yamāya" (salutation to Yama). This should be done on the thirteenth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.

"One should offer seven handfuls of water with these seven mantras of salutation: 'To Yama, to Dharmarāja, to Mṛtyu, to Antaka, to Vaivasvata, to Kāla, and to Sarvabhūtakṣaya. By this, one is liberated from all sins," according to the prose Smṛti of Vyāsa. Regarding a specific detail here, Vṛddhamanu says:
Having prepared three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds for each individual,
the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having turned toward the south, being himself composed,
one should offer with sesame seeds through the *devatīrtha* for the sake of divinity, and with sesame seeds for the Lord of the Departed (*pretādhipa*).
Vṛddha-Manu states the fruit for one who acts in this way:
"Whatever sin has been committed in this life and whatever has been committed in other lives,
one dispels it by performing the libation on the fourteenth day of Aṅgāraka."
Yama also says: "Having bathed in any river whatsoever on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, and having offered libations to Dharmarāja, one is liberated from all sins. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the libation for Yama in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the libation for Bhīṣma: they prescribe the libation for Bhīṣma on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha. To that effect, a Purāṇa states:
Whoever offers a respectful salutation with joined palms to Bhīṣma on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
the sin committed throughout the entire year perishes at that very moment.
In this regard, the mantra is as follows: "To Bhīṣma, who belongs to the Vaiyāghrapāda gotra, whose pravaras are the Saṅkṛtis, and who is the son of Gaṅgā, I shall offer water with sesame seeds."
"I give this water to Bhīṣmavarman, who is without a son. Thus ends the procedure for the libation to Bhīṣma in the *Smṛticandrikā*. [531]
Now, regarding the worship of the deities,
Hārīta says:
"One should perform the worship of the deities immediately after the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña)."
Whether on a sacrificial mound, in an image, in water, in fire, or even in the heart;

The sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is the sacrifice of sacred knowledge (*brahmayajña*). Regarding this, with reference to the sacrifice of sacred knowledge, Yājñavalkya records: "For the successful accomplishment of the sacrifice of recitation, one should recite the spiritual knowledge (*ādhyātmikī vidyā*). Marīci also [states]:
Having performed the worship of the deity immediately after the morning fire-oblation,
[one should do so] either upon a sacrificial mound, in an image, in the fire, or in the lotus of the heart.
Also in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"Having paid homage to the Lord in the water, the wise man should then go home;
he should then worship Viṣṇu with the *Puruṣasūkta*."
In this regard, their assignment [of deities] should be understood as follows. On this point, Yogayājñavalkya says:
"One should place Govinda on the thumb, Mahīdhara on the index finger, Hṛṣīkeśa on the middle finger, and Trivikrama on the ring finger."
One should place Viṣṇu on the little finger and Mādhava in the middle of the hand;
likewise, what is offered in the fire, what is given, and the worship of the deities [should be assigned to the respective fingers].
"By the power of the placement upon the hands (*hastanyāsa*), everything becomes inexhaustible. Thus it is said.
And that worship was described by Nārada:
"In former times, the venerable sage Nārada was questioned regarding this matter."
And by those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, together with the lord of sages, he was joined.
You ought to speak for us so that we may hear the ritual procedure for the worship of Nārāyaṇa,
by which one attains the abundant goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and apavarga.
Having heard this and reflected for a long time,
he remembered that which was heard of old in the Ocean of Milk, as it issued from the mouth of Puṣkarākṣa.
O sages, listen properly to the worship of Puruṣottama,
by performing which all sages may attain the Brahman-nirvāṇa.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite, facing the east with a pure mind,
and having performed the rituals taught in his own Vedic branch as well as the *āhitāgni* fire-oblation;
One should perform the worship of Viṣṇu, the god of gods who bears the discus,
in water, in fire, in the heart, in the sun, on a sacrificial mound, and in images.
The sages have declared that the perfect worship of Hari occurs in these six ways:
for those engaged in ritual action, the God is in the fire; for the wise, the God is in heaven.
For yogins of limited intellect, Hari resides in the heart within images;
since water is indeed His abode, Hari is always present in them.
For water is indeed his abode; therefore Hari is always present within it.
And because he is omnipresent, he is also present upon the sacrificial ground for those of purified soul.
In the Ṛgveda, the Puruṣasūkta is praised as the most secret and supreme;
it is a hymn composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter, ending with verses in the Triṣṭubh meter, and has the Divine Being (Puruṣa) as its deity.
The Puruṣa who is the seed of the universe is remembered as the seer Nārāyaṇa;
one should place the first [syllable] on the left hand and the second on the right hand.
The third [syllable] is on the left foot, and likewise the fourth on the right;
the fifth is on the left calf, and similarly the sixth on the right.
One should place the seventh on the left hip, the eighth likewise on the right;
the ninth in the center of the navel, and the tenth in the heart.
One should place the eleventh day on the region of the throat, the twelfth on the left arm,
the thirteenth on the right, and the fourteenth on the region of the mouth.
Having placed the fifteenth [digit] on the two eyes, one should place the sixteenth on the head;
one should perform the rite of placement (nyāsa) upon the deity just as one does upon oneself.
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner, the wise one should afterwards worship the deity and honor himself with fragrant perfumes and garlands.
Then, having propitiated Pīta with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
one should invoke the Lord Puruṣottama with the first Ṛk verse.
One should offer a seat with the second [verse], and water for the feet with the third;
the guest-offering (arghya) should be presented with the fourth, and water for sipping (ācamanīya) with the fifth.
One should perform the bath on the sixth day, the clothing on the seventh,
the sacred thread on the eighth, and the fragrant unguents on the ninth.
On the tenth day there should be the offering of flowers; on the eleventh, incense;
on the twelfth, likewise a lamp; and on the thirteenth, likewise sacrificial porridge (caru).
One should perform the salutation on the fourteenth day, the circumambulation on the fifteenth, and the dismissal on the sixteenth; the remaining rites are as before.
During the bathing, the putting on of garments, the sacred thread, and the food offering, one should perform the sipping of water (ācamana).
Having offered oblations with sixteen mantras, there is also an oblation at the end of each of those sixteen.
One should offer the remainder to him and then give water for sipping (ācamana);
thereafter, one should present sixteen flowers with sixteen mantras.
One should then recite all of that, as well as the supreme Puruṣasūkta once more;
thereafter, one should circumambulate the healthy Nārāyaṇa.
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu, who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace in his hands, one should worship him;
by worshipping him in this very manner, one attains perfection within six months.

By that very year, one attains union with Him. Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with armlets, shark-shaped earrings, and a crown, wearing a necklace, possessing a golden body, and bearing the conch and the discus— He is to be meditated upon at all times.
Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"There is no Vedic rite more meritorious than the worship of Viṣṇu;
therefore, one should constantly worship Hari, who is without beginning, middle, or end."
With the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ" or with the Puruṣa Sūkta—
no mantra equal to these two has been declared even within the four Vedas.
Alternatively, one who is purified by inner disposition should worship the god Īśāna, the Blessed One, the eternal Mahādeva, the Great Lord Maheśvara.
With the Rudra-Gāyatrī mantra, or again with the Praṇava,
or with the Īśāna mantra, or with the Tryambaka Rudras, one should remain composed.
"Or one may recite with this mantra, 'Tathom namaḥ śivāya'. Thus [it is said]. Bodhāyana also [states]:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the daily service of the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*). Having bathed, being pure, and having smeared a clean place with cow-dung, one should fashion an image of the God, worship it with unbroken rice grains, perfumes, and flowers as they are available, and then invoke the Great Person along with water and flowers: "Oṃ *bhūḥ*, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ *bhuvaḥ*, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ *suvaḥ*, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*, I invoke the Puruṣa. Having thus invoked him, he says: "May the Blessed Great Person come. Then he welcomes him with a greeting: "Welcome! You have arrived, O Blessed Great Person; this seat has been prepared; may the Blessed Great Person sit here. Here he gives him a grass mat (*kūrca*), saying: "This is the Blessed One's grass mat, made of *darbha* grass, triple-stranded, green, and golden; please enjoy it. Here he prepares the bath and other offerings: "In front, I prepare for the Conch; I prepare for the Discus; on the right, I prepare for the Mace; I prepare for the Forest Garland; behind, I prepare for the Śrīvatsa mark; I prepare for Garuḍa; on the left, I prepare for Śrī; I prepare for Sarasvatī; I prepare for Puṣṭi; I prepare for Tuṣṭi. Then, having washed the vessel with water using the *Sāvitrī* mantra, and having poured water across the strainer, he consecrates the water again with that same mantra and shows it to the Sun while reciting "Oṃ" until the end of his breath. Of those waters, he gives the foot-water while reciting the verse: "He strode out three steps. Then, having removed the remains of the previous offering with the *Vyāhṛtis*, he should give the respectful water (*arghya*) while reciting: "Viṣṇu strode across this. The water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) is given with: "Or from heaven, O Viṣṇu. Then he bathes him with the three verses beginning "The waters are indeed our source of bliss," with the four verses beginning "Golden-colored, pure, purifying," with this section (*anuvāka*) beginning "Pavamāna, born of light," with the *Brahmajajñāna*, with the *Vāmadevya* hymn, and with the *Yajus-pavitra*. Then he satiates him with water: "I satiate Keśava; I satiate Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara. Having offered garments, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and water for sipping to the deities with the *Vyāhṛtis*, and having sprinkled water clockwise around the area with the *Vyāhṛtis*, he gives a garment with the *Praṇava* (*Oṃ*), a sacred thread with the *Sāvitrī*, water for sipping with "Viṣṇu strode across this," perfume with "Gandhadvārām," unbroken rice grains with "Irāvatī," flowers with "Tad viṣṇoḥ," incense with the *Sāvitrī*, and a lamp with "Uddīpyasva. For the food offering (*naivedya*), he says: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I offer this pleasing sacrificial pap (*caru*) to the Blessed Great Person. Then he should give twelve flowers to him by means of the twelve names (Keśava and the others). Then: "Salutation to the Conch; salutation to the Discus; salutation to the Mace; salutation to the Forest Garland; salutation to the Śrīvatsa; salutation to Garuḍa; salutation to Śrī; salutation to Sarasvatī; salutation to Puṣṭi; salutation to Tuṣṭi. Then, having adorned the Brahmins with the remaining perfumes and garlands, and having adorned himself with what is left over, they praise him with hymns from the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas. Some say they should recite the *Dhruva-sūkta*, the *Puruṣa-sūkta*, and other Vaiṣṇava mantras. Having set aside the sacrificial pap with "Oṃ *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar mahar* Oṃ, I set aside the pap for the Blessed Great Person," at the time of dismissal, he says: "Oṃ *bhūḥ*, I dismiss the Puruṣa; Oṃ *bhuvaḥ*, I dismiss the Puruṣa; Oṃ *suvaḥ*, I dismiss the Puruṣa; Oṃ *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*, I dismiss the Puruṣa. Having dismissed him, he says: "May the Blessed Great Person depart, satisfied by this oblation, for the sake of returning again and for the sake of being seen again. In the case of images, in water, or in fire, the invocation and dismissal are all the same. This is called the "Great Propitiation" (*mahat savastyayanam*); so said the blessed Bodhāyana. Thus ends the passage.
In this regard, after the worship, the *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
"Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods and meditated for a moment upon the stainless [Brahman], one should then look at the sun with the *ṛc*: 'The Swan (Haṃsa) dwelling in purity'."
"He goes to the abode of Brahmā, provided he meditates and beholds [the Lord] with this [mantra].
Thus the Blessed One declares the fruit for one who acts in this way:
"Those who always worship Viṣṇu, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace..."
Completely liberated from all evil, they enter into Brahman.
Also in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"Those men on earth who perform the worship of Viṣṇu in this manner go to the eternal, infinite, and supreme abode of Viṣṇu. [539] Thus it is said.
On this point Vyāsa says:
"Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is the teacher of all the worlds;
his worship must be performed, for it indeed removes all sins."
The fruit of worshipping Śiva is shown in the Śivadharmaśāstra:
"If one were to give a hundred thousand milch cows to those who have mastered the Vedas,
the merit of one who worships a Liṅga for a single day is greater than that."
"Whether one should feed the best of the twice-born month after month for as long as one lives, or whether one should worship the Liṅga even once—these two are equal; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, the fault incurred by failing to act accordingly is shown in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
He who, out of delusion or laziness, eats without having performed the worship of the deities,
goes to the hells and is born here among swine.
Thus ends the section on the worship of deities in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, some other statements concerning the bathing of deities and related matters are also written down. In that regard, Pulastya says in the *Viṣṇudharma*:
Whatever fruit may come from giving a hundred cows to Brahmins, that same fruit is obtained by bathing Viṣṇu with a prastha of ghee; of this there is no doubt.
It is said that the earth with its seven islands was obtained by Bhūridyumna through the bathing of an image of Govinda with a drona-measure of ghee.
O tiger among Daityas, bathing Lord Hari with cow-derived oblation on the twelfth or fifteenth day destroys even the greatest of sins.
When the northern solstice has arrived, he who bathes Keśava with a prastha of ghee indeed dispels all his sin.
For he who gives a tawny cow daily to a preeminent Brahmin,
that indeed becomes equal to a bath of clarified butter for the Lord at that very time.
And those who behold him being bathed with ghee during the northern course of the sun go to the same world as Viṣṇu, freed from all sins.
Just as curds and other derivatives arise from milk,
even so do all desires arise from bathing Lord Hari with milk.
In the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa as well:
"Having bathed Viṣṇu once with curd— He who is stainless and of pleasing appearance—
one attains the world of Viṣṇu, being served by the best of the gods."
Yama also says:
"Removing the garlands from deities, cleaning the temples of the gods,
and bathing all the deities are recorded as equal to the gift of a cow."
In the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"O King of kings, by anointing the form of Acyuta with a paste of saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood out of devotion, one shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas."

Śaṅkha also says: "One should apply an ointment consisting of sandalwood, saffron, and musk, excluding nutmeg," provided these are available—this is the understood remainder of the statement. Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Among fragrances, sandalwood is meritorious; agallochum is better than sandalwood;
black agallochum is superior to that; but saffron is better still."
In the *Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa* as well:
"One should worship Hari with flowers that are not stale, free from holes, untouched by insects, or even those grown in one's own garden."
Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving ten pieces of gold,
that same fruit he obtains by offering a *droṇa* of *puṣpa* flowers to Viṣṇu.
Among a thousand *doṇa* flowers, the *khadira* flower is supreme;
among a thousand *khadira* flowers, the *śamī* leaf is distinguished as superior.
Indeed, a single bilva leaf excels a thousand śamī leaves;
indeed, the bakula flower is superior to a thousand bilva leaves.
The *nadyāvarta* is superior to a thousand *bakula* flowers;
indeed, the *karavīra* is superior to a thousand *nandyāvarta* flowers.
A single *pālāśa* flower is superior to a thousand *karavīra* flowers;
a *kuśa* flower excels a thousand *pālāśa* flowers.
For a forest garland is indeed superior to a thousand *kuśa* flowers;
and the *campaka* flower is supreme even over a thousand forest garlands.
From a thousand *campaka* flowers, the *aśoka* flower is superior;
from a thousand *aśoka* flowers, the *sevantī* flower is superior;
from a thousand *sevantī* flowers, the *gorjaṭā* flower is superior.
Of the thousand varieties of *gorjaṭā* flowers, the *mālatī* flower is the most excellent.
The sandhyā-red [flower] is unsurpassed by a thousand mālatī flowers;
indeed, the kunda flower excels a thousand sandhyā-red flowers.
For indeed, among a thousand *kunda* flowers, the *mallikā* flower is supreme;
and among a thousand *mallikā* flowers, the *jātī* flower excels.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who, with devotion and according to the prescribed rite, offers a garland made of a thousand *jātī* flowers to Viṣṇu.
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
that glorious one, possessing prowess equal to Viṣṇu, shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu.
Also in the Viṣṇurahasya:
"Just as the Brāhmaṇa is among the castes, as the Jāhnavī is among sacred fords,
as Viṣṇu is among the gods, so is the Mālatī among flowers."
He who daily worships the Lord whose banner is Garuḍa with *mālatī* flowers shall be liberated from birth,
death, old age, and disease, and shall attain liberation.
A flower offered to Hari becomes *nirmālya* (remains of an offering) the very moment it is given;
however, Hari enjoys the *mālatī* flower for a full day and night.
Having worshipped Acyuta with fragrant jasmine flowers, a person,
liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
He who worships Hari, the remover of all sins, with *pāṭalī* flowers—
that meritorious soul goes to the supreme, stainless abode of Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped Acyuta with white and red karavīra flowers of great merit, one goes to where he who has Garuḍa as his banner resides.
Having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa with devotion using fragrant, pure, and beautiful flowers produced from the kubjaka tree, a person shall go to Śvetadvīpa.
Having worshipped Adhokṣaja with bright, pure, and highly fragrant lotus flowers, a person goes to the abode of Hari.
Having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa with flowers produced from the ketakī plant,
one goes to that meritorious and painless abode of Keśava.
Having worshipped Keśava, the remover of sins, with flowers from the sacrificial pit,
he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is praised by sages and celestial singers.
The meritorious man who worships the Lord of the worlds with *āḍharūpika* flowers goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped the infallible Lord Acyuta with beautiful Aśoka flowers— which remove the fear and sorrow of rebirth— one goes to the healthy Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped Madhusūdana with the brilliant flowers of the *tilaka*,
one who has shaken off sin and is free from fear shall become an attendant of Kṛṣṇa.
Having worshipped Keśava with fragrant flowers of the nīpa, arjuna, kadamba, and bakula trees, the doer of merit attains the world of Viṣṇu.
By worshipping Hṛṣīkeśa with beautiful Kiṃśuka flowers that have been soaked in the water of Agastya, one is liberated from the suffering of birth.
Having adorned the mountain with flowers made of dūrvā grass, as well as those grown from kāśa and kuśa grass, a person shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
The *māruta* flower, the *ketaka*, and likewise the *dāmanaka*,
produce for Hari a supreme affection that lasts for a hundred years.
The fruit that is obtained by men who adorn Janārdana with flowers grown in city gardens is tripled when using wild forest flowers.
Fruit, flower, leaf, durva grass sprout, or water offered with devotion— Keśava accepts these without delay, for he is one who is won over by devotion alone.
Also in the Viṣṇudharma: "The Supreme Lord Hari, when worshipped with devotion by men using dūrvā sprouts, indeed bestows a fruit that is very difficult to obtain even through all sacrifices."
Also in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"A person who has worshipped Govinda even once with a *bilva* leaf shall become a partaker of liberation, free from affliction, and an attendant of Kṛṣṇa."
Those men who worship Keśava even with śamī leaves, though out of negligence,
attain the supreme goal when Hṛṣīkeśa is pleased.
Even those men who worship Hari, the Lord of the gods, with water from a golden pitcher,
are liberated from old age and disease and go to the abode of Hari.
Those who worship Hari, the remover of sins, with *ālasya* leaves—
that virtuous man goes to the abode of Acyuta, cleansed of all evil.
Tulasī may be dark or fair; by worshipping Janārdana with it, a person, upon casting off the body, attains the eternal Vaiṣṇava goal.
Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
"He who covers the image on all sides without leaving any gaps with fragrant tulasī leaves shall obtain infinite fruit."
Among all varieties of flowers, the golden flower is supreme;
by giving even as much as a sesame seed's measure of it, one shall obtain half of Śakra’s throne.
"Even if it is merely the size of a drop or a minute atom. Also in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"When given to Kṛṣṇa by men endowed with devotion, the merit of gold is more than a hundred thousandfold, while that of a garland is ten million times greater."
"Thus, Janārdana should always be worshipped with pure flowers;
one should never worship the Lord with prohibited flowers that cause suffering.
Prohibited flowers are also shown in that very same source:
One should not worship the deity with dry flowers, nor with those that have fallen to the ground,
nor with those whose petals are withered, nor with those already offered, nor with those that are unwholesome, nor with those that are not in full bloom.
One should avoid putrid odors, pungent odors, and sour odors.
Also in the Padma Purāṇa: "One should not accept leaves that are infested with insects or hair, decayed, stale, broken, or tainted by worms; nor should one bring such."
One should avoid anything scented with spider silk even if it is beautiful;
one should not pluck flowers growing on land, but one may cut those growing in water.
One should avoid those things touched by those who are untouchable and by the Lokāyatikas.
Hārīta also says:
"Whatever twice-born ones indeed take flowers after having performed their ablutions,
the deities do not accept them, nor do the twice-born accept them."
The ancestors do not accept him; he turns to ashes like a piece of wood.

This refers to the midday bath (*madhyāhna-snāna*). Regarding the second part [of the day], it is stated in the *Dakṣasmṛti*: "No specific time is prescribed for fuel-sticks (*samidh*), flowers, *kuśa* grass, and so forth. This is also stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*.
To those people who worship Janārdana, the Lord of the Three Worlds, with *arakapuṣpa* flowers,
Viṣṇu, out of anger, bestows inexhaustible suffering upon them.
To those fools who worship Trivikrama with madness,
the one whose banner is Garuḍa grants a terrible madness in return.
To those who worship the Enemy of the Asuras with flowers made of gold,
Viṣṇu bestows poverty abounding in suffering.
"Madhusūdana brings about the terrible destruction of the lineage of those ignorant people who worship Viṣṇu with *girikarṇikā*.
On this point, Hārīta says:
Mahiṣākṣa, kaṇa, dārusallaka, sāgara, mada, śaṅkha,
and jātiphala— these are the glorious incenses dear to Hari.
One should not bring anything for the sake of a lamp except ghee and oil.
Saṃvarta also says:
By giving a lamp at a temple, to brahmins, or at a crossroads,
a man is born intelligent, endowed with knowledge, and possessed of sight.
Also in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"Having lit a lamp with camphor for the God of gods,
one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage."
Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
"I shall describe the vessel for the food offering (naivedya) for the great-souled Keśava:
it may be made of gold, silver, bell-metal, copper, or even clay."
A vessel made of *pālāśa* wood or a lotus leaf is exceedingly dear to Viṣṇu;
the oblation should consist of divine rice cooked with milk, mixed with clarified butter and sugar.
One should offer as an oblation to the God of gods barley-gruel and milk-rice;
however, if the materials for the oblation are unavailable, one should instead present fruits.
But even in the absence of fruits, one should offer grasses, shrubs, and herbs;
and in the event that herbs are not available, one should offer even waters.
But in the absence of that, mental worship is everywhere considered supreme.
Also in the Varāha Purāṇa: "The destination that one who worships with prostration, having bowed like a staff upon the ground, attains— that cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices."
Also in the *Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa*:
"By means of a single prostration with eight limbs, one shall go to Hari.
The characteristics of the eight limbs are shown in the Purāṇa.
With the chest, the head, the gaze, the mind, and also with the intellect;
with the two feet, the two hands, and speech—this is called the eight-limbed prostration.
In this regard, Brahmā said:
"The man who performs even a single circumambulation with devotion around Viṣṇu’s temple obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices."
Also in the Purāṇa:
"O Goddess, by eating the food offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu, one obtains that fruit which comes from thousands of Agniṣṭoma sacrifices and even hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices."
"He who has the form of Hari in his heart, His name in his mouth, the food offering in his stomach,
the water from the washing of His feet and the remains of His garlands upon his head— he is Acyuta himself.
Thus ends the section concerning the bathing and other rites for the deity in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, regarding the worship of Śiva,
Bodhāyana says:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the daily service of Mahādeva. Having bathed and become pure, having smeared a level spot with cow-dung and fashioned an image, one should worship it with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), perfumes, and flowers as they are available, and then invoke Mahādeva along with water and flowers: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke Mahādeva; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke Mahādeva; Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke Mahādeva; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, I invoke Mahādeva. May the Blessed Mahādeva come hither. Then he welcomes him with a greeting: "Welcome! You have arrived, O Blessed Mahādeva. This seat has been prepared; may the Blessed Mahādeva be seated here. Here he offers a *kūrca* (seat-grass mat): "This is the Blessed One’s *kūrca*, made of *darbha* grass, triple-stranded, green, and golden; please accept it. Here he prepares the places: "In front, I prepare a place for Brahmā; I prepare a place for Viṣṇu. To the south, I prepare a place for Skanda; I prepare a place for Vināyaka. To the west, I prepare a place for Śūla; I prepare a place for Mahākāla. To the north, I prepare a place for Umā; I prepare a place for Nandikeśvara. Having thus prepared them, he consecrates the vessel with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, washes it, pours water across the strainer, and consecrates it again with that same mantra. He should show it to the Sun together with the strainer, saying "Oṃ," until the end of the invocation. He should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) with the *Tvaritarudra* hymn, and the respectful offering (*arghya*) with the *Praṇava*. Then, having removed the remains of the previous offerings (*nirmālya*) with the *Vyāhṛtis*, he says to the north: "Salutation to Caṇḍīśvara. Then he bathes the deity with the three verses beginning "The waters are indeed our source of bliss" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*), with the four verses beginning "Golden-colored" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*), and with this entire section beginning "Pavamāna, the light-maker" (*pavamānaḥ svarjanaḥ*). Having bathed him, he satiates him with water: "I satiate the god Bhava; I satiate the god Śarva; I satiate the god Īśāna; I satiate the god Paśupati; I satiate the god Rudra; I satiate the god Ugra; I satiate the god Bhīma; I satiate the god Mahānta. Having thus satiated him, he offers clothing, a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and ornaments with water while reciting the *Vyāhṛtis*. Having sprinkled water clockwise around the deity with the *Vyāhṛtis*, he should offer perfume with the verse "Salutation to you, O Rudra, in your wrath" (*namas te rudra manyave*). He should offer unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with the verse "You are the Lord of beings, the sovereign glory" (*īśānaṃ tvā bhuvanānām adhiśriyam*). He should offer incense with the *Sāvitrī*, and a lamp with "Make it shine" (*uddīpyasva*). He should offer the sacrificial food (*naivedya*) with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I present this pleasing sacrificial pap (*caru*) to the Blessed Mahādeva. Then he should offer eight flowers with the eight names: "Salutation to the god Bhava; salutation to the god Śarva; salutation to the god Īśāna; salutation to the god Paśupati; salutation to the god Rudra; salutation to the god Ugra; salutation to the god Bhīma; salutation to the god Mahānta; salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation to Skanda; salutation to Vināyaka; salutation to Mahākāla; salutation to Umā; salutation to Durgā; salutation to Nandikeśvara. With the remainder of the sacrificial pap, he offers eight oblations with the eight names, beginning with "To the god Bhava, svāhā," and so on. Then, having adorned the Brahmins and himself with the remaining perfumes and garlands, he should recite thousands of hymns from the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas, or the section beginning "Thousands upon thousands" (*sahasrāṇi sahasraśaḥ*), and other Raudra mantras according to his ability—so say some. Finally, he should dismiss the sacrificial pap with: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar mahar oṃ, I dismiss the Blessed Mahādeva. At the time of dismissal, he says: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I dismiss Mahādeva; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I dismiss Mahādeva; Oṃ suvaḥ, I dismiss Mahādeva; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, I dismiss Mahādeva."

"May the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, the ultimate refuge of all worlds, depart satisfied by this oblation, so that he may return again. Thus, in the case of images, or in water, or in fire, everything is the same except for the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*). "There is a great path," so they say; "there is a great path," so says the Blessed Bodhāyana. Thus it is said.

With the *anuvāka* beginning "Tvaritarudra" and "Sarvo vai rudra," Nandikeśvara states in the *Purāṇa* the fruit for one who acts in this manner: "The merit of one who worships a *liṅga* for a single day is greater than that of one who might give a hundred thousand milch cows to those who have mastered the Vedas."

"Whether one should feed the best of the twice-born month after month for as long as one lives, or whether one should worship the Liṅga even once—these two are equal; of this there is no doubt. Thus ends the section on the procedure for the worship of Śiva in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, regarding the subject of Śiva’s ablution and so forth,
Nandikeśvara says in the *Śivadharma*:
"Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of crores of kalpas..."
By bathing with clarified butter, one burns all that away, just as fire consumes fuel.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of years,
one undoubtedly burns it all away by anointing the Liṅga with ghee.
Having performed a bath with ghee on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, a man who applies it once to the Liṅga uplifts twenty-one generations of his lineage and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
He who performs the ritual bath with clarified butter continuously for a month, accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage, attains the state of the Lord.
The merit of bathing [an image] with milk is equal to that of one who gives ten thousand milch cows, adorned with garments, gold, and other ornaments, to a master of the Vedas.
That man who bathes the Liṅga even once with devotion using curd is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having fasted on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should bathe the Liṅga with curd;
having delivered seven generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having bathed [the image] once with honey with devotion,
a man indeed casts off the cloak of sin and is glorified in the world of Agni.
Whoever performs the bathing of the Liṅga even once with sugarcane juice shall attain the world of the Vidyādharas, endowed with all objects of desire.
He who bathes the Liṅga even once with water filtered through a cloth shall attain a self fully satisfied in all desires and reach the world of Varuṇa.
The man who bathes a *liṅga* even once with water infused with *kuśa* grass is honored in the world of Brahmā, traveling upon a golden celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
If one bathes the Lord even once with water scented with sandalwood,
having reached the world of the Gandharvas, one is highly honored by the Gandharvas.
Having reached the world of Savitṛ with water from flowers, that of Kubera with golden water,
and that of Indra with water containing jewels, he rejoices.
If one performs the ritual bath once with the five products of a tawny cow according to the prescribed method, it is declared that for others [the merit] is a hundredfold; of this there is no doubt.
A bath is known to yield a hundredfold fruit, while an anointing yields twenty-five;
however, a great bath (mahāsnāna) is proclaimed to yield two thousand fruits.
O Śivā, one should offer garments that are most variegated, substantial, soft, scented, hairless, and new.
For as many thousands of years as there are threads in that garment, for that long one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Having given a three-stranded sacred thread (*upavīta*) made of silk thread or similar material, white or yellow, to Rudra, one becomes a master of the Vedānta.
One should perform an anointing of the Liṅga with divine and fragrant perfumes;
such a person is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred times ten million divine years.
The merit from anointing with fragrant ointments is twice that of sandalwood;
the merit from agallochum is known to be eight times that of sandalwood.
The fruit of black agallochum is especially desired to be double that;
from it, the merit of saffron is ordained to be a hundredfold.
Having thoroughly anointed the liṅga with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron finely ground together,
one shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas.
Having fanned [the image] with a palm-leaf fan and having anointed it with divine perfumes,
one is honored in the world of Vāyu for thousands of millions of years.
By giving a peacock-feather fan that is exceedingly beautiful to Śiva,
one is honored in the world of Rudra for a hundred crores of years.
With flowers grown in the forest, or leaves produced on the mountains—
fresh, without holes, sprinkled with water, and avoided by living beings.
Or one may worship Śiva even with flowers grown from one's own garden;
through particularly excellent flowers, merit becomes especially great.
When even a single Arka flower is offered to Śiva,
one obtains that same fruit which is gained by giving a hundred pieces of gold.
The karavīra flower is superior to a thousand arka flowers;
the bilva leaf is superior to a thousand karavīra flowers.
A single lotus flower is superior to a thousand bilva leaves;
likewise, a bakula flower is superior to a thousand lotuses.
A single *duttūraka* flower is superior to a thousand *baka* flowers;
a *bṛhatī* flower is the most excellent among a thousand *duttūraka* flowers.
A *droṇa* flower is superior to a thousand *bṛhatī* flowers;
indeed, an *apāmārga* flower is superior to a thousand *droṇa* flowers.
A single *kuśa* flower is superior to a thousand *apāmārga* flowers;
a single *śamī* flower is superior to a thousand *kuśa* flowers.
O Illustrious One, a single blue lotus is superior to thousands of *śamī* flowers;
among all species of flowers, the blue lotus is the most excellent.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who, with devotion and according to the prescribed rite, offers a garland made of a thousand blue lotuses to Śiva.
For thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of eons,
the illustrious one, possessing prowess equal to Śiva, shall dwell in the city of Śiva.
The *śamī* flower and the blossom of the *bṛhatī* are said to be equal;
the *jātī*, *vijayā*, and *pāṭalā* are to be known as equal to the *karavīra*.
The white mandāraka flower is like a white lotus;
the nāga, campaka, and punnāga flowers are known to be similar to the dhattūra.
The man who worships the Liṅga even once with a Dhattūra flower attains the fruit of a hundred thousand cows and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Whoever devoutly worships a liṅga even once with bṛhatī flowers shall attain the fruit of giving ten thousand cows and go to heaven.
Mallika, utpala, and padma; jāti, punnāga, and campaka; asoka, mandāraka, karṇikāra, and bakula.

[One should perform the rite] with flowers from the *karavīra*, *arka*, *dhattūra*, *śamī*, *nāgara*, and *kesara*; or even with those produced from *kuśa*, *apāmārga*, *kusuma*, *kādamba*, and *droṇa*.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the fruit that a man obtains who worships Śiva with these flowers according to his availability.
With celestial chariots that resemble ten million suns, which are available at all times,
encircled by garlands of flowers, and resounding with the music of songs and instruments;
With the sweet sounds of lutes and musical instruments, where one may wander at will,
crowded with the daughters of Rudra, and difficult even for gods and dānavas to attain.
Being fanned by yak-tail whisks and praised by gods and asuras,
he shall go to the divine city of Śiva, or wherever else may please him.
Whoever should construct a very dense flower-pavilion over Śiva,
adorned with flower garlands and other ornaments hanging down as far as the *āpīḍa* (head-ornament).
Surrounded by all these most wonderful Great Vehicles adorned with divine flowers, the glorious one shall go happily to the city of Śiva.
He who should offer even a mere fragment of gold upon the head of the Liṅga shall occupy half the throne of Indra for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
In this same manner, the fruit should be understood according to the sequence, in brief,
for all the jewel-lotuses, especially for the purpose of the crown.
Shiva himself, out of constant devotion to him, personally accepts those flowers which one plucks oneself and offers in worship to Shiva.
Or, in the absence of flowers, one should offer even leaves;
and if leaves are also unavailable, one should offer even grasses, shrubs, or medicinal herbs.
If medicinal herbs are unavailable, he becomes worshipped through devotion;
groves of kadamba trees should be offered to Śambhu at night.
During the day, one should avoid all flowers except for the *mallikā*; during both day and night, one should avoid flowers that are scentless or have a pungent odor.
One should avoid even those leaves that possess fragrance;
however, one should accept even that which lacks fragrance, provided it is pure, such as *kuśa* grass and the like.
One should discard flowers that are infested with insects or hair, those that are withered or stale, those that have fallen on their own, and those that are otherwise defiled.
One should not worship the deity with unopened buds, nor should one offer anything that is unripe;
for incense made from the resin of black aloe-wood is like a fire of chaff to gold.
One should purify a person joined with sin; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should offer incense made of black agallochum and camphor to Maheśvara.
Listen to the fruit of his merit for practicing this continuously for half a month:
for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
He enjoys pleasures in the city of Śiva, and at its conclusion he becomes a lord of the earth;
Śaṅkara himself directly accepts the guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter.
By giving for half a month, one is honored in the world of Śiva;
he who burns guggulu resin with clarified butter on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight dedicated to Śiva [attains the same].
One thousand offenses committed here or in the hereafter are consumed by two thousand fruits of guggulu resin mixed with buffalo ghee.
Having burned that [offering] mixed with clarified butter, one becomes equal to Śiva;
by the gift of a ghee lamp to Śiva, [one attains a realm extending] for a hundred yojanas.
Leaving that abode of Yama with celestial chariots resembling the sun,
that man shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas under that God of gods.
One should prepare a prastha of rice grains from śāli paddy and cook it into well-prepared food;
one should offer that caru-oblation to Śiva, especially on the fourteenth lunar day.
For as many grains of rice as there are in that food offering,
for that many thousands of eons one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
When offerings of jaggery, sugar-candy, ghee,
and various foods cooked with ghee are presented, the fruit of giving them is a hundredfold.
Half a fruit is prescribed for those who consume marrow and syrups;
half of that again is for scented water, especially so.
One should offer ripe fruits such as the mātuluṅga;
whatever fruit is offered to Śiva, that same fruit belongs to him who makes the offering.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who offers betel leaf endowed with the five fragrances to Śiva and likewise to the Guru.
With a fragrant body, radiant and beautiful in every limb,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred divine crores of years.
One should place a beautiful, stainless mirror before Śiva,
having adorned it with a couch and decorated it with white garlands.
Stainless as the rays of the moon, glorious, fortunate, and assuming forms at will,
he is honored in the world of Rudra for thousands of tens of thousands of kalpas.
The destination that a man attains by circumambulating a temple of Śiva with devotion cannot be reached even by a hundred sacrifices;
he easily obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Also in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"The pure man who performs a circumambulation in every direction with prostrations, moving slowly according to the rule of right and left, [attains merit]."

"At every step one shall obtain the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. Thus ends the section on the bathing of Śiva and related matters in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follow the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*).
In this regard, Saṃvarta says:
"Thereafter, a twice-born man should perform the five great sacrifices day after day;
a wise man should not neglect them, for they are indeed heard of even in the Śruti."

Then, after the worship of the deity— that is, immediately following it— one should worship Viṣṇu with the *puruṣasūkta*. Thereafter, one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* rite and likewise the *balikarman*.
Thus it is stated in the *Nārasiṃha Purāṇa*. Yama also says:
"Five slaughterhouses exist for the householder, operating day after day, always:
the reaper, the grinder, the hearth, the water-jar, and the household utensils."
"For by employing these [senses], a Brahmin is indeed bound again and again;
therefore, five sacrifices have been prescribed for the purpose of purifying them. Thus it is said.

*Sūnās* are places of violence; for the traditional law (*smṛti*) of Hārīta states: "Now we shall explain *sūnās*: they are called *sūnās* because they slaughter living beings, whether mobile or immobile. A *khaṇḍinī* is a mortar and so forth. A *peṣiṇī* is a grinding stone and so forth. A *cullī* is a hearth for cooking. A *jalakumbha* is a water-jar. An *upaskara* consists of winnowing baskets and other such implements. The meaning is that by maintaining these—that is, by performing their respective functions—one is slain, which is to say, one becomes joined with sin. Although here the mention of a specific occasion suggests that this is an occasional duty (*naimittika*), nevertheless, because it is both obligatory and occasional, it is indeed a constant duty (*nitya*). For this very reason, Śaṅkha says:
A householder has five slaughter-houses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water jar; for the expiation of their sin—
A householder must never neglect the performance of the five sacrifices. Vyāsa also says:
"Even in times of dire distress, one should not omit the five sacrifices."
And those sacrifices were shown by Yama:

"The sacrifice to Brahman, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, as well as the sacrifice to beings and the sacrifice to men—these are proclaimed as the five sacrifices. Thus it is said.
Manu and Devala state their characteristics as follows:
"Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña); the libation to the ancestors (tarpaṇa) is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña);

the burnt offering (homa) is the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña); the bali-offering is the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña); and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña). Thus [it is said].

Teaching, studying, and the recitation of mantras constitute the *brahmayajña*; for it is recorded in the Smṛti of Kātyāyana: "That which is declared as the recitation of the *Śruti* is known as the *brahmayajña*. Libation (*tarpaṇa*) refers to the libation for the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), the ancestral funeral rite (*pitṛśrāddha*), and the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). As Manu has said:
Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests—these expect [support] from householders; therefore, one who understands his duty must act for them.
"One should honor the sages through the private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), the gods with fire-oblations according to the rule,
the ancestors with the *śrāddha* rite, men with food, and the elemental spirits with the *bali* offering.
Alternatively, that which was stated by Kātyāyana should be consulted.
Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña); the libation to the ancestors is the sacrifice to the Pitṛs (pitṛyajña);
the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña); the bali offering is the sacrifice to the elements (bhūtayajña); and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña).

"Or it may be a *śrāddha*, or a *pitṛyajña*, or even an offering (*bali*) to the ancestors. In this matter, the arrangement follows one's own specific *śākhā*. Here, "śrāddha" refers to the obligatory daily *śrāddha* (*nityaśrāddha*). Thus, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
"One should constantly feed at least one Brahmin, dedicating [the meal] to the ancestors."
"That is designated as the *nityaśrāddha*, a sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*) that bestows a [favorable] state of existence.
By this, it is stated that this is a *śrāddha* without a deity (*adaiva*). And it has been said by Manu:
"In the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pāñcayajñika*), one should feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors."
"And a twice-born man should not cause anyone to fast on account of the Vaiśvadeva," [it is said].

Regarding the *pāñcayajñika* (the rite consisting of the five sacrifices), which forms a constituent part of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), the word "even" (*api*) implies that he may feed many people if he possesses the means. For this very reason, the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states:
"One should perform the *śrāddha* every day with food, etc., or even with water."
"One should feed Brahmins or even a single Brahmin, intending it for the ancestors.
Regarding this, Hārīta states the specific detail:
"The daily *śrāddha* (nitya-śrāddha) should be without the gods; it is devoid of the *arghya*, the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), and so forth."
Pracetas also says:
"The best of the twice-born should not perform the invitation, nor the oblation, nor the summoning, nor the dismissal, nor the offering of rice-balls, nor the *svadhā* invocation, in the daily rite."
Having seated him and provided a seat, having honored him with flowers and other offerings,
having assigned him his place and fed him, one should dismiss him after giving a small gift.
Also in the Purāṇa:

"That which is called the daily śrāddha (nityaśrāddha) is said to be devoid of the deities; it should be known as extending to six generations of ancestors, and it is to be performed without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) or a rice-ball (piṇḍa)."
Vyāsa also says:
"In the daily *śrāddha*, having honored the twice-born with water for the feet (*arghya*), perfumes, and other offerings according to one's ability,
one should feed them all properly while duly dedicating the rite to all the groups of ancestors."

In the daily *śrāddha*, one should omit the invocation (*āvāhana*), the utterance of *svadhā*, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), the ritual of placing food in the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and so forth; one should simply prepare the food to be eaten.
Having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability, one should dismiss the guests with salutations.
A householder should feed even a single Brahmin every day, even if he has six guests.
In this regard, that which is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa should be consulted. "If one should feed a single Brahmin, intending him for the three ancestors"—
regarding this alternative procedure, Kātyāyana says:
One should feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the ancestral sacrifice;
however, if such a person does not exist, one may instead consume [the offering] oneself, or else [feed] another who is worthy of the food.
Having also extracted some food according to his ability and in accordance with the rules,
and having said, "This for the ancestors," he should utter the word *svadhā*.

And one should give that food to a Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, the Kūrma Purāṇa, concerning the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña), states: "Or, having set aside some food according to his ability, being composed, he should present it to a twice-born who knows the true meaning of the Vedas."
Regarding inability [to perform the rites], that which was stated by Manu is as follows:
"One should offer the *śrāddha* day after day with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors."
"Homo daiva" means "homa for the Viśvedevas"; the meaning is that this is the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña). And so it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Whether in the domestic fire, or in the common fire, or in water, or even upon the ground, the Vaiśvadeva must be performed; that indeed is remembered as the sacrifice to the gods."

The *śālāgni* is the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*). Regarding this, Bodhāyana states: "Day after day one should offer *svāhā* to the gods, even if only with a piece of wood; thus one completes the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*). The phrase "even with a piece of wood" refers to a situation where there is a lack of food. For this very reason, Pracetas says: "Therefore, one should offer oblations day after day to the gods with whatever [is available], even if it is only a piece of wood, in the absence of food. The term *balir bhautaḥ* means that the offering of the *bali* is the sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūtayajña*). And so it is said in the Kūrmapurāṇa: "From the remains of the food offered to the gods, one should present the *bali* to the spirits."
That is to be known as the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña), which bestows prosperity upon all embodied beings.

Hārīta also states: "The offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*) to the guardians of the dwelling and the spirits (*bhūta*) is *ahuta*. *Ahuta* refers to the sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūtayajña*). Regarding that as well, in the absence of food, Bodhāyana says: "One should offer the oblation to the spirits day after day, even down to flowers; thus one completes this sacrifice to the spirits. "The sacrifice to men (*nṛyajña*) is the honoring of guests"—the meaning is that the honoring of guests, which is the giving of food to guests, is the sacrifice to men;
the giving of food to guests is indeed the *nṛyajña*, and it is the fifth [sacrifice].

Thus, from the Smṛti of Yama. Hārīta also says: "In that one offers oblations to the gods, by that one conquers the world of the gods; in that one offers to the ancestors, by that the world of the ancestors; in that one studies the Veda, by that the world of the ṛṣis; in that one presents the *bali* offering to the beings, by that the world of the beings; in that one gratifies the Brāhmaṇas, by that the world of men. Therefore, having given food to the ancestors, one should wait until the milking of the cows. Also in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "Because he stays for no fixed time, he is therefore called a guest (*atithi*)."
When he is satisfied, the householder is released from his debt regarding the purpose of the human sacrifice (nṛyajña).
Regarding this, Nārāyaṇa states the specific rule:
"Having appointed one or many Vedic scholars facing east, [the performer], wearing the sacred thread around his neck (nivīta),
with his mind fixed on them, composed and meditating upon the sages..."
Thereafter, one should offer a seat, the water for honor (arghya), and the water for sipping (ācamana) after the meal.
Regarding the sages beginning with Sanaka, because they were human beings— even Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana was so—
thus should a twice-born man perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for human beings every day.
With the exclamation "Hanta," the householder should perform the *hantakāra* sacrifice every day.
That in which "hanta" is employed is *hantakāra*. The meaning is that one should sacrifice after uttering "hanta. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"The *svāhākāra*, the *vaṣaṭkāra*, and the salutation (*namaskāra*) belong to the inhabitants of heaven;
the *svadhākāra* belongs to the ancestors, and likewise the *hantakāra* belongs to human beings."
The term *hantetikaraṇa* means making the utterance *hanta*. Regarding this, Nārāyaṇa states an alternative procedure (*anukalpa*):
"In case of inability, having set aside some food, one should simply designate it with the word *hanta*.

Bodhāyana also says: "Day after day one should give food to Brāhmaṇas, even down to roots, fruits, and vegetables; thus one completes the sacrifice to men (*manuṣyayajña*). Following the primary procedure (*mukhyakalpa*), Kārṣṇājini also says:
Whether it be alms, or an abundant meal, or even a morsel of food—
if these are not available, one should always give at least a vessel of water.
"He should give to the guest"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. For this very reason, the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, introducing the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*), states:
"A twice-born man should always give to a guest either a *hantakāra* (a morsel of food), or the first portion, or alms according to his ability; thus he should perceive the Supreme Lord."
The definitions of *bhikṣā* and so forth have been stated by Śātātapa:
"A single morsel (*grāsa*) constitutes a *bhikṣā*; four times that is a *puṣkala*;
and the wise know that four *puṣkala*s constitute a *hantakāra*."
Manu also says:
"A single morsel constitutes alms; four morsels constitute an *agra*;
and by quadrupling an *agra*, an *hantakāra* is prescribed."

However, when neither a Brāhmaṇa is available for the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*) nor for the giving of alms (*bhikṣādāna*), the rule for disposal (*pratipatti-niyama*) is shown in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"But if none at all are available, one should offer what has been given to the cows.

And thus, by Manu and others, the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*) and the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*) are shown to be performed specifically within the *vaiśvadeva* and the *baliharaṇa*. However, in the commentary on that [text], it is stated that Āpastamba, due to the difference in mantras and the difference in designations, taught these two sacrifices as entirely distinct. On this point, Bodhāyana says:
He who has no one in his house to perform these five great duties when departing on a journey departs together with those very sacrifices.
"While traveling, he should offer these [oblations] with whatever food is available;
if no food is obtained, he should complete them with water.
Regarding this, Dakṣa states the rule for the timing:
"And in the fifth part, a distribution according to their merit is prescribed for the ancestors, the gods, human beings, and all living creatures.
This refers to the distribution of food. It occurs during the fifth part of the day divided into eight portions. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says:
"But when midday has arrived, having offered the *bali* in his own home to the gods, ancestors, and men, he should eat the remainder with speech restrained.
Regarding the fruit for one who acts thus, Hārīta says:

"A Brahmin who gratifies the gods, the ancestors, the sages, as well as all beings and other Brahmins according to the prescribed rule, is fit for becoming one with Brahman. Thus [says] Śambhu as well.
Whatever fruit a wealthy twice-born man obtains through the Soma sacrifice,
a poor man may attain that same result by properly performing the five great sacrifices.
Now, the fault in not performing [the rite] has been shown by Garga:
"Those who are tainted by the impurity of the slaughterhouse are all remembered as *vṛṣalas*;
there is no eligibility for those evil-minded ones in any religious duty whatsoever."
A *vṛṣala* is a *śūdra*. Vyāsa also says: "But for that householder who, out of delusion, does not perform the five sacrifices, neither this world nor the next exists according to the Dharma."
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "One should not share one's house, seat, or household utensils with anyone whose body has been struck by the breath of a god or other such being."
Thus concludes the section on the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for the *vaiśvadeva* offering.
Regarding this, Nārāyaṇa says:

"Accompanied by his wife, pure, having bathed, having sipped water according to the rule, and restrained in speech, he should enter and perform the Vaiśvadeva rite in a well-kindled fire. [The phrase] "in a well-kindled fire" refers to either a non-Vedic or a Vedic fire. And so says Śātātapa:
Whether in a worldly or a Vedic fire, or having offered oblations into water or upon the ground,
the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must be performed for the removal of the five slaughtering grounds.
[571] Regarding the Vedic and the nuptial fires, as Manu has said: "A householder should perform the domestic rites according to rule in the nuptial fire,
as well as the performance of the five sacrifices and the daily cooking."
The specific distinction regarding the twenty-four [tithis] has been shown:
"Having performed the morning oblation and having removed [the fire] from the hearth,
one should place the remainder in the kitchen and there carry out the cooking."

Alternatively, the cooking may take place in a worldly fire (*laukika-agni*). Thus Aṅgiras says: "One should always cook food in the domestic fire (*śālāgni*) or even in a worldly fire. The domestic fire is the *gṛhya* fire. But when the cooking is done in a worldly fire, then the oblation (*homa*) must be offered in that very same fire. This has been stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"If the cooking were done on a worldly fire, then the food would be offered therein;
if it is done in the domestic fire (*śālāgni*), then the food [is offered there]—this is the eternal rule.

With this very intention, Āpastamba also states: "One should offer with the hand, using each of the first six mantras, either in the *aupāsana* fire or in the cooking fire (*pacana*). Regarding this, the phrase "or in the cooking fire" has been explained in its commentary as referring specifically to one who has performed the *sarvādhāna* (the complete installation of the sacred fires). And this has been stated by Viṣṇu as well.
"From the time of the establishment of the *agnihotra* until the setting up of the *āvasathya* fire, in whichever fire one cooks food, in that very fire the *homa* is prescribed. [572]

For one who has performed the *sarvādhāna* (the complete establishment of the sacred fires), since there is no separate *agnihotra* outside the *āvasathya* fire, and thus no *gṛhya* (domestic) fire, the meaning is that the *homa* is to be offered in whatever worldly fire the cooking was done. When it is asked how even that [is to be done], Śaunaka says: "Then, in the evening and morning, one should offer of the prepared sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) to the deities of the *agnihotra*: to Soma, to Vanaspati, to Agni-Soma, to Heaven and Earth, to Dhanvantari, to Indra, to the Viśvedevas, and to Brahmā, with the word *svāhā*. Then follows the offering of the *bali*. The term *haviṣyasya* means "of that which is fit for sacrifice. "To the deities of the *agnihotra*" means to Sūrya, Agni, and Prajāpati. Āpastamba also says: "One should offer with the hand, using the first six [mantras] respectively, either in the *aupāsana* fire or the cooking fire. There is sprinkling around on both sides, as previously described. "With the first" means with those beginning with "to Agni, *svāhā*" and ending with the *Sviṣṭakṛt* mantra. "On both sides" means at the beginning and at the end of the rite. Gṛhya-Kātyāyana also says: "Having sprinkled water around the food intended for the *vaiśvadeva*, one should offer portions with *svāhā*-utterances to Brahmā, Prajāpati, the Households, Kaśyapa, and Anumati. Gautama also says: "The offerings are to Agni, Agni, Dhanvantari, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, and Sviṣṭakṛt. In this matter, the arrangement is according to one's own *śākhā*.
Thereafter, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā),
using consecrated food or sacrificial oblations (havis) accompanied by sacrificial side-dishes.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. Kātyāyana also says:

"Having taken up the sacrificial oblation and poured clarified butter or other suitable offerings over it, one should offer the oblation according to the rules of one's own Vedic school and then present the *bali* offering with what remains."

The connection here is as follows: having taken out the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), having sprinkled it with a sacrificial substance such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and so forth, and having poured [the butter] over it, one should offer that oblation. In this context, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is intended to include curd (*dadhi*) and other such substances. For this very reason, Vyāsa states:
"One should offer what is smeared with clarified butter, avoiding oil and alkaline substances;
or smeared with curd, or smeared with milk; or, in the absence of these, even with water."
But when sacrificial materials are unavailable, a specific rule is shown in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:

"In the absence [of proper materials], one should perform the Vaiśvadeva with whatever is available— such as fruits, vegetables, water, and so forth— or indeed with milk, curd, and ghee, using the *sruva* ladle."
"One should perform [the offering] with food and so forth by means of the hand, or with water by means of the hollowed palms (añjali) in the water.
This means that it may be done by whatever instrument is available. Here too, the oblation (homa) is performed with that very thing which is to be eaten. As it is stated in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"Whether it be a vegetable, or a leaf, or a root, or a fruit..."
"Whatever one intends regarding food, with that one should also offer oblations into the fire.
[574] Regarding this, there is a specific rule stated by Āpastamba:
"With the hand turned upward, [the offering is made] pressed by the tip of the thumb..."
With fingers and palms joined together and restrained in speech, he should offer the oblation.
Kātyāyana also says:
