"He who, out of delusion, offers oblations into a fire that has no flame or whose coals are extinguished,
is born with weak digestion, afflicted by disease, and impoverished."
Therefore, one who desires health, long life, and ultimate prosperity should offer oblations only when the fire is well-kindled, and never when it is not kindled.
Śaunaka also says: "When the fire has many dry fuels, is well-kindled,
especially when it is smokeless and flickering, one should offer oblations for the successful accomplishment of the rite."
Kātyāyana also says:
"Those desiring prosperity should offer oblations using their hands, winnowing baskets, mouths, or wooden ladles;
they should not blow on the fire, nor should they fan it with fans or similar objects."
"One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for it was born from the mouth.
[575] Regarding this, he (the author) himself states the settled rule:
"One should not apply the expression 'with the mouth' to the case of a worldly fire."

Āpastamba, however, prescribes specific observances at the commencement of the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites: "When these mantras are employed, there shall be sleeping on the ground and celibacy for twelve days; furthermore, for the final [mantra], there is a fast for one night, excluding pungent and salty foods. These refer to the mantras intended for the *vaiśvadeva* offerings. The "final" refers to the mantra beginning with "ye bhūtāḥ" (*Those beings who...*). Then follows the *vaiśvadeva* *caru* (oblation), because it has been stated by that very author: "In the *vaiśvadeva*, the Viśvedevas [are the deities]. The meaning is that in whatever rite is to be performed during the *vaiśvadeva*, the Viśvedevas are the presiding deities. Regarding this, Āpastamba further states: "When the food is prepared, standing, he should announce to the host: 'It is ready' (*bhūtam*); the response is: 'May that well-prepared food, which is the Virāj, not perish' (*tan mā kṣāyi*). Then follows the *vaiśvadeva* and subsequent rites. And this is to be performed both in the evening and in the morning.
The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and the offering of bali must be performed both evening and morning;
it must be done even by one who is fasting, otherwise he becomes a sinner.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Kātyāyana. By this, it is stated that [the rite] serves as a purification of the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*). And it is said in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:

"If one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should ever depart on a journey due to the passage of time, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must indeed be performed in whichever fire the cooking takes place."
In that regard, the man who eats without having first offered oblations eats only sin;
even when away from home, he should certainly perform the purification of himself without hesitation.

Gobhila also says: "If rice and barley were to be prepared at this time, one should offer the oblation with one of them, and the task is accomplished by means of the other. If food should be cooked again and again at this time, one should perform only a single *bali* offering there. If much food should be cooked at one time, the householder should perform only a single *bali* offering there from the kitchen itself. The meaning of this is as follows: if at this time there is the cooking of various foods such as rice and barley, then one should perform the *homa* and other *bali* offerings from only one cooking, not from every individual cooking. Even if food should be cooked repeatedly at this time due to the arrival of guests and the like, then too one should perform only a single *bali* offering once from that one cooking. Likewise, even if there is cooking in many ways at this time for brothers, sons, and others who subsist on the same fire, one should perform it only once from the householder's cooking. Regarding one who maintains no sacred fire (*anagnika*), Atri says:
One who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *balikarma* up to the end of the *pitṛyajña*;
one without fires, however, should offer the *kākabali* using the remnants of the [ancestral] oblation.

"There is no great sacrifice for one who maintains no sacred fire except the sacrifice of the person (puruṣayajña). Thus it is said. Furthermore, Vasiṣṭha has shown that even the fire-oblation for such a person is as follows:
"But that Brahmin who maintains no sacred fire should himself offer food with the vyāhṛtis."
Having offered oblations with the Śākala mantras, one should present the remaining portion as the *kākabali* (offering to the crows).
The Śākala mantras are those beginning with "devakṛtasyainasaḥ" (of the sin committed against the gods) and so forth. Viṣṇu also says:
"Having offered food repeatedly with the Vyāhṛtis and with the Śākala mantras, and having offered the oblation to Prajāpati, one should thereafter honor the guest."
On this matter, Yama says:
"Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having performed the Vaiśvadeva offering go to the womb of a crow by virtue of that food cooked in vain."
Vyāsa also says:
"That twice-born man who, when not in a state of distress, eats without having first performed the Vaiśvadeva rite,
is a fool who goes headfirst to the Kālasūtra hell."
Thus ends the section on the Vaiśvadeva ritual in the Smṛticandrikā. Now follows the offering of the bali-oblation;
regarding this, Kātyāyana states:

"Having drawn out the oblation and having poured clarified butter or other sacrificial substances over it, one should offer the sacrifice according to the rules of one's own Vedic school and then present the *bali* offering with what remains. Here, the connection is as follows: having drawn out the oblation (*havis*), having poured sacrificial substances such as clarified butter over it—that is, having sprinkled it—and having sacrificed with that oblation. On this point, Gobhila states: "As long as he himself resides in the house, he should perform the *bali* offering; or another Brāhmaṇa may do so. This means that for as long as he dwells in the house, either he himself or another should perform the *bali*. The mention of a "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to include sons and others. For this very reason, Atri says:
"A son, a brother, a sacrificial priest, a pupil, a father-in-law, a maternal uncle, a wife, a Vedic scholar, and one for whom one sacrifices—these are prescribed as witnesses at the *balikarman*.
This refers to cases such as being away on a journey; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
If one who has maintained the sacred fires should ever depart on a journey due to the passage of time,
the Vaiśvadeva offering must indeed be performed in whichever fire the cooking takes place.
In that regard, the man who eats without having first offered [the oblation] eats only sin.
Even when away from home, he should perform the purification of himself without hesitation;
his son, brother, wife, or disciple may offer the *bali* on his behalf. Thus it is said.

"If the wife [is present], she should offer the silent oblation of the cooked food in the evening"—so states the traditional law of Manu. However, when there is no other performer in the house, then even while traveling abroad, he himself should perform it. Thus says Bodhāyana.
He who has no one in his house to perform these five great duties while he goes on a journey departs together with the sacrifices themselves.

Regarding this, Śaunaka says: "Now follows the offering of the *bali* (food-oblation). To these very deities—to the waters, to the plants and trees, to the house, to the household deities (*gṛhadevatā*), to the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*), to Indra and Indra’s men, to Yama and Yama’s men, to Varuṇa and Varuṇa’s men, to Soma and Soma’s men—thus in each direction; to Brahmā and Brahmā’s men—in the middle; to the All-gods (*viśvedevāḥ*), to all beings who roam by day—in the daytime; to those who roam by night—at night; to the *rakṣas* (demons)—to the north; *svadhā* to the ancestors—with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*)—he should pour the remainder toward the south. The meaning of this is as follows: "To these" refers to the deities of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, because they are the subject under discussion. The particle *ca* (and) serves to include the deities about to be mentioned. The particle *eva* (only/very) is intended to exclude the *bali*-offerings prescribed in other *Gṛhya* texts. Furthermore, starting from "to the Sun" up to "to the deities of the site," the offerings are made ending toward the east, so that the rule applies to the east, according to the technical definition: "movements are directed toward the east. Then, at the end of that, he offers in each direction to Indra and the others, and in their midst to Brahmā and Brahmā’s men. To the All-gods is offered at the very end of everything, as they are the primary recipients. "To all beings" is offered in the middle, because that is its domain. To the *rakṣas* is offered to the north of Brahmā and the others, because they are the subject under discussion. For this very reason, to the south of them is the offering " *svadhā* to the ancestors. All the mantras end with *svāhā*. Here, the mention of "he should pour" (*ninayet*) is to indicate that this is a separate ritual act for the sake of the *pitṛyajña*, distinct from the *bali*-offering. This distinction is made to exclude the use of the word *svāhā*. If it were a separate act, it might occur at a different time; to prevent this, the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is used. All of this has been stated in the *Gṛhyavṛtti*. Āpastamba also says: "To the west of the fire, with the seventh and eighth [mantras], ending toward the north; near the well, with the ninth; in the middle of the house, with the tenth and eleventh, ending toward the east; in the north-eastern part of the house, with the next four; in the place of the bed, with the mantra containing the word 'desire' (*kāma*); on the threshold, with the mantra containing the word 'intermediate space' (*antarikṣa*); on the upper covering, with the northern [mantras]; in the place of Brahmā, to the south, with the mantra containing the word 'ancestor' (*pitṛ*), wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder and with the palm turned downward. The one to Rudra is the last, just as the offerings to the deities [were made]. The sprinkling of water around those two is separate because of the difference in their ritual rules. Only at night, with the final [mantra], the offering to the sky (*vaihāyasa*). The meaning of this is: with the next four [mantras], ending toward the east, because that is their domain. "In the place of Brahmā" means in the middle of the house. There too, "ending toward the east" is understood to carry over. To the south of the place of Brahmā, with the mantra containing the word 'ancestor', because that is the subject under discussion. "The one to Rudra is to the north"—the remainder is "from the ancestral [direction]. "The sprinkling of water around those two is separate"—because of the statement further on. "Just as to the deities": just as the offering to the deities was made with the palm facing upward, so it is here too, and not like the ancestral offering. Regarding the rules for the *bali* offerings, he himself says: "For each of the *bali*s in its respective place, there is a consecration: having wiped it with the hand, sprinkled it, and placed the food, the sprinkling follows after. However, for those offerings gathered in one place, the sprinkling is done once only, as it is possible; this too has been stated by him: "Thus, for the *bali*s gathered in various places, the sprinkling is done once at the end, provided they have been touched by the ladle. An exception to this is: "The sprinkling around those two is separate because of the difference in their ritual rules. This means that although the ancestral and the Raudra offerings are gathered in one place, the sprinkling is separate and distinct, even though the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder, because of the difference in their ritual rules. "Only at night, with the final [mantra], the offering to the sky"—meaning one should give the *vaihāyasa* offering with the mantra "Those beings... only at night. Some maintain that only with the final mantra is it given at night, and not with any other, thus seeking to exclude other mantras during the night. All of this has been stated by the Commentator. Gṛhyakātyāyana also says: "At the water-jar (*maṇika*), three [offerings]: to Parjanya, to the Waters, and to the Earth; to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ; at the two door-posts; in each direction to Vāyu and to the Directions; in the middle, three [to] Brahmā, to the Intermediate Space, and to Sūrya; to the All-gods and to all Beings; to the north of them, to Uṣas and to the Lord of Beings; further, to the ancestors: *svadhā namaḥ*; to the south, to the three ancestors; in the north-western direction, he should pour out [the remainder]: 'That which is security, that is your cleansing water. The meaning of this is: "At the water-jar" means near the well. "In each direction to Vāyu and likewise to the Directions"—the phrase "in each direction" is understood here. The application is "to the eastern direction," and so forth. "In the middle"—the phrase "of these" is understood. To the north of the three [is the offering] "to the All-gods," which makes two. "Further" means to the north of those two, "to Uṣas and to the Lord of Beings. To the south of the three, "to the ancestors"; having washed the vessel with "that which is security, that is your cleansing water," he should pour it out in the north-western direction. All of this has been stated by the Commentator on that. Here, all the mantras end with *namaḥ*.

"The offering of the bali is prescribed with the formula, 'Salutation to such-and-such,'" according to the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana. In this matter, the arrangement follows one's own Śākhā; a twice-born man should never undertake a rite prescribed in another Śākhā.
Thus, from the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha. On this point, the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa states:
"Having thus performed the domestic offering (gṛhyabali), the master of the house, being pure, should respectfully perform the ritual release (utsarga) for the nourishment of all beings."
The offering of food—when the question arises as to how that is to be done, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states:
"Gods, humans, animals, birds, Siddhas, along with the hosts of Yakṣas, Uragas, and Daityas; Pretas, Piśācas, trees, and all others who desire food—may it be given by me."
May the ants, insects, and winged creatures, who are emaciated and bound by the fetters of karma, attain satisfaction;
this food has been relinquished by me for them—may they be happy.

For those who have no mother, no father, no kinsman, and for whom there is neither the preparation of food nor such satisfaction—may this food offered on the earth for their gratification reach them; may they find contentment and be joyful.
All beings, as well as this food and I myself—Viṣṇu—are not other than that.
Therefore, for the welfare of beings and for their prosperity, I bestow this food, which is a living being.
This fourteenth class of beings—whatever hosts of spirits dwell therein—for their satisfaction this food has been released by me; may they rejoice in it.
"Having uttered this, a man endowed with faith should give food for the benefit of beings upon the earth, since the householder is the refuge of all.
Then he should give food to dogs and other such creatures; that too has been stated in that very same place.
Then the man should give [food] on the ground to dogs, caṇḍālas, and birds,
as well as to any others who are outcasts and have arrived with unbaked clay vessels.
Manu also says:
"One should gently place on the ground for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, crows, and worms."
In this regard, the mantras for the offering to the dogs and the crows as spoken by Vyāsa are as follows:
"To these two dogs, one dark and one brindled, born of the lineage of Vaivasvata—to them I shall give this ball of rice; may they always protect me on the path."
May those who belong to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, and Nirṛti—
those crows— accept the rice-ball offered by me upon the ground.

In this context, the giving of gifts to outcasts (*patita*) and others is not mandatory, because their presence is uncertain. However, some say that one should give even to those who have arrived. Thus says Āpastamba: "One should indeed make all [beings] sharers in the *vaiśvadeva* offering, down to the dogs and *caṇḍālas*; however, some say one should not give to those who are unworthy. Here, "unworthy" refers to *caṇḍālas* and the like. Regarding this, Vyāsa states:
"Having given the *bali* according to this rule, one should afterwards perform the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśet*).
Manu describes the fruit for one who acts in this manner:
"Thus, the Brāhmaṇa who constantly honors all beings goes by a straight path to the supreme abode, his form consisting of light.

Āpastamba also says: "He who performs these [rites] constantly, undistracted and according to instruction, attains heaven and prosperity; and the first portion must be given"—the remainder [of the sentence] being "to one learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*). Likewise, Vasiṣṭha states: "One should offer the *bali* to the household deities after giving the first portion to one learned in the Vedas and immediately thereafter to a student (*brahmacārin*); one should give to the ancestors [after that]. The meaning is that one should give alms to the student. For this very reason, Yama says:
"And one should give alms to a mendicant who observes the vow of celibacy according to the prescribed rule.

This rule was also shown by Gautama: "The giving of alms is preceded by the pronouncement of *svasti* (well-being). The meaning is that after causing the begging brahmacārin to say "svasti," one should give water into his hand and then perform the giving of the alms. For the ascetic (*yati*), however, the giving of water must be performed at both the beginning and the end. And thus Vyāsa says: "One should give water into the hand of the ascetic, give the alms, and again give water."
That alms-food would be equal to Mount Meru; that water would be like the ocean.

Since both of these two statements use the expression "one should give," it is understood that one should not refuse a mendicant (*yati*) or a student (*brahmacārin*). For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "When women refuse [a guest], they seize his merit, his gifts, his oblations, his offspring, his cattle, his spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and his food; therefore, one should never refuse a group of students as they wander. It is also stated in the *Purāṇa*:
"For they did not honor the ascetic who had approached, O descendant of Kakutstha."
And in the next world, he who eats the flesh of others shall eat his own flesh in a state of suffering.
Vyāsa also says:
"Both the ascetic and the celibate student are the masters of cooked food;
having eaten without giving food to those two, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
On this point, Parāśara says:
"A wandering mendicant (parivrāj) and a student (brahmacārin) should each be given three portions of alms;
thereafter, one may give according to one's desire, provided there is wealth, without restriction."
This also refers to the domain of yoga, such as vows and Vedic study,
because of the traditional teaching of Yājñavalkya: "Alms should be given with due respect to a mendicant, or to one who observes excellent vows."
The king should punish that village where twice-born men wander for alms while being unobservant of their vows and unlearned in the Vedas; for such a village provides sustenance for thieves.
And because of this traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "But when a mendicant arrives before the Vaiśvadeva has been performed, then that which was spoken by Vyāsa should be observed:
'If a mendicant comes to the house while the Vaiśvadeva remains unperformed, one should set aside food for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva, give him alms, and then dismiss him.'"
A mendicant is capable of removing the fault incurred by performing the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice;
however, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice does not remove the fault incurred by the mendicant.
The mendicant (bhikṣu) is the wandering ascetic (parivrāj). The same should be understood for the religious student (brahmacārin) as well. For this very reason, the Viṣṇupurāṇa states:
"One should give alms to the mendicant, the wandering ascetic, and the religious student, having set aside from the unprepared food a portion provided with all kinds of condiments."
Regarding alms-food, Yama says:
"But that alms-food which is handed over by hand, as well as water and condiments—
the eater becomes impure, and the giver does not go to heaven."
But when there is no acquisition of alms, it was said by Viṣṇu:
"In the absence of alms, one should give the food to cows or cast it into the fire.
And those mendicants have been shown by Vyāsa:
A student of sacred knowledge, an ascetic, a seeker of learning, one who supports his teacher, a traveler, and one whose livelihood is exhausted— these six are remembered as those entitled to alms.
Also in the Purāṇa:
"For one who is diseased, for one who is destitute of wealth, for one who has fallen away from his family,
or for one who has set out upon a journey, the practice of begging is prescribed."
The measurement of alms and so forth has been stated by Manu:
"A single morsel shall be a *bhikṣā*; four morsels are an *agra*;
and by quadrupling the *agra*, a *hantakāra* is prescribed. Thus it is said.
Regarding the fruit for one who acts in this way, Yama says:
"The Blessed One, Yama, has declared that the merit of a person who respectfully offers alms to a mendicant is equal to the gift of a cow."
Also in the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "He who bestows alms sufficient to fill a bowl upon ascetics shall be liberated from all sins and shall not fall into an evil rebirth. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the section on the offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the worship of guests (*atithipūjā*).

Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "Having given alms, one should further attend to the honoring of guests. The meaning is that after giving alms, one should remain in the courtyard of the house for some time in order to observe whether other guests have arrived. To this effect, the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* says:
Having sipped water for purification, the wise man should then look toward the door;
for one should wait for a guest during the eighth part of a muhūrta.

"Looking at the door" means *dvārāvalokanam*. Brahmagarbha also says: "A twice-born man, having offered the *bhūtabali*, should wait for the time of milking the cows. This restriction of time is intended to indicate that looking [at the guest] is necessary even at other times. For this very reason, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa states:
"Then, standing in the courtyard of his house for the duration of a cow’s milking,
or for longer than that according to his desire, he should remain there for the purpose of receiving guests.
When it is asked what the characteristics of such a person are, Śātātapa says:
Whether he be a friend or a servant, a fool or even a scholar—
whoever arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering is a guest who serves as a bridge to heaven.
Manu also says:
"A Brāhmaṇa who stays for even one night is traditionally called a guest (atithi);
because he remains for only a non-permanent time, he is therefore called a guest."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa as well:
"One should not treat a friend as a guest, nor one who dwells in the same village,
nor one whose family and name are unknown, even when he has arrived at the time for a meal."
"One who is hungry, who has arrived weary, who begs, and who possesses nothing—such a person they call a *brāhmaṇa* guest; he should be honored by the wise according to their ability.
The mention of the *brāhmaṇa* here is for the purpose of excluding the *kṣatriya*. For this very reason, Manu says:
"A Kṣatriya is not called a guest in the house of a Brāhmaṇa;
rather, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a friend, kinsmen, and even a teacher [are so designated].
As for that which is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"One who is neither fierce nor confused, neither ignorant nor a knower of distinctions, who has no connection to a lineage and is not intent on service—such a person is not a guest.

This should be understood as referring to one who is like a guest (*atithivat*). For this very reason, Śaṅkha states: "But if he is unable [to feed] many, he should give to only one; or he should give to that śrotriya who arrived first, or to whoever is such [a śrotriya]. A distinction regarding the giving [of food] is shown by Mārkaṇḍeya:
A wise man should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, conduct, or even his Vedic study;
he should regard him, regardless of whether his appearance is beautiful or ugly, as Prajāpati himself.
Also in the *Purāṇa*: "Without having asked about one's Vedic study, lineage, conduct, or likewise family,
the householder should regard that guest as Hiraṇyagarbha."

"Likewise, O Lord of Men, Prajāpati, Śukra, Vahni, the Vasu-gaṇas, and Yama—these enter the guest himself and consume the food. Thus, even the eater should not mention his lineage. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:
"He who announces his country, lineage, family, learning, or need for food—he is declared a 'vomiter of food' (vāntāśin) according to the laws of Vaivasvata.
Thus [it is said]. Manu states what must be done regarding a guest:

"But to a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water, as well as food according to one's ability, having honored him according to the prescribed rule. Here, the mention of "water" is intended to indicate the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, because of the traditional teaching of Hārīta: "He should offer him, according to his means, the *arghya*, water for sipping (*ācamana*), and a seat. Parāśara also says:
One should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and other courtesies,
as well as by providing a seat and washing his feet.
With faith, by the gift of food, by pleasant inquiries and replies,
and by following him as he departs, the householder should inspire joy in [the guest].
Yama also said: One should give sight, one should give mind, and one should give pleasant speech;
and rising up, one should offer a seat—this is the fivefold dharma.

The phrase "having made him rise" refers to the case of a *śrotriya* guest. For this very reason, Āpastamba states: "To a Brāhmaṇa who is not learned in the Vedas, one should give a seat, water, and food; one should not rise for him. One should rise only for the purpose of greeting him, provided he is worthy of being greeted. Regarding the specific details of giving a seat and so forth, he says the same: "If a guest arrives claiming to be a *śrotriya* but is not truly accomplished (*asamudeta*), one should give him a seat, water, and food with the words, 'I am giving these to a *śrotriya*. In this way, his [gift] becomes complete. One devoid of learning, wealth, and other such qualities is called *asamudeta*. Furthermore, a specific rule regarding a guest who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) has been shown by that same author: "If a guest who maintains the sacred fires should arrive, the host should personally rise to meet him and say: 'O *vrātya*, where did you stay? 'O *vrātya*, [here is] water. 'O *vrātya*, satisfy yourself. The meaning is that after addressing him with the mantra, "O *vrātya*, where did you stay?", one should give him water and food with the two subsequent mantras. On this point, Āpastamba further says: "Food with milk poured over it is equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; with ghee, it is equal to the Ukthya; with honey, it is equal to the Atirātra; with meat, it is equal to the Dvādaśāha; and with water, there is an increase of progeny and longevity" (ĀpDh 2.7.4). And regarding the absence of food, he says: "At the proper time, the master and mistress should not refuse one seeking food. In its absence, [there should be] ground, water, grass, or kind words. These indeed never fail in the house of a virtuous person. However, regarding a multitude of guests, it has been stated by Manu:
One should provide a seat, lodging, a bed, escorting, and attendance—
of the highest quality for those who are superior, of lower quality for those who are inferior, and equal for those who are equal.
However, food and other such items should be shared equally among those seated in a single row. As Hārīta has said:
"For those who possess superior learning and austerity, the first seat is prescribed;
but for those seated together in a row, eating and so forth are traditionally held to be equal."
For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states the fault in giving unequally:
"If one gives unequally in a single row out of affection, fear, or for the sake of wealth,
the sages declare that to be the murder of a Brahmin, as seen in the Vedas and sung by the seers."
On this point, the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa states:
"One should not eat for oneself meat, grain, or vegetables that have been prepared in the house, if one does not first honor a guest with them."

Āpastamba also says: "He who eats before his guest eats away the vigor, nourishment, progeny, cattle, and the merit of sacrifices and charitable works belonging to his house. Regarding the period after the guest has eaten, Vasiṣṭha states: "Then he should follow him as he departs, whether he is walking or sitting, until the boundary of the village, or until he receives permission to leave. The phrase "until the boundary" refers specifically to a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas); for it is recorded in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*: "One should follow a *śrotriya* guest until he is satisfied and reaches the boundary of the village. Manu describes the fruit of acting in this manner:
Whoever honors a guest who is weary and pure of mind,
it is my conviction that by him a hundred cows along with a bull have been given.
Viṣṇu also says:
"A householder does not attain such worlds through Vedic study, the Agnihotra, sacrifice, or austerity as he does from honoring a guest."
Likewise, Vyāsa has shown the fault in failing to do so:
"He who does not honor with devotion a guest on the road who is weary, unknown, and afflicted by hunger and thirst— him they call a slayer of a Brahmin."
Also in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he departs having given that person his own misdeeds and taking away their merit."
Devala also says:
"The guest who returns from a house having been unhonored and disappointed, immediately destroys that family."
Therefore, the sense is that one should not reject him. This should be understood to apply even when he has arrived at sunset. And so Manu says:
"A guest who arrives at sunset should not be turned away by the householder;
whether he arrives at the proper time or the improper time, he should not remain in the house without eating."

"At the proper time" means when the time for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has arrived; "or when the sun has set" means that another guest arriving in the evening must not be turned away—that is, he must not be rejected. Pracetas states the definition of one who arrives with the setting sun: "He who comes of his own accord to the house either at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva or in the evening—he is to be honored like a god; such a guest is known as a *sūryoḍha*."
In this regard as well, the fault incurred when a guest turns away is shown in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:

"O King, whatever sin is incurred when a divine guest departs disappointed, that very same sin is multiplied eightfold for men when a guest who has come by the sun (at the proper time) departs disappointed."

For this very reason, when there was a lack of food for a hunter who had arrived as a guest, the pigeon offered even its own self for the sake of a meal. Thus Vyāsa said: "In the dialogues between the gods and the sages, I have repeatedly heard of the great dharma regarding the honoring of guests."
That guest who has arrived from a great distance, emaciated by hunger, thirst, and fatigue,
and who is properly honored— he is indeed a sacrifice without a sacrificial post.
Having spoken thus, that righteous-souled one, with a joyful inner self, circumambulated that fire three times and entered it as if it were his own home. Thus [it is said].
But when a Kṣatriya or others arrive in the form of guests, then that which was spoken by Manu [applies]:
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, one may,
at will, feed him as well once the Brahmins have finished eating and the benediction has been recited.

[595] “Even if a Vaiśya or a Śūdra have arrived at the household as guests, he should feed them along with his dependents, practicing kindness (*ānṛśaṃsya*). Here, *ānṛśaṃsya* means the absence of harshness. *Bhṛtyāḥ* means those who are to be maintained or nourished. Regarding Śūdras, Āpastamba states a specific rule: “One should employ an arriving Śūdra in work. And those who are to be nourished are indicated by Dakṣa:
Mother, father, teacher, wife, offspring, the destitute, those who have sought refuge,
the guest, and the sacred fire— this group is declared to be the circle of those to be supported.
And this [maintenance] is necessarily dependent upon supporting one's dependents, for otherwise a fault is heard [in the scriptures]. Thus says Atri:
"The maintenance of the group of those to be supported is praised as a means to attain heaven;
hell results from their neglect; therefore, one should support them with effort."
Manu also says:
"He who does not offer [oblations] to these five— the deities, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— though he breathes, he does not truly live."

As for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya—"One should feed friends, relations, and kinsmen when they arrive at the proper time"—that should be understood to apply when food is available provided it does not conflict with the needs of one's own family. As Āpastamba says: "The distribution [of food] must not interfere with those who are entitled to a regular portion; one may, however, restrict oneself, one's wife, or one's son. *Bhakta* means food; those who depend on it are the *bhāktikas*. *Saṃvibhāga* refers to the sharing of food. Manu also says:
"He who performs the funeral rites for the deceased without causing hardship to his dependents—that results in unhappiness both while he is alive and after he has died.
Therefore, it should be understood that this rule regarding the feeding of kinsmen and others applies only to one who possesses wealth. And it is stated in the *Ādipurāṇa*:
Relatives, kinsmen, the destitute, and likewise those who have come for refuge—
even others— are declared to be the circle of dependents for one possessed of wealth.
The maintenance of this [fire] is also absolutely necessary; for it was stated immediately thereafter:
"If one eats while these [guests] have not yet eaten, he indeed consumes sin;
and having died, that man goes to hell and is reborn as a consumer of phlegm."
Also in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"If a relative, having approached a wealthy relative, falls into distress,
he incurs all the sin committed by that distressed person."
After the worship of the guest, according to the Viṣ�pu Purāṇa:
"Then the householder should first feed the married women, the distressed, the pregnant, the elderly, and the children with well-prepared food."
On this point, Vyāsa says: "He who, for one year, gives daily fodder to another's cow while not taking food himself— that vow is perpetual."
In this regard, the mantra is as follows:
"O daughters of Surabhi, benefactors of all, pure, and destroyers of sin;
may you, the mothers of the three worlds, accept my morsel of food. Thus.
Thus concludes the section on the honoring of guests in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, as an incidental matter, some statements concerning the gift of food are recorded; regarding this, Vyāsa says:
He who gives even a single mouthful of food day after day attains the heavenly world and beholds no hell.
These two persons stand above the sun in this world:
the giver of food during a famine, and the giver of gold and garments during times of plenty.
The fruit obtained by making an oblation into the fire and through giving gifts—
equal to that, or even superior, is the fruit when a Brāhmaṇa is gratified.
A gift of food given to Brahmins is inexhaustible, while food given to a Śūdra yields great fruit;
indeed, the gift of food to a Śūdra is equal to that given to a Brahmin without distinction.
Viṣṇu also says:
"But he who, having committed a sinful deed, gives food to one who asks—
especially to a Brāhmaṇa— is not tainted by that sin."
On this point, Devala says:
"He who, while ghee is available in his house, feeds a Brahmin food without ghee,
undoubtedly goes to a terrible hell in the next world."
"Having himself eaten choice food, if a foolish man subsequently feeds Brāhmaṇas with wretched fare, he shall dwell in hell for a long time.
And those Brāhmaṇas must indeed be learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). As Vyāsa said:
When a learned brahmin, girded with the knowledge of the Vedas, comes to one's house, all the medicinal herbs rejoice, thinking: "We shall attain the highest state."
To a Brahmin who has neglected the twilight prayers, fallen from his vows, and abandoned the Vedas, food being offered weeps; what evil deed have I committed?
Manu also says:
"That which is offered into the fires of the mouths of Brahmins, kindled by knowledge and austerity,
delivers one from misfortune and even from great sin."
Regarding this, Yama states a specific distinction:
"He who, bypassing one who does not cook, feeds one who does cook,
shall dwell in the womb of a female rat for more than a hundred years."
Thus concludes the section on the rules for the gift of food in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the rule for eating; regarding this, Manu says:
When the Brahmins, the servants, and others have indeed finished eating,
the husband and wife should afterwards eat that which remains.
*Vighasa* is that which remains after eating. And so Vyāsa says: "One should always be an eater of *vighasa*, and always an eater of *amṛta*;
for *vighasa* is what remains after eating, and likewise, *amṛta* is what remains from a sacrifice."
By this it is implied that one should never cook food for one's own sake alone. And it has been stated by Devala:
"One should not cook food for one's own sake, nor should one slaughter animals for one's own sake;
one who cooks for the sake of the gods and for the sake of Brahmins incurs no taint."
Manu also says: "He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for this food of the virtuous is ordained as that which remains from sacrifice."
Regarding this, the same author states the rule for the directions:
"One eating while facing east gains longevity; facing south, one gains fame;
facing west, one gains prosperity; and facing north, one eats the Truth."

That which is beneficial for life is *āyuṣyam*; one should eat that facing the east. That which is beneficial for fame is *yaśasyam*; one should eat that facing the south. Desiring prosperity (*śrī*), one should face west. *Ṛtam* means truth; the meaning is that one desiring that should face north. Viṣṇu also says: "One should eat facing the east or facing the south. Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "One should eat facing the south; however, they teach that eating while facing in this manner [westward] is not conducive to long life for a mother. Furthermore, this meal should be taken in private. Thus says Devala.
"One should take food and even perform one's movements in secret;
for one who is concealed shall be endowed with fortune, whereas in public one is deprived of prosperity. [600] Thus it is said. "Secret" (rahas) means a hidden place. Also in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"In a secluded place, facing either the east or the north,
seated comfortably on a pleasant seat with his feet placed upon the ground"—
regarding this, Devala states a specific detail:
In a clean and well-smeared place, having washed his feet and restrained his speech,
he should eat his food facing the east, pure and seated upon a seat.
Also in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"But when the floor has been freshly smeared, one who has rinsed his mouth outside,
restrained in speech, facing north or east, and properly prepared for the meal [should enter]."

The remainder [of the verse] is "from outside the dining hall. However, that Brahmin who, desiring to eat in the dining hall, should sip water while remaining on his seat and not elsewhere, is a defiler of the row.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Āpastamba. The phrase "on which cow-dung has been smeared" is the understood supplement. And so says Baudhāyana:
"Having sipped water twice with the mantra itself on ground smeared with cow-dung, or else with ashes or even with water, one should then cause a mandala to be made."
Regarding this, Śaṅkha states the specific detail:
"The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and Brahmā the Grandfather subsist upon the circles; therefore, one should draw the circle."

"A square for the foremost of the twice-born, a triangle for the Kṣatriya, a circular shape for the Vaiśya, and sprinkling with water is prescribed for the Śūdra. Thus [it is said]. On this point, Yama says:
"One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
eating with wet feet, one shall attain a long life.
Here, the mention of "feet" is intended as an illustration for the five limbs. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
One should take food while facing east and observing silence;
"wetness in five" is considered to consist of the two hands, the two feet, and likewise the mouth.
Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"A man should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor from a broken vessel; likewise, he should not eat with his hands and feet unwashed, nor with his head unwashed."

The phrase "not with a broken vessel" refers to vessels other than those made of copper and the like. For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi states: "There is no fault [in eating] from broken or unbroken vessels made of copper, silver, gold, conch-shell, mother-of-pearl, stone, or crystal. Pracetas also says:
"A twice-born man should not eat from a broken vessel, nor with those whose internal disposition is defiled; except for vessels made of copper, silver, lotus-metal (bronze), or gold."
The "lotus-born" refers to the conch and so forth. Regarding the vessel for eating, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"He who eats continuously for one month from a *brahmapatra* [leaf] achieves a result equal to thirty *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts; it destroys even the most grievous sins (*mahāpātaka*)."
Whether eating from a golden vessel, a silver plate, a copper one, or from the petals of a lotus— at every meal, for three nights, he enjoys a *pala* of food.

The *brahmapatra* is the leaf of the *palāśa* tree. It is also stated in the Purāṇa: "O Bhārata, for him who eats his meal from the middle leaves of the *palāśa*, there is the merit of a *prājāpatya* penance day after day."
He who desires to go upward to the supreme and eternal state should consume [food] upon a lotus leaf continuously for one month.
Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"But he who eats alone from a pure bronze vessel,
at every meal, enjoys the fruit of a three-night fast."
But he who eats alone from a pure bronze vessel—his four qualities increase: longevity, wisdom, fame, and strength.

The rule regarding the bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsyabhājana*) applies to cases other than those involving ascetics (*yati*) and the like. Thus Pracetās stated: "An ascetic, a student (*brahmacārī*), and a widow should avoid betel, the application of oil, and eating from a bell-metal vessel."

Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi states the things to be avoided: "One who desires prosperity should never eat from the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *arka*, *aśvattha*, *kumbhī*, *śrī*, *udumbara*, *kovidāra*, or *karañja* trees."
Hārīta also says:
"One should not eat from a vessel made of black iron or of clay. Pracetās also says:
"One should neither eat nor drink from an earthen vessel, a leaf-cup, a cotton one, or likewise a woven one; nor [should one eat] from the hand, nor from a seat.
Furthermore, the types of seats that are to be avoided have been shown by that same author:

"A wise person should always avoid a seat made of cow dung, one made of clay, one that is broken, one made of *pālāśa* wood, one bound with iron, or one made of *arka* wood. Regarding this, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
One should eat while the five [limbs] are still moist, having placed the vessel upon the ground;
Prajāpati Manu has declared that this is equal to fasting.
Vyāsa also says: He who, being pure and restrained in speech, places his vessel upon the ground and eats,
obtains the fruit of three nights' fasting at every single meal.
Having set down his bowl, O great sage, he should eat five morsels;
the remainder should be set aside before eating—listen now to the reason for this.
"O best of Brahmins, there is no fault in contact with droplets, nor with the dust from the feet or clothing;
one may eat with ease, for one is not defiled when eating for the sake of the ancestors.

This means that when placing the vessel on the ground for the sake of the ancestors, its surface should not be smeared; rather, having lifted the food from there, one should eat it from that vessel. Regarding the restraint of speech, it is also stated in the Purāṇa:
"Varuṇa may take away the power of one who bathes; Agni may take away the prosperity of one who offers oblations;
Death may take away the lifespan of one who eats. Therefore, silence is prescribed for these three occasions.
As for that which was stated by Atri:
"The vow of silence is extremely difficult to maintain; it is destroyed even by the utterance of 'huṃ'.
Since such a great fault would otherwise arise, one should therefore observe it with strict discipline.
This refers to the intention of "silence like a log" (kāṣṭhamauna). And this should be understood as applying to the period after a meal.
One should always eat food without censuring it, remaining silent and not disparaging it;
taking five mouthfuls is the "great silence," which is beneficial for nourishing the vital breaths and other faculties.

This is because of the recollection of Vṛddha-Manu. "Without censuring" means without finding fault with; such is the meaning. On this point, Śātātapa says: "Food given by hand, as well as salt [added] directly [to the dish], and likewise the eating of clay, is declared to be equal to the eating of cow-flesh."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha also says: "If a Brahmin eats either ghee or oil that has fallen on the ground due to a fingernail, Yama declares him impure; it is equal to the eating of cow's flesh."
Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"One should not eat salt, condiments, clarified butter, oil, or various kinds of foods to be licked or drunk, if they are given by hand."
When it is asked, "By what [utensil] then should it be given?", Manu says:
"Clarified butter and rice, as well as all side dishes, should be given with a ladle;
likewise water and cooked food—whosoever desires to give these should do so with a ladle."
He is a killer of an embryo, a drinker of liquor, a thief, and one who violates the teacher’s bed.
On this point, Bodhāyana says:

At the conclusion of all necessary duties, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet and sipped water (*ācamana*), he sits down facing the east in a place that has been swept and smeared with cow-dung. Having offered reverence (*upasthāna*) to the food being brought with the words, "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvar Om," he should restrain his speech. He sprinkles water clockwise around the placed food with the *Mahāvyāhṛtis*. Without releasing his hand from the left side, he first drinks water with the mantra, "Thou art the under-layer for the nectar" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*). Then, with the food, he offers the five oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhutis*): "Seated in the breath, I offer nectar; may thou enter me as auspiciousness, not causing burning; svāhā to the breath! Having offered the five oblations to the vital breaths with the food, he should eat further in silence while meditating on Prajāpati in his mind. Without eating to excess, he drinks water over the top with the mantra, "Thou art the covering for the nectar" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*). Having sipped water again, he touches the region of his heart with the mantra, "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; may Rudra, the destroyer, enter thee; swell with this food. Having sipped water once more, he lets the remaining water flow off his hands onto his right big toe with the mantra: "The Person the size of a thumb resides within the thumb; the Lord of the entire world, the Master, the consumer of all, is pleased."

With his hands raised, he should perform the consecration of the oblation (*hutānumantraṇa*), saying: "In faith, having entered into the breath (*prāṇa*), may the offered nectar nourish the breath with food. In this same manner, he should do so for the five [breaths]: *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*. With the syllable "Om," he should unite his self with the thought: "May my self be joined with Brahman for the sake of immortality. It is said that among those who sacrifice with all the ritual formulas (*kratuyājins*), the one who sacrifices to the Self (*ātmayājī*) is preeminent. Furthermore, they cite this: "Just as a tuft of reed-wool cast into a fire is consumed by the flame, even so are all the sins of the one who sacrifices to the Self burned away."
Gobila also says:

Now, therefore, follows the ritual for the oblation of breath (*prāṇāhuti*). Having consecrated the water with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *gāyatrī*, one should pour it around [the food] at evening with the mantra: "I sprinkle you, the Right (*ṛta*), with Truth (*satya*)," and in the morning: "I sprinkle you, the Truth (*satya*), with the Right (*ṛta*). "You move within all beings, hidden in their secret place, facing in every direction. You are the sacrifice; you are Viṣṇu; you are the *vaṣaṭ*-call; you are the sacred formulation (*brahman*); you are Prajāpati. Water, light, essence, immortality, the sacred formulation—*bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ*. You are the under-layering of nectar. Having thus drunk the water, one should mentally recite the *daśahotṛ* formula and, without hurrying, take five mouthfuls, saying: "To Prāṇa, svāhā! With this [formula], one offers into the *gārhapatya* fire. Saying: "To Apāna, svāhā!", one offers into the *anvāhāryapacana* fire. Saying: "To Vyāna, svāhā!", one offers into the *āhavanīya* fire. Saying: "To Udāna, svāhā!", one offers into the *sabhya* fire. Saying: "To Samāna, svāhā!", one offers into the *āvasathya* fire. Thus it is said.
These mantras end with *svāhā* and begin with the *praṇava*. Thus says Śaunaka:
"The mantras for Vāyu consist of his names, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *svāhā*.
While offering the oblation, one should consume the food and touch it with the teeth."
Regarding this, he [the same author] states a specific detail:
"In the offering of the vital breath (prāṇa), the index finger should be joined with the middle finger and the thumb;
the wise man should offer the downward breath (apāna) with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb."
One should offer the oblation into Vyāna with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb;
the wise one should offer into Udāna while keeping the index finger outside;
into Samāna, the offering should be made with the entire hand joined together.
Viṣṇu also said: "Listen, I shall tell you here how it is offered into the mouth:
having placed the vessel upon the ground, joined with the syllable Om."

"One should place that food into the mouth using all five fingers. Thus it is said. Following the preparation of the food, the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* states: "One should indeed offer a portion of food from the meal as an oblation (*bali*) to Dharmarāja."
Then, having offered the bali-oblation to Chinnagupta, who is indeed Dharmarāja.

"Wherever they may dwell, for the satisfaction of those hungry ghosts whose selves are afflicted by hunger and thirst, may this be inexhaustible according to their pleasure. Thus [it is said]. On this point, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states:
One should eat with a focused mind, beginning with sweet flavors;
then salt and sour in the middle, and thereafter bitter, pungent, and so forth.
A person should eat liquid food first, solid food in the middle, and liquid food again at the end; thus, strength and health do not forsake him.
Marīci also says:
After eating, one should not take curd with water as a post-prandial drink;
nor, after eating rice with milk, should a wise man touch water when he is not yet fully satiated.
Vṛddha Manu also says:
"Having sipped the *āpośana* water, one should eat what has been placed on the vessel and is not forbidden;
then one should leave the remainder as food for one's wife, hired servants, and slaves."
Regarding this, Pulastya states an exception for certain cases:
"A wise person should never leave any food uneaten, except for curd, barley-meal, clarified butter, sesame paste, milk, honey, and water. [609]

*Palalam* means meat. This too must be performed in the evening and in the morning, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "One should eat food offered with reverence at evening and morning, without finding fault with it. By this, it is implied that one should not eat in between. And it has been stated by Manu:
"The twice-born should eat their meals at evening and morning as enjoined by the Vedas;
they should not take food in between, for this rule is equal to the *agnihotra* sacrifice."

By the statement "equal to the *agnihotra*," he indicates that eating is necessary at both times [morning and evening]. For this very reason, the Śruti says: "Therefore, eating must be obligatory in the evening and in the morning. Regarding eating, Āpastamba states: "Eight mouthfuls are the food of a sage (*muni*), sixteen for a forest-dweller (*āraṇyavāsin*), thirty-two for a householder (*gṛhastha*), and an unlimited amount for a student (*brahmacārin*)."

"The one who has maintained the sacred fires, the ox, and the student—these three attain perfection only while eating; for them, there is no perfection through fasting. Thus it is stated by Bodhāyana regarding fasting and similar observances.
If a householder or a student who practices austerity while fasting should neglect the fire-sacrifice of the vital breaths (prāṇāgnihotra), he becomes one who has broken his vow of chastity.
"One should mutter the mantras of the *prāṇāgnihotra* when food is withheld,
just as one mutters the mantras of the *tretāgnihotra* when sacrificial materials are unavailable.
Thus says Devala immediately after the discussion on eating.
"Having taken a little of the remnants from all [the food] after eating, and having sipped water,
one should offer it with water upon the ground to those entitled to the remnants.
As for the mantra:

"May the water given to those who dwell in the Raurava hell—the abode of demerit—and to those who reside in Padma and Arbuda, reach those petitioners as inexhaustible. Regarding this, Vyāsa states in prose: "Then, being satisfied, having sipped water with the mantra *amṛtāpidhānam asi*, and having stepped back slightly from that place, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) according to the rules. Vyāsa himself also describes a specific rule for the sipping of water.
He who, deluded by sin, rinses his mouth after washing his hands,
accomplishes neither the rites for the gods nor those for the ancestors, nor does he purify himself.
Having drunk half, one should then rinse the mouth; the other half is to be discarded upon the ground.
By this, one constantly gratifies the Nāgas dwelling in the subterranean realm.
On this point, Devala says:
Having eaten and sipped water, being composed, one should cleanse the mouth and hands according to the prescribed rule, using earth and rubbing agents as well.
Having sipped water (ācamana), one should then perform the chewing of a tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha);
and after removing food particles stuck between the teeth during a meal, one should perform the ritual sipping of water.
One should regard a coating stuck to the teeth that cannot be removed as being like the tooth itself;
one should not exert excessive effort toward its extraction.
"There would be excessive impurity if a wound were inflicted by piercing with grass.
On this point, Vyāsa says:
"Do not touch hand with hand, nor shanks, nor the eyes."
"Touch your knees, O son of Kuntī; you must support a great multitude of people. Śātātapa also says:
"Having sipped water and set aside the vessel, [one should touch the ground] with the hand slightly moistened."
Having touched the principal vital breaths and the navel with the palm of his hand.
Having eaten, he should depart, neither with wet hands nor by placing his hand upon his head; rather, being composed, he should touch fire.
"A man skilled in the performance [of rituals] attains preeminence among his kinsmen.

Āpastamba also says: "Having sipped water, he should hold his hands upwards until they become wet; then he should touch fire. Those two by which water has flowed away are "prodakau. Also in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"But one who is healthy and of tranquil mind, having taken possession of a seat..."
A wise person should perform the recollection of their chosen deity.
May Agni, impelled by the wind, cause the food of the earth to swell;
may the sky provide space for it, and may my mouth digest it.
May this food serve for my strength, as well as for that of water, fire, and wind;
may it be fully digested, and may there be unimpeded happiness for me.
May food be nourishing for the prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna breaths; may there be for me unimpeded well-being.
May Agasti, Agni, and the submarine fire digest the food I have eaten without exception;
may they grant me the ease arising from its digestion, and may there be freedom from disease within my body.
Just as the Lord Viṣṇu is the sole sovereign of all the senses, the body, and the embodied soul,
by that truth may this entire food, when consumed, bring me health and reach its proper transformation.
Viṣṇu is the eater, and likewise he is the food and its transformation;
by that truth, may this food which I have eaten be digested for me.
Having recited this, one should rub the abdomen with one's own hand;
then, being untiring, one should perform activities that do not cause exhaustion.
Thus says Mārkaṇḍeya as well.
Having sipped water once more, one should then consume betel-leaf and listen to the Itihāsas or the Rāmāyaṇa.
The word "should do" (*kuryāt*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. Viṣṇu also says:
"Having eaten and being seated at rest, one should reflect upon some portion of the Veda.
Dakṣa also says:
"One should spend the sixth and seventh [parts of the day] with the study of Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
in the eighth, however, one should attend to worldly affairs; thereafter comes the external twilight [ritual].
Thus ends the section on the rules for eating in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding the rules for the eater:

on this matter, Hārīta states, "One should perform the acts of sprinkling, worship, offering oblations, and eating with the *daiva* tīrtha. The *daiva* tīrtha is the tips of the fingers. Āpastamba also says:
"A Brahmin should carefully hold the purifier (*pavitra*) in his right hand."
But one who eats [in this manner] is especially not defiled by the faults of food.
Atri also says:
"In the Brahma-yajña and in the recitation of prayers (japa), the Brahma-granthi is prescribed;
at the time of eating, it is said to be circular; thus the dharma is not lost."
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well:
"A householder, being pure and holding excellent jewels in his hands, should eat;
O Lord of Men, he should never eat food from which the essence has been extracted."
Vasiṣṭha also says: "One should not make a smacking sound with the mouth; one should eat using all the fingers, and one should not shake the hand. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"The consumption of water is equivalent to bathing at all sacred fords;
Manu has declared that food which is stepped over by the arm is unfit to be eaten."
He who eats with his palms facing upward, he who eats while making a hissing sound like the wind,
and he who lifts up a finger while eating— all this is declared to be equivalent to the eating of cow's flesh.
"With wind" means he eats making a sound; that is the meaning. Also in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*:
"One should not eat the remnants of a village meal, nor should one drink the remnants of what has been drunk;
one should not chew vegetables, roots, fruits, or sugarcane with the teeth."

Bodhāyana also says: "One should not bite with the teeth all kinds of food, cakes, bulbs, roots, fruits, and meat; nor should one be *atisuhita*. *Atisuhita* means excessively satiated. Manu also says: "Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to attaining heaven; it is meritless and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it."
Yama also says: One should never eat anything that is leavings, nor ever while walking;
one should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor ever with food held in the hand.

In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa as well: "A man who has not bathed, nor one who is lying down, nor one whose mind is elsewhere, nor one on a bed, nor one on the ground, nor one seated, nor one making noise [should not recite it]."

A man who has bathed should eat according to the rule in the evening and in the morning, neither wearing only a single garment, nor speaking, nor looking at those who are watching him, and without having first given [food] away.
Regarding the continuation [of the rule] "one should not eat," Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"Having stretched out one's feet, nor with the head wrapped. Uśanas also says:
One should not eat delicacies without having first given [to others], nor while many are looking on;
likewise, many should not eat while one person looks on.
Hārīta also says: "And one should not eat that food with which one would fail to perform the sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and men. Vṛddha-Manu also says:
"A twice-born man should neither drink nor eat with his left hand;
he should not drink water with only one hand, nor water offered by a Śūdra."
If water should fall from one who is drinking while food has escaped from his mouth, that food becomes unfit for consumption;
the eater would incur sin.
Having made it yellowish by leaving some residue, a Brahmin may drink it again;
however, he must observe a vow for three nights if he drinks from his left hand.
The meaning is that the water is poured out with one hand. This is also stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"One should not eat water other than from the hand, nor drink from anything other than a vessel. Viṣṇu also says:
"One should not consume ghee while still impure from food, nor should one consume it when excessively hungry. Thus it is said.
Also in the Ādi-purāṇa:
"One should not cause another to take the clarified butter while impure from food, nor should one discard what remains after eating."
"Furthermore, one should not eat what remains after a Śūdra has eaten, nor likewise that which remains in a vessel. Devala also says:
"One should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor with the door closed."
Whether standing on a vehicle, on a cart, or even near sandals;
Atri also says:
"If a Brāhmaṇa ever eats while placing his foot upon his seat,
or eats food blown upon with the mouth, it is equal to the eating of cow-flesh."
Bodhāyana also says:
"Eating, recitation, giving, offering, and receiving—these acts should not be performed with the knees outside [the garment]; the same is prescribed for sipping water (ācamana)."
Bṛhaspati also says:
While eating, one should never touch the food with the left hand;
nor should one touch one's feet, head, or bladder, nor should one touch the vessel with the foot.
The bladder is below the navel. Āpastamba also says:
"One should avoid wearing sandals in the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of gods or Brahmins, during the recitation of prayers, and at the time of eating."
A twice-born Snātaka should not eat having placed his vessel on his lap,
nor having placed it on the palm of his hand, nor on a bed, nor on a seat.
Also in the Ādipurāṇa:
One should not eat while lying down, nor while seated on another seat;
never during the two twilights, nor at midday, nor at midnight.
One should not study while wearing wet clothes, nor with a wet head, nor without the sacred thread;
nor with feet placed upon a footstool, nor together with one's wife.
One should not eat in an empty house, nor in the temple of a deity or a fire-sanctuary;
however, a child eating the remnants of his mother and father shall be happy.

Also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "One should not eat together with one's wife, nor in the open air, nor likewise while standing, nor while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having placed a cloth between the knees."

"Prāuḍhapādaḥ" means one who has placed his feet upon a seat or similar support. "Avasakthikā" is the binding of the space between the knees [and the chest] with a cloth or other material. As for the verse:
"If one should ever eat together with a Brāhmaṇī, or eat her leavings, the wise do not consider that to be a fault at all."
If a Brāhmaṇa should ever eat the leavings of the other three [castes], he should be known as one requiring expiation; he is a confused man of deluded intellect.
Thus, this does not intend to establish the total absence of fault in all circumstances, because of the expression "at any time" (*kadācana*). For this very reason, the *Ādipurāṇa* states:
"One may eat with a Brāhmaṇa wife at some point on the road;
but having eaten with a woman of a lower caste, one falls from that very moment."

On this point Paiṭhīnasi says: "One who is not invited should not go to the seat of honor"; the word "to eat" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Śaṅkha also says: "One seated at the seat of honor should not eat first. Śātātapa also says: "But that ignorant twice-born man who eats first while seated at the seat of honor, while many look on, takes upon himself the sins of the entire row."
Gobhila also says:
"When Brahmins are seated in a single row for a communal meal,
if even one should set aside his vessel, the others shall not eat either."

But he who eats there out of delusion should perform the Sāntapana penance. However, he who abandons his vessel while the Brahmins are eating is a creator of obstacles at the meal; he is likewise called a slayer of a Brahmin.
Also in the Ādipurāṇa:

"If, while seated in a single row, another person should sip water for purification (ācamana) without rising, then the others should leave the remainder and thereafter properly perform the ritual sipping of water."
"One should not eat even in a single row with Brahmins, even if they are one's own kinsmen;
for who knows what hidden sin he might possess? (619). The intention is that by doing so, the sin becomes shared by all. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"Whatever evil deed is committed by wicked-souled persons sitting in a single row,
it belongs equally to all of them as long as the row is not broken.
The breaking of the row has also been shown by that same [author]:
The wise have declared that a breach in the row [of mourners] occurs through fire, or ashes, or a pillar, or water, as well as through a door or a path.
Hārīta also says:
"Water, grass, ashes, a door, and likewise a path—
having placed an interval between [the eaters] by means of these, no fault regarding the row (paṅkti) occurs."
Regarding this, Atri says:
Even after sipping water, one remains impure as long as the vessel has not been set aside;
even when it has been set aside, one remains impure as long as the ground is not smeared [with water].
"For even on ground that has been smeared [with cow dung], a man remains impure as long as he has not touched the earth after rising from his seat.
Thus ends the section on the rules for the eater in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, in connection with the rules regarding food, something else concerning that same subject is also stated;
on this point, Manu says:
"During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should not eat; one may eat after bathing once they have been released."
"Having seen [the eclipse] while they have not yet been released, one should bathe on the following day.

[620] Here, by the terms "lunar eclipse" (*candragraha*) and "solar eclipse" (*sūryagraha*), the day and night associated with them are indicated. Thus, it is stated that on a day and night joined by a lunar or solar eclipse, one should not eat prior to their release. And it was said by Mārkaṇḍeya:
"O Bhārgava, on whichever day there is an eclipse of the Moon or of the Sun..."
In that case, there may indeed be the act of grasping, but not the prior act of eating.
"One should not eat while that [planet] is in conjunction, nor likewise when it has set;
one should not eat at all until its rising occurs there.

In this context, "there" means during that day and night. Regarding this, some have explained the mention of "rising" so that eating may take place provided the sun rises, even if the planet is somehow not visible. With this very intention, Śātātapa also says:
"One should not eat for a day and night when there is an eclipse of the moon or the sun;
however, having seen it released, one may eat after performing a bath according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding the lunar eclipse specifically, Mārkaṇḍeya says:

"But the eclipse of the moon [should be understood as occurring] after the first watch; one may eat before the turning of the sun [i.e., before midday]. In the case of the first [watch], [one should eat] below the first. The phrase "after the first" means "after the first watch. "Turning" refers to midday. By this, it is stated that one should eat having avoided three watches prior to the watch in which the eclipse occurs. Regarding a solar eclipse, however, there is a specific rule mentioned in another Smṛti.
During a solar eclipse, one should not eat for four watches (yāmas) beforehand;
during a lunar eclipse, however, for three watches, except in the case of children, the elderly, and the sick.
The terms "children," "the elderly," and "the sick" apply to both cases. For this very reason, Mārkaṇḍeya states:
"If an eclipse occurs at sunset, one should not eat in the afternoon;
if it occurs in the afternoon, not at midday; if it occurs at midday, not during the morning (saṅgava) period."
"One should eat at the time of *saṅgava* (the third *muhūrta* of the morning) if there has been no prior act of eating.
And thus it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"One should not eat before a solar eclipse during the day, nor before a lunar eclipse in the evening."
One should not eat during an eclipse, but one may eat after bathing once both [the sun and the moon] have been released.
One may eat when the moon has been liberated, provided it is not the dead of night;
however, if both [the sun and the moon] have been eclipsed and set, one should eat after bathing and seeing them on the following day.

In this context, it should be understood that the words "here" (*atra*) and "evening" (*sāyam*) are either restatements (*anuvādaka*) or indicators of times already established by other scriptural injunctions. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"All land is [as sacred as] a gift; all twice-born men are equal to Brahmā;
and all water is equal to the Gaṅgā when the sun is seized by Rāhu."
The merit [of bathing] at the moon is a hundred thousandfold, and that at the sun is a hundred times greater than that;
but when the waters of the Gaṅgā have arrived, the merit is ten millionfold for the moon and ten times that for the sun.
Whatever fruit a man obtains from [bathing at] ten million moons,
that same fruit he obtains by bathing in the Ganges when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu.
Whoever bathes in the Jāhnavī during an eclipse of the moon or the sun has bathed in all sacred fords; why should he wander the earth?
If there is a solar eclipse on a Sunday and likewise a lunar eclipse on a Monday, it is known as the Cūḍāmaṇi; therein one obtains infinite fruit.
Whatever merit is obtained on other days during the eclipses of the moon and sun,
that merit is said to be multiplied ten millionfold during the eclipse of the Cūḍāmaṇi.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* as well:
"Upon the sighting of Rāhu, there is impurity (sūtaka) for all castes alike;
having bathed, one should perform one's rites, but one should avoid cooked food."

The mention of *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) is for the purpose of obtaining the rule of bathing with one's clothes on. For this very reason, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says: "In the case of *sūtaka* caused by Rāhu [an eclipse], for all castes alike, that bath must be performed with one's clothes on; and one should avoid food from those in a state of *sūtaka*."
"Sūtaka-anna" refers to food [received during] the impurity caused by Rāhu [eclipses]. Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"The śrāddha must be performed even at the cost of one's entire property when the conjunction with Rāhu occurs;
however, he who does not perform that śrāddha sinks like a cow in the mud."
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga also said:
"When the sun is swallowed by Rāhu, whoever performs a Śrāddha—
by that very act, the entire earth is indeed placed into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa."
Bathing, giving gifts, austerity, and ancestral rites yield infinite merit during an eclipse of Rāhu;
at other times it is a demonic night, therefore one should avoid it.
The mention of "the sight of Rāhu" (an eclipse) is intended to illustrate the occurrence of other events as well, such as the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti) and so forth; for it is said:

"One should perform bathing, giving, and other rites during the night on occasions such as the sight of Rāhu, the transit of the sun, marriage, times of distress, and festivals of prosperity, as well as during optional vows."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Devala: "atyaya" means death. Regarding the materials for the śrāddha, Śātātapa has stated:

"In times of distress, when there is no sacred fire, at a holy place (tīrtha), and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a twice-born man (dvija) may perform an āma-śrāddha (using raw grains); indeed, a Śūdra may always do so."
Bodhāyana also says:
"In the absence of food, in the absence of twice-born men, during travel, upon the birth of a son,
and during an eclipse, a Śūdra may indeed always perform a gold-śrāddha."
Regarding this, the rule for the timing has been shown by Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:
"The gods are satisfied at the time of contact, likewise the ancestors;
humans [are satisfied] during the middle period, but the Rākṣasas at the time of release."
On this point, the *Liṅga Purāṇa* states:
"One should bathe during an eclipse of the moon or sun, even during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*).
One who does not bathe meets with death; one who bathes incurs no sin."
In the case of both birth-impurity and death-impurity, there is no fault during an eclipse of Rāhu;
purification shall remain in effect only so long as the planet is not seen to have been released.
Having fasted for three nights during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
and having bathed and given gifts according to the rules, one rejoices together with Brahmā.
Having fasted for a single night, bathed, and given according to one's ability,
there is liberation from the sheath of sin, just as a snake is freed from its slough.
Śātātapa also says: "During the solstices, the equinoxes, and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses,
one who has fasted for a day and night and bathed is liberated from all sins."
And thus, as it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "When there is a solar eclipse at night, or likewise a lunar eclipse during the day,
one should not perform ablutions there, nor should one ever give a gift."
Therefore, it should be understood that the fact that an eclipse is not seen by those situated on the earth's surface pertains to that specific location.
Thus ends the section on the lunar and solar eclipses in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*);
regarding this, Vyāsa says:

"When the sun has gone to the peak of the setting mountain, having performed the rite of washing the feet, one should perform the evening twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) outside, holding kuśa grass in hand and being composed.
The phrase "having reached the peak of the setting mountain" means when it is half-set. For this very reason, Saṃvarta says:
One should perform the morning twilight devotion according to the rules while the stars are still visible;
likewise, one should perform the evening twilight devotion when the sun has half-set and the solar disk is present.

Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "At the two twilights, one should sit outside the village and remain silent; in case of conflict, that which is characterized by direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*) is more authoritative. This means that for one who performs the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) outside the village while remaining silent at both the morning and evening twilights, there is no issue. However, for one whose performance of the twilight rite outside the village would result in a contradiction with the limbs (*aṅga*) of the ritual procedure as prescribed by *śruti*, it is not contradictory to perform both twilights even within the house. For this very reason, Atri says: "The twice-born must perform the two twilights for the purification of the self."
"Both twilights must be performed by Brahmins even within their own homes.
On this point, Vyāsa says:
"The twilight rite performed outside is ten times more meritorious; it is likewise so at pools and springs."
At a renowned sacred site it is a hundredfold, and at the waters of the Ganges it is a thousandfold.
Śātātapa also says:
"The performance of the twilight devotions outside [the village] purifies the food of a Śūdra, even if it contains falsehood, the smell of liquor, or sexual intercourse during the day."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"The twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) performed at home is said to have a single-fold merit; in a cow-pen it is a hundred-fold;
by a river it is a hundred-thousand-fold; and in the presence of Viṣṇu it is infinite."

In this regard, there is a specific rule from Śātātapa stating, "Infinite [merit is gained] in the presence of Śiva. The procedure here is as follows: having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the evening twilight worship (sāyaṃsaṃdhyā)," one should drink water at the end of the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), as before, with the verse beginning "Agniś ca. On this point, Yājñavalkya and Śaunaka have stated in sequence: "Having restrained the breaths and sprinkled oneself, one should drink water with the verse addressed to the Waters (ab-daivata). Having said 'Agniś ca me' in the evening, and 'Sūryaś ca me' in the morning."

Its *prakṛti* is *chandas*; Sūrya is the *ṛṣi*; Agni, Anu, Manu, and the days are the deities (*devatās*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the twilight rinsing (*ācamana*) at evening.
