Then, the procedure beginning with the sprinkling (*mārjana*) is the same up until the recitation of the *gāyatrī*. Regarding the specific details therein, Vyāsa says:
"Seated facing west, restrained in speech and well-composed, one should then recite the *gāyatrī* joined with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*."
Having taken up the rosary, one should practice correctly until the rising of the stars.

Śaṅkha also states: "Seated upon a grass mat (brusī) or one covered with Kuśa grass, with Kuśa blades as a purifier in hand, facing north or toward the sun, and having taken up a rosary, one should perform the recitation (japa) while meditating on the deity. Here, *brusī* means a seat; *kuśottarā* means covered with Kuśa grass. And the deity here is Gāyatrī, who is to be approached [at the beginning]; for Bṛhaspati records: "Silence [is required], as is reflection on the meaning of the mantra. Then, having performed the rites as before up to the dismissal of Gāyatrī, one should worship the Sun with the mantras studied in one's own Vedic branch (*śākhā*).
One should perform the ritual attendance of the Sun with its own mantras.

Thus, according to the *Smṛti* of Vasiṣṭha. And those mantras were shown by Nārāyaṇa: "Having worshipped the Sun with the *Vāruṇī* verses, while performing a circumambulation, one should pay homage to the quarters and to the lords of the quarters individually. The *Vāruṇī* verses are: "imaṃ me varuṇa," "tat tvā yāmi," "yaccid dhite," "yaktiṃ cedam," and "kita vāsaḥ. Of these, the meter (*chandas*) of the first and third is *Gāyatrī*; of the second and fifth, it is *Triṣṭubh*; and of the fourth, it is *Jagatī*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) of the first three is Śunaḥśepha; of the latter two, they are respectively Vasiṣṭha and Atri. Varuṇa is the deity (*devatā*). Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the worship of the Sun. But Bodhāyana prescribes the worship of Night at the conclusion of the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*: "One worships Night with two *Vāruṇī* verses: 'imaṃ me varuṇa' and 'tat tvā yāmi. In this regard, Aṅgiras says:
"The Brahmin who remains composed and observes silence during both twilights is honored in the world of Brahmā for a thousand divine years.
Thus ends the procedure for the evening twilight (sāyaṃsaṃdhyā) in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the rule for retiring to bed.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having performed the evening twilight devotion, having offered oblations into the fires, and having attended upon them,"
Surrounded by his servants, he should eat without excessive greed and then retire to rest.

"Saṃviśet" means he should sleep; the word "ca" (and) serves to include the Vaiśvadeva and other rites as well: "The Vaiśvadeva and the bali-offering must be performed every evening and morning, even by one who does not eat; otherwise, he becomes a sinner."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana. And this [rite] should be performed by taking [food] from another cooking, but not with the remains of what has already been eaten;

nor [should it be done] with that which is the remnant of a *śrāddha*, or that which has stood overnight in the house, or the remains of what was eaten by the husband and wife, for having consumed such, one must perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.

Thus, because of the traditional rule that such a person is unfit to be fed, and because of the traditional rule of Āpastamba stating, "One should not perform a sacrifice with that which would be unfit food for the noble ones," for this very reason the Viṣṇu Purāṇa says:
"O Lord of the Earth, having again prepared the cooked food, even at evening,
one should offer the *bali* for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva rite together with one's wife."
There too, one should likewise offer food even to outcastes and others;
then, one should honor any guest who has arrived there according to one's own ability.
O King, whatever sin is incurred when a guest who is a deity departs disappointed,
that very same sin is multiplied eightfold for men when the sun has set and he departs disappointed.

"O King, having performed the purification of his feet and so forth, and having eaten in the evening, the householder should then go to a bed made of solid wood that is not cracked. The phrase "he should go to the bed" implies "for the purpose of lying down. When it is asked how that is to be done, Hārīta says:

Having thoroughly washed his feet, performed protection on all sides, and equipped himself with auspicious items such as a jar filled with water, he should occupy a bed that is pleasing to him and free from defects while reciting the verse beginning with "sutrāmāṇam. Having muttered the *Rātrisūkta*, paid homage to Viṣṇu, and recited the two verses beginning with "sarpāpasarpa bhadraṃ te," he should remember his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), enter into meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and mutter other Vedic mantras and the *Sāvitrī*. Then, listening to auspicious sounds and the blowing of a conch shell, he should sleep with his head toward the south. Thus it is said.
And here, protection should be performed with Gāruḍa mantras;
having placed an auspicious full water-pot upon the head,
one should then sleep after having established protection with Vedic and Gāruḍa mantras.

Thus, according to the *Purāṇa* tradition. The *Rātrisūkta* consists of eight verses beginning with "rātrī vyakhyad āyatī. The phrase "with the head toward the south" is intended as an illustration; for it is said: "O King, for a man who always sleeps with his head toward the east or toward the south, it is auspicious; however, the opposite brings about disease."

Thus it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*. Regarding this, Vyāsa states a specific rule: "A wise man should always smear a clean and secluded place with cow dung, and he should lie down upon ground that slopes toward the east or the north."

"Secluded" means in private. Gobhila also says: "Having bathed, at the time of going to bed, he places a bamboo staff near his bed for the entire night, remaining motionless for the sake of auspiciousness. It is also stated in the Purāṇa:
"One should mutter the Rātrisūkta while remembering the gods who sleep peacefully;
having paid homage to the imperishable Viṣṇu, one should sleep at night established in meditative absorption (samādhi)."
Gobila has shown those who sleep in happiness:
Agastya, Mādhava, the mighty Mucukunda,
the sage Kapila, and Āstīka— these five are those who sleep in happiness.
Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
One should not sleep in an empty house, in a cremation ground, under a solitary tree at a crossroads, nor in the temple of Mahādeva or in the dwelling of the Mothers.
Nor in a shrine of yakṣas or nāgas, nor likewise in a shrine of the Skandhas; nor in the shade of riverbanks, nor on gravel, clods of earth, or dust.
One should never sleep upon *darbha* grass except during a consecration (*dīkṣā*), nor should one ever sleep upon grain,
cattle, deities, Brahmins, or one's teachers.
Nor should one study on a broken bed, nor in an unclean place, nor while being impure oneself;
nor while wearing wet clothes, nor naked, nor with the head pointing north or south.
Neither in the sky, which is entirely empty, nor likewise in a sacred tree.

Pracetas also says: "One should not sleep during the twilight hours, nor near a deity, nor upon the completion of a rite to a deity; nor while impure, nor naked, nor on a broken bed, nor by sleeping with one of another caste, nor on a seat of stone, nor in abodes of spirits, yakṣas, or grahas, nor in the shade of cremation grounds, anthills, or large trees. Viṣṇu also says: "One should not sleep with wet feet or clothing, nor on a bed of palāśa leaves, nor on one made of five kinds of wood, nor on one made from wood broken by an elephant, nor on one scorched by lightning, nor on one consumed by fire, nor on one made from a tree watered by a jar; nor in cremation grounds, empty houses, or temples of deities; nor in the midst of meat, nor in the midst of women, nor above grain, cows, gurus, fire, or gods; nor while impure from food, nor during the day. This is also stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa.
"One should not occupy a bed that is not spacious, nor one that is broken, uneven, or dirty; nor one infested with insects, nor one that is uncovered. Thus [says the law].
Dakṣa also says:
One should spend the two watches of the night—those of evening and the last—engaged in the study of the Vedas;
by sleeping for only two watches, one becomes fit for union with Brahman.
On this point, the Kūrma Purāṇa states:
"O twice-born ones, all this has been declared day after day—
the entire collection of duties for Brāhmaṇas, which bestows the fruit of liberation."
He who does not perform the rites for a Brahmin, whether out of atheism or laziness,
goes to terrible hells and is born into the womb of a crow.
"There is no other path to liberation except by following the rules of one's own stage of life (āśrama).
Therefore, one should perform ritual actions for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord.
Thus [ends the work] by the son of the venerable Keśavāditya Bhaṭṭopādhyāya, who was a master of all branches of knowledge.
The section on daily observances (*āhnika-kāṇḍa*) in the *Smṛticandrikā* composed by Yājñikadevaṇabhaṭṭopādhyāya is completed.
